This section of the text presents a series of theological refutations (Reprehensio) and responses (Responsio) regarding the nature of Christ, the superiority of the apostles over prophets, and the distinction between the divine and the physical. It cites authorities such as St. Ambrose of Milan, St. Gregory the Great, and the prophet Daniel to argue against Arianism and for the unity of Christ's divinity and humanity. The text also includes a defense of the sanctity of the Church and the validity of worshipping Christ as the true God.

This text is a collection of scriptural and patristic citations used to support the legitimacy of venerating sacred images. It includes excerpts from St. Augustine (on the Trinity and the Psalms), St. John Chrysostom (on the ladder of the Church), and a letter from Pope Gregory the Great to Bishop Serenus of Marseille regarding the distinction between worshipping an image and learning the history of what is worshipped through an image.

The text discusses the theology of sacred images (iconodulism), citing a letter to Januarius of Calari and a letter from Secundinus of Gaul. Pope Adrianus addresses a letter to King Carolus of the Franks and Lombards regarding the reconciliation of heretics who returned to the orthodox faith and the restoration of sacred images. The text argues for the legal and spiritual rights of the Roman Church over its properties and the authority of the papacy as the successor to Saint Peter. It concludes with a theological defense of the keys of the kingdom and the authority of the pontiffs.

This collection of early modern Latin poetry by Michael Abel consists of 'Carminum' (odes) and 'Elegiarum' (elegies). The work is organized into twenty sections featuring a blend of devotional, pastoral, and occasional poetry. It contains meditations on Christology, the Passion, the Eucharist, and the life of the saints, alongside classical themes involving Apollo, Venus, the Muses, and the Hesperides. The text includes specific dedications to figures such as Maximilian II, the Duke of Savoy, Andreas Ebersdorffer, and Johannes Sambucus. Geographical references include Dresden, Vienna, Assisi, the Ister (Danube), and the city of Thebes. Additional subjects include medical descriptions of podagra and thermal springs, a polemic against Muhammad, and reflections on the sacrifice of Abel.

This collection of Latin poems and epigrams includes a dedication to the reader, a defense of the author's poetic style, and several themed sections. The texts address religious themes such as the 'Crown of Piety,' the 'Vocation of the Nations' to Christ, and the 'Icon of Christ the Patient,' alongside more classical and allegorical subjects like the 'Poets' (Helicon), the 'Night of the Messiah's Birth,' and a meditation on the passage of time and mortality.

This section of the Latin poetry contains a series of short, often allegorical or moralizing stanzas and fragments. This section of Michael Abel's poetry contains a series of short lyrical and devotional poems. It includes a meditation on the Passion of Christ (IN CRUCEM REDEMPTORIS), a biblical reflection on the sacrifice of Abel (DE ABELE), a poem on the birth of Christ (TEMPUS FILII DEI natale), and a reflection on the conversion of Saul (DE SAULE R.).

This section of the collection contains a series of poems and hymns including a psalm, a prayer by a monk named Nicolaus, and a piece titled 'In Novum Annum'. The texts address themes of divine judgment, the suffering of the Church, the fall of man, and the nature of sin. Specific references are made to figures such as Serapis, the serpent of the Styx, and the city of Babylon.

This section of the collection contains several poems and inscriptions with varied themes: the spiritual and physical properties of wine (Vineyard of the Church, Wine from Water), the figure of Ganymede, and a reflection on the fate of a poet. It also includes a religious meditation on the Resurrection (Day of Easter), a critique of Pharisaic hypocrisy, and a concluding poem on the fortunes of a figure named Pericleus.

This section contains a collection of short Latin poems and inscriptions including a pastoral scene in a garden, a lament for a friend, a Christological meditation, and a tribute to Saint Bartholomew. It also includes a satirical piece on 'assentators' (likely a reference to those who agree to things without thinking), a reflection on the passage of time, and a concluding meditation on the afterlife.

This section contains a series of short poems and meditations on religious and mythological themes. It includes a plea to the elements (Borea, Frigora) for safe passage, a lament for the lack of fruit addressed to Ceres, and a narrative regarding the birth of a king and the actions of Herod. The text also features a tribute to a friend, a reference to the city of Assisi, and a concluding section based on Psalm 117 (Psalm 116 in modern numbering).

This collection of poems and fragments includes a series of religious hymns praising the goodness and mercy of God, a section on music and its relation to the soul, and a series of shorter poems on themes of parsimony, nature, and fate. The text includes specific references to the figures of Achilles, Venus, and the poet Simiolos, as well as a personal address to a friend and a critique of a poet named Philip.

This section contains a series of short poems and epigrams including a lament for a lost legacy, a description of a squirrel navigating a timber ridge, and a formal invocation to the Muses. It includes a religious section on Saint Peter (Divus Petrus) and a brief narrative regarding the flight of the Messiah into Egypt.

This section contains a series of religious and poetic fragments, including a hymn to Christ, a meditation on the Easter lamb, and a passage on the illness of King Hezekiah. It includes an epitaph for a mathematician named Valentinus Engelhart and a concluding section regarding pagan idols and the worship of Jupiter.

This section of the poems contains a series of short, often cryptic, lyrical and religious fragments. It includes a poem addressed to a friend regarding the vanity of seeking fortune in the stars, a reflection on the nature of death and resurrection (Vita ex Obitu), and several brief meditations on the divine word, the seasons, and the endurance of faith.

This section contains a series of poems and epitaphs, including a lament on mortality, a dedication to a friend, and a commemorative piece for the year 1787. It features specific dedications and mentions of figures such as Christ, Moses, Elijah, and a woman named Ranzovia. The text includes a formal epitaph and a concluding piece for a patron.

This section contains a series of short Latin poems and inscriptions, including a dedication to Emperor Maximilian II and a reference to Emperor Rudolph II. The text also features mythological references to figures like Leucothea, Venus, and Daphne, and a description of a garden (Hortus Caesarium).

This section contains a collection of short poems and dedications. It includes a poem about the siege of a Pannonian castle by the Turks, a dedication to a prefect of Vienna (D. Hugonem Bloti), a poem about a poet named Haslobius, and several shorter pieces including a lament for a girl named Margaris, a poem on the theme of 'Convivium', and a poem dedicated to a woman named Bigeri.

This section contains a collection of diverse Latin texts including lyrical verses on beauty and mythology, a funeral epitaph for Count Christian of Oldenburg, and several shorter poems or inscriptions. Specific subjects include the figures of Pallas, Icarus, and the deityes of the Heliconian forest, as well as a satirical piece regarding a scholar's lack of temperance and a warning against mixing absinthe with wine.

This section contains a series of short poems and dedications, including a poem on friendship (De Amicitia), a dedication to the Duke of Savoy (Duci Sabaudiae) mentioning Emanuel Philibert, and a poem addressed to Apollo (De Bruma ad Apollinem). This section contains a series of poetic fragments and dedications, including a passage titled 'TRITON HASLOBIANUS' and a section 'DE EODEM' featuring a figure named Triton Haslobianus. It includes a religious and polemical passage regarding the 'execution of the hearts' of those who 'shed the blood of Christians,' a section titled 'PALAE TRANSVERSAE Caspar' involving a character named Caspar, and a concluding section 'DE PINDARIS SENTENTIA'.

This section contains a series of short poems and dedications including an 'In Aemulum', a 'Amico Deficienti', an 'Epicedii Commendatio', a 'De Adolescente Naivo', and a 'De Angelis'. The texts address themes of artistic merit, the physical and spiritual resurrection of Christ, the defense of the faith against skepticism (specifically addressing a 'Thomas'), and a concluding invocation of the Muses and the Camenae.

This section contains a series of dedicatory poems and celebratory verses. This section of the poem contains a series of addresses to two specific individuals: Andreas Ebersdorffer, a physician from Vienna, and a woman from Lidel (referred to as the 'gemmula patriae Lideli'). The text contains a series of Latin poems and dedications. It includes a personal reflection on the influence of Martin Luther's doctrine and a dedication to Carolus Utenhovius. The latter section features a formal address to a poet, discussing themes of literary art, the study of sacred mysteries, and the interpretation of complex figures and symbols.

This section contains a series of panegyrics and dedications addressed to various figures, including a poet/historian identified as Sambucus (Johannes Sambucus) and a figure associated with the name 'Praestus'. This section contains a series of Latin poems and dedications, including a tribute to D. Hugoni Blotius and a memorial for Oswaldus Scriba of Nivimontum. The text contains a series of poetic addresses and dedications involving figures such as Lideli, Prideni, and the poet Ebersdorffus. It features a lengthy allegorical discussion regarding the purity of wine versus water, specifically referencing 'Cananaea' and 'Lyaei', and concludes with a poetic description of a garden and a warning against 'Talpas' (moles).

The text contains a series of poetic and didactic reflections on friendship (De Amicitia), the virtues of shared purpose, and the dangers of impulsive passion. The final section features a series of short, allegorical, or satirical fragments involving biblical and mythological references, including Moses, Christ, and the Garamantes.

This section of the elegies contains a series of religious and allegorical poems.
