The final portion features a hymn of praise to peace and a concluding passage on the 'immaturi' (unripe/unprepared) death.

This section contains a series of religious and devotional poems or meditations, including a 'PERSEVERANDUM IN' prayer and a 'PERICULOSA VERBI' warning. The text features theological reflections on the resurrection of Christ, the fall of Adam, and the triumph over death, interspersed with liturgical-style exhortations and a concluding passage attributed to the Bishop of St. Basil.

This section contains a series of poetic and didactic passages, including a hymn to the Church (De Ecclesia) and a warning to a prince (Ad Principem Paraenis). It features references to biblical and mythological figures such as David, Solomon, Midas, and Apollo, and describes a diverse gathering of nations including Phoenicians and Indians at Zion. The text also includes a passage regarding the Temple of Peace in Rome and a concluding section titled 'Solomon's Youth'.

The text contains a series of elegiac verses and a New Year's address. It features a moralizing exhortation to youth (pubes) to avoid the fleeting pleasures of the body and the 'cyclopean' excesses of lust, followed by a transition to a religious and commemorative section. The latter part includes a dedication to Hugo and Maxendies, mentions of figures like Christ, and a commemorative list of names and locations such as Sithonia and Idalia.

This section contains a series of elegies and carmina featuring several distinct dedications and poetic sequences. It includes a funerary or commemorative passage for 'Hildebrandus' and 'Georgius' involving themes of death, the afterlife, and the 'Book of Life,' followed by a 'Natalis Poetae' (Poet's Birthday) and a 'Guillemo Hildenio' sequence. The text concludes with a 'Dedicatoria' addressing 'Virtus' and 'Erato' regarding the nature of poetic craft and sacred severity.

This section of the 'Carminum' contains a hymn to the angels (De Angelis Hymnus) and a series of allegorical or mythological verses. It features a celestial and martial narrative involving figures such as Michael, Lucifer, and Cacus, and describes a spiritual conflict between holy orders and demonic forces. The text includes references to various entities like the 'Sanguinis', 'Pharmaca', and 'Mancipi', set against a backdrop of divine judgment and celestial protection.

This section contains a series of distinct poetic and dedicatory texts. It includes a religious allegory involving a 'Redeemer' and a 'multicephalous beast,' a dedication to a 'Baron' and 'Pector,' a formal dedication to 'Johann Rucard' (a physician and poet), and a celebratory panegyric for the 'Augustus' (Elector of Saxony) regarding the establishment of peace and the spread of the Christian faith.

This section contains a series of dedicatory and commemorative poems. It includes a praise of a poet named Elias Huter, a celebratory poem for a marriage (IN MATRIMONII), a dedication to a new spouse (PRO NOVIS CONIUGIBUS), a celebratory poem for a poet (PROPEMPTICUM), and a funeral elegy for Christoph Roeberstorfer of Vienna. The text also includes a final dedication to a poet (AD POETAM).

The text contains a series of religious and allegorical poems, including a section of 'Carminum' and an 'Elegia' (Elegia I). The content features a transition from a description of the Republic and the figure of Sophia to a series of prayers and meditations involving Christ, the figure of Moses, and the 'Aquila' (Eagle) as a symbol of the Church. The final section includes a polemical defense of the faith against 'Mahometis' (Muhammad) and a call to arms against an 'invisa gente' (invaded people).

This section contains a series of elegies and a dedicatory note. The text includes a passage on the 'Ship of the Church' (Navicula Ecclesiae) and a poem titled 'The Justice of the Exiles' (Justitia Exulans) which references figures such as Venus, Bacchus, and Niobe, as well as the laws of Sparta and the names of Aeacus, Minos, and Rhadamanthus. The final elegy is a prayer or address to a divine protector or 'Angel' regarding the poet's status and the service of the Lord.

This section contains a series of elegies and an epitaph featuring mythological and religious imagery. It includes a passage titled 'De Puperra ex Apocalypsi' referencing Apollo, the Moon, and the Apocalypse, and a section titled 'De Tyrannorum Insanid' involving the rivers Ister and Albis. The final section, 'Epitaphium Albi Submersorum,' describes a maritime disaster involving a ship and a figure named Festus.

The text contains a series of elegies and poems, including a section on a 'Good Shepherd' (Bonus Pastor) and a dedication to Henry Nicard, Secretary of the Military Courts. The poems feature mythological and pastoral imagery, referencing figures like Apollo, Admetus, and Venus (Cypria), and locations such as Hybla and Enna. The final section includes a dedication to a 'Nicarde' and a series of verses involving floral and pastoral metaphors.

This section of the elegies contains a series of pastoral and mythological verses featuring figures such as Philabella, Philomela, and Venus. The text describes a transition from winter to a blooming spring, invoking the goddess Ceres and the deity Phoebus, while incorporating imagery of gardens, vineyards, and birds. It concludes with a transition toward a more celestial focus on a man whose head is 'filled with stars' and who moves the paths of the heavens.

The text contains a series of poems, including a section of 'Carminum' and 'Elegiarum' (Elegies). The passages feature a mix of mythological and natural imagery, including references to Phoebe, the Temple of Solomon, and the figure of Adam. The final section, Elegia X, is a lament for a son named Elia, mentioning his parents, the loss of a daughter named Anna, and a final reference to the Danube (Ister) and the Austrian court.

The text contains two elegies (XI and XII) and a dedicatory note to a physician, Andreas Eberstorffer. Elegia XI features a dedication to the 'symbolum' of Nicolai Reicheli and reflects on themes of fate, divine will, and the struggle of the soul against adversity. Elegia XII contains a more complex, metaphorical meditation on physical suffering, the nature of pain, and the role of the poet.

The text contains a series of elegiac verses featuring a mixture of mythological, medical, and geographical imagery. It mentions specific locations such as Hesperia, Idalia, Cyprus, and Prague, and references figures or entities like Efferus, Gazula, and the goddess Trux. The passage contains heavy medical and physical imagery involving 'podagra' (gout), 'morbus' (disease), and 'crura' (legs/feet), alongside references to horses, chariots, and a 'shepherdess' of a flock.

The text contains a series of elegiac verses describing a grim, allegorical landscape of disease, physical suffering, and medical treatment. It mentions mythological figures such as Pluto, Tisiphone, Apollo, and the Eumenides, alongside geographical and cultural references like the River Norica, the Graeae, and the city of Rome. The passage also references specific names like Eberstorff, Titius, and the physician-like role of the poet, while describing the preparation of medicinal mixtures and the physical toll of illness.

The text contains a series of elegiac verses and a concluding medical dedication to Dr. Eberstorfer. The poems contain a mix of mythological imagery (Apollo, Jove, Ganymede), geographical references (Dresden, Lipsia, the river Silesus), and medical descriptions involving ailments like gout (podagra) and the preparation of medicinal herbs. The final section explicitly praises the medical skills and pharmacological knowledge of the physician Eberstorfer.

The text contains a series of Latin poems, including a section of 'Carminum' and 'Elegiarum' and a specific 'Elegia XV' regarding Austrian thermal springs (Thermae Austriacae). The passages mention figures such as Delius, Chiron, and the author Abel, while referencing medical themes, the healing properties of mineral waters, and the fertility of women. A specific mention of 'D. Eberstorff' appears in the context of the thermal springs.

The text contains a series of elegiac verses and a formal dedication to 'Augustino a Lidlau'. It features a celebratory section involving figures such as Lidelius, Judith, and Eberstorferus, and includes a drinking song (Elegia XVI) with references to the Muses, the river Ister, and the deity Portunum. The final section transitions into a religious meditation on Christ, the redemption of the Jewish people, and the dangers of the Danube.

The text begins with a religious meditation on salvation, divine mercy, and the suffering of the faithful. It transitions into a mock-heroic or satirical epigram featuring a lion, an ass, and a rooster in a comedic confrontation. The final section is a dedicated elegy to D. Christophorus Pelargus, describing a maritime voyage involving mythical and geographical references such as the Isthmus of Grai, the city of Rostoch, and the lands of the Pomeranians.

The text transitions from a maritime voyage and a journey toward the East, mentioning the Euphrates, the Aegean, and the conversion of the Gentiles. It features a shift to a medical narrative where the speaker describes suffering from a severe illness (rheum, cough, and asthma) and the subsequent administration of medicines and wine by physicians.

The text is a series of elegiac verses containing a mix of pastoral imagery, mythological references, and personal dedications. It mentions specific figures such as Bacchus, Apollo, and several individuals with German-sounding names (Schraderus, Haslobius, Cornerus, Copernicus). The passage describes landscapes involving the Rhine, the Alps (Lycaeus), and various vineyards, while also referencing historical or literary figures like Aonius and the poeter Sabinus.

This section contains a series of elegies and dedications. It includes a poem dedicated to the Queen of England regarding the constellation Cassiopeia, a memorial for the physician Petrus Monavius (referred to as 'D. Petri Monavii'), and a formal address to Jacob Colerum in Berlin. The text mentions several mythological figures such as Tritoniger, Dionysus, and Perseus, and references geographical locations like Britain, Italy, and the city of Berlin.

The text contains a series of elegiac verses and poems featuring several named figures, including Haslobius, Marchia, and the poet Fabricius. It contains personal reflections on the hardships of life, the preservation of literary works, and the enduring fame of certain authors. The passage also mentions specific locations and entities such as the Aonii fountain, the land of Gaul, and the court of Pollio.

This section contains a series of elegies and a funerary inscription (Epitaphium) featuring names such as Dimidius, Colere, and Haslobius. The text includes a dedication to the study of sacred scriptures and languages, and a specific elegy (Elegia V) referencing geographical and mythological locations like the Hyperborean lands, the land of the Saxons, and the city of Martigene. The passage also mentions figures such as Pallas, Solomon, and Pierius, while referencing themes of divine mystery, poetic fame, and the preservation of ancient traditions.

This section of the 'Carminum' contains a series of lyrical and mythological verses featuring figures such as Mathusalah, Apollo, Minerva, and various deities like Ceres, Nereus, and Faunus. The text describes pastoral and sacred landscapes, including the Hesperides, the Garden of Hesperides, and the lands of Enna and Hybla, while referencing mythological locations like the Lyceum and the shores of the sea. It concludes with a series of invocations and descriptions of divine grace and musical performance.

The text contains a series of Latin poems, including a section of odes and a dedicated elegy (Elegia VI) addressed to Abraham Risen, a mathematician. The poems feature mythological and geographical references including Chloris, the mountains of Orea, the Borean realm, and the Isthmus of Cymbricus. The final section addresses the recipient's mathematical expertise, referencing Pallas, Pythagoras, and the geometry of the sphere.

The text contains a series of poetic and didactic reflections, including a formal address to 'Eliam Hutterum' regarding works in Dresden and the study of the Bible. It features a scholarly defense of scholarly labor, the preservation of ancient languages, and the distinction between profound scholarship and 'vulgar' usage. The passage mentions specific figures or entities such as Elia, Thamirac, Tiresias, and the city of Fulgida.

The text contains a series of elegies (Elegia VIII and IX) and a concluding section of a larger work. The passages feature religious and allegorical imagery involving the Gospel, the Eucharist, and the transition from 'piety' to 'religion,' while also incorporating classical and mythological references such as Ulysses, Aeneas (Atrides), and the city of Pergamum. The text concludes with a dedication to Andreas Reussius and includes specific mentions of the names Reussius and Vulnificus.
The text contains a single line of verse regarding the construction of eternal monuments. It references a 'Caesar' who has bestowed favor upon a recipient as a reward for wisdom.

This collection by Johannes Atrocianus consists of an elegy, a selection of epigrams, and a hortatory letter. The primary work, 'Elegia De bello rustico' (1625), utilizes mythological figures such as Ceres, Bacchus, and Sardanapalus to critique moral decay, rural life, and the destruction of books during the German war. The text features a series of 'Non didicit Christum' refrains criticizing ecclesiastical practices and the use of icons. Subsequent sections include personal addresses to figures such as Theodoricus of Engelsperg, Gebhardus Wagner, and Henricus Glareanus, alongside a narrative poem set in Lugdunum. The collection concludes with a literary defense of the author's style compared to Virgil and Caton, a hymn to the Virgin Mary, and a final prayer for peace.

This section contains an elegy titled 'De bello rustico' by Johannes Atrocianus, composed in 1625 in Germany. The text employs a series of allegorical and mythological comparisons—referencing figures like Ceres, Bacchus, and the Eumenides—to describe a perceived moral and social decay in the countryside. It specifically laments the subversion of social order, the desecration of sacred objects, and the decline of natural and celestial elements.

This section of the 'Elegia De bello rustico' contains a series of moral and religious critiques regarding the state of the world and the church. It features a long series of 'Non didicit Christum' (Christ taught not) refrains that criticize specific behaviors, such as the use of icons, the wearing of Franciscan habits, and the conduct of the clergy. The text also references mythological figures like Sardanapalus, Enceladus, and Cerberus, and mentions locations such as Athens.

The text contains a series of elegiac and satirical verses concerning the destruction of books and rural life during a war in Germany (1625). It features a satirical critique of a man named Thestilius and his actions during a conflict, mentions historical and mythological figures like Sisyphus, Scyron, and Sardanapalus, and includes a specific address to Valerius Arimaspum regarding his long beard.

This section contains a series of elegies and epigrams addressed to specific individuals, including Theodoricus of Engelsperg, Johannes Gilherus, and Joannem Valtenbergium. The texts address themes of virtue versus avarice, the distinction between true faith and false piety, and include a satirical critique of a man named Pamphagus. It also features a brief address to a scholar regarding the recitation of legends and an epitaph for Baldasaris.

This section contains a series of elegiac and epigrammatic poems. It includes a poem on the vanity of worldly glory and a 'speculum' (mirror) addressed to Onophrum Atrocianus regarding the distinction between physical appearance and inner virtue. It also features a collection of Aesopic fables and two dedicatory poems: one to Gebhardus Wagner regarding the vanity of certain 'boasters' and another to Leonardus Susher concerning the 'mad love' of a character named Pamphilus for a woman named Glycera.

This section contains a series of poems and dedications. It includes a narrative poem about a lover named Pamphilus and a woman named Glycera in Lugdunum (Lyon), a panegyric to Maximilian Caesar regarding his military prowess against barbarian nations, a meditation on the transience of worldly glory addressed to Count Christoph of Lupfen, and a formal dedication to the poet Henricus Glareanus praising his mastery of Greek, Latin, and mathematics.

This section contains a collection of epigrams and dedications. It includes a satirical 'In Irrisorem' mocking a figure who laughs at the world and the gods, a dedication to the physician Bonifacius Amorbacchius, a lament for a man named Cornelius, an epitaph for Ioannes Aquilae, a dedication to a 'Turcarum' image, and a final address to Ioannes Gloterus.

This section contains a series of poetic exchanges and formal addresses. It includes a literary defense of the author's style compared to Virgil and Caton, a personal correspondence with a man named Glothere regarding friendship and shared texts, a hymn to the Virgin Mary, and a concluding Latin prayer (Precatio) for peace, divine protection, and the removal of envy.

This work is an instructional elegy (elegia monitoria) titled 'Iter Dantiscum' by Nathan Chytraeus. It is organized into five parts that combine geographical descriptions of the Baltic region with moral and practical advice for travelers. The first three parts detail specific itineraries through Pomerania, mentioning the rivers Rostochius, Luburgi, Demminum, Viadrus, and Oder, as well as cities such as Stettinum, Barnim, Breslau, and Gedani. The text includes references to historical figures like Ericus Guelfius and Hannibal, and mentions the Sarmata and Henetes tribes. The final two sections provide didactic counsel to a traveler named Johann, focusing on the dangers of the Alps, the risks of intoxication, and the importance of social discretion. The work concludes with invocations to Minerva and Fortuna.

The text describes a journey through the Pomeranian region, naming specific geographical features such as the rivers Rostochius, Luburgi, and Demminum, and the towns of Stettinum and Barnim. It mentions local landmarks like the bridge of the Cygnifer, the forest of Sidinorum, and the city of Oppidulus. The narrative includes references to historical tribes (Henetes, Sarmata) and local flora and fauna, specifically regarding fishing and local estates.

The text describes a journey through various landscapes, mentioning the river Viadrus, the city of Breslau (Bratisilai), and the river Oder. It features a narrative involving figures such as Ericus Guelfius and mentions geographical locations like the Thames, the city of London (implied by the 'Anguino' and 'Tamesi' context), and the city of Breslau. The passage concludes with a description of a large linden tree and a nocturnal scene of nature.

This section of the itinerary describes the geography of Pomerania, specifically the regions of Coslin, the Balthic sea, and the river systems of the Zana, Slagam (Sclaua), and the Laba. It mentions local landmarks such as the mountain of the 'Great Sackell', the port of Gedani, and the settlement of Bogislai. The text also references historical figures and entities including the Duke of Pomerania, the Sarmatians, and various local rulers and mythical/poetic figures like the Muses and the goddess Minerva.

This section of the poem is an instructional elegy (elegia monitoria) addressed to a young traveler (Johann) regarding the perils of journeying. It provides practical advice on enduring harsh weather, navigating the Alps, and the dangers of excessive drinking, while also warning against the physical and mental tolls of travel. The text mentions specific geographical features like the Alps and historical/mythological figures such as Hannibal and Bacchus.

This section of the 'Elegia monitoria' provides moral and practical advice to a traveler, specifically addressing the dangers of the Alps and the importance of discretion in speech. It warns against unnecessary talk and the risks of starting quarrels, while emphasizing the importance of observing local customs and sacred rites. The text concludes with a mention of a 'Fabritius' and a final invocation of Minerva and Fortuna.

Georg Fabricius's 'Poemata sacra. Pars prima' is a collection of sacred Latin poetry, odes, and hymns that integrates Christian theology with classical poetic forms such as Alcaic, Sapphic, and Archilochian meters. The work is structured into sections containing 'Paeans' and 'Hymns' that address Christology, the Trinity, and angelology, specifically naming the Archangels Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, Uriel, and Jeremiel. The text includes extensive biblical narratives featuring Abraham, David, Moses, and the apostles Peter and Paul, alongside historical figures such as Charles V, Sultan Suleiman, and Theodosius. It incorporates technical metrical commentaries on Greek and Roman forms and includes a cycle of nuptial poems and dedications for figures such as Sebastian Hillinger and Prince Wilhelm of Orange. The collection also features moralizing allegories involving botanical and zoomorphic imagery, as well as specific dedications to individuals like Nicolaus Eblebius and Laurentius Stroer. Themes range from the defense of the Church against the Turks and the fall of Constantinople to the sanctity of marriage and the transition from the Old Law to Grace.

This section contains three odes (Oda I-III) concerning the excellence of Faith (Fides) and the spiritual life. The text includes a series of biblical and mythological allusions, including Abraham, the Israelites' crossing of the sea, the defeat of Goliath, and the fall of the first parents. The author provides technical descriptions of the poetic meters used in the odes, referencing Archilochus and various classical meters.

The text contains a series of religious and didactic poems (Odes) and technical descriptions of poetic meters (such as the Asclepiadean and Alcaic). The content includes prayers for Christian rulers to govern justly, a plea for protection against the 'tyranny of the Turks,' and a series of theological reflections on divine providence and the duties of Christian leaders. It references biblical and historical figures such as Jethro, Laban, and Pharaoh.

This section contains a series of religious poems and prayers (Odes VI-VIII) composed in various meters, including the Alcaic and Dicolos distrophos. The text addresses the fall of Constantinople to the 'Mahometans' (Muslims), the suffering of Christians, and the destruction of holy sites. It features invocations of Christ and mentions geographical locations such as Byzantium, the Euxine Sea, and various historical/mythological figures like the Parthians and the Sybarites.

The text contains a series of religious poems (Odes) and technical descriptions of poetic meters (Hipponactics, Glyconics, Aselepiads). The content includes prayers to Christ and the Holy Spirit, invocations of angels as protectors against enemies, and references to biblical figures such as Lot, Daniel, and Tobias. It also mentions specific names like Isaides and Pellacius in a theological context.

The text contains two sacred poems (Odes XI and XII) concerning Christian doctrine and ecclesiastical unity. Ode XI focuses on the Trinity, the merit of Christ's sacrifice, and the distinction between divine grace and human effort. Ode XII addresses the preservation of concord within the Church, specifically pleading for the removal of schismatics and the recognition of the Pope and his ministers.

This section contains three odes (Ode XIII, XIV, and XV) that utilize various classical meters (Sapphic, Adonic, Asclepiadean, and Archilochian) to address religious and moral themes. The text includes a prayer for the unity of the Church and the protection of the faithful against the 'beasts' of worldly passions and heresy. The final ode reflects on the diverse pursuits of humanity, mentioning the Gymnosophists, the Antipodes, and the pursuit of wealth (Mammon).

This section contains a series of religious and patriotic odes (Odas XVI-XVIII) written in various classical meters, including Archilocian iambics and Sapphic trimeters. The text includes prayers for the Church, the defeat of enemies like the Turks and the 'Sultan' (Sulimanum), and mentions of historical figures such as Charles V (Carolus V), Theodosius, and the Pipini lineage. It concludes with a reference to the defense of Germany against foreign powers.

The text contains a series of sacred poems and hymns addressed to Christ, contrasting the 'frivolous' pagan worship of figures like Diana and Neptune with Christian devotion. It includes a section of technical commentary on poetic meters (heroic hexameter, Archilochian, and Sapphic odes) and a concluding prayer of thanksgiving for the natural world, including animals and the cosmos.

This section contains a series of devotional poems (Ode I, Ode II, and the beginning of Ode III) and technical metrical notes. The text includes a prayer of submission to Christ, a lamentation of personal sins and the passage of time, and a plea for spiritual renewal. The author includes specific technical descriptions of poetic meters, referencing figures such as Catullus, Glycon, Ithyphallicus, and Hipponax.

This section of the poem contains a series of religious and moral exhortations, referencing biblical figures such as Jacob, Rachel, Deborah, and the tribe of Judah, as well as historical figures like Saul, Goliath, and Absalom. The text transitions into a formal defense of faith and the endurance of the soul against physical suffering and worldly vanity. The final portion includes a technical note on the Phrynichian meter and a meditation on the transience of earthly life versus the permanence of spiritual reward.

This section of the 'Poemata sacra' contains a series of devotional poems and prayers. It includes a meditation on Christian virtue and the 'true happiness' of the faithful, a prayer for the soul's journey toward the afterlife, a prayer for an infant's baptism, and several technical descriptions of poetic meters (such as Phalaecian and Antispastic verses).

This section of the collection contains a series of religious poems and hymns, including a transition to the works of Prudentius and a series of odes. The text includes a devotional poem regarding the Eucharist and the communion of saints, followed by 'Ode IX' and 'Ode X', which utilize Archilocan meters to address themes of divine judgment, the rejection of paganism (mentioning figures like Delilah and Herodias), and the spiritual struggle against worldly temptations.

This section of the 'Poemata sacra' contains a series of religious and moralizing poems, including the titles 'Monocolos' and 'Tricolos'. The text includes biblical references to Jonah, David, and Achab, and addresses themes of sin, repentance, and the contrast between worldly pleasures and spiritual devotion. It also contains a concluding section regarding the punishment of the Turk and the justice of God.

The text contains a series of religious and allegorical poems, including 'Oda XIV' and 'Oda XV'. The first section features a lamentation and a call to divine judgment against enemies, referencing biblical and historical figures such as Antiochus, Sennacherib, and the Israelites. The second section, 'Oda XIV', focuses on the fall of Adam, the role of Christ in redeeming humanity, and the defeat of the serpent. The final section, 'Oda XV', includes a brief prayer for the souls of friends and a reference to the opening of hearts to Christ.

The text contains a series of sacred poems (Poemata sacra) and odes (Oda XVI, XVII, and I) featuring religious and moral exhortations. It includes references to biblical figures like Christ and Malachi, geographical locations such as Calabria, Hybla, and the river Tiber (Iberus), and mythological figures like Hercules and Geras. The author provides technical descriptions of poetic meters, including Alcaic, Pherecratean, and Boethian forms.

This section of the 'Poemata sacra' contains a series of prayers and theological meditations. It includes a plea for divine favor and protection against enemies, mentions of biblical figures such as Moses, Manasseh, and the Virgin, and a specific reference to the threat of the Turks. The text also includes a technical commentary on poetic meters, specifically the heroic hexameter and the Alcmanic dactylic.

This section contains a series of sacred poems (Odes III-VI) composed in various classical meters, including Ithyphallic, Archilochian, and Asclepiadean. The texts function as devotional prayers and hymns, addressing the Trinity, the role of Christ as a savior and mediator, and the offering of personal devotion and praise to God. The poems include specific references to biblical figures like Job and the serpent of the Hebrews, as well as invocations of divine protection against enemies.

The text contains a series of religious and allegorical poems (Odes VII and VIII) addressed to Christ. The first section contains a plea for the protection of the Church against 'beasts' and 'tyrants' (symbolized by a dragon and a hyena) and a description of the 'poor house' of Christ. The second section, composed in anapestic dimeters, calls for the defense of the Church's princes and cities, and lists figures such as David and Achas.

This section of the 'Poemata sacra' contains two odes (IX and X) and a concluding fragment of a third (XI). Ode IX addresses the defense of Christian doctrine against the 'wicked' and 'sacrilegious' influences of the world, specifically mentioning the threat of the Turks and the 'tyranny of Rome.' Ode X focuses on the divine light of Christ, the Virgin's womb, and the spiritual struggle of the faithful against the 'lust of pontiffs' and 'tyrannical kings.'

This section of the collection contains two odes (XII and XIII) addressed to students, focusing on moral and religious instruction. Ode XII emphasizes the importance of Christian virtue, the rejection of worldly vices like pride and deceit, and the guidance of the Church. Ode XIII addresses the role of masters in educating youth, using metaphors of growth and cultivation to describe the transition from childhood to a life of holy service.

This section contains two odes (Ode XIV and Ode XV) and a concluding technical note. Ode XIV is a prayer for the preservation of Christian doctrine and the safety of schools and churches, invoking the Trinity and seeking peace and the removal of the 'hardships of war.' Ode XV addresses the celestial order of the sun and moon, the unity of the Church, and the divine governance of the world.

This section contains a series of religious and didactic poems (Odes) and instructional notes on poetic meters. The text includes a prayer to the Creator (Custos hominum) featuring imagery of nature and maritime navigation, a section on the defense of the Christian faith against enemies like the Getae and Thracians, and a passage regarding the leadership of figures like Peter and Theodosius. It also contains technical instructions on the structure of Cretic and Paeonic meters.

This section contains a series of religious and moral poems (Odes) featuring biblical figures such as Susanna, Naboth, and Zedekiah, as well as references to Christ and the Eucharist. The text includes technical metrical descriptions of Greek and Roman poetic forms (Euripidean, Anacreontic, and Alcmanic) and concludes with a vivid apocalyptic description of a celestial vision involving falling fire, blood, and sulfur.

The text contains a series of sacred poems (Odes) and technical metrical descriptions. The first section contains a religious plea for divine mercy and protection against enemies, while the subsequent sections provide technical commentary on the meters of the odes, referencing figures such as Anacreon, Asclepiades, Aristophanes, and Boethius.

The text begins with a poetic hymn of praise to God, referencing biblical figures like Paul of Tarsus and classical figures such as Aurelius Clemens and Juvenal. It transitions into a theological meditation on the incarnation of Jesus Christ and the mystery of the divine becoming human. The final section addresses the author's brothers (Blasius, Jacobus, and Andreas) regarding the virtues of patience and faith in the face of personal loss and the trials of the human condition.

Fabricius addresses a group of students or 'brothers' (Fratres), reflecting on their education in the arts, sciences, and the faith of Christ. He defends the inclusion of hymns and the use of classical models (such as those of Plato, Minos, and Horace) as tools for religious devotion. The text concludes with a series of liturgical-style verses and scriptural references (John 13) regarding the Eucharist and Christ washing the feet of the apostles.

This section of the 'Poemata sacra' contains a series of devotional poems and liturgical-style reflections following the Passion of Christ. It details specific biblical scenes including Christ's journey to the Mount of Olives, his trial before Caiaphas, and his denial by Peter, interspersed with references to specific Psalms and the hours of the day.

This section of the 'Poemata sacra' provides a poetic narrative of the Passion of Christ, structured by the traditional hours of the day (Third through Ninth). It incorporates scriptural references from the Psalms and the Book of Isaiah, and includes specific liturgical and dramatic descriptions of Christ's trial before Pilate, the accusations of the crowd, and his appearance before Herod Antipas.

This section of the poem contains a series of devotional meditations on the Passion of Christ, structured by the hours of the day (First, Second, Third, Tenth, and Eleventh). It incorporates scriptural references from the Gospel of John and Isaiah 53, and includes liturgical-style prayers and descriptions of the crucifixion, the two thieves, and the resurrection.

This section of the 'Poemata sacra' contains a series of hymns and meditations on the Passion of Christ, specifically detailing the burial, the hours of the Passion, and the trials before various authorities. It references biblical figures such as Nicodemus, Joseph of Arimathea, and Caiaphas, and cites specific scriptural passages from Isaiah and the Gospels of Matthew and Psalms.

This section contains a series of ten hymns (Hymnus V-X) detailing the Passion of Christ, specifically focusing on his trials before Pontius Pilate and Herod. The text incorporates scriptural references (Isaiah 53, Psalm 2) and describes the accusations of prophanity, the crowd's demands, and the physical suffering of Christ.

This section contains a series of sacred hymns (Hymni) and prayers centered on the Passion of Christ, the role of Pilate, and the suffering of the Virgin Mary. It includes specific scriptural references to the Gospels of Luke and John, and the Psalms, while incorporating liturgical elements such as the 'Hymn of the Cross' and petitions for the Church. The text mentions specific locations like Calvary and the city of Cyrene, and includes a sequence of prayers for the forgiveness of sins and the comfort of the faithful.

This section contains a series of sacred poems (Hymns I-III) and devotional verses centered on the Passion of Christ and the liturgy of the Eucharist. The texts include specific references to biblical passages (Luke 22, Matthew 26, Mark 14) and incorporate traditional prayers for protection, patience, and the preparation of the soul for death. The poems utilize imagery of the wounds of Christ, the betrayal by others, and the spiritual purification of the believer.

This section contains a series of sacred poems (Hymns IV through XI) concerning the Passion of Christ. The text describes specific biblical scenes including the mocking of Christ, his trial before Herod and the high priests, the crowning with thorns, and his sentencing, referencing passages from the Gospels of Matthew, Luke, and John.

This section contains a series of devotional hymns (Hymns 12-19) concerning the Passion of Christ. The texts focus on Christ's trial before the high priests, scribes, and elders, and his appearance before Pilate, while incorporating theological reflections on his kingship, the mockery of his followers, and the physical reality of his wounds and clothing.

This section contains a series of hymns (XX-XXVI) depicting the Passion of Christ. The text includes scenes of Christ being mocked by the crowd, the soldiers' interaction with him, the offering of the sponge and vinegar, the thief's plea for salvation, and the crowning with thorns. The author includes brief theological reflections on adoption, the role of the priest, and the physical suffering of Christ.

This section contains three sacred hymns (Hymns 27, 28, and 29) focused on the Passion of Christ, specifically the stripping of his body, the piercing of his hands and feet, and the piercing of his side. Following the hymns, Georg Fabricius addresses a letter to Johannes Giga, discussing the decline of classical arts, the history of his own compositions, and the influence of various musicians and scholars such as Martinus Agricola and Johannes Waltherus. The text concludes with a dedication to Andreas Ernst of Quedlinburg.

This section contains a series of eight hymns (Hymnus I-VIII) concerning the life and theology of Christ, including his incarnation, birth, circumcision, appearance to the Gentiles, offering in the temple, baptism, and transfiguration. The text includes specific references to biblical figures such as Isaiah, Moses, and Elijah, as well as the Holy Trinity and the transition from the Law to Grace.

This section of the collection contains a series of religious hymns (Hymns IX through XIV) and liturgical markers for the liturgical calendar. The texts focus on the Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension of Christ, as well as the roles of the Trinity and the Holy Spirit. Specific mentions include the names David, Melita, and various theological figures or locations like Tartarus and the Temple.

This section contains a series of sacred poems (Poemata sacra) and hymns dedicated to various religious figures and themes. It includes hymns for the 'Caste of Angels', the martyrs 'Flosculi', John the Baptist, Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, the converted Paul, and a hymn for a 'received sinner' (Peccatrice Recepta).

This section contains a series of sacred hymns (Hymns 21-23) and prayers addressed to the Trinity. The texts include specific invocations to the Apostle Peter, the Apostle Thomas, and the Holy Spirit, featuring themes of redemption, the overcoming of demons, and the protection of the Church. The passages are structured around liturgical dates, specifically the Calendar of April.

This collection of sacred poems includes liturgical and devotional hymns for the midday (Horis Meridianis), evening (Vespertino Diei), and the Nativity of Christ (De Nativitate Christi). It also contains specific prayers for the protection of students during calamities, the preservation of the universe, and the liberation of the Church. The texts feature traditional invocations to the Trinity and various petitions for protection against enemies, disease, and famine.

This section of the 'Poemata sacra' contains a series of liturgical and devotional poems dedicated to Christ, the Holy Spirit, and the Trinity. It includes specific hymns for the Nativity, the Resurrection, and the Epiphany, as well as a lamentation of the sinner's plight and a plea for protection against 'Turkic' weapons and 'tyrannical' forces.

This section of the 'Poemata sacra' contains a series of devotional hymns and prayers addressed to God and Christ. The text includes specific petitions for peace, the protection of the Church, the remission of sins, and the hope of the afterlife, featuring traditional liturgical themes and references to biblical figures like Abraham and the apostles Peter and Magdalene.

This section of the poem contains a series of invocations and hymns to the Trinity and the angelic host, specifically naming the Cherubim, Seraphim, Gabriel, Michael, and Raphael. It includes a transition from a discussion of pagan rituals (the Telchines and Bacchic dithyrambs) to a Christian defense of sacred music and the sanctity of the angelic realm. The text mentions specific geographical locations such as Normandy, Cornwall, Bithynia, and Libya, and references biblical figures like Tobias and Manoah.

This section of the 'Poemata sacra' contains a series of hymns (Paeans) and invocations addressed to the angelic hierarchy. The text describes the celestial host's role in protecting the faithful, the order of the cosmos under God's governance, and specific attributes of the Archangels and the Angel of Counsel. It references biblical figures such as Christ, David, and Jacob, and mentions specific angelic ranks like the Principality and the Throne.

This section of the poem contains a series of hymns (Paeans) and theological reflections concerning the role of angels as protectors, guides, and warriors. It references biblical figures such as Joseph, Abraham, Moses, and John, as well as historical or mythological figures like Cambyses, Hagar, and various groups like the Alani and Sarmatae. The text concludes with a meditation on the spiritual warfare of angels against Satan and the dangers of worldly temptations.

This section of the poem contains a series of religious and allegorical hymns (Paeans) and invocations of angels. It features specific figures such as Michael, Peter, John, and the biblical figures of Gideon, Jonathan, and the prophetess (or figure) at the Euphrates. The text describes a spiritual struggle against demons, the judgment of the impious, and the ultimate triumph of the Word of God over the physical senses.

This section of the 'Poemata sacra' contains a series of hymns (Paeans) and angelic meditations. It features a theological defense of faith and the role of Christ as the ultimate teacher, a description of the devil's multifaceted and deceptive forms, and a narrative of the announcement of the Messiah's birth to the patriarchs and the descent of God into the earth.

This section of the 'Poemata sacra' contains a series of religious poems and paeans. It includes a meditation on the birth of Christ in Bethlehem, a description of the angelic host, and three specific paeans titled 'Angelus Luctator', 'Angelus Liberator', and 'Angelus Salutis'. The text references biblical figures and themes such as the defeat of the dragon, the role of the Holy Spirit, and the contrast between the divine and the human.

This section of the poem contains three paeans and several liturgical-style hymns concerning the protection of the Church and the roles of the Archangels Gabriel, Michael, and Raphael. It references biblical figures such as David, Daniel, and the Virgin Mary, and mentions geographical locations including the Tiber, Ganges, Euphrates, and the Baltic Sea. The text also references historical figures like Nero, Maxentius, and Licinius, and describes a celestial defense against demonic forces.

This section of the poem contains a series of 'Paeans' (IV-VII) and 'Angelus' titles that weave biblical narratives and figures into a meditative structure. It references specific scriptural scenes including the Annunciation (Gabriel), the feeding of the five thousand, the healing of Tobit, and the story of Judith, while invoking the roles of angels as protectors and messengers.

This section contains a series of sacred poems (Paeans) and invocations concerning guardian angels. The text mentions biblical and mythological figures such as Tobias, Lot, Judith, Susanna, and David, alongside specific locations like Gomorrha and the city of Semiramis. It describes the protection of the innocent, the defeat of enemies like Herod and Nero, and the role of angels in guarding the body, modesty, and the betrothed.

This section of the poem contains a series of hymns (Paeans) and angelic invocations concerning the sanctity of marriage, the protection of children, and the healing of the sick. It mentions biblical figures such as Isaac, Rebecca, Tobias, and Sarah, as well as the angel Raphael. The text also references the Rhine, the Lake of Gomorrah, and the biblical figures John, Isaac, and Samson.

This section of the poem contains a series of hymns (Paeans) and liturgical-style proclamations concerning the end times, the judgment of the wicked, and the glorification of Christ. It describes the transition of the soul to heaven, the punishment of the damned in a hell of fire and sulfur, and the celestial worship of the Trinity by the angelic host. The text includes specific references to figures such as Lazarus, the Apostle Peter, and the prophet Jacob, alongside descriptions of the celestial kingdom.

This section of the 'Poemata sacra' contains a series of three paeans and several angelic invocations. The text features a series of theological reflections on the nature of Christ and the Trinity, the dangers of forbidden knowledge (curiositas), and the role of specific angels such as Uriel and Jeremiel. It also includes a narrative segment involving Michael in Persia and a concluding section on the spiritual duties of the pious.

This section contains three paeans (V, VI, and VII) concerning the spiritual warfare of the Church and the protection of the faithful. Paean V describes the defeat of a 'Slanderer' and a 'demon' by the Word of God and the intervention of angels. Paean VI focuses on the plight of the Jewish people (Iudaea) and the historical role of the Church as a refuge. Paean VII addresses the status of the Church as a wandering, yet divinely guided, institution, referencing figures like Christ, Jacob, and various biblical locations.

The text contains a series of sacred poems (Paeans) and descriptions of angelic beings. It features a theological defense of the Christian faith against pagan influence, mentions biblical figures such as Laban and Esau, and includes a series of hymns to Christ and the angelic host. The final section describes the physical decay of pagan idols and the spiritual reality of the divine.

This section contains a series of sacred poems (Paeans) and invocations of angels. The text includes a hymn to the 'Angel of the Contubernal' regarding the Holy Spirit and the role of prophets, a poem on the 'Angel of the Scholars' regarding the value of learning and the names of Daniel and Helcan, and a final paean concerning the 'Angel of Victories' featuring a narrative involving Tobias, the city of Salmanassaris, and the river Ammus.

This section of the poem contains a series of 'Paeans' (XV-XVII) and related verses featuring angelic figures (Angelus Obiurgator, Prohibitor, and Inspector). The text references biblical and mythological figures such as David, Gideon, and Ahaziah, and mentions historical/geographical locations including Colchis, Pontus, and Bithynia. The narrative warns against idolatry, the dangers of alliances with enemies, and the spiritual consequences of deceit and pride.

This section of the poem contains a series of liturgical or devotional hymns (Paeans XVIII and XIX) and a concluding prayer. It features a series of mystical and allegorical descriptions involving the 'Angel of Martyrs,' the 'Angel of Nomenclators,' and various figures such as Christ, the Lamb (Agnus), and several specific names like Numquam, Vitam, and others. The text describes scenes of martyrdom, the recording of names in the Book of Life, and the final judgment of the pious against the wicked.

The text begins with a sacred poem (Paean XX) concerning the dual nature of Christ, the resurrection of the dead, and the role of angels as guides to heaven. It is followed by a formal Latin dedication and eulogy for a young man named Albertus, son of Albertus, and a tribute to the virtue of a scholar named Nicolaus Eblebius. The author, Jacobus Fabricius, concludes with a personal correspondence to a contemporary, mentioning the locations of Misenae and Argentoratum.

This section contains five sacred hymns (Hymnus I-V) recounting biblical figures and narratives. It features figures such as Adam, Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, and others like Deborah, Gideon, and Samson, often framed within a theological context of faith and divine judgment.

This section contains a series of sacred poems (Hymns VI through X) and related liturgical fragments. The text features biblical figures such as Saul, David, Joseph, Moses, Samuel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and John, alongside references to the prophets and various kings. It includes descriptions of divine judgment, the transition of kingdoms, and the role of prophets in the history of the Church.

This section contains a series of sacred hymns (Hymns XI through XIV) and a 'Dies Heroicus' entry. The text features biblical and historical figures including Serubbabel, Ezra, Nehemiah, Jonah, Paul, and the four Evangelists (Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John), as well as mentions of Nero, Herod, and various geographical locations like Africa and the Isthmus.

This section contains a series of sacred poems and hymns detailing biblical narratives, including the fall of Adam, the sacrifice of Abel, the trials of Noah, the sacrifice of Isaac, and the journey of Lot. It follows with a narrative of the life of Christ, including his birth, the trial of the centurion, and the resurrection. The final portion is a formal dedication by Georg Fabricius to Caspar Nevius, where the author critiques the inclusion of pagan elements in sacred verse.

This section of Fabricius's poetry contains three distinct allegorical poems titled 'RELIGIO', 'PUDICITIA', and 'CONCORDIA', followed by a polemical defense of women against the works of Euripides. The text features a transition from a critique of pagan deities (Apollo, Jupiter, Astarte) and their 'monstrous' attributes to a celebration of Christian virtues and the 'holy' lineage of the faithful. The final section specifically addresses the marriage of Sebastian Hillinger and Catharina Losseliana, concluding with a defense of women against the 'malice' of Euripidean drama.

This section contains a series of nuptial poems and blessings for several couples: Valentino Gravio and Helena Wellera, Melchior Pisoni and Anna Creucera, and Wolfgang Meurero and Margaritha Blasebalgae. The text includes theological reflections on the creation of woman from man, the sanctity of marriage, and specific invocations to Christ and the river Dravus. It also features traditional blessings for domestic harmony, fertility, and the protection of the household.

This section contains a series of nuptial poems and blessings for several couples: Christophorus Leuschner and Margaritha Glycae, and Blasius Fabricius and Odilia Cratomyliana. The text includes a series of 'Angelus Pronubus' (pre-nuptial angelic messages) referencing biblical figures such as Isaac, Rebecca, and Sarah. The poems utilize traditional wedding imagery, such as the 'flame' of marriage and the 'bond' of piety, while invoking divine protection against poverty and illness.

This section of the collection contains a series of nuptial poems and blessings for several couples: Hieronymus Buchner and Anna Rivia; Johannes Chentman and Magdalena Sporera; and Johannes Brambacco and Martha Sporera. The verses invoke themes of divine favor, marital fidelity, and the sanctity of the marriage bond, often incorporating biblical allusions and traditional virtues like 'Caritas' and 'Castitas'.

This section contains a series of wedding poems and dedications for several couples: Simon Rostius and Margaritha Thurlerae, Iohann Wideman and Cordula Thurlerae, and Valerius Cracovius and Maria Thurlerae. The text includes religious exhortations to the newlyweds, references to biblical figures like Solomon and the Virgin Mary, and poetic descriptions of the brides' virtues. It also includes two distinct sections labeled 'Siracides' (chapters XV and XXVI) containing allegorical and moralizing verses on marriage, virtue, and the role of the wife.

This section of the poem contains a series of moral and religious meditations on marriage, obedience, and creation, interspersed with specific dedications to individuals such as Jacob of Strasbourg and Magdalena Blasebalgae. It includes a biblical-style passage on the creation of Adam and Eve, and a concluding section incorporating a modified Psalm 127 (cited as CXII) regarding the blessings of a household and the duties of a husband.

This section contains a series of devotional poems and dedicatory inscriptions for various individuals, including the couple Serua and Jacob, the couple Valentinus and Sabina, and the couple Tobias and Sarah. The text includes specific dedications to individuals such as Georg Fabricius, Calixto Sheino, and Odiliae Heida, often incorporating religious imagery of the Cross and the sanctity of marriage. It also features a prayer for Sarah and a concluding stanza on the shared aging of a married couple.

This section contains a series of nuptial poems and dedications for several couples, including Wolfgang Eilenburg and Margaritha Othbach, and Prince Wilhelm of Orange and Anna of Saxony. It includes a defense of marriage and the role of women against the criticisms of the comic poets Alexin and Philemon. The text also features a dedication to Paul Vogelio and Magdalena Nevia, praising their lineage and personal virtues.

This section of the collection contains a series of nuptial poems and dedications for various couples, including Andreas Mylius and Margaritha Rotermundae, Tilemano Stella and Helena Rotermundae, Ambrosius Clavigerus and Susanna Stumpelae, and Bartholomaeo Clamorino and Walpurgi Troezeniae. The verses celebrate the virtues of husbands and wives, the sanctity of marriage, and the blessings of the union. The text also includes a brief biblical reference to the Epistle to the Ephesians and a concluding stanza for Iacobus Colbingero and Annae Smidiae.

This section contains a series of nuptial poems and blessings for several couples: Iohannes Hippocrenius and Ursula Stentia, Sebastianus Frolichius and Maria Harderia, Alexius Hanius and Annae Faustae, and Aegidius Morchio and Magdalenae Sulciae. The verses utilize traditional allegorical imagery of marriage, such as the 'yoke of marriage,' the 'bond of the husband,' and the 'purity of the bride,' while invoking divine protection and the virtues of faith and modesty. The text also includes a section for Abrahamus Fusio and Anna Hausmanus, incorporating references to the Church, the Republic, and the House of Hausman.

This section of the collection contains a series of poems and moralizing verses. It includes a series of dedicatory or celebratory verses for Laurentius Stroer, Anna Neubera, Gabriel Tholae, and Maria Thola; a series of allegorical poems using the spider (Aranea), the ant (Formica), and the bee (Apis) to illustrate virtues of industry and domesticity; and a concluding section of 'Praecepta Connubialia' (Marriage Precepts) and a passage on the education of free men.

This section of the collection contains a series of short poems and epigrams, many of which are wedding toasts or dedications for specific couples. It includes specific dedications to the couples of Catherine and her husband, Andrew and Anna, and Ioannius Rosianus and Rosinae Heuslera. The text also features a series of allegorical and descriptive poems centered on botanical themes, specifically the vine (Vitis), the bramble (Labrusca), the fig (Ficus), and the rose (Rosae).

This section of the collection contains a series of nuptial poems and dedications for several couples: Paulus and Odilia, Tobias and Elisabeth, Johannes and Ursula, Nicolaus and Eva, and Iohannes and Veronica. Each poem utilizes a specific botanical metaphor—the rose, the lily, the autumn narcissus, and the winter hellebore—to symbolize virtues such as chastity, fidelity, and the enduring nature of marital love. The text also includes a final, shorter passage regarding the 'aspis' and 'venena' (poisons).

This section contains a series of dedicatory poems and epigrams addressed to several couples: Felix Zimmerman and Sibylla Mathesius, Adam Gryphius and Maria Kirchbach, Johann Oporino and Elisabeth Holdzach, and Bartolomaeo Losano and Magdalena Freidinger. The verses celebrate marital virtues, parental devotion, and the professional achievements of the men, particularly the scholarly and literary labors of Oporino. The text includes mythological allusions to Medea, Pontia, and Hercules, as well as pastoral imagery regarding the rewards of labor.

This section contains a series of nuptial blessings and poetic dedications for several couples: Wolfgang Hausmann and Rosina Gravia, and Heinrich Schirner and Judith Dasipodia. It includes traditional themes of marital virtue, the importance of patience and charity, and references to biblical scenes such as the wedding at Cana. The text also includes specific laudations for individuals like Peter Buchero and Badhorn.

Poemata sacra. Pars altera is a multi-part collection of sacred Latin poetry by Georg Fabricius (Chemnicensis) comprising devotional, liturgical, and didactic verses. The work is structured into nineteen sections that progress from Old Testament narratives—including the Creation, the Flood, the Tower of Babel, and the lives of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—to Christological meditations on the Nativity, the Eucharist, and the Trinity. The text features specific biblical vignettes such as the trials of Joseph, the Exodus, the siege of Jerusalem, and the exploits of David and Samson. It incorporates liturgical elements like the Oratio Dominica and pastoral instructions for students, while also including 'Triumphs' depicting the fall of enemies like the Syrians and the House of Ahab. The collection concludes with a series of elegies and funerary inscriptions for figures such as Duke Fridericus and the scholar Cornarius. Notable geographical references include Bethlehem, Babylon, and the Rhine.

This collection of sacred poems (Poemata sacra) covers biblical themes including the creation of the world, the fall of man, and the lineage of the patriarchs (Adam, Seth, Enos, Methuselah, Noah). It includes specific sections on the 'Institution of Marriage,' the 'Fall of Abel,' and the 'Greatness of the Giants' (Gigantum Immantitas), while invoking the Trinity and the role of the Holy Spirit.

This section of the poem describes the biblical narrative of the Great Flood and the subsequent fate of Noah's descendants, specifically mentioning Sem, Eber, Peleg, and the confusion of tongues at the Tower of Babel. It includes a series of prayers and liturgical-style exhortations regarding the preservation of the Church, the sanctity of the Eucharist (alluded to via the 'ark' and 'sacred offerings'), and the defense of the faith against pagan idols and worldly influences.

This section of the poem contains several biblical and historical vignettes, including the migration of Abraham and the Chaldeans, the captivity of Sarah in Egypt, and the separation of Lot from Abraham. It also includes a passage on the victory of Abraham over five kings, the flight and return of Hagar, and the birth of Ishmael. The text incorporates prayers for divine protection, the preservation of faith during exile, and the importance of domestic harmony.

This section contains a series of devotional and biblical poems. It includes a prayer for divine guidance and peace, a meditation on the covenant with Abraham and the institution of circumcision, a narrative of Abraham's hospitality to three angels and the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, and a brief mention of the judgment of Lot and the actions of King Abimelech.

This section of the poem contains a series of devotional and biblical meditations. It includes prayers for purification from sin, a section on the virtues of kings and the protection of the poor, and several biblical vignettes including the lineage of Isaac and Sarah, the sacrifice of Isaac on Mount Moriah, and the birth of Christ from the Virgin. The text concludes with a reflection on the frailty of human life compared to the eternal seed of Abraham.

This section contains a series of sacred poems and meditations. It includes a meditation on death and the afterlife, a narrative regarding the marriage of Rebecca (daughter of Laban) and the journey of Abraham to Mesopotamia, a prayer for the protection of virgins and the sanctity of marriage, and a concluding section on the trials of Isaac and the plight of the Israelites against the Palestinians and Gerarensians.

This section of the sacred poems contains a series of prayers and liturgical-style verses concerning the biblical figures Isaac, Jacob, and Esau. It includes specific invocations for the protection of the household, the conversion of enemies into friends, and a vision of Jacob in exile. The text also addresses themes of divine providence, the rejection of hypocrisy, and the spiritual guidance of the faithful.

This section of the poem contains a series of devotional and moralizing verses, including several stanzas specifically referencing the biblical narrative of Jacob and Laban. It addresses themes of divine protection against enemies, the rewards of the pious, and the contrast between sincere faith and the deceitful practices of the wicked. The text includes specific references to the 'servitude' of Jacob in the house of Laban and the 'perfidy' of Laban.

This section of the poem contains a series of devotional and allegorical verses, including a prayer for protection against the devil and a meditation on the light of faith (Hesperus). It features several biblical and mythological references, specifically the figures of Jacob, Esau, Rebecca, Rachel, and Isaac, as well as the names of women like Dina and Heva. The text concludes with a series of moral exhortations regarding purity, the rejection of idolatry, and the steadfastness of the soul in the face of adversity.

This section of the poem contains a series of religious and allegorical verses, including a narrative on the biblical figure Joseph (Iosephus). It features specific references to the patriarchs Isaac and Jacob, the land of Edom (Idumaei), and the city of Sichem. The text alternates between liturgical-style exhortations to the faithful and a dramatic retelling of the biblical narrative of Joseph's sale into slavery and the subsequent mourning of his father.

This section contains a series of devotional poems and meditations, including a lamentation on the dangers of lust and the need for divine protection, and a series of prayers for strength and purity. It features a specific narrative section regarding Joseph (Iosephus) in prison, interpreting dreams for a king and a eunuch, and a concluding prayer for the oppressed. The text mentions figures such as Judas, Thamar, and the biblical Joseph, and references locations like Egypt and Olympus.

This section of the poem contains a series of moral and spiritual exhortations regarding humility, the avoidance of worldly vanity, and the endurance of suffering through faith. It includes a narrative sequence based on the biblical story of Joseph and his brothers in Egypt, specifically mentioning the famine in Canaan, the identification of the brothers, and the plight of Benjamin.

This section of the collection contains a series of religious poems and meditations. It includes a moralizing poem on the judgment of the self-righteous, a series of hymns to God's providence and healing, and a narrative sequence concerning the biblical figures Joseph and Jacob, specifically focusing on Joseph's life in Egypt and the reunion with his father.

This section of the poem contains a series of devotional and theological meditations on the nature of God as a protector, judge, and source of salvation. It includes specific biblical references to the figures of Pharaoh, Joseph, and Jacob, and concludes with a series of exhortations regarding the duties of the faithful and the rewards of the pious.

This section of the poem contains a series of moral and theological exhortations, beginning with a call for harmony among the faithful and a discussion on the biblical figures of Ephraim, Isaac, and Esau. It moves into a series of 'blessings' (benedictiones) and warnings concerning the biblical figures Jacob, Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judas, focusing on themes of divine justice, the rejection of sin, and the exaltation of the kingdom of God.

This section of the collection contains a series of sacred poems and blessings. It includes the 'Benedictiones Sex Filiorum' (Blessings of the Six Sons) regarding the tribes of Zebulon, Issachar, Dan, Gad, Asher, and Naphtali, followed by the 'Iosephi Benedictio' concerning the sons of Joseph, Ephraim, and Manasseh. The text concludes with a meditation on death and the incarnation of Christ as the 'seed of the Virgin'.

This section contains a series of religious and allegorical poems. The first part addresses the spiritual liberation of the soul through faith, referencing the 'Ephronites' and 'Hethites' before transitioning into a series of meditations on the life of Christ, the suffering of the faithful, and the role of the Church. The second part, titled 'Triumphus I,' recounts the biblical narrative of the Tenth Plague of Egypt, detailing the destruction of the Egyptian people and the transition from slavery to the 'true home.'

The text contains a series of religious and allegorical poems, including a section on the judgment of the wicked and the protection of the faithful. It features a narrative concerning a figure named Isaides (or Isacidis) who faces divine judgment and a plague, and a passage concerning the military actions of Joab and the geography of the Levant, including Sidon, Damascus, and the Jordan. The final section offers a moralizing reflection on trust in God's mercy versus human pride.

This section contains two 'Triumphs' (III and IV) depicting biblical scenes of divine intervention and judgment. Triumph III focuses on the siege of Jerusalem and the defense of the city against the Assyrians (specifically the figure Rabsac), while Triumph IV depicts the defeat of the Syrians and the fall of Ahab. The text references specific biblical passages from Isaiah, the Chronicles (Paralipomeni), and Maccabees.

The text describes a military conflict involving the Syrians, the Samaritans, and the figures Benhadad and Hethau. It depicts a siege of Samaria characterized by famine and a subsequent retreat of the Syrian forces following a divine intervention or angelic appearance. The narrative concludes with the mention of the prophet Elisaei and the temple of Bahal.

This section of the poem contains a series of exhortations to trust in God and find comfort in divine providence amidst hardship, followed by a narrative and moral reflection on the city of Sodom. It specifically references the biblical account of Lot (Lothus) and the destruction of Sodom as a warning against luxury, impiety, and the abandonment of sacred teachings.

The text contains two sacred triumphs (Triumphus VII and VIII) featuring poetic reflections on piety, the dangers of impiety, and the protection of the faithful. It includes a narrative involving a prophet (vates) and the King of Syria, referencing biblical locations such as Samaria and Dothan, and mentions figures like Benhadad and the prophet Balaam.

The text contains a series of biblical and historical narratives, beginning with the conquest of the territories of Sihon and Og and the subsequent interactions between the prophet Balaam and an angel. It transitions into a theological reflection on the corruption of sacred things and the moral failings of figures like Heliodorus and the treacherous actions of individuals like Simon. The passage concludes with a condemnation of sacrilege and the betrayal of religious trust.

The text begins with a narrative involving Heliodorus, a man accused of sacrilege and greed, and the subsequent judgment of his actions and the restoration of temple honor. It then transitions into a biblical and mythological section titled 'Triumphus I,' focusing on the Exodus of the Hebrews, the miracles of Moses, and the crossing of the Red Sea.

This section of the poem contains a series of biblical and mythological allegories, including the crossing of the Red Sea (mentioning Amramides, Joseph, and the destruction of Egypt), the fall of Jericho (under the command of Joshua), and the victory of Gideon over the Midianites. It also includes a theological reflection on original sin, the fall of man, and the redemptive power of baptism. The text concludes with a description of the destruction of the Midianite camp through the use of trumpets and torches.

This section contains a series of religious and biblical poems (Triumphs) detailing the exploits of Samson (Maxilla Simsonis), the actions of Samgar, and the story of Jonathan (Gladius Ionathae). The texts describe the defeat of the Philistines, the punishment of thieves and robbers, and the defense of the Ark of the Covenant. Specific figures mentioned include Samson, Samgar, and Jonathan, set against the backdrop of biblical warfare and divine judgment.

This section contains two sacred poems (Triumphs VII and VIII) depicting biblical and mythological scenes. Triumph VII recounts the victory of David over the giant Goliath and the defeat of the Philistines, while Triumph VIII depicts the victory of Benaias over an Egyptian opponent. The text includes theological reflections on faith, divine strength, and the contrast between human audacity and divine power.

The text contains two biblical-themed poems (Triumphs IX and X) depicting the fall of enemies of Israel. Triumph IX describes the assassination of the King of Moab by Ehud, while Triumph X recounts Judith's actions against the Assyrian commander Holofernes. The poems include references to the cities of Pelusium, Betulia, and the regions of Ephraim and the Jordan.

This section contains two sacred triumphs (Triumphus XI and XII) depicting biblical narratives. Triumphus XI recounts the defeat of Sisera by Barak and Deborah, featuring the names of Sisera, Jabin, and the locations of Taanach (implied by 'Tauris' context) and Kishon (Chison). Triumphus XII begins a narrative concerning the Israelites and the Midianites, specifically mentioning the figures Simri and Casbia.

The text contains two 'Triumphs' (I and II) featuring biblical and mythological narratives. Triumph I recounts the story of Phinehas (Pinehas) and the judgment of the people, the conquest of the Midianites, and the fate of the Ark of the Covenant. Triumph II focuses on the sword of King Saul and the actions of the Thariads regarding the spoils of war.

The text describes a biblical narrative involving King Saul and the prophet Samuel, specifically the moment Saul rejects God's commands and is told he will lose his kingdom. It transitions into a scene involving a priest named Doeg (Doegus) and a man named Isaius, who are involved in a conflict involving the Philistines and the city of Nobah. The passage concludes with the violent actions of Doeg against those who betrayed the king.

This section of the poem describes the rebellion of Absalom against his father, portraying him as a deceitful and ambitious figure who uses fraud to gain the favor of the people and the military. It details the military movements of figures such as Joab, Zerviadae, and Maachides, and concludes with the tragic consequences of Absalom's pursuit of power and the subsequent desecration of his remains.

This section of the poem contains a series of moralizing and didactic verses addressed to kings, warning them against the dangers of pride, the fickleness of fortune, and the betrayal of trust. It includes a specific narrative sequence involving the figures of Achitophelus, Gilon, and Husaius, set against a backdrop of biblical and mythological imagery. The text concludes with a series of moral exhortations regarding the duties of rulers and the consequences of impiety.

This section of the poem contains a series of moralizing and narrative vignettes, beginning with a warning against the consequences of ambition and deceit. It features a narrative involving figures named Gabalus, Amanus, and the Iairidae, set against a backdrop of Judean and Macedonian themes. The final portion uses the winds and the figure of Aeolus as an allegory for the dangers of unchecked power and the necessity of pious governance.

The text describes a dramatic scene involving a king, a group of Hebrew youths, and a Chaldean who approaches the royal court. It depicts a confrontation involving a 'fiery path' (caminus igneus) and a furnace, where the youth are accused of idolatry and the king is portrayed as a tyrant. The narrative concludes with a theological defense of faith over earthly power, specifically referencing the Hebrew God and the figure of Abraham.

The text begins with a theological meditation on Christ's victory over fire and his suffering in a human body. It then transitions into a narrative involving a king (Darius) and a figure named Daniel, set against a backdrop of Medes, Persians, and a lion's den (Spelunca Leonum). The narrative describes a scene of judgment, the presence of a crowd, and the miraculous survival of individuals amidst lions.

The text contains a series of religious and moral poems. The first section uses biblical allegories (Daniel, Joseph) to contrast the behavior of just and unjust rulers, while the second section, marked 'ELEG.', is a devotional poem celebrating the Nativity of Christ, his incarnation, and the humble circumstances of his birth in Bethlehem.

This section of the poem contains two distinct parts. The first part is a prayer to Christ for the protection of the Church and the spiritual guidance of children, referencing the Virgin's veil, the crossing of the Red Sea, and the role of teachers. The second part, a hymn to the Christ child, describes the Incarnation, the Nativity in Bethlehem, and the theological significance of the 'manger' and 'stable' as the seat of the King.

This section of the poem describes the birth of Christ in a stable, contrasting the humble circumstances of the manger with the majesty of the divine child. It mentions specific locations such as Solymae and Bethlehem, and includes a narrative involving Herod, the shepherds, and the recognition of Christ as the new light for all nations. The text concludes with a direct address to the child as the image of the Father.

This section of the poem contains a series of religious and devotional verses concerning the Nativity of Christ, the incarnation of the Word, and the role of the Messiah as a savior. It references biblical figures and lineages, including the house of David, the lineage of Jesse, and the figures of Adam and the woman. The text also includes a series of pastoral and liturgical-style verses describing the stable, the protection of the infant from wolves and cold, and the cosmic significance of the Word.

Sylvae Tubingenses is a collection of early modern Latin poetry and academic prose by Christoph Kaldenbach. Mythological and pastoral elements are prominent, featuring figures like Apollo, Ceres, and Dido. Geographical references include Tübingen, Jena, Leipzig, the Vistula, the Alps, and the lands of the Habsburg dynasty. Additional subjects include a treatise on anagrams, botanical descriptions, and an account of the execution of Charles I of England.

Opuscula poetica is a collection of Latin poetry by Christian Adolph Klotz, organized into thirteen sections containing odes, elegies, and satirical verses. This collection contains three satirical declamations (Declamationes Satyricae Tres) performed at the Academy of Rostock. The work addresses the moral and intellectual decay of the early 17th century, specifically critiquing the corruption of the legal system, the degradation of academic standards, and the lack of student discipline. The author utilizes classical and mythological allusions to figures such as Aristophanes, Juvenal, Hercules, and the Eumenides to contrast contemporary conditions with ancient virtues. The text identifies specific local figures including Duke Philip II of Pomerania, the scholar Thomas Lindemann, and the lineage of Ulricus and Henry Swicheli. The final sections transition from satirical critique to formal funeral orations for members of the Pomeranian nobility. The work also incorporates themes of the defense of Latin and Greek education and the contrast between sacred and profane life.

This opening section of a satirical declamation, performed in 1602 at the Academy of Rostock, addresses a gathering of scholars and a 'dear young man.' The author justifies his use of satire and 'rough' language as a necessary response to the moral decay of the current age. The text invokes a long list of classical and satirical poets—including Eupolis, Cratinus, Aristophanes, Juvenal, and Lucilius—to establish his literary lineage. The passage concludes with a transition from classical antiquity to early Christian history, referencing martyrs like Polycarp and the apostles Peter and Andrew.

This section of the declamation contains a series of rhetorical questions and polemics regarding the corruption of the legal system and the degradation of sacred values. The text concludes with a plea for the judge to pause and weigh the evidence before a final ruling.

The text contains a series of satirical declamations concerning the corruption of the legal system, the moral decay of the Roman Empire, and the actions of specific figures. The passage concludes with a rhetorical defense of justice and a reference to the jurist Papinian.

The author delivers a satirical critique of various academic and professional groups, including the 'Sophians' (philosophers), grammarians, rhetoricians, and astrologers.
