Lyrische Gedichte is a collection of early modern Latin lyric poetry, odes, and meditations by Simon Rettenpacher, OSB. The work is organized into nineteen sections that blend moral didacticism, religious devotion, and classical mythology. It contains a variety of genres, including martial odes, devotional hymns, and pastoral scenes. Notable figures include biblical figures such as the Virgin Mary, the Holy Spirit, and Saint Paul, alongside classical figures like Augustus Caesar, Pericles, Orpheus, Hercules, and the Muses. The text features specific geographical locations such as the Rhine, the Danube, the Ister, and the Taurus Mountains, as well as historical settings like the defense of Vienna against the Turks. Themes include Stoic and Socratic philosophy, the vanity of worldly wealth, and the moral consequences of lust and pride.

This collection of five poems explores themes of stoicism, Marian devotion, and spiritual ascent. The texts include a meditation on virtue and the cross, a hymn to the Virgin Mary (Deiparae), a mystical ascent of the mind toward the divine, a seasonal poem on winter and the solace of wine, and a maritime allegory regarding the dangers of trusting worldly leaders.

This collection of lyric poems includes a sequence on Fortune and Cupid, a hymn to the Holy Spirit, a poem regarding a girl's marriage, and a reflection on the vanity of old age. The text features mythological and biblical figures such as Alcides, Juno, and St. John the Evangelist, and references geographical locations like the Taurus mountains and the island of Clauderius.

This collection of lyric poems includes a meditation on the rarity of virtue (Virtus) and the duty of the intellectual to serve the state, a theological poem regarding the Nativity of Christ in Bethlehem, and a lament addressed to a man named Plance regarding a woman named Tyndaris. The text also includes a descriptive passage on the pleasures of nature and the passage of time.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a warning against a dangerous path toward death, a meditation on historical truth and the role of the historian, and a poem on divine love. It also features a reflection on the state of the world (war, fraud, and justice), a musical interlude referencing the Muses and the Pindus mountains, and a concluding invitation to a frugal feast featuring references to Plato and Atticus.

This collection of lyric poems includes a series of vignettes featuring figures such as Bromius, Tullius, and Melander. The poems address themes of aging, the rewards of victory, the dangers of lust, and the moral contrast between the wealthy and the poor. Specific references are made to historical or mythological figures like Nero, the poet's role in old age, and the plight of the impoverished.

This collection of lyric poems includes dedications to Tullius, Faustinus, Flaccus, and Alfonsus, as well as a concluding poem on the fruits of repentance. The texts address themes of solitude, the dangers of greed and worldly wealth, the sanctity of friendship, and the transition from earthly desires to spiritual devotion. Specific figures mentioned include Thersite, Ulysses, and the biblical figures of the Hebrew people and the Temple of Sion.

This section contains a series of lyrical poems and addresses. It includes a moralizing exhortation to a traveler or seeker, a dialogue-style poem addressing Pericles regarding various lands (Venice, Rome, Asia, Africa, etc.), a critique of intellectual inconsistency and the abandonment of Stoic and Socratic values, a dedication to 'Fernandum' regarding the rejection of worldly wealth, and a final address to 'Priscum' regarding the vanity of accumulating gold.

This section contains a series of lyrical poems including 'Ad Caesarem' (To Caesar), 'Ad Plancum' (To Plancus), 'Ad Avarum et Libidinosum Divitem' (To the Avaricious and Lustful Man), and 'Fidelium Animarum Planctus' (Lament of the Faithful Souls). The texts address themes of immortality, the vanity of earthly wealth, the dangers of lust, and the ritualistic mourning of the dead.

This section contains a series of lyrical poems and odes. The first poem addresses a 'leader of the world' (rector orbis) regarding a troubled mind and the loss of spiritual light. The second, titled 'Saeculi Ignavia,' laments the decline of ancient virtues, the ruin of the priesthood, and the loss of historical glory in favor of modern luxury and vanity. The third, 'Ad Metellum,' offers solace to a figure named Metellus, referencing Hagar, the sun (Phoebus), and the endurance of hardship. The final fragment reflects on the memories of past sufferings and the desire for oblivion.

This collection of poems includes a meditation on the fleeting nature of joy and the weight of past hardships, a celebratory ode to Bacchus and the contrast between youth and age, and a series of exhortations regarding the fragility of health and the pursuit of poetic fame. The text also features a warning to a figure named Cleobulus regarding the dangers of pride and a concluding passage on the exposure of hidden crimes by the sun.

This collection of lyric poems includes a meditation on the dangers of excessive physical size and strength, a consolation to a man named Cleander regarding the superiority of the mind over a failing body, a praise of the steadfastness of Saint George, and a warning to a man named Fabian regarding the deceptive nature of women. The text also includes a brief elegy for a deceased wife addressed to a man named Candidus.

This collection of lyric poems includes a meditation on the virtues of a wife (Candide), a lament for Orpheus, and a series of poems on the dangers of excessive fortune and the virtues of prudence. The text features specific references to the figures of Orpheus, the tyrant Polycrates, and a dedicatory passage to Nearchus regarding the praise of heroes.

The text consists of four lyrical poems or sections. The first section uses mythological imagery (Melpomenes, Mars, Pindar) and classical allusions (Nearchus, Sithonia) to describe artistic inspiration and the dangers of passion. The second section, titled 'Corrupti Saeculi Mores,' critiques moral decay, the commercialization of religious life, and the loss of traditional virtues. The third section, 'Contemptus Mundi,' reflects on mortality and the fleeting nature of life through the figures of Orpheus and Eurydice. The final section, 'Iuventus Praeceps,' addresses a 'Tribennius' regarding the impulsive nature of youth versus the gravity of statecraft.

This collection of poems includes a prayer to the Holy Spirit, a critique of the common people's preference for private interests over public ones, and a dialogue between the Spirit (SP.) and the Flesh (CA.). The text also features a pastoral scene involving a shepherd, the figures of Themistocles and Scipio, and references to mythological locations like Olympus and the regions of Egypt and Syria.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a meditation on rural solitude and the rejection of urban fortifications, a poem addressed to Nearch regarding the unpredictability of the sea and the fate of Hector, and a piece addressed to Probum regarding celestial love. The final sections contrast ancient and modern eras, and a poem dedicated to the virtue of Augustus Caesar (referred to as 'Augusti Caesaris' and 'Leopolde') invokes the names of various geographical locations and mythological figures.

This collection of poems includes a moralizing exhortation to a young man regarding the dangers of pride, the importance of military discipline, and the consequences of deceit. It features a dialogue regarding the 'spirit of Labi Metellus' and a series of warnings against the 'crime of treachery.' The final section, titled 'Bellum Turcicum,' describes a military scene involving the defense of Vienna against the Turks and mentions locations such as Pannonia, Thrace, and the Ister (Danube).

This collection of lyrical poems includes a martial scene involving the defeat of a 'Teuton' army and the conquest of Thracian and Asian lands. It transitions into a series of devotional and allegorical poems, including a meditation on the 'Eternal Presence' of the divine, a praise of the goddess Cybele, a martial lament regarding the death of a soldier named Miscere, and a moralizing poem on the virtues of virginity and chastity.

This collection of lyric poems includes a meditation on the brevity of human life and the vanity of worldly pursuits, a dedicatory poem to 'Fernandus' regarding the preservation of human laws and charity, a prayer to the Virgin Mary, and a critique of 'Pison' regarding the fleeting nature of fame and the dangers of ambition. The text also includes a passage regarding the architectural vanity of 'Paulus' and the construction of villas.

This section contains a series of lyrical poems and dedications. It includes a sequence of allegorical and mythological verses referencing figures such as Melpomene, Cupid, and Hyperion, followed by a formal address to 'Tullius' regarding courtly manners and a concluding poem titled 'Suspiria' concerning the sighs of a lover's soul.

This section contains a series of lyrical poems and religious exhortations. It includes a plea to 'Vita' (Life) to return, a laudatio of Thomas Aquinas as a model of divine wisdom and scholarship, a hymn to the virtues of a holy man (Laus Viri Iusti), a meditation on the martyrdom of Saint George under Diocletian, and a concluding poem addressed to Cloelia regarding the dangers of pride.

This section contains a series of lyrical poems and meditations. The poems address themes of vanity, the brevity of life, the pursuit of virtue over worldly pleasures, and the dangers of deceit. Specific references include the Greek figures Lachesis, Tisiphone, and Cephalus, as well as a dedicatory poem to Polycarp.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a prayer for protection against war and famine, a warning against the forbidden pursuit of divine knowledge, a meditation on the fleeting nature of youth and virginity, and a moralizing exhortation against the dangers of a path of vice. The texts reference figures such as Mars, Pallas, Phaeton, and the Punic general Cunctator, and mention locations like Capua and the underworld (Styx, Erebus).

This collection of lyrical poems includes a critique of worldly ambition and the pursuit of material wealth versus spiritual truth. It features a section on the 'Vita Quieta' (quiet life) contrasting it with the violence of Mars, and a series of poems regarding the vanity of promises, the corruption of money, and the fall of earthly rulers. Specific references are made to figures such as Bromius, the god Apollo (Phoebus), and the mythological figures of Danae and Perseus.

This collection of poems includes a meditation on the permanence of divine law versus the shifting nature of human laws, and a series of moralizing poems. The texts feature specific figures such as Moses, Lycurgus, Dracon, and various fictionalized or allegorical figures like Cyrillus, Titus, and Leo. The poems address themes of religious devotion, the corruption of the 'ungrateful' (ingrati), and the rarity of faith (Fides) in a world of material greed.

This section contains a series of lyrical poems and epigrams. It includes a hymn to chastity (LAUS CASTITATIS) featuring a virtuous maiden, a satirical poem addressed to Lyce regarding the vanity of an elderly woman's beauty, a critique of a ruler's lack of counsel (CONSILII NECESSITAS) referencing Xerxes, and a consolation to a man named Sabinus mourning his deceased wife.

The text contains a series of lyrical poems and hymns. Section XV describes the transition from winter to spring, featuring imagery of melting snow, blooming flowers (lilies, roses, hyacinths), and the figure of Narcissus. Section XVI addresses the horrors of war among Christians, naming specific regions such as Gaul, Germany, Britain, and Bavaria, and mentions the tribes of the Danes and Suevians. Section XVII focuses on divine vengeance and the punishment of crimes, followed by a 'Carmen Saeculare' and a hymn praising the Order of Saint Benedict.

The text contains a series of lyrical poems and meditations on religious and moral virtues. It references historical and biblical figures such as Winfridus, the Semites, and the martyrs, while contrasting the 'purity' of monastic life and the 'sacred' with the 'profane' allure of worldly wealth and pagan imagery. The second section, titled 'Ecclesiae Antiquae Facies,' focuses on the steadfastness of martyrs and the sanctity of the early Church.

This collection of lyric poems includes sections on the dangers of avarice, the deceptive nature of physical beauty, and a description of winter. The text references mythological and geographical elements such as Ceres, the Caspian Sea, the goddess Astraea, and the gardens of Alcinous. It contrasts spiritual purity with material wealth and describes the physical transformation of the landscape during the winter season.

This section contains a series of lyrical poems and hymns. It includes a lament on poverty and divine gratitude, a hymn for the Feast of Saints Peter and Paul featuring imagery of Rome and the celestial hierarchy, a mystical poem regarding the 'Desire of the Beloved Soul' and the 'Triad,' and a dream sequence involving the monastery of Sion and the 'Sion' mountains. The final poem contrasts profane love with celestial love, mentioning figures such as Telesilla and Cleobulus.

This collection of lyric poems addresses the themes of slander (calumnia), the protection of the innocent, and the dangers of pride. The text includes a series of numbered poems (XII-XV) featuring mythological and classical references, including figures such as Titus, Tisiphone, and the god Mars, as well as references to the Stygian underworld and the Roman military.

This collection of lyric poems includes a series of numbered pieces (XVI-XXII) featuring various themes. Notable sections include a religious meditation on Christ's passion (Christus Patiens), a critique of slander (Calumnia Spernenda) featuring historical figures like Catiline, Brutus, and Cassius, and a moralizing poem on the dangers of lust and the pursuit of wealth. Specific figures mentioned include the mythical Phaethon, the biblical figures Moses and Isaac, and the historical figures Catiline and Brutus.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a series of numbered sections (XXIII-XXVIII) exploring themes of modesty, the inevitability of death, the value of friendship, and the consequences of offense. The texts feature various proper names and mythological references, including Meliton, Theseus, Pylades, Orestes, and the goddess of the hunt (implied by the mention of the 'forbidden fruit' and 'Olympus').

This collection of poems includes a lament over the destruction of cities and the Rhine's defenses, a warning against the dangers of lust and the betrayal of faith, and a series of moralizing verses. It features specific references to figures such as Hercules (Alcides), the saint Barbara, and various mythological entities like the Hydra and Geryon. The text also includes a section on the rules of comedy and a meditation on the purity of the virgin.

This collection of lyric poems includes a meditation on the dangers of pride (hubris) using the myth of Icarus, a celebration of wine (Laus Vini) referencing the myth of Pandora and the god Bacchus (Bromius), and a series of poems on virtue, friendship, and chastity. The text features mythological figures such as Icarus, Daedalus, Pandora, and Bacchus, and includes a dialogue involving Orcus and a virago.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a series of addresses to specific individuals (Priscus, Cleobulus, Crispus) and a section on the Muses. The texts explore themes of virtue versus appearance, the dangers of excess (specifically drinking), the unpredictability of fortune, and the nature of the cosmos. Specific names mentioned include the Muses, the Pierides, and various tribes such as the Britons, Batavians, and Suevi.

This section contains a series of lyrical poems and epigrams. It includes a critique of a 'lascivious' poet (Melander) and a warning to a man named Meletius against slander and loose speech. The final sections feature a poem addressed to Venus regarding the dangers of lust, and a poem regarding the equality of skin colors (Maurus, Aethiops, and the crow) and the vanity of outward appearance.

This collection of poems includes a series of lyrical and didactic verses. Notable sections include 'Mundi Deceptio', which critiques worldly vanity and the deception of the senses; 'Clarissimo Viro Leoni Allatio', a formal panegyric to a man named Leo regarding his role in Roman drama; and 'Solitudo Amanda', a meditation on secluded devotion. The text also features brief reflections on human misery, moderate love, and the contrast between earthly vanity and spiritual light.

This collection of poems includes a moralizing piece on the 'punishment of libido' featuring references to the Ganges, Libya, and the figure of Phyllis. It contains a poem on the 'Fortune' of a man named Metellus, a prayer to a guardian angel, and a laudatory piece for Emperor Henry II. The final section, 'Sacrae Scripturae Praestantia,' contrasts the study of profane books with the study of sacred scriptures.

This collection of poems includes a section on the Elector of Saxony and the King of Poland, referencing the Sarmatians, the land of Bistonia, and the tribe of the Geloni. Other sections feature a hymn to Bacchus, a meditation on the power of prayer (obsecrationis) involving figures like Solymis and Iessaeus, and a concluding poem on the endurance of virtue.

This collection of poems includes a meditation on the transience of life and the pursuit of higher knowledge, a dialogue between Virtue (Vir) and Pleasure (Vol), and a plea for justice against a cruel ruler. The text features references to figures such as Elijah, Astraea, and Melpomene, and mentions locations like Thrace, Africa, and Asia.

This collection of lyric poems includes a meditation on inner virtue versus public fame, a martial ode praising a soldier's bravery against enemies, and a devotional hymn to the Virgin Mary near Salzburg. The text also contains a satirical piece on aging and physical decay, and a concluding exhortation on the value of concise, graceful speech.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a series of numbered meditations on themes such as the vanity of wealth, the value of marriage, and the pursuit of divine peace. The text references mythological figures and locations including Midas, Danae, the city of Troy (Priam), and the goddess Venus, while also referencing historical or literary figures like Solon and Mucius. The final section provides an allegory of a soul's affliction set against a backdrop of a violent storm.

This collection of lyric poems includes a sequence of numbered sections (XXV-XXX) exploring themes of personal transformation, the dangers of envy, and the inevitability of death. The text references mythological figures and locations such as Venus, Melpomenes, Pindus, Castalia, and the River Styx, while employing classical imagery of floods, sea monsters, and divine intervention.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a personal reflection on the author's rise to status and subsequent illness, a defense against slander, a meditation on the fear of death, and a critique of false friendship. The text features specific references to the names Titus, Diodore, and Daniel, as well as a reference to the 'gentis Teutonicae' (Teutonic people).

This collection of lyrical poems includes a critique of luxury and vanity, a description of the dangers of lust and the influence of Venus, and a series of poems on the virtues of Stoicism. The text mentions several mythological and historical figures, including Eurynome, Iolas, Hector, Paris, Zeno, and Cleanthes, while referencing geographical locations such as Libya, the Ganges, and the Sarmatic throne.

This collection of lyric poems includes a series of vignettes and moralizing verses. It features a poem addressed to Leuconoe regarding maternal love and a maiden's virtue, a critique of lustful elderly men (including a reference to Paphos), and a prophetic vision of a people from the islands reclaiming a sacred tomb. The final section, 'Quamdiu Haec Erunt?', lists various historical and mythological figures such as Antinous, Catullus, Lesbia, and Crispus in a series of rhetorical questions regarding their status and passions.

This section contains a series of lyrical poems and meditations. The first part addresses the vanity of worldly pursuits, the value of hard work, and the deception of appearances. The second part, titled 'Vaticinium de Turca Evertendo,' contains a prophetic passage regarding the fall of the Turks and the rise of a ruler in Gaul (France) and the fate of Austria. The final section, 'Peregrinatio,' describes a journey through Asia and the lands of the Persians.

This collection of poems includes a didactic exhortation to intellectual prudence and the avoidance of sensory distractions, a personal address to a friend named Cratippus regarding their shared studies of Pindaric and Heliconic themes, and a poem titled 'Festina Lente' advocating for deliberate action. The text also features a martial and mythological sequence involving Aeneas, the destruction of Ilium, and the transition from pagan imagery to a Christian context. The final poem, 'Calamitatis Utilitas,' explores the refining power of adversity and the pursuit of virtue.

This collection of lyrical poems includes several numbered sections (VIII, IX, XI) and a concluding passage on the praise of constancy. The texts address themes of moral fortitude against worldly temptation, the corruption of lineage and the dangers of ambition, and the internal conflicts within the Christian faith. Specific names mentioned include Cleander, Melisse, and the figure of the 'tyrant of Asia'.

This section contains a series of lyrical poems and fragments. It includes a patriotic and anti-Ottoman exhortation to the Germans, a prayer for Metellus, a satirical or moralizing dialogue regarding a soldier's conduct in a forum, and a mythological/lyrical scene involving a fleet near Lilybaea and a reference to the Trojan War.

The text contains a series of lyrical poems and meditations on mortality, the passage of time, and the loss of traditional virtues. It includes a section titled 'Militia Venalis' which critiques the corruption of military honor and the commercialization of war, and a section titled 'Humanae Vitae Calamitas' which reflects on the stages of human life from childhood to death. Specific references are made to the figures of Mars, Jupiter, and the historical names Scipio, Decii, and Fabii.

This collection of poems includes a hymn to the Virgin Mary (Breve Encomium Beatae Virginis) and a secular poem (Carmen Saeculare) detailing military conflicts involving the Batavians, Teutons, Gauls, and Turks in regions like Pannonia and the Rhine. The final sections include a meditation on the life of youth and a description of a man of 'fastus' (prestige) in humble attire.

This collection of lyric poems includes a dramatic scene involving a 'rustica' figure and a 'king' amidst a crowd, followed by a spiritual lament regarding the 'Desiderium Caelestis Patriae' and the plight of the soul in Babylon and Memphis. The text includes a critique of false promises in poetry and a funeral elegy (epicedion) for a young man named Maximilian Sigismund, mentioning figures such as Apollo (Phoebus), Narcissus, and Hyacinthus.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a series of numbered sections (VIII-XIII) featuring themes of mortality, the passage of time, and the dangers of the sea. The text references historical and mythological figures such as Caesar, Demeter, and the Nereids, while describing military conflicts involving the Thracians, Gauls, and Teutons in regions like Pannonia and Asia.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a martial scene involving Germans and Odrysians, a penitential prayer of the soul to God, and a meditation on the life of a scholar. The text also features a hymn to the Eucharist (Calix Bibendus), a philosophical exhortation to seek higher truths over worldly vanity, and a concluding section on the precepts of Christian life.

This collection of lyric poems includes a series of moral and philosophical exhortations. The texts address themes of stoicism against the future, the rejection of worldly vanity, the virtues of Christian philosophy, and the necessity of hard work. Specific figures mentioned include Telesilla, Gelasine, and the mythological figures Phoebe and Eos.

This collection of lyric poems includes a meditation on the virtues of old age (Senectutis Encomium) and the pursuit of spiritual knowledge over physical pleasures. It features a religious and martial poem regarding the victory of the Virgin Mary over the Turks, and several shorter pieces concerning the contrast between earthly desires and celestial contemplation. Specific references include the Muses (Calliope), the Pierides, and various mythological/geographic locations like the Castalian springs and the Phlegethon.

This collection of lyric poems includes several numbered sections (30-35) featuring moralizing and allegorical themes. Specific subjects include the dangers of ambition, the corruption of judges and rulers, the fall of a king named Solymus (or Solymae) for lust and idolatry, and the contrast between inner virtue and outward appearance. Named figures and places include Fronto, the Aeneads, the Tyrians, and the mythical/literary figures Clymene and Magnus.

This collection of lyric poems includes a passage on the military life of Pompey and the discipline of soldiers, a meditation on the omnipresence of God and the scrutiny of the soul, and a reflection on the ideal form of government (monarchy vs. republic). The final sections describe the inevitability of death, the terror of the final judgment, and the punishments of the underworld, referencing figures such as Sisyphus, Tityus, and Tantalus.

This collection of lyric poems includes a series of vignettes describing mythological and infernal scenes, such as the suffering of a prophet in the Phlegethon and the description of a celestial city. The text transitions into a series of numbered sections (IV-IX) featuring themes of divine glory, the contemplation of death and tombs, the birth of Christ, and the transition of the new year. Specific names mentioned include figures like Vulcan (implied by 'Veneris' context), Lucifer, and various proper names like Carmine, Brachius, and Egeris.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a New Year's greeting to a nephew named Largiar, a critique of a woman's vanity and a man's lack of discipline, and a description of a soldier's experience in battle. The texts also feature moralizing poems on the vanity of hope, the dangers of deceitful speech, and the physical consequences of gluttony.

This collection of lyric poems includes a series of numbered sections (XVII-XXIII) featuring themes of divine order, the corruption of earthly power, and moral warnings. Specific subjects include the 'Concordia' of the universe, the fall of a 'Turpis' adulterer, the dangers of pride, and a critique of a 'Mendax Historicus' who confuses historical dates. The text mentions figures or entities such as Enyo, Venus, Jupiter, and various proper names like Pontice, Suetus, and Bistonum.

This collection of lyric poems includes a series of numbered sections (XXIV-XXX) featuring various themes such as the dignity of the priesthood, the consequences of greed, and the preparation for death. The texts mention specific figures and locations including the figures of Hector, Pelias, and the goddess Ceres, as well as the names of individuals like Titus, Longius, and the figure of Mulciber.

This collection of lyrical poems includes several numbered sections exploring themes of virtue, the dangers of lust, and the rewards of moderation. Specific figures mentioned include Lycurgus, Cleobulus, Philomus, and the mythical figures of Achilles (Alcides) and Priam. The text also features a section on the duties of a servant and a concluding piece on the leisure of the wise.

This collection of lyrical poems includes sections on the futility of medicine for physical ailments, the moral distinction between true virtue and simulated piety, and the internal struggles of the soul. It features references to mythological figures and locations such as Lachesis, the Styx, Avernus, and the goddess Cypris (Venus), as well as a specific narrative involving a man named Fabius and a physician's failed treatment of a 'lustful' disease.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a series of numbered sections (XV-XXI) featuring various themes such as the hardships of exile, the dangers of lust, and the pursuit of virtuous leisure. Specific names and places mentioned include Lysander, the cities of Athens, Argos, Pisa, Sicyon, and Sparta, as well as figures like Melander and the deity Phoebus. The text also contains allegorical descriptions of nature, military imagery, and religious devotion.

This collection of lyric poems includes meditations on mortality, the virtues of honesty over utility, and the necessity of religion. Specific sections feature the deaths of figures such as Julius, Sidera Crispus, and Claudius, while others address the divine power of the Creator over the cosmos and the spiritual redemption of the soul.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a prayer for the removal of 'old-fashioned night' and 'wickedness,' followed by a series of numbered poems (XXVII-XXX) exploring themes of inner peace, the alignment of speech and life, and the dangers of deceit. The text features several proper names and mythological references, including Mars, Cerberus, and the Stygian marshes, while contrasting the virtues of a 'good mind' against the 'scoundrel's' life of fraud and physical suffering.

This collection of lyrical poems includes several numbered sections dealing with moral and spiritual themes. Specific subjects include the brevity of life and the judgment of the world's rulers, the inner peace found in faith in God, the distinction between masters and servants, and the physical signs of aging. The text mentions figures such as Phaeton, Philemon, and the King of Babylon, and references mythological locations like Olympus, Phlegethon, and the Styx.

This collection of lyric poems includes several numbered sections (IX-XV) featuring moral and allegorical themes. Specific figures mentioned include Cleobule, Melisse, Xenophon, and Corinnae, while the texts address themes of justice, the vanity of wealth, the dangers of lust, and the duty to the poor. The poems utilize classical imagery, referencing locations like Olympus and the Styx, and contrast virtuous living with the follies of the crowd.

This collection of lyric poems includes a series of moralizing and allegorical verses. Key sections include a meditation on the vanity of hoarding wealth (the 'empty brain' and 'gold of the Orient'), a didactic poem on self-knowledge (Nosce Te Ipsum), a narrative regarding a marriage to a barren woman (Leander), and a concluding prayer for divine protection against poverty and fear.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a series of numbered sections (XXII-XXVI) featuring various allegorical and historical scenes. Notable elements include a description of the conquest of Germany (Germania) involving the Rhenus and Ister rivers, a critique of the rewards for poets and artists, and a series of moralizing verses regarding the fleeting nature of fame and the pursuit of true joy.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a series of numbered sections (XXVII-XXXIII) featuring various themes. Notable content includes a description of a battle involving figures like Fidus, Sternus, and Paene; a warning against pride and the pursuit of vain glory; a satirical piece regarding a man named Cymbalion visiting a temple; and a concluding poem on the spiritual peace found in poverty and trust in God.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a series of numbered sections (III-VIII) exploring themes of physical beauty, the vanity of clothing, and the dangers of impulsive judgment. The text features several mythological and historical references, including Phaethon, the city of Babylon, the Ganges river, and the figure of Metellus. The poems contrast physical allure with moral virtue and the fleeting nature of time and youth.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a critique of a 'shameless' preacher (Ecclesiastes Improbus) who favors rhetoric over action, a narrative of a virgin's longing and a clandestine marriage involving Demophon and the Clytian, and a meditation on the enduring value of antiquity. The final sections include a lament on the 'plagues' of Venus and the physical decay of old age, featuring references to figures such as Cupid, Cypris, and various mythological or allegorical entities.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a spiritual quest for the divine through geographical landmarks like the Syrtes, Caucasus, and Thule, followed by a series of moral and allegorical meditations. The text features several numbered sections (XVI-XXI) addressing themes of asceticism, the vanity of wealth, the proximity of death, and the internal struggle of the soul. Specific figures and locations mentioned include Philodeme, Alcaeus, the Styx, and various personified entities like Pectus and Atropos.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a series of numbered sections (XXII-XXVII) featuring various themes. Notable subjects include a pastoral scene of the Ister river and spring growth, a lament on the 'Original Sin' of Eve, a critique of 'inept poets' (mentioning Cleophon), and a concluding fragment regarding a noble banquet.

This collection of lyric poems includes a series of moral and didactic verses. Notable sections include a warning to a youth named Vellet about the dangers of greed and lust, a meditation on the brevity of life and the inevitability of death (addressed to Delium), and a series of poems regarding the duties of a prince, the dangers of hatred, and the consequences of excessive clemency.

This collection of lyrical poems addresses themes of mortality, the vanity of earthly pursuits, and the necessity of divine submission. The text includes specific references to the figures of Mars, Pallas, and Xerxes, as well as a passage regarding the life of a king of the Hebrews. It contrasts the fleeting pleasures of the senses and the accumulation of wealth with the spiritual rewards of piety and the acceptance of divine providence.

This collection of lyric poems includes a meditation on nature and the divine judgment of the wicked, a description of the morning and the celestial order, and a reflection on the virtue of modesty. It also contains a hagiographic account of the conversion of Saint Paul the Apostle and a concluding exhortation regarding the choice of companions.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a warning against the madness of the Maenads and the rituals of Cybele, a meditation on the fleeting beauty of youth and the physical decay of the body, and a critique of the vanity of worldly fame and the dangers of the 'theatre' of life. The final sections contrast the fleeting pleasures of the world with the enduring virtues of theology, specifically charity, faith, and hope. Named figures and locations include Mopsus, Cybele, Venus (Cypris), Vestal Virgins, Rome, Theseus, Pirithous, and various allegorical or local figures such as Menalca, Choerilus, and Servetus.

This collection of lyric poems includes a critique of the arts and the vanity of worldly pursuits, a meditation on the rarity of peace and the dangers of war, and a series of moralizing verses on humility and the virtues of the poor. The text features references to historical and mythological figures such as Maron, Augustus, Maecenas, and the Pierides, as well as a concluding passage describing the celestial kingdom of the Virgin and the Martyrs.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a description of a celestial or sacred city with gates of gems and walls of metal, followed by a series of numbered poems. The texts address themes of spiritual fortitude, the dangers of sloth (Craton), the role of Saint Peter as a rock of the church, the vices of the human soul, and the brevity of life. Specific figures mentioned include Peter, Nicodemus, and the biblical figures Abel and Adam.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a lament for a fallen figure (possibly a ruler) and a series of mythological and allegorical verses. It features specific references to figures such as Ibycus, Cleander, and St. Joseph, as well as mythological entities like Clotho, Nereus, and the Muses. The poems explore themes of fate, the fickleness of Fortune, and the contrast between life and death.

This collection of poems includes a meditation on the vanity of human life and the equality of all in death, a defense of the native tongue against foreign languages (Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, etc.), and a critique of the misuse of public office. The final sections include a poem on comets and a metaphorical 'shipwreck' of celestial love involving celestial imagery and mythological references.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a maritime allegory of a voyage, a lament for a lost wife (Uxor) and the dangers of lust, and a critique of female inconstancy. It features several numbered sections including a description of a Thracian seer (Thracius) in a Stygian cavern, a pastoral scene of a landowner (Meliboeus) seeking wealth, and a meditation on human fragility and the death of a figure named Tyrius.

This collection of lyrical poems includes a series of numbered sections (XVIII through XXIII) featuring themes of divine judgment, the transience of beauty, and the dangers of worldly desire. The text references mythological figures such as Sisyphus, Tantalus, and Tityus, and includes specific names like Telesilla, Tyndaris, and various Latinate names like Cosmotime and Semita. The poems alternate between moralizing on the vanity of earthly pleasures and praising the enduring nature of spiritual friendship.

This collection of lyric poems includes a pastoral scene of nature and the Graces, a moralizing poem on the dangers of lust and the bondage of desire, a warning against the perils of hunting and the fleeting nature of pleasure, and a meditation on old age and the passage of time. The texts feature various mythological and allegorical figures, including Philomela, the Graces, Cerberus, and the Megaera, while addressing themes of virtue, mortality, and the contrast between youth and age.

This section contains a series of lyrical poems and odes. One poem addresses the plight of the oppressed and the pursuit of spiritual peace, while another, titled 'Animus Salutis Cupidus,' reflects on the contrast between physical bondage and spiritual longing. A subsequent section, 'Animus Vigilans Corpore Dormiente,' describes a soul's nocturnal journey toward the divine, followed by a panegyric for Count Rutgerus Ernestus of Starmberg, which celebrates military victories over the Turks and the defense of Vienna.

The text contains two distinct lyrical poems. The first section is a martial and religious ode celebrating a military victory over the Turks (Turcicas) and the 'barbarians,' featuring references to the Danube (Danubius/Padus), the Rhine (Rhenus), and the Thracian frontier. The second section is a panegyric for Maximilian Emanuel, Elector of Bavaria, utilizing classical allusions to Greek mythology and the Iliad to praise his leadership and the defense of the German lands.

Annales Hibernie is a medieval Latin chronicle documenting the history of Ireland, England, and Scotland from 1162 to 1370. The work is organized into seventeen chronological sections covering ecclesiastical successions, military conflicts, and political shifts. It records the activities of the Archbishops of Dublin, the Order of Templars, and prominent lords such as Richard de Clare, Hugo de Lacy, and the Earls of Ulster. Key geographical locations include Dublin, Drogheda, Kilkenny, Ulster, and the port of Dondalk. The text details specific events such as the sieges of Dublin and Acre, the siege of Damietta, and the 1348 pestilence. Additionally, it records legal proceedings regarding heresy and land seizures, as well as the movements of Robert the Bruce and Edward Bruce.

This section of the annals records a chronological history of Ireland and related events from 1162 to 1187. It documents the successions of the Archbishops of Dublin and Canterbury, the deaths and military actions of figures such as Richard de Clare (Comes Ricardus), and the founding of various abbeys including those at Rossglas and Waterford. Notable entries include the death of Hugo de Lacy, the capture of Jerusalem, and the arrival of papal legates.

This section records a series of historical events in Ireland and England between 1189 and 1204, including the deaths of King Henry and King Richard, the founding of several abbeys (Cnokmoy, Tyntern, Dowisky), and the translation of the relics of Saint Malachy. It details the capture of Richard by the Duke of Austria, the imprisonment of King John, and a specific military conflict between John Courcy and Hugo de Lacy over the lordship of Ulster.

The text describes a vision or dialogue involving John Courcy, who is depicted as a warrior and defender of the realm who participated in a duel against a French champion to secure a victory for the King of England. It details his subsequent rewards, including the granting of lands in Ireland (Ultonia) and the establishment of a cell for monks. The chronicle then lists several historical events between 1205 and 1212, including the founding of the Abbey of Wetheneia, the rise of the Franciscan Order, the banishment of William de Brewes, and the capture of the sons of Hugh Lacy by King John.

This section records the deaths and successions of high-ranking clergy and nobility in Ireland and England, including the Archbishops of Dublin, John Comyn and Henry 'Scorchevilleyn'. It details the lineage and inheritance of the Mareschall family (Marquesses of Marls and Pembroke) and the deaths of several knights and lords, including Walter de Lacy. The text also notes the siege of the castle of Trim and the capture of Damietta.

This section of the annals records a series of deaths, appointments of the Justiciar of Ireland (Justiciarius Hibernie), and military actions between 1162 and 1182. Notable figures include Hugo de Lacy, Walter de Burgo, and various Justiciaries such as Robert Dufford and Stephen of Fulborne. The text also records the coronation of King Edward in 1177, including his oath, and mentions specific locations like Tothomonia, Dessemonia, and the castle of Roscoman.

This section records a series of deaths, military actions, and ecclesiastical appointments in Ireland and England between 1273 and 1292. It details the deaths of Moritagh and Art Macmurgh, the death of King Edward's son Alfonsius, and the death of Queen Eleanor of England. The text also describes the siege of Acre by the Saracens, the marriage of Gilbert of Clare to Joan of Acon, and the submission of Scottish lords to King Edward.

This section records a series of events in Ireland and England between 1194 and 1195, including the death of Peter of Geneville, the capture of Richard, Earl of Ulster, and the appointment of William Doddingzele as Justice of Ireland. It details the military actions of the Normans, the capture of Madocus by John de Haverynges, and the execution of Thomas de Torbevile for treason. Specific locations mentioned include Dublin, Kildare, and the construction of a castle at Beaumaris.

The text records military and political events in Scotland and Ireland between 1196 and 1200. It details the capture of Berwick, the surrender of John Balliol to the King of England, and the death of Edmund of England in Vasconia. In Ireland, it notes the appointment of John Wogan as Justiciar and the burning of villages by the Hibernians.

This section records a series of historical events between 1162 and 1370, including a peace treaty between the Kings of England and France mediated by Pope Boniface VIII, and military campaigns in Scotland involving King Edward. It details specific casualties at Fowkirk, a siege in Flanders at Courtrai involving several counts and nobles, and various local Irish events such as the burning of Dublin and marriages between lords like John of Montfort and the lords of Geneville.

This section of the annals records military actions and deaths in Ireland and Scotland, including the defeat of Jacobus de Sancto Paulo, the death of several lords (Walranus de Wellesley, Robertus de Percivall), and the execution of Moritagh O'Conghir. It details ecclesiastical appointments and deaths in Dublin, such as the consecration of Thomas Cantok and the succession of archbishops. Notable figures mentioned include Robertus de Brus (Robert the Bruce), who is recorded as being crowned King of Scotland at Scone.

This section records a series of military and political events in England and Ireland between 1162 and 1370, including the resignation of an Archbishop of Dublin, the military actions of King Edward I against the Scots, and the capture of several Scottish rebels. It details the execution of Robert the Bruce's associates, the arrest of the Templars, and the downfall of Peter of Gaveston. The text also documents local skirmishes in Ireland involving figures such as Macnochi, Thomas of Sueterby, and the outlaw Willelmus Macbaltor.

This section records various events in Dublin and Ireland between 1162 and 1370, including the construction of a marble cistern and a bridge by John le Decer, and the military activities of Richard de Clare and Peter de Gaveston. It details the movements of figures such as Roger de Mortuomari, the death of Dermot Odymcy, and the appointment of Alexander de Bigenore as Archbishop of Dublin. The text also notes several military engagements at places like Thomond, Tassagard, and Rathcoule, and mentions a Parliament held in London.

This section records the political turmoil surrounding the banishment and execution of Peter of Gaveston in England, followed by a series of Irish events including the deaths of local lords and the appointment of Edmund Le Botiller as Justiciar. It details the siege of the Order of Templars, the construction of a bridge at Clontarf, and the death and succession of the Archbishop of Dublin. Specific figures mentioned include Robert of Verdon, John Wogan, and various local lords in the regions of Ulster and Dublin.

The text records military actions and deaths in Ireland and Scotland between 1162 and 1370, specifically detailing the movements of Robert de Brus (Edward Bruce) and the conflicts between Scots and the English. It names specific figures such as Edmund le Botiller, John of Staunton, and William de Burgo, and details battles at locations including Dublin, Dondalk, and the waters of Banne. The narrative includes the seizure of lands, the burning of castles like Athlon and Randon, and the transport of men to Scotland.

This section records military movements and skirmishes in Ireland involving Edward Bruce, the Scots, and various local lords and clans. It details the destruction of several sites (including the castle of Cragfergus and the village of Kenlis), the death of several figures (including Richard of Lan and Fergus Andressan), and the capture of Northburgh. It also notes a formal oath of loyalty taken by several Irish magnates (such as Richard of Clare and Arnaldus le Pover) to the King of England.

This section records military actions and casualties in Ireland between 1315 and 1316, specifically involving the deaths of the Scots and Hibernians at the hands of lords such as Richard de Bermyngham and William Comyn. It details a specific skirmish at the castle of Cragfergus involving the Bruce, the capture of Scots, and the siege of the monastery of Brught. The text also notes the death of Thomas, son of the Count of Ulster, and the death of John, son of Thomas, near Laraghbryne.

The text records the succession of the Lord of Kyldarie, the capture of the Earl of Ulster (Robert Notyngham) near Dublin, and the subsequent military movements of 'le Brus' (Bruce) and the Earl of Ulster. It details the destruction of Dublin's suburbs and the church of St. John, the seizure of land by the Earl of Kyldarie (Thomas, son of John), and the subsequent famine and pestilence in the region. The narrative concludes with military actions against the Lacy family and the movements of figures such as Edmund le Botiller and Mortimer.

This section records a series of military and legal events in Ireland and England between 1360 and 1370, including the capture of Adomarus of Valencia, the execution of thieves, and the movements of Roger de Mortimer. It details the siege of Drogheda, the appointment of Alexander of Bigenore as Archbishop of Dublin, and a report of a famine-induced massacre of Ultonians. The text concludes with the appointment of William of Causellens as Chancellor and Archbishop of Dublin.

This section records the death of Richard de Clare and the subsequent burial of his remains in Limerick, followed by the legal proceedings of John Lacy de Castro. It details a military engagement near Dundalk between the Scots, led by Edward de Brus, and the English forces under John de Bermyngham, resulting in the death of Edward de Brus. The text concludes with the founding of the University of Dublin under Archbishop Alexander de Bykenore and the listing of its first masters and officials.

This section of the annals records events in Ireland between 1311 and 1326, including the construction of the town of Leghelyn by Maurice Jak and the death of Edmund Botiller. It details a heresy and sorcery trial involving Alicia Ketyll, who was accused of consorting with a demon and performing rituals at a stone bridge near Kilkenny. The text also records the death of Richard de Burgo, Earl of Ulster, who died at Athisell and was buried near the feast of St. John the Baptist.

The text records a series of military conflicts and legal proceedings in Ireland between 1327 and 1328 involving Dominus Mauricius (son of Thomas), Dominus Arnaldus (le Pover), and their respective allies, including the Bourkeyns. It details the burning of lands in Ofath, Momonia, and Kenlys, the capture and imprisonment of the rebel leader David Otothil, and the execution of the heretic Adam Duff. The passage concludes with the appointment of William de Burgo as Earl of Ulster and the convening of a Parliament at Northampton to arrange a peace treaty involving the marriage of the Earl of Ulster.

The text records diplomatic negotiations between Robert the Bruce, William de Burgh (Earl of Ulster), and Scottish magnates regarding peace between Scotland and Ireland. It details the heresy trial and imprisonment of Arnaldus le Pover, the accusation and subsequent clearance of Brother Roger Utlawe (Justiciar of Ireland), and a series of banquets and legal proceedings in Dublin. The passage concludes with a list of casualties in a skirmish in Ulster and a legal petition by the Gernon brothers.

The text records military movements and casualties in Ireland, including the death of Thomas le Botiller and his subsequent burial with the Preachers. It details the activities of Justiciar John Darcy, the siege of various locations by Maurice, son of Thomas of Desmond, and the capture of Donaldus Arte Macmurgh. The passage also records natural disasters, including a severe flood of the Boyne and a significant famine, alongside local skirmishes and the birth of a son to the Countess of Kildare.

summary: This section records a series of military actions and legal proceedings in Ireland between 1310 and 1311. It details the capture of several figures, including Maurice, son of Thomas (Count of Desmonie), and William Bermyngham, as well as the capture of Henry Maundeville. The text also describes the seizure of livestock, the burning of churches at Ffreynestoun, and a specific incident involving the capture of fish in Dublin harbor during a famine.

The text records a series of military and civil events in Ireland between 1332 and 1333, including the execution of the Hibernians at the river Slane and the death of Lord William (Willelmus) of Bermyngham. It details the movements of Justiciaries such as Anthony of Lucy and John Darcy, the siege of Limerick and Nenagh, and the death of William of Burgh, Earl of Ulster. The passage concludes with the gathering of nobles and the Count of Ormonie at the Carmelite house in Dublin.

This section of the annals records a series of events in Ireland between 1337 and 1340, including the death of Maurice, son of Thomas, Count of Dessemonie, and a miraculous occurrence involving seven birds flying over Dublin. It details the movements of high-ranking officials such as John Charleton, Thomas, Bishop of Hereford, and David O'Reilly, as well as a severe winter of 1338 where the River Liffey froze. The text also describes military actions, the capture of Maurice, son of Nicholas, and a large livestock raid in the region of Odrone.

The text records the deaths and appointments of officials in Ireland, including Rogerus Outlawe and John Darcy, and notes a miraculous occurrence in Leicestershire involving a man and a 'prodigium' of a plague. It describes a political and legal conflict between the English administration and local interests, specifically regarding a 1341 Parliament in Kilkenny. The final section contains a condemnation of Radulphus Ufford, the Justiciarius of Ireland, for his predatory and unjust rule.

The text records the military and legal actions of Radulphus de Ufford, Justiciarius Hibernie, against the lands of the Comitatus Dessemonie. It details the seizure of lands in Momonia, the arrest of the Count of Dessemonie, and the subsequent forfeiture of lands and legal rights from twenty-six specific men, including several named knights and the Count of Ultonia. The passage concludes with a note on the death of Radulphus de Ufford on the feast of the Rams (April 9th).

This section records the death of a Justice of Hibernia and the subsequent movements of his remains and the royal treasury. It details the military actions of Maurice, son of Thomas (Comes Kildarie), and Walter of Bermyngham against the forces of Omorda, the burning of the settlements of Ley and Kylmehede, and the massacre of 300 Englishmen by the Ultonians. The text also notes the death of Lady Johanna FitzLeones, the siege of Calais, and the arrival of a major pestilence in Ireland in 1348.

This section of the annals records the successions of the Justiciaries of Ireland (Justiciarius Hibernie) between 1349 and 1369, specifically naming Walter of Bermyngham, Thomas Rokysby, Maurice FitzThomas, and Almaricus de Sancto Amando. It details the death and burial of Kenwricus Sherman in Dublin, the construction of fortifications by Robertus Savage, and a legal dispute between Archbishop Richard FitzRow and the Mendicant orders. The text also notes the death of Countess Johanna de Burgo and the translation of the bones of Archbishop Richard FitzRow to Dondalk.

This section records the deaths and military actions of several figures in Ireland, including Robertus Savage, who is noted for a victory near Antrum, and the movements of Leonellus, Earl of Ulster. It details administrative appointments for the office of Justice of Ireland, specifically involving Maurice, son of Thomas, and Jacobus le Botiller. The text also records local events such as a storm in Dublin, the burning of St. Patrick's Church, and a conflict between the Berminghames of Carbry and the men of Midia.

The text records the appointment of Geraldus Fitz Morice as Justice of Ireland in 1268 and the subsequent capture of several high-ranking officials, including Thomas Burley and Robert Terell, in Carbry. It notes the burning of the church of St. Mary of Trim, the death of Duke Leonard of Clarence, and the outbreak of a major plague in 1270. The passage concludes with a list of deaths among the nobility, including Simon Flemyng and John Taylor, and mentions the ownership of the manuscript by William Preston.

Annales de Monte Fernandi is a medieval Latin chronicle organized into seven parts, documenting a chronological progression of ecclesiastical and secular history. The first section focuses on early Christian history, hagiography, and the conversion of the Franks and Britons. Subsequent sections track the reigns of figures such as Charlemagne, William the Conqueror, and the English kings Henry, Richard, and John. The text provides detailed records of the successions of popes and archbishops in centers such as Canterbury, Dublin, and York. Later sections focus heavily on Irish geography and politics, mentioning the de Burgo and Geraldine families, the siege of Bedford, and the conquest of Wales. The work concludes with specific regional records concerning Hibernia, including the actions of Eustachius de Prendergast and the siege of castles like Roscoman.

This text is a chronological list of historical and ecclesiastical events, primarily focusing on the lives of saints, popes, and early Christian figures. It records specific dates (often in the years since the Incarnation) associated with the actions of figures such as Peter, Paul, Augustine, and Jerome, as well as the conversion of kings like Clodoveus and the expansion of Christianity in Britain and France.

This section of the annals records a chronological list of historical events and figures from the 8th through the 11th centuries. It documents the reigns and actions of figures such as Charlemagne (Karolus), William the Conqueror (Willelmus Bastard), and various English kings, alongside the founding of abbeys and the movements of the Normans. Specific events include the conversion of the Saxons, the siege of Antioch, and the translation of Saint Nicholas.

This section of the chronicle records a series of historical events, ecclesiastical successions, and natural phenomena. It documents the reigns and successions of kings in France, England, and Scotland, the appointments of various bishops and archbishops in centers such as Canterbury, Dublin, and Lincoln, and mentions specific events like the burning of churches, comets, and eclipses.

This section of the annals records a chronological sequence of ecclesiastical and political events in England, France, and Ireland between the 12th and 13th centuries. It documents the successions of popes and archbishops (including those of Canterbury, York, and Dublin), royal movements of Kings Henry, Richard, and John, and the confirmation of religious orders like the Templars and the Minors. Notable events include the coronation of Philip of France, the siege of Jerusalem, and the conflict between King John and his barons.

This section of the chronicle records a series of annual entries from 1120 to 1170, documenting ecclesiastical appointments in Ireland and England, royal movements, and military actions. Notable figures include Henry III, Pope Innocent IV, and various archbishops of Dublin and Armagh, alongside events such as the siege of Bedford and the conquest of Wales.

This section of the chronicle records a series of military actions, deaths, and ecclesiastical appointments in Ireland and England between 1252 and 1272. It details the movements of figures such as Richard of Exonia, the conflict between the de Burgo and Geraldines, and the deaths of several high-ranking officials, including the Justiciar of Ireland, James de Audele. Notable events include the siege of castles like Roscoman and Sligaht, a famine in Ireland, and the transition of various church offices.

This section records a series of events and appointments in Ireland (Hibernia) and surrounding regions. It mentions individuals such as Brother Eustachius of Prendergast, Brother Thomas of Suynisfeld (appointed justice of Hibernia), and Lord Galfridus of Genevile. The text records deaths, a drowning of brothers Simon and Magus near Saint David, and the succession of bishops in Limerick and Clonens. It also notes the capture of Totomomam by Mauricius and Teobaldus, and the imprisonment of nobles at Glendelore.

Annales Breves Hiberniae is a Latin pseudo-historical chronicle of Ireland and its surrounding regions. The work is organized chronologically, beginning with a scriptural genealogy featuring Bartholenus and the giant Ruanus, followed by accounts of Norse and Saxon conquests. The narrative transitions into a medieval and early modern record of military conflicts, ecclesiastical appointments, and land disputes involving the Butler and Geraldine families. Specific locations mentioned include Dublin, Waterford, Kilkenny, Sligo, and the Isle of Orkney. The text records the actions of figures such as Saint Patrick, Henry II, Edward III, Henry VIII, Elizabeth I, and Philip of Spain. Later sections document the suppression of rebellions by O'Neill and O'Brien, the plague in Dublin, and the confiscation of monastic lands.

This text provides a pseudo-historical chronicle of Hibernia (Ireland) featuring a lineage of figures including Bartholenus, Bergon, and the giant Ruanus, who is said to have lived for 2,400 years until the arrival of Saint Patrick. It details a series of conquests and settlements involving figures like the sons of Dale, the Scythians, and the king Gurguntius, while recording specific dates and locations such as the island of Orkney and the site of Carrekfergus. The narrative concludes with the missionary activities of Pope Celestine and the mention of figures such as Brigida and Saint Columba.

The text chronicles the Norse conquest of Hibernia (Ireland) starting from the era of Laigerius and St. Patrick, specifically detailing the actions of Gurmundus (also called Caradocus) and his successor Burchardus. It describes the founding of the priory of Leighlen, the siege of the King of the Medes by Turgesius, and various military conflicts involving the Danes, the Saxons, and the kings of Hibernia and Lagenia.

This section records a series of military conflicts and political transitions in Ireland (Hibernia), Wales (Wallia), and England involving figures such as Brian Bowrow, Murchardus, and various leaders of the 'Ostomanni' (Danes, Normans, and Suevians). It details the deaths of several monarchs, the movement of captives between Hibernia and Northwallia, and the ecclesiastical appointments of Patricius in Dublin. The text also notes the construction of the abbey of Tyntern and the specific circumstances of the execution and burial of Murchardus.

This section of the annals records a series of conflicts and diplomatic negotiations in Ireland (Hibernia) and Wales (Wallia) involving figures such as Richardus Marshall, Llewelyn, and the kings of Conatie. It details the military movements of Richardus Strangbo near Waterford, the siege of the city, and the subsequent marriage of Dermot Laginensis to Eve. The text also notes the founding of the abbey of Mellefont and the various titles and lineages of local lords like Roderik Conchurk and Robertus fitz Stephans.

The text records a series of legal and military disputes regarding the conquest of Ireland, specifically involving the seizure of Dublin, Waterford, and the actions of figures such as Roderick, Henry II, and various local lords. It details the capture of Dublin by Hastulph and the subsequent execution of Heywood, followed by a list of eight ecclesiastical decrees issued by the clergy at Cashell under the authority of Popes Adrian and Alexander to reform the Irish church.

This section records a series of ecclesiastical and military events in Ireland, including the appointment of Gelasius as bishop of Dublin, the capture of Maelgunus, and the death of Richardus Strangbo. It details the construction of various fortifications (Fernes, Sliggagh), the founding of the Cathedral of St. Patrick in Dublin and the Abbey of Jeripont, and the deaths of several lords including Hugo Lacy and Walterus Mariscallus. The text also notes land grants and legal disputes regarding inheritance and titles in regions such as Ulster, Kildare, and Penbrochium.

This section records a series of military actions, deaths, and appointments in Ireland (Hibernia) and surrounding regions. It names figures such as Mauritius fitz Gerald, Theobald Butler, and various bishops of Ossoria and Leighlen, while detailing conflicts involving the Geraldines and Burkes. The text also notes the construction of castles at Sligo and Roscoman, a period of famine and pestilence, and the movements of figures like Edward Baliol and William Veschi.

This section records military actions, rebellions, and judicial proceedings in Ireland (Hibernia) during the late 13th and early 14th centuries. It details the movements of figures such as John Wogan, Richard of Burgo, and Peter of Gaveston, while documenting the deaths of local lords like Mortaghus O Conchur and the suppression of the Branenses. The text also notes the seizure of Templar lands, the establishment of Hospitaller sites, and legal disputes in the parliaments of Kildare and Kilkenny.

The text chronicles the military campaigns of Edward of the Bruce in Ireland, detailing his conquest of areas such as Dundalk and his proclamation as monarch of Hibernia. It records the subsequent administrative appointments of figures like Edmundus Butler and Johannes Bremyngham, the establishment of the University of Dublin by Alexander Bignor, and the construction of bridges at Kilcullen and Leighlen. The final section describes a local account of a noblewoman, Alicia Kettell, and her alleged occult practices in Kilkenny.

This section of the annals records a series of historical events, executions, and ecclesiastical appointments in Ireland and England. It details the execution of Adam Niger for heresy, the military actions of Edward III in Scotland and France, and various appointments of Irish justices such as Maurice Fitzgerald and Thomas Rocksey. The text also notes the translation of Saint Fyntani and the bequest of Kymbrichus Sherman.

This section records a series of administrative acts, military engagements, and legal proceedings in Ireland (Hibernia) involving figures such as the Duke of Clarence, Rogerus Mortimer, and various justices. It details the fortification of Catherlough, the execution of Donatum Mc Murchard, the confirmation of the Charter of the Liberties of Hibernia and the Statutes of Kilkenny, and several instances of pestilence and military conflict in regions including Kilkenny, Wexford, and Kildare.

summary: This section records the deaths and military actions of various figures in Ireland, including Jacobus Buteler, Hugo Mc Adam Mc Gillamor, and Stephanus Scrope. It details military engagements involving the Comes Ormonie and the Prior of Kilmaynam, the capture of Donatus More Cavenagh Mc Murchardus, and the movements of Thomas le Butler in France. The text also notes administrative changes in Dublin and the tenure of various bishops and archbishops.

This section of the annals records a series of military conflicts and political transitions in Ireland and England during the 15th century. It details the actions of figures such as Jacobus le Butler, the Duke of York (Dux Eboracensis), and various Irish lords like Mac Geoghagan and the McMahons. The text also chronicles the reigns of Henry VI and Edward IV, the siege of Roone, and the ecclesiastical disputes involving Richard O. Hiden and Thomas Crawley.

This section records a series of historical and ecclesiastical events in Ireland and England, including the reigns of Henry VI, Edward IV, and Henry VII, and the marriage of Mary to the Archduke of Austria. It details specific local disputes involving the Bishop of Leighlen, the Duke of Kildare (Gerald), and the actions of Edward Poynyngis in Hibernia. The text also notes the death of several figures, including the bard Milo Roch and the knight Gerald of Kildare, and mentions the Battle of Knocktoa.

This section records a series of historical and ecclesiastical events in Ireland (Hibernia) and England, including the deaths of Walter (archbishop), Maurus Nemorosus, and Geraldus Kevanagh. It details legal and military conflicts involving the Butlers of Ossorie and the Earl of Kildare, specific local incidents such as the 1525 execution of a man named Maurus, and the movements of Thomas Howard (Duke of Norfolk). The text also notes local occurrences like a severe flood of the Thames and the 1532 insurrection of the Ultonians.

This section records a series of military conflicts and administrative changes in Ireland (Hibernia) during the 16th century, specifically involving the actions of Thomas fitz Gerald, Leonardus Gray, and the suppression of rebellions by figures such as O'Neill and O'Brien. It details the seizure of monastic lands, the execution of Leonardus Gray for his ties to rebels, and the subsequent appointment of officials like William Brereton and Anthony Saintleger. The text also lists specific casualties, the confiscation of lands from absent lords, and the creation of titles for Donatus O'Brien and others.

This section records military engagements and casualties involving figures such as Cahir Cavenagh Mc Art, Gerald Mc Cahir, and Edwardus Randolf in regions including Tipperary, Knockfergus, and Dyrrhy. It details ecclesiastical appointments and disputes in Ireland (Leighlen, Ossorie, Dublin) involving bishops like Robertus Travers and Johannes Bale, and notes the deaths or actions of royal figures including Henry VIII, Elizabeth, and Philip of Spain.

This section records military conflicts and local governance in Ireland, specifically involving figures like Henry Sidney, Peter Carew, and Rory O'Moore. It details the deaths of several figures, including Shane O'Neill and Lysac O'Moore, and describes a significant plague in Dublin and surrounding areas. The text also notes the introduction of printing in Dublin and the legal status of various lands and clergy.

This section records military and administrative movements in Ireland, including the deaths and appointments of figures like Willelmus Gerard, Willelmus Drury, and Arthurus Gray. It details specific military engagements at Down Moyr and near Leighlen, the capture and execution of rebels such as Geraldus fitz James and Orwairk, and a detailed inventory of ships and men in various coastal locations like Sligo and Tyreconill.

Annales Dominicani de Roscoman is a medieval Latin chronicle documenting historical events in Ireland (Hibernia) and neighboring regions from the 12th through the 14th centuries. The text is organized into sequential sections recording deaths, successions, military conflicts, and ecclesiastical appointments. It details the activities of the Dominican Order and the movements of figures such as William de Burgo, the de Lacy family, and various Irish lords including the O'Donnells and O'Connors. Notable geographical locations include the cities of Tuam, Athlone, and Roscommon, specifically regarding the construction of fortifications and castles. The chronicle records the tenure of the Archbishops of Armarchanus and Dublin, as well as various bishops of Elphin. Environmental and social hardships, such as severe frost, famine, and plague in Meath, are also noted.

This section records a series of historical events in Ireland (Hibernia) and the surrounding regions, including the deaths and successions of local rulers like Toirdelach, Roddericus, and Cahell Crobderg. It details the activities of ecclesiastical figures such as the Archbishops of Armarchanus and Dublin, the construction of fortifications at Tuam and Athlone, and the movements of military figures like William de Burgo and the de Lacy family. The text also notes climatic events, such as severe frost and snow, and the arrival of religious orders and envoys.

This section of the annals records a series of deaths, military conflicts, and ecclesiastical appointments in Ireland and England between the 12th and 14th centuries. It names specific figures such as Geraldus filius Mauritii, various bishops of Elphin, Tuam, and Dublin, and several Irish lords like O'Donnell and O'Connor. The text also notes the construction of castles at Roscommon and Tuam, the arrival of the English under Henry fitz Empress, and the appointment of various preachers and prelates.

This section of the chronicle records a series of deaths, battles, and appointments of Irish clergy and nobility between the late 12th and early 13th centuries. It documents specific figures such as the O'Brien and O'Connor kings, various bishops of Elphin and Tuam, and the activities of the Dominican friars. Notable events include the construction of Roscommon Castle, the siege of Athlone, and a period of famine and plague in Meath.

A 12th-century Latin hagiography detailing the life, miracles, and mystical experiences of the virgin Yta. The narrative follows Yta from her noble Irish (Hyberni) lineage and her initial consecration to her role as a spiritual mother in the region of Hua Conayll. The text is structured as a series of miraculous interventions, including resurrections, healings, and the identification of sins. Notable figures include the artisan Beoanus, the man Comhganus, and the abbots Luchtichernus and Lasreanus. Geographical locations mentioned include the hills of Luachra and the province of Connacht. The work concludes with Yta's death and her identification as the 'second Brigid.'

The text recounts the life and miracles of the virgin Yta, a noblewoman of the Irish (Hyberni) lineage descended from Feidhlimidh Reachtmair and the kingdom of Temoria. It details her childhood, a vision of an angel giving her three stones representing the Trinity, and her struggle to obtain her father's permission to consecrate herself to Christ. The narrative concludes with an angel appearing to her father to command him to allow her to take the veil.

The text recounts the spiritual life and miracles of the blessed virgin Yta, including her protection by angels against demons and her reception of a 'veil of virginity' in a church. Following an angelic vision, she is instructed to move to the region of Hy Conayll near the hills of Luachra, where she becomes a spiritual mother to the people of Hua Conayll. The narrative concludes with her receiving celestial food from an angel and a dialogue with a visiting religious woman regarding her mystical experiences and prophetic graces.

The text recounts a dialogue between the holy virgin Yta and a man named Comhganus, followed by Yta's miraculous actions: raising three dead nobles, healing a paralytic man, and identifying a fornicating nun. It further describes Yta's intervention in the life of a woman from the province of Connacht and the miraculous restoration of the severed head of a craftsman named Beoanus.

The text recounts a series of miraculous events involving the holy figures Yta (or Yta/Jethus) and the virgin Chinreche. It describes the resurrection of a man, the birth of a son named Mochoemhog to the artisan Beoanus, and the restoration of a man's speech through the prayers of the 'ancilla Dei'. The narrative concludes with a dialogue between a wealthy man and the virgin regarding the distribution of alms, and a list of three virtues pleasing to God.

The text recounts miracles and interactions involving the holy virgin Yta (or Yta prophetissa). It describes a bishop visiting Yta to seek a blessing for his nurse, Richena, and a man who was miraculously resurrected after being killed in battle. The final section mentions a theft in the cell of Doyre Cusgryd and the involvement of a nun seeking Yta's judgment.

The text recounts several miraculous interventions by the holy virgin Yta (or Jeta). These include the recovery of a stolen veil from a woman in a forest, the healing of a man named Feargus, and the resurrection of a man's son for a period of seven years, seven months, and seven days. It concludes with the arrival of abbots Luchtichernus and Lasreanus at Yta's monastery, where they are met by virgins.

The text recounts miracles and prophecies of the virgin Yta, including the identification of a man named Lasreanus (son of Colman) and the prediction of a fatal conflict between two brothers. It describes a military victory for the people of Hua Conaill through Yta's prayers and the subsequent healing and repentance of a wounded soldier. The final section details Yta's identification of a family member's sin of fornication and her mission to rescue a sister held as a slave by a magician in the land of the Connachtians.

The text concludes the hagiography of the virgin Yta, describing her final days and her prophecy regarding the blessing of water for the ailing Abbot Aengus. It records her death on the 18th of February, her burial in a monastery she consecrated, and her identification as the 'second Brigid.' The narrative concludes with a formal doxology and the closing formula 'Explicit vita sanctissime virginis Yte.'

This 11th-century Latin theological treatise provides a symbolic exegesis of the four Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John). The author employs a series of fourfold allegories to describe the nature of the Word and the characteristics of each Evangelist. The text compares the Gospels to four types of liquids (honey, wine, milk, and oil), four elements (earth, water, air, and fire), and the four seasons of the year. It also incorporates numerical symbolism, specifically the number four and the twelve apostles. The work cites Jerome and references the divinity of Christ and the sacraments.

This Latin medieval dialogue features a tripartite structure exploring the relationship between the body (corpus) and the soul (anima). The first section depicts a dialogue between a spirit and a body in a state of spiritual slumber, where the spirit rebukes the body for its indulgence in wealth and sin. The second section continues the dialogue, focusing on the moral consequences of earthly pleasures and the fate of the damned. The final section provides a descriptive vision of the infernal realm, featuring four monstrous demons with horns, serpent-like nostrils, and lion-like teeth. The text concludes with a soul crying out the name of 'Jesus, son of David' and a narrator's reflection on the vanity of worldly riches. The work utilizes allegory to contrast spiritual devotion with worldly vanity.

A dialogue between a spirit and a body in a state of spiritual slumber. The spirit rebukes the body for its indulgence in worldly pleasures, the accumulation of wealth, and its fall into sin, while the body's response is characterized by groans and a lack of coherent defense.

A dialogue between the Body (corpus) and the Soul (anima) regarding the moral consequences of earthly pleasures and the state of the damned. The Body defends its role and the nature of its failings, while the Soul laments the corruption caused by worldly vanities and the lack of hope for those who sought riches and power over spiritual devotion.

The text describes a vision of the damned and the punishments of the infernal realm. It depicts four demons with monstrous physical features—horns, serpent-like nostrils, and teeth like lions—who torment a soul and cast it into hell.
