It addresses specific petitions from the people regarding three main areas: the rights of women to wear religious veils regardless of age, the legal status and protections of free men held by patrons, and procedures for homicide trials and the verification of charters. The document concludes with a provision regarding the silence of those involved in certain disputes. The text includes a specific reference to the laws of the Lombards and the era of Charlemagne (Karoli).

This 9th-century Latin text, titled 'Capitula Papiae optimatibus ab imperatore pronuntiata', consists of a series of seven chapters (capitula) issued by the Emperor Louis the Great (Hludowicus augustus) in the city of Tycinum (modern-day Thionville). The document functions as a legal and administrative decree concerning the governance of the realm, the protection of the Church, and the maintenance of public order. It addresses specific issues such as the prevention of robbery, the protection of widows and orphans, and the regulation of monastic and clerical life. The text emphasizes the enforcement of peace and the preservation of traditional privileges for religious institutions. It concludes with a warning to officials and subjects regarding the consequences of negligence in upholding these imperial mandates.

A medieval Latin legal and administrative text titled 'Legatio' (Capitulare missorum). The document is structured into five chapters providing instructions for envoys (missi) or officials. It mandates the investigation of ecclesiastical justice, the protection of the property of orphans and widows, and the hearing of public grievances. The text outlines specific administrative duties, including the collection of annual gifts and public tributes, the restoration of bridges and palaces, and the identification of land holdings. It further instructs abbots to oversee monasteries and 'senodochia' (likely ecclesiastical estates or jurisdictions) to ensure they are managed according to established rules. The final section commands the restoration of hospitals for the poor in mountainous regions.

This ninth-century Latin document is a military and logistical decree concerning an expedition from the Po River to the Trebia. The text is organized into two primary sections detailing troop organization and movement. The first section establishes recruitment criteria based on wealth and utility, defines the roles of counts, bishops, and masters, and assigns specific geographic sectors to individuals including Iotselmus, Eriulfus, Erembertus, and Landebertus. It also codifies disciplinary measures for theft, desertion, and adultery. The second section details a specific itinerary through Ravenna, Rome, Capua, and Benevento, including a rendezvous for Tuscans at Luceria before the Kalends of April. The text concludes with legal warnings against homicide and notes on local trade.

This text outlines military and logistical regulations for a campaign from the Po River to the Trebia. It details the selection of soldiers based on their wealth and utility, specifies the roles of various leaders (counts, bishops, and masters) in the field, and assigns specific geographic sectors to named individuals such as Iotselmus, Eriulfus, Erembertus, Landebertus, and others. The document also establishes disciplinary measures for desertion, theft of supplies, and moral offenses like adultery.

The text outlines military logistics and movement orders for an army traveling through Ravenna, Rome, Capua, and Benevento. It specifies a route for the Tuscans and others arriving from 'beyond' to meet at Luceria on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. The passage also contains a legal warning against reckless homicide and a note on local trade between neighbors.

This 9th-century Latin decree, the Karoli II capitulare Papiense, was issued by Charlemagne in February 776 at the palace of Ticino. It was drafted in consultation with Archbishop Anspert of Milan to establish ecclesiastical protections and privileges. The text is organized into two primary sections focusing on church immunity and clerical discipline. It mandates the recognition of the authority of Pope John III and prohibits the seizure of church property or the carrying of weapons by priests. The second section details the management of church assets, the required residency of bishops, and the penalties for illegal seizures. The document concludes with a list of signatories including bishops Ansbertus, Iohannes of Ticinensis, and Adalgaudus of Vercelli, alongside counts Bernardus, Bodradus, and Cunibertus.

This decree by Emperor Charlemagne (Karolus), issued in February 776 in the palace of Ticino with the counsel of Archbishop Anspert of Milan, establishes ecclesiastical protections and privileges. It mandates the respect of the Roman Church and the authority of Pope John III, prohibits the seizure of church property, and regulates the conduct and residency of the clergy. The text specifically forbids priests from hosting women in their homes or carrying weapons, while ensuring that church lands and assets are returned to their proper legal status.

This section of the Karoli II capitulare Papiense establishes regulations for ecclesiastical discipline, the management of church property (erogatoria and eleemosynariae), and the conduct of bishops and counts. It mandates that bishops remain in their own residences to avoid disputes and outlines the penalties for those who seize church assets for personal use. The text concludes with a list of signatures from several bishops (including Ansbertus, Iohannes of Ticinensis, and Adalgaudus of Vercelli) and several counts (including Bernardus, Bodradus, and Cunibertus).

This 9th-century Latin text is a royal charter and decree concerning the election of King Wido. The work is organized into two parts: the first establishes a charter of liberties in the court of Ticence following a period of violence and sacrilege. It details protections for the Roman Church, rights for clergy and laity, and regulations for Palatines and those entering the realm. The second part records a formal decree by a collective body confirming Wido's election as king and senior of the realm. This decree cites his military victories as divine favor and his commitment to ecclesiastical law and the suppression of robbery. The text concludes with a note on the clergy's role during sedition and a formal signature by Wido.

A group of bishops from various parts of the Papacy meet in the court of Ticence with King Wido to establish a charter of liberties following a period of violence and sacrilege. The text outlines protections for the Roman Church, the rights of clergy and laypeople, and the duties of the Palatines and those entering the realm. It concludes with a justification for electing Wido as king and protector following the death of Emperor Charles and a period of instability.

The text records a formal decree by a collective body to elect Widon as king and senior of the realm, citing his victory over enemies as a sign of divine favor. The participants pledge their unanimous consent to his rule based on his professed commitment to the Roman Church, ecclesiastical law, and the eradication of robbery. The final lines contain a brief note regarding the clergy taking up arms during sedition and a signature identifying Wido as king.

This 9th-century medieval Latin text consists of additions to the Capitulare Papiense under the authority of Widonis. The work is organized into two primary sections focusing on local governance and judicial penalties. The first section details the cooperation between bishops and counts in maintaining peace and regulating trade. It establishes specific legal procedures for the notarial authentication of documents and defines property rights, including the usufruct of land by wives and the rights of women to alienate property. The second section prescribes specific fines, including a widrigild for insulting judges and a 1,000-pound gold fine for murder committed during judicial proceedings. The proceeds of the latter fine are divided between the victim's heirs and the royal chamber.

This section of the Capitulare Papiense establishes regulations for local governance, specifically regarding the cooperation of bishops and counts in maintaining peace and managing trade. It details legal penalties for those who refuse to assist neighbors or who engage in illegal seizure of property, and provides specific procedures for the authentication of legal documents (cartae) involving notaries and twelve witnesses. The text also addresses property rights, specifically regarding the usufruct of land by wives and the rights of women to sell or gift property.

This section of the Papian additions to the Capitulary of Widonis establishes penalties for judicial misconduct. It mandates a fine (widrigild) for any individual who insults or dishonors judges during court proceedings, and prescribes a fine of 1,000 pounds of high-quality gold for those who commit murder in the context of a judicial proceeding, with the proceeds divided between the heirs of the victim and the royal chamber.

This 9th-century Latin legal and ecclesiastical text, titled Lamberti capitulare Ravennas, consists of a series of prescriptive clauses (capitula) concerning the regulation of imperial and ecclesiastical administration. The text addresses the rights and obligations of imperial officials, the status of 'arimanni' (likely a specific class of landholders or soldiers), and the management of public and church property. It specifically outlines the separation of ecclesiastical lands from secular jurisdiction and the distribution of tithes. The document also details the hierarchical organization of the clergy, specifically the role of 'archipresbyterum' in overseeing the 'plebes' (the common people). Key themes include the preservation of 'antiquam consumptum' (ancient custom), the regulation of 'placitum' (judicial assemblies), and the definition of jurisdictional boundaries between the state and the church.

This medieval Latin text, dated to the 9th century, consists of a series of legal fragments or 'capitula' derived from Roman law and the Novellae of Justinian. The passage begins by identifying a specific decree issued by Emperors Theodosius and Valentinian to the prefect Albinus. The content focuses on the legal protections and penalties associated with the clergy, specifically bishops, presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and readers. It outlines specific fines in gold (solidi) for those who strike or accuse members of the ecclesiastical hierarchy. The text also addresses the legal status of the 'palatium Christi' and the consequences for those committing acts of sedition or violence against church officials.

This 9th-century Latin manuscript records a formal treaty of peace and mutual defense (sacramentum firmitatis) between the kings Hludowicus, Karolus, and Hlotharius. The text is organized into three parts, beginning with a list of witnesses including bishops Hincmarus and Vulfadus, and lay nobles such as Chuonradus and Adalardus. The first section establishes conditions for brotherly harmony and the consequences for violating the peace. The second section details ecclesiastical procedures for penance, the seizure of property, and a royal decree by Hludowicus at Confluentes. The final section focuses on the legal status of defectors, the protection of the poor, and the prohibition of robbery and abduction. The document concludes with formal exchanges and proclamations delivered in both Latin and the Germanic (Theodisca) language.

The text records a formal agreement of peace and mutual defense (sacramentum firmitatis) between the kings Hludowicus, Karolus, and Hlotharius, witnessed by a list of bishops and lay nobles in the year 860. It includes a list of specific participants, including bishops such as Hincmarus and Vulfadus, and lay figures like Chuonradus and Adalardus. The document outlines conditions for maintaining brotherly harmony, the consequences for those who violate the peace, and the procedures for handling those who commit capital crimes or face excommunication.

This section of the decree outlines legal and ecclesiastical procedures for dealing with sinners, specifically regarding their punishment, potential reconciliation, and the role of bishops in the process. It mandates that those who refuse correction be separated from the church and establishes protocols for the seizure of property and the restoration of public order. The text concludes with a formal oath of adherence by the signatories and a note regarding a proclamation by King Hludowicus at Confluentes in the Germanic language.

This section records a formal agreement between Karolus and Hludowicus (Hlotharius) regarding the status of men who defected to the other's side. The text outlines legal protections for the poor, the prohibition of robbery and the abduction of women, and a specific negotiation regarding the restitution of lands (alodes) and honors. The passage concludes with a formal exchange between the two leaders in both Latin and Germanic (Theodisca) languages to finalize the terms of peace.

This 9th-century medieval Latin text records a series of formal diplomatic and theological correspondences between two rulers, Hludowig and Carol, regarding ecclesiastical law and internal governance. The first sections document a dispute over the marriage of Balduinus to a widow named Judith, focusing on the failure of the grandson Hlotharius to enforce excommunication. The text cites the authority of the Pope, Gregory the Great, and the Apostle John to address issues of scandal and slander. The middle section contains two formal declarations (Adnuntiationes) by Hludowig and Carol regarding a joint agreement at Confluentes and Marsna concerning the reconciliation of a common nephew and the reform of church rights. The final section contains reciprocal declarations by Hlothar and Karolus (Charles) regarding feudal obligations, justice, and the protection of shared interests. Key locations mentioned include Tusiacum, Confluentes, and Marsna.

The text records a formal correspondence between two rulers (likely Carolingian) regarding a breach of a mutual agreement and the actions of their shared grandson, Hlotharius. The authors discuss a specific case of a man named Balduinus who married a woman named Judith, a widow under ecclesiastical protection, and the subsequent failure of Hlotharius to enforce the resulting excommunication. The passage cites papal authority, the writings of Gregory the Great, and scriptural warnings to condemn the violation of sacred canons.

The text is a formal diplomatic and theological correspondence regarding a legal and moral dispute involving a 'nepos' (grandson) and a 'rex' (king). The author argues for the reconciliation of the grandson with the church and the community, citing scriptural and patristic authorities (such as Gregory the Great and the Apostle John) to address issues of 'scandalum' and 'calumnia' regarding the grandson's actions and his wife. The passage concludes with a call for the grandson to act out of fear of God to rectify his public standing and the reputation of the kingdom.

This section contains two formal declarations (Adnuntiationes) by the rulers Hludowig and Carol regarding a joint agreement made at Confluentes. The texts address the reconciliation of a common nephew, the mediation of disputes between the two rulers, and the shared commitment to reforming ecclesiastical and legal matters in their respective kingdoms. They reference specific locations, including Confluentes and Marsna, and emphasize the roles of bishops and the preservation of the rights of the Church.

This section contains the formal declarations (Adnuntiationes) of Hlothar and Charles (Karolus). Hlothar acknowledges the favor shown by his father-in-law Hludowicus and pledges to uphold the laws, justice, and ecclesiastical honors of the realm. Charles responds by affirming his commitment to the mutual protection of their respective parties and the preservation of their shared interests.

This 9th-century Latin text is a formal agreement or pact (pactum) between Hludowici and Karoli. The document begins with a preamble establishing the sincerity of the participants' intentions and their commitment to the common good of the Church and the realm. It contains a formal declaration of mutual support, a commitment to the defense of the kingdom, and a specific agreement regarding the status of wives and children. A significant portion of the text is dedicated to a disciplinary and conciliatory matter concerning a man named Hlotharius, who is accused of violating the laws of marriage. The authors propose sending envoys to him to offer counsel and restoration of his status within the community. The text is structured with a formal opening, a numbered chapter, and a concluding section regarding diplomatic communication.

This 9th-century Latin legal document is a formal treaty or convention (conventio) between the rulers Hludowicus (Louis the German) and Karolus (Charles the Bald). The text outlines the division of the kingdom of Hlotharia and specifically addresses the status of the kingdom of Italy. It is organized into nine chapters covering themes of mutual alliance, the handling of pagan or pseudo-Christian uprisings, inheritance rights for heirs like Hludowicus and Karlomannus, and the management of internal dissent. The document also establishes protocols for ecclesiastical governance, the prosecution of those who disturb the peace, and the adjudication of property disputes. Key figures mentioned include Karolus, Hludowicus, and Karlomannus, with a focus on the preservation of 'amicitia' (friendship) and the unity of the Christian people.

This 9th-century Latin legal text, titled Pactiones Aquenses, records a formal agreement regarding the division of territory between two rulers. The document outlines a mutual pledge of non-aggression and territorial integrity between King Karolus (Charles) and his brother King Hludowicus (Louis). The text is structured as two parallel clauses: the first is a pledge from the side of Karolus to Hludowicus, and the second is a reciprocal pledge from the side of Hludowicus to Karolus. Both clauses specify that neither ruler shall deceive or coerce the other regarding the portion of the kingdom of Hlodhari (Lothair) they have agreed upon. The document concludes with a list of witnesses and participants, including the counts Ingelramnus, Liutfridus, Theodericus, and Radulfus, as well as the high-ranking clergy Leutbertus, Altfridus, and Odo.

This ninth-century Latin text records the territorial division of a kingdom between two rulers, Hludowicus (Lothair) and Karolus (Charles). The document is structured as a formal list of geographical entities, including cities, abbeys, monasteries, and specific villages. It details the holdings of Hludowicus, which include regions such as Treveris, Stratsburch, and various monasteries like Sancti Maximini and Sancti Deodati. The text also specifies additions made for the sake of peace and charity, notably the city of Mettis and the abbey of Sancti Petri. The second section lists the territories received by Karolus, including Lugdunum, Vesontium, and portions of Frisia. The document utilizes precise geographical markers, such as the river Urta and the road to Bedensium, to define boundaries.

This 9th-century Latin document is a formal ecclesiastical and civil agreement (conventus) concerning the governance of the Church and the state. The text is organized into two primary sections. The first part establishes the preservation of religious honors, clerical privileges, and the maintenance of royal authority through the unity of clergy and laity. The second part details the legal obligations of the faithful to uphold the king's honor and the terms of a specific treaty. It mandates judicial integrity by forbidding officials from acting out of greed or personal kinship. The text concludes with a conditional clause regarding the consequences for those who either obey or rebel against royal and pontifical authority.

The text is a formal ecclesiastical and civil agreement regarding the governance of the Church and the state. It addresses the preservation of religious honors, the privileges of the clergy, and the maintenance of royal authority and administrative stability. The document emphasizes unity between the clergy and the laity, calling for a singular voice in matters of common utility and the avoidance of personal discord.

This section of a 9th-century Latin legal or diplomatic agreement (Conventus) outlines the obligations of the faithful to uphold the king's honor, authority, and the terms of the treaty. It mandates that officials must not be influenced by private greed, kinship, or friendship when making judgments, and it establishes a process for correcting those who violate the bond of charity or the peace of the realm. The text concludes with a conditional clause regarding the consequences for those who either obey the decree or persist in rebellion against the royal and pontifical authority.

This 9th-century Latin decree, issued at Tolosa, addresses ecclesiastical governance and the regulation of clerical fees in Septimania. The first section establishes specific limits on the amounts of grain, wine, and currency (denarii and solidi) that bishops may accept from presbyters for dispensations, citing the precedents of Toledo and Barcelona. It further regulates the logistics of pastoral visits, the construction of altars, and prohibits the division of parishes for profit. The second section outlines the canonical procedures for establishing churches and appointing priests, mandating that bishops act for the benefit of the local population. It also addresses the management of tithes, the conduct of synods, and the treatment of presbyters within those synods.

This decree addresses the grievances of presbyters in Septimania regarding the treatment of their ministry and the fees charged by bishops for the reception of dispensations. It establishes specific limits on the amount of grain, wine, and currency (denarii and solidi) that bishops may accept from presbyters, referencing the precedents of Toledo and Barcelona. The text also regulates the logistics of pastoral visits, the establishment of additional altars for the convenience of the faithful, and prohibits the division of parishes for profit.

The text outlines procedures for the establishment of churches and the appointment of priests, emphasizing that bishops must act with canonical counsel and for the benefit of the local population rather than for profit. It mandates that bishops adhere to established canons and royal authority regarding the management of tithes and the conduct of synods. The passage specifically addresses the roles of presbyters in synods, requiring bishops to treat and absolve them based on the truth of their ministry.

This 9th-century Latin text is a collection of canons and regulations concerning the administration of the church, confirmed by King Charles (Karolus). The document is organized into a series of 'commemorations' (commemoratio) that group specific ecclesiastical and legal regulations. The content covers the honor and worship of churches, the status of bishops and servants of God, and the discipline of the clergy, including prohibitions against them bearing arms. It addresses specific issues such as simonical heresy, the conduct of monks at the palace, the handling of tithes by the laity, and the location of burials. The text also references the 'villa Colonia' (Cologne) in relation to the royal and princely confirmations.

This medieval Latin text records the proceedings of a synod held in 853 at the monastery of Saint Medard and Saint Sebastian near Soissons. The document details the attendance of King Charles the Bald and several high-ranking prelates, including Hincmar of Reims, Guenilon of Sens, and Amalric of Tours. The first section addresses specific ecclesiastical disputes involving the illicit re-entry of Bishop Ebon of Évre into office, the health of Bishop Herimann of Nevers, and the candidacy of Burchard for the see of Carnot. It also includes a letter from Bishop Aldric of Sens and a petition from Pippin regarding discipline in Aquitaine. The second section details disciplinary actions against monks and the deacon Ragamfridum of Remens, concluding with the promulgation of new chapters for the kingdom by King Karolus.

The text records the proceedings of a synod held in 853 at the monastery of Saint Medard and Saint Sebastian near Soissons, attended by King Charles the Bald and several bishops including Hincmar of Reims, Guenilon of Sens, and Amalric of Tours. The assembly addresses the illicit re-entry into office by Bishop Ebon of Évre, the disciplinary issues and health of Bishop Herimann of Nevers, and the candidacy of Burchard for the see of Carnot. Additionally, the text mentions a letter from Bishop Aldric of Sens regarding his health and a petition by Pippin for the restoration of ecclesiastical and military discipline in Aquitaine.

The text describes the disciplinary actions taken against two monks who attempted to abduct Pippinus and the subsequent punishment of the deacon Ragamfridum of Remens for compiling false precepts. Following these cases, King Karolus (Charles) proposed and confirmed a series of chapters to be promulgated throughout his kingdom by the bishops. The passage mentions the monastery of Sancti Medardi, the bishop of Suessionum, and the diocese of Remens.

This 9th-century Latin text records the proceedings of a synod held in 853 at the monastery of Saint Medard and Saint Sebastian near Soissons. The first section documents the presence of King Charles the Bald and several bishops, including Hincmar of Reims, Guenilon of Sens, and Amalric of Tours. It addresses specific ecclesiastical disputes involving Bishop Ebbon of Évre, Burchard of Carnot, and Herimannus of Nevers, as well as a request for prayers from Bishop Aldric of Sens. The second section details the capture and imprisonment of Pippinus by two monks at the monastery of Saint Medardus. It records the subsequent investigation by the local monastic community and the Bishop of Suessione, Rothadi. The text concludes with decrees regarding ecclesiastical immunity, the prohibition of public trials in sacred spaces on holy days, and regulations concerning church property and monastic discipline.

The text records the proceedings of a synod held in 853 at the monastery of Saint Medard and Saint Sebastian near Soissons, attended by King Charles the Bald and several bishops including Hincmar of Reims, Guenilon of Sens, and Amalric of Tours. The synod addresses the illicit re-entry into office by Bishop Ebbon of Évre and the status of Burchard of Carnot. It also addresses the conduct of Herimannus of Nevers and a request from Bishop Aldric of Sens for prayers. The final section mentions Pippin and the state of ecclesiastical and military discipline in Aquitaine.

The text recounts the capture and imprisonment of Pippinus at the monastery of Saint Medardus by two monks, followed by the investigation of their actions by the community of monks and the Bishop of Suessione (Rothadi). It details the subsequent sentencing of the conspirators and a series of decrees by a holy synod and a prince regarding ecclesiastical immunity, the prohibition of public trials in sacred places on holy days, and the regulation of church property and discipline.

This 9th-century Latin decree, the Capitulare missorum Suessionense, provides instructions for royal envoys regarding the oversight of ecclesiastical institutions. The text is organized into two primary sections. The first section mandates the audit of monasteries, parishes, and churches, specifically focusing on clergy numbers, tithes, and the maintenance of church property under the authority of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious. It reinforces the immunity of church grounds from secular activities such as markets. The second section addresses the liturgical calendar, prohibiting specific public assemblies and feasts during the period between the fourth fair before the forty days and the eighth day after Easter. It further regulates the use of corporal punishment by bishops, the administration of penance, and the prohibition of unauthorized exchanges of ecclesiastical lands or titles.

This decree instructs royal envoys to inspect monasteries, parishes, and churches to audit their assets, clergy numbers, and maintenance. The envoys are tasked with investigating the status of tithes (the ninth and tenth parts), the condition of church property, and the conduct of prelates. It specifically mentions the authority of the ancestors, Emperor Charles and Emperor Louis (Hludowici), and mandates that church grounds remain exempt from secular activities like markets or public gatherings.

This section of the Capitulare missorum Suessionense contains instructions for envoys regarding the timing of public assemblies and feasts, specifically prohibiting them during the period between the fourth fair before the start of the forty days and the eighth day after Easter. It further mandates that bishops and their ministers must not use excessive corporal punishment (flogging) on colonists without proper cause, and it establishes that royal authority shall be used to compel penance for those the church cannot reach. The text concludes with prohibitions against the unauthorized exchange of ecclesiastical lands or titles, ensuring that church property remains in ecclesiastical servitude while individuals who exchange titles for liberty may do so.

This 9th-century Carolingian capitularie contains royal instructions from Charlemagne to his missi regarding the administration of justice and the enforcement of royal and ecclesiastical law. The first section details procedures for handling the abduction of women and children, the protection of church property and clergy, and the identification and punishment of thieves (latrones). The second section establishes protocols for pursuing fugitives across borders, the role of advocates, and the handling of refugees from Norman and British oppression. It concludes with a list of specific bishops and envoys, including Hincmarus, Ricuinus, and Pardulus, assigned to locations such as Lauduniso and Catalaunio. The final section provides a geographical list of ecclesiastical and secular officials, such as Adalardus, Folcoinus, and Wenilo, assigned to specific counties (comitatus) including Noviomiso, Paris, and Saxony.

This text is a royal instruction (capitulare) from Charlemagne to his messengers (missi) regarding the administration of justice and the enforcement of royal and ecclesiastical law. It details specific procedures for handling the abduction of women and children, the protection of church property and clergy, and the identification and punishment of thieves (latrones). The text also outlines legal consequences for those who harbor outlaws, including physical punishment for commoners and the forfeiture of land for others.

This section outlines legal and administrative protocols for capturing and punishing thieves (latrones) who flee across borders or into private homes. It establishes the duties of messengers (missi) to pursue fugitives, the role of advocates in legal disputes, and the specific procedures for handling refugees from Norman or British oppression. The text concludes with a list of specific bishops and envoys assigned to various locations, including Hincmarus, Ricuinus, and Pardulus, and mentions locations such as Lauduniso and Catalaunio.

This section lists groups of ecclesiastical and secular officials (bishops, abbots, and others) and the specific geographic regions or counties (comitatus) to which they were dispatched. The text names numerous individuals such as Adalardus, Folcoinus, and Wenilo, and identifies numerous locations including Noviomiso, Paris, Saxony, and various local districts like Trecasino and Alciodris.

This 9th-century Latin manuscript, titled Capitulare missorum Attiniacense, is a royal decree or administrative instruction issued by King Charles (Karolus) in the year 754. The text outlines specific instructions for his officials (missi) regarding judicial and administrative matters in the kingdom. Key subjects include the prosecution of thieves (latronibus), the maintenance of maritime security, the reopening of waterways, and the restoration of bridges. It also addresses the legal status of refugees from the Normans and Britons, the regulation of counterfeit coins, and the investigation of church lands. The document concludes with a formal oath of allegiance (sacramentum fidelitatis) and lists numerous individuals, including local lords and clergy, who swore their loyalty to the King at Remi.

This medieval Latin text consists of a set of instructions (capitula) addressed to the Franks and Aquitanians regarding the Mass of St. Carisiacus. The first section details legal and administrative procedures issued by King Charles (Karolus) to resolve disputes and cases of unfaithfulness among his servants, specifically naming the envoys Adalardus, Rodulfus, Richuinus, Adalgarius, and Berengarius. The second section establishes a disciplinary code and governance protocol for a religious community, referencing the palace of Vermerium and a gathering of bishops, abbots, and laity on August 14. The final section is a brief fragment asserting certainty and security in the context of liturgical instructions. The work combines elements of royal administrative law, ecclesiastical discipline, and liturgical preparation.

A set of instructions (capitula) sent by King Charles (Karolus) to the Franks and Aquitanians in 756. The text outlines legal and administrative procedures for resolving disputes, cases of unfaithfulness, and the restoration of justice among those in the king's service. It specifically addresses the roles of his envoys—Adalardus, Rodulfus, Richuinus, Adalgarius, and Berengarius—and the conditions under which a subordinate's actions may be judged as justified by necessity or corrected through the counsel of the king's faithful.

This section of the Carisiacum minutes outlines a formal agreement and disciplinary code for a religious community, specifically addressing the duties of members to correct errors and maintain order. It establishes a protocol for addressing the actions of the 'senior' (the leader), who is identified as Carolus (Charles), and defines the procedures for handling internal dissent or the desire to leave the order. The text mentions a specific location, the palace of Vermerium, and a date, the 14th of August, in relation to a formal gathering of the faithful, including bishops, abbots, and laity.

The text contains a brief assertion of certainty and the ability to act with security. It is a fragment of a larger liturgical or instructional work (Capitula) addressed to the Franks and Aquitanians regarding the Mass of St. Carisiacus.

This 9th-century Latin text is a formal missive or diplomatic communication addressed to the Franks and Aquitanians. Sent by the King of Basia (Basque) via the intermediaries Hadabran and Betton, the document contains a single chapter of instructions. The text addresses a breach of prior agreements regarding a 'placitum' (an agreement or settlement) and demands that the recipients adhere to previously established terms. It specifies a meeting at the villa of Nielfa and references a prior arrangement dated to the Kalends of September. The rhetoric concludes with a religious exhortation, urging the recipients to remain faithful to the Church and the Christian name in the face of enemies and persecutors.

This 9th-century Latin text is a formal missive (missaticum) addressed to the Franks and Aquitanians. It was issued by King Charles (Karolus) and transmitted through a group of officials including the abbot Adalardus, Richuinus, Rodulfus, and Berengarius. The document serves as a formal mandate and exhortation regarding the defense of the holy church against pagan persecution. It addresses the unity of the faithful and offers a conditional pardon for those who return to the king's service and the defense of the church. The text is structured with a formal opening and a single chapter containing legalistic and religious instructions.

The Capitulare Carisiacense is a 9th-century royal decree issued by King Charles (Karolus) following a synod at Carisiacum. The text establishes a legal and ecclesiastical framework to combat looting, robbery, and the depopulation of lands caused by pagan incursions and the movement of subjects. It is organized into sections that combine royal mandates with scriptural and patristic justifications, specifically citing the Gospels, Isaiah, Paul, John, and the sermons of St. Augustine. The decree mandates cooperation between bishops, envoys (missi), and counts (comites) to enforce both church censures and royal penalties. Specific legal provisions are detailed for the theft of grain, livestock, and church property, as well as the violation of the 'peace' (pax). The text also distinguishes between the legal status of free men and slaves regarding theft and property damage.

This text is a royal decree issued by King Charles (Karolus) following a synod of bishops and a gathering of the faithful at Carisiacum. It addresses the issues of looting and depopulation caused by both pagan incursions and the mobility of subjects, establishing a legal and ecclesiastical framework for punishing those who commit such crimes. The decree mandates that bishops, envoys (missi), and counts (comites) must enforce both church censures and royal penalties against offenders, including specific provisions for cases involving the kin of the king.

This section of the Capitulare Carisiacense addresses the crime of theft, specifically the robbery of the poor, the clergy, and the property of the Church. It cites scriptural warnings from the Gospels and the Prophet Isaiah, the writings of St. Paul and St. John, and the decrees of Popes Anacletus, Urban, and Lucius to condemn thieves and those who consent to their actions. The text concludes with a reference to St. Augustine's sermon on the Gospel of John regarding the sacrilege of Judas.

This section of the Capitulare Carisiacense contains ecclesiastical regulations regarding the anathema, the duties of bishops, and the conduct of counts (comites) in their administration of justice. It includes specific instructions for the clergy and laity regarding holy days, and provides legal penalties for crimes such as theft, robbery, and the violation of the 'peace' (pax). The text references the 'capitula' of Emperors Charlemagne (Karolus) and Louis (Hludovicus) and mandates specific fines for housebreaking.

This section of the Capitulare Carisiacense establishes legal penalties for theft and looting of grain, hay, livestock, and houses, distinguishing between the actions of free men and slaves. It prohibits unauthorized looting within the kingdom, imposing a fine of sixty solidi and corporal punishment for slaves, while mandating that masters be held liable for their servants' crimes. The text concludes by addressing the theft of church property as sacrilege, requiring the removal of such individuals from the borders of the church.

This 9th-century Latin text is an 'allocutio' (official proclamation) issued by a royal messenger regarding a set of capitula (chapters) issued by King Charles (Karolus). The document outlines legal and ecclesiastical protections for the realm, specifically focusing on the preservation of church immunities and the protection of the clergy. It details prohibitions against the robbery of sacred goods, the exploitation of widows and orphans, and the theft of crops and livestock. The text establishes a judicial hierarchy for punishing offenders, involving bishops, counts, and royal officials. It also addresses specific crimes such as theft of 'mancipia' (property/slaves), illicit marriage, and crimes committed during travel. The document concludes with instructions for local priests to identify and report various crimes, including robbery, adultery, and homicide.

This 9th-century medieval Latin text records the formal proceedings of a meeting (conventus) held at the sanctuary of Quintinum on the Kalends of March, 857. The document contains the joint declarations of King Carolus II and his nephew Hlotharius II. The first section focuses on the reaffirmation of their mutual unity following the death of Carolus's brother, Hludowicus, and addresses the defense of the kingdom against pagan incursions. It further details legal and ecclesiastical decrees regarding the jurisdiction of bishops and envoys over criminals and the enforcement of royal penalties. The second section contains a formal prayer and petition for divine favor, requesting loyalty and reciprocity from the recipients based on the traditions of previous generations.

This text records the formal declarations of King Carolus II and his nephew Hlotharius II at a meeting (conventus) at the sanctuary of Quintinum on the Kalends of March, 857. The participants reaffirm their mutual commitment and unity following the death of Carolus's brother, Hludowicus, and address the threat of pagan incursions. The document includes specific legal and ecclesiastical decrees regarding the jurisdiction of bishops and envoys over criminals fleeing between regions, and the enforcement of canonical and royal penalties.

This section contains the third announcement of Charles (Karolus). The text is a formal prayer or petition requesting that God grant the speakers the merit to receive the loyalty and assistance of the recipients, just as previous generations shared mutual benefits. The speaker expresses a desire to reciprocate the recipients' kindness with equal goodness.

This 9th-century Latin document records a formal oath of fealty (sacramentum) taken at the court of Carisiacum in the year 1358 of the Incarnation (reign of Charles XVIII). The text is structured into two distinct oaths: the 'Sacramentum fidelium' (oath of the subjects) and the 'Sacramentum regis' (oath of the king). The subjects pledge to assist the king and uphold his authority, while the king pledges to provide justice, mercy, and protection to his subjects according to their respective ranks. The document concludes with a list of high-ranking clergy, including Hincmarus, Immo, Yrminfridus, and Hilduinus, followed by a list of names of individuals present, such as Engilramnus, Isembardus, and Ratbodus.

This 9th-century Latin text contains a series of capitularies issued by King Carolus (Charles the Bald) following a meeting at Confluentes. The document is organized into three parts, beginning with the establishment of peace terms, the restitution of alodes, and the prohibition of robbery and sedition. The second section details specific legal regulations regarding the protection of church property, the punishment of thieves, and the regulation of military conduct. It also addresses the pardoning of those who wronged the King and the management of livestock. The final section provides instructions to envoys regarding the rectification of illegal land holdings in public and ecclesiastical forests. The text explicitly notes the omission of certain topics, such as the abduction of women and the misconduct of counts, due to their complexity.

This text records a set of capitula (chapters) issued by King Carolus (Charles) following a meeting at Confluentes. It outlines terms for peace and legal order in the kingdom, specifically addressing the reconciliation of rebels, the restitution of lands (alodes), and the prohibition of robberies, seditions, and the abduction of women. The document includes a formal oath of loyalty and a summary of the agreements made with the 'seniores' (elders/lords) and their followers.

This section of the capitularies outlines legal regulations regarding the protection of church property, the punishment of thieves and kidnappers, and the regulation of military conduct. It specifically addresses the pardoning of those who wronged King Carolus (Charles the Bald), the restitution of stolen goods, and the management of land and livestock during seasonal movements. The text also establishes penalties for the theft of church items (sacrilege) and the unauthorized plundering of neighbors' property by soldiers.

The text instructs envoys to warn those who hold lands from destroyed or sold forests (both public and ecclesiastical) to rectify illegal acts to avoid the penalties prescribed by previous capitularies. It notes that specific laws regarding the abduction of women, conspiracies, ecclesiastical offenses, and the misconduct of counts are omitted here because they require more extensive treatment. The envoys are instructed to work with the counsel of senior envoys to ensure the full observance of these capitularies for the peace and safety of the kingdom.

This is a medieval Latin legal decree, specifically a monetary edict (constitutio de moneta), issued by King Carolus (Charles) in the year 861. The text begins with a standard invocation of the Holy Trinity and a formal royal titulary identifying the king as ruler by the grace of God. The document mandates that the current constitution be preserved and observed in accordance with the precedents of previous rulers. It specifies that the decree is to be read, acknowledged, and observed in various public and administrative locations, including palaces, cities, marketplaces (mallis), and trading places (placitis).

The Capitula Pistensia is a 9th-century Latin ecclesiastical and legal text containing moral exhortations and legislative decrees. The work opens with a formal invocation and a lamentation on moral decay and the abandonment of spiritual virtues, specifically mentioning King Charles (the Bald) and the site of Pistis near the Seine. It transitions into a theological treatise on the consequences of sin, the role of the Devil, and the necessity of repentance and almsgiving. The text then incorporates specific legal decrees concerning the punishment of theft, robbery, and sacrilege in the regions of Carisiacus and Confluentes. These decrees involve figures such as King Hludowig and the prince Hlotari, and establish deadlines linked to the feast of Saint Remigius. The final sections codify penalties for arson and sedition, citing the Councils of Chalcedon and Toletani to reinforce the authority of the church and the crown.

The text begins with a formal invocation and a gathering of the faithful, including King Charles and various clergy, at a site called Pistis near the Seine in 852 AD. The author laments the moral decay of the realm, attributing the 'devouring' of the land by outsiders to the internal abandonment of spiritual virtues like faith, hope, and charity. The passage concludes with a critique of the clergy and people who have rejected the Holy Spirit through pride and lust, leading to the desecration of churches and the violation of sacred boundaries.

The text presents a moral exhortation and theological warning against the consequences of sin, specifically focusing on the loss of celestial peace and the 'selling' of justice. It utilizes scriptural citations to warn against the influence of the devil, the betrayal of Christ, and the degradation of the clergy. The passage concludes with a call to repentance, confession, and almsgiving to regain divine favor and avoid the 'harsher vengeance' of the judgment.

The text provides moral and spiritual instructions on repentance, comparing the persistent sinner to a pig in mud or a dog eating its vomit. It transitions into a legal and ecclesiastical decree regarding the punishment of thieves and plunderers in the regions of Carisiacus and Confluentes. The decree mentions King Hludowig and the prince Hlotari, establishing a deadline of the feast of Saint Remigius (October) for criminals to make amends or face double banishment and exclusion from the church.

This section of the Capitula Pistensia establishes legal and ecclesiastical penalties for robbery, sacrilege, and the failure of superiors to discipline their subordinates. It cites scriptural warnings against robbers and murderers, and mandates excommunication for those who steal from the church or for leaders who fail to correct their men. The text also outlines procedures for the seizure of property, the reporting of crimes to bishops, and the specific roles of counts (comites) in enforcing these regulations.

This section of the Capitula Pistensia establishes legal and ecclesiastical prohibitions against theft, arson, and sedition within the kingdom and during military campaigns. It outlines specific penalties for crimes, including fines for free men and capital punishment for slaves, while also defining the roles and consequences for bishops and counts who fail to enforce these laws. The text references the Council of Chalcedon and the Council of Toletani to reinforce the authority of the church and the crown in punishing those who defy both divine and human laws.

This 9th-century Latin decree, the Capitulare Tusiacense in Burgundiam, is a royal mandate issued by King Charles for the region of Burgundy. The text is organized into two primary sections focusing on land tenure and military administration. The first section mandates the enforcement of royal authority over church property, the regulation of tithes, and the reclamation of 'alodes' from 'infideles' who hold land without fealty. The second section outlines the duties of 'missi' (envoys) in providing justice and coordinating the defense of the realm. It specifically details the roles of bishops, abbots, and counts in military defense, as well as protocols for naval security and the reporting of cases beyond local jurisdiction.

This decree, issued by King Charles in 765 (or 865) for the region of Burgundy, mandates the enforcement of royal authority over land tenure, church property, and clerical appointments. It specifically targets 'infideles' (unfaithful ones) who hold land or positions without swearing fealty, and commands envoys to investigate illegal land transfers, 'dead hand' (mortmain) holdings, and the collection of tithes. The text references previous capitularies of the king's ancestors to justify the reclamation of 'alodes' and the regulation of 'commendations' within the church.

This section of the Capitulare Tusiacense outlines administrative and military protocols for the defense of the realm against 'infideles' (enemies). It details the duties of 'missi' (envoys) to provide justice to the needy, the coordination of bishops, abbots, and counts in military defense, and the specific management of naval defenses and maritime security. The text also establishes procedures for reporting cases that exceed the authority of local officials and defines the scope of compensation and personnel for the envoys.

The Capitula Pistensia is a 9th-century Latin legal and ecclesiastical document establishing laws and privileges at Pistis. The text begins by defining the immunity, protection, and status of the clergy, including archbishops, bishops, and priests, while establishing the reciprocal duties between the crown and the church. It details disciplinary procedures for presbyters, specifically condemning simony with reference to Saint Gregory and outlining the processes for excommunication and reconciliation. The final section contains royal decrees from King Charles (Karoli regis) regarding the collection of tithes from various lands and the military obligations of the faithful. The work emphasizes the unity of the clergy and nobility in the face of external threats.

This text contains the opening of the Capitula Pistensia, a set of laws and privileges established by King Charles in 869 at Pistis. The first chapter establishes the honor, immunity, and protection of the clergy (archbishops, bishops, priests, and servants of God) and the sanctity of the churches. It outlines the obligations of the king to uphold both secular and ecclesiastical laws, and the reciprocal duties of the clergy to provide counsel and obedience to the crown.

This section outlines disciplinary procedures for clergy, specifically addressing the role of bishops in correcting presbyters and the prohibition of simony. It cites Saint Gregory to condemn those who accept or offer payment for sacred offices and details the legal process for excommunicating and reconciling sinners. The text concludes by invoking the authority of the kingdom and the biblical warning to judges regarding the justice they dispense.

This section contains a series of exhortations and legal decrees concerning the unity of the clergy and nobility, specifically addressing bishops, abbots, and vassals. It includes a formal proclamation by King Charles (Karoli regis) regarding the preservation of traditional rights, the collection of tithes (decimae) from various land types, and the obligation of the faithful to provide immediate military defense against pagans or enemies of the realm.

This 9th-century Latin document records a formal oath of fealty and a religious profession of faith taken at Gundulfi-villam on September 13, 772. The text records a formal assembly involving the bishops and laity of the kingdom of King Carolus (Charlemagne). It notes the presence of Queen Ingilberga and the papal legates Formosus and Gadericus. The document is structured into two distinct sections: the 'Professio episcoporum' (Profession of the bishops) and the 'Sacramentum laicorum' (Oath of the laity). Both sections contain formulas of commitment to defend the realm, uphold the honor of the king, and maintain the interests of the holy church.

The Capitulare Carisiacense is a 9th-century Frankish legislative decree (dated 773) concerning criminal law, property rights, and judicial procedures. The text is organized into three primary sections. The first section establishes protocols for the apprehension of thieves, fugitives, and 'infidels,' detailing the use of sureties and the legal status of repeat offenders. The second section addresses the management of tax collectors, the use of 'judgment of God' (ordeals) in cases of insufficient evidence, and the prohibition of sorcery and witchcraft. The final section defines the legal distinctions between royal fisc, ecclesiastical property, and private inheritance, while mandating that corporal punishments occur outside of sacred spaces. The document emphasizes the authority of the count (comes) and the royal envoy (missi) in maintaining order.

This section of the Capitulare Carisiacense (dated 773) establishes legal procedures for the pursuit and punishment of thieves, criminals, and 'infidels' (unfaithful persons) within the jurisdiction of counts and envoys. It details protocols for the apprehension of fugitives, the use of sureties (fideiussores) to ensure their appearance at the 'mallum' (market/court), and the specific penalties for those who fail to appear or who refuse to assist in the capture of criminals. The text references earlier capitularies of the king's ancestors to define the legal status of repeat offenders and those who have been previously pardoned.

This section of the Capitulare Carisiacense outlines legal procedures for handling fugitives, tax collectors (fiscalini), and runaway servants, prescribing the use of 'judgment of God' (ordeals) when evidence is lacking. It mandates that counts and officials identify and eliminate sorcerers and practitioners of magic (malefici, venefici) from the realm. The final portion addresses the legal distinction between royal property and ecclesiastical property, specifically targeting the fraudulent claim of church lands as private inheritance.

This section of the Capitulare Carisiacense establishes legal distinctions between private inheritance and property belonging to the royal fisc or the Church. It outlines procedures for the verification of legitimate inheritance, the management of ecclesiastical property exchanges, and the appointment of 'scabinei' (jurors) to ensure impartial justice. Additionally, it mandates that judicial punishments, such as executions and floggings, be conducted outside of sacred spaces like churches or presbyters' houses.

This 9th-century Latin synodal record documents the proceedings and decrees of the Synod of Pontigon. The first section records the formal confirmation of Charlemagne's election as Emperor by the bishops and nobles of Italy, France, Burgundy, and Aquitaine, featuring signatures from figures such as Hincmarus of Rome and Johannes of Tuscany. The second section lists signatories from regions including Vesontio and Ruthenensium, issues a formal protest against the actions of King Hludowicus and his son, and includes a decree regarding the priest Adalgardus. The final section details specific decrees regarding the authority of bishops in Gabin, Forosemproniatis, and Tuscany, while confirming the primacy of Ansigisus and Senon in Gaul and Germany. The text concludes by reaffirming the condemnation of King Hludowig and the synod's submission to apostolic sanctions.

This text records the formal confirmation of the election of Emperor Charlemagne by the bishops and nobles of the Kingdom of Italy and various regions of France, Burgundy, and Aquitaine. It includes a formal declaration of submission to the Emperor and a list of signatures from numerous bishops and prelates, including Hincmarus of Rome and Johannes of Tuscany, who attest to the proceedings at Pontigon and in the palace of Ticinius.

This section contains a list of signatories including bishops of Vesontio, Autisiodorensis, and Ruthenensium, and abbots of Bethleem and other houses. It includes a formal protest against King Hludowicus and his son regarding acts of violence, sacrilege, and adultery in their realm, followed by a decree regarding the priest Adalgardus. The text concludes with a historical account of the 1176 Synod of Pontigon, detailing papal envoys sent to admonish the King.

This section of the synodal record documents the formal decrees of the synod regarding the authority of specific bishops, including Leo of Gabin, Peter of Forosemproniatis, and the Tuscan and Aretine bishops, in handling ecclesiastical matters. It confirms the primacy of Ansigisus and Senon in Gaul and Germany as sanctioned by Pope John and Emperor Charles. The text also reaffirms the condemnation of King Hludowig's actions and confirms the synod's obedience to apostolic sanctions.

This text is a legal decree or proclamation regarding the crime of robbery (rapina). It was promulgated by King Charlemagne (Karolomann) in the year 783. The document specifies the date as the Kalends of March, the sixth feast day, in the first year of his reign in France. It establishes a formal prohibition against robbery and mandates that those who commit the crime be punished with a corresponding penalty (harmiscaram). The text outlines legal procedures for the apprehension of offenders, including the obligation of those who harbor fugitives to bring them before the authorities. It concludes with a formal ban against any individual fleeing justice.

The Karolomanni capitulare Vernense is a 9th-century Carolingian decree issued by Charlemagne at the palace of Vernus in March 784. The text functions as a legal and ecclesiastical mandate aimed at suppressing robbery, theft, and the exploitation of the poor. It is structured into three main sections: the first establishes legal penalties and scriptural justifications using citations from Isaiah and Paul; the second details procedures for excommunication and the roles of priests and missi dominici in punishing moral and property offenses; and the third defines the roles of counts (comites), their messengers, and the bishop's envoys in adjudicating theft and ensuring hospitality. Key themes include the integration of secular and ecclesiastical law, the protection of the vulnerable, and the enforcement of royal authority through local officials.

Charlemagne issues a decree at the palace of Vernus in March 784 to renew and enforce laws against robbery, theft, and the exploitation of the poor. The text uses scriptural citations from Isaiah and Paul to argue that those who plunder their neighbors are spiritually and physically harming the kingdom. The decree establishes specific legal penalties, including a triple fine and a 'dominicum banno', for those caught committing robbery or disturbing the peace.

This section of the Karolomanni capitulare Vernense establishes legal and ecclesiastical procedures for punishing crimes such as theft, robbery, and sexual offenses. It details the process of excommunication for those who refuse to comply with a bishop's admonition and outlines the roles of local priests and 'missi dominici' in maintaining order. The text also specifies the involvement of secular officials, including counts, vicars, and legal experts, to assist the clergy in judicial matters.

This section of the Karolomanni capitulare Vernense establishes legal procedures for dealing with robbery and the subsequent punishment of offenders. It outlines the rights of victims' relatives to seek compensation, the role of counts (comites) and their messengers in adjudicating cases of theft, and the specific duties of priests to provide hospitality and prevent robbery. The text also mandates that local priests and officials coordinate with the bishop's envoys to ensure legal corrections are made according to established law.

This medieval Latin text consists of a formal decree and set of capitula issued by King Charles regarding the bishopric of Tungres. The document is organized into two primary sections detailing the legal and ecclesiastical condemnation of a man named Hilduinus. Hilduinus is accused of sacrilege, the theft of church treasures from Tungres and Aquisgrani, and the illicit sale of ecclesiastical offices. The text justifies these condemnations by citing scriptural passages, the Council of Nicaea, the Council of Chalcedon, and the writings of Augustine. It specifically addresses the forced consecration of Herimannus of Agrippina. The work concludes with a formal appeal to Pope Richer to provide stability for the Diocese of Tungres following the seizure of its assets.

The text is a formal legal and ecclesiastical decree by King Charles (Karolus) regarding the bishopric of Tungres (Tongeren). It condemns a man named Hilduinus for his actions against the king's authority, specifically for his involvement in the theft of church treasures from Tungres and Aachen (Aquisgrani) and for the forced consecration of Herimannus of Agrippina (Aix-la-Chapelle). The king cites scriptural passages, the Council of Nicaea, and the decrees of Pope Anacletius to justify the condemnation of Hilduinus as a sacrilegious thief.

This section of the capitula details the legal and ecclesiastical proceedings against Hilduinus, who is accused of sacrilege, theft of church property, and selling ecclesiastical offices. The text cites scriptural and conciliar authorities (including the Council of Chalcedon and the writings of Augustine) to condemn the sale of church offices and the actions of the 'Judas-like' thief. It concludes with a formal request to the pontiff Richer to provide support and stability for the Diocese of Tungres following the seizure of its assets by Hilduinus.

This text is a collection of 'capitula' (headings) from a medieval Latin legal or administrative treatise, likely dating to the 8th century. The entries focus on judicial procedures, the conduct of officials, and the integrity of legal testimony. It addresses specific roles such as 'scabini' (jurors/judges), 'advocati', 'vicedomini', 'vicecomites', 'archidiaconi', and 'prepositi'. The text highlights issues of corruption, specifically regarding 'pravis' (deceitful or false) officials and 'testimonia mala' (false testimony). One section addresses the status of individuals who may have been formerly enslaved ('servi') and the legal implications of their actions or status. The final entry concerns the potential for advocates to influence the desertion of soldiers from an army.

This 8th-century Latin text is a capitularies (Capitulare) addressed to bishops regarding the governance of the church and the conduct of clergy in the Lombard territories. The document is organized into thematic sections covering the status of the clergy, the physical restoration of churches and monasteries, and the management of synagogues (senodochia) within the royal domain. It mandates that priests, monks, and nuns adhere to traditional norms and that illegal acts, such as perjury and false witness, be corrected through local and royal oversight. Specific provisions are made for the protection of widows, orphans, and the poor, as well as the collection of tithes. The text concludes by establishing a dual system of jurisdiction, subjecting clergy to canonical judgment and laypeople to the judgment of the lords and their successors.

This 8th-century Latin capitulary, issued by King Pippin of the Lombards, establishes regulations for ecclesiastical and judicial administration in Italy. The first section details the governance of churches and monasteries, mandating canonical order for bishops and abbots while defining the roles of advocates and commissioners. It outlines specific judicial procedures for crimes including theft, murder, and adultery among Frankish and Lombard populations. The second section addresses the apprehension of runaway slaves and servants in regions including Austria, Neustria, Emilia, and Tustia. It commands local officials, such as sculdasii, decani, and saltarii, to surrender fugitives to the king's representatives. Additionally, it establishes a fine of 60 solidi for the killing of pilgrims traveling to Rome and includes a decree in the name of King Charles (Karolus) regarding the administration of justice.

This 8th-century Latin capitulary, issued by Pippin the Short, establishes legal and administrative regulations for the Frankish and Lombard populations in Italy. The text is organized into two primary sections. The first section details ecclesiastical order, the roles of bishops and abbots, and the duties of local commissioners and advocates in criminal justice and infrastructure maintenance. The second section focuses on judicial procedures regarding runaway slaves in Austria, Neustria, Emilia, and Tustia, as well as the protection of pilgrims traveling to Rome. The text concludes by invoking the authority of King Charles (Carolus) to enforce these mandates.

This 8th-century legislative text is a capitulary issued by King Pippin of the Lombards concerning the administration of Italy. The work is organized into two primary sections covering judicial and ecclesiastical governance. The first section establishes regulations for Frankish and Lombard populations, focusing on canonical order, the roles of bishops and abbots, and the procedures for prosecuting crimes such as murder, theft, and adultery. It specifically addresses the protection of widows and orphans and the protocols for legal testimony. The second section addresses the apprehension of runaway slaves and servants in Austria, Neustria, Emilia, and Tustia. It further mandates penalties for the killing of pilgrims traveling to Rome and includes a decree issued in the name of King Charles regarding the administration of justice.

This decree by King Pippin of the Lombards establishes regulations for the administration of churches, monasteries, and the judicial system in Italy. It mandates that bishops and abbots maintain canonical order, defines the roles of advocates and commissioners in legal disputes, and outlines procedures for adjudicating crimes such as theft, murder, and adultery among both Frankish and Lombard populations.

This section of the Pippini capitulary establishes legal and administrative regulations for the Frankish and Lombard populations in Italy. It mandates that bishops and abbots maintain canonical order, defines the roles of local commissioners (comites) and advocates in adjudicating disputes, and outlines specific procedures for prosecuting crimes such as murder, theft, and adultery. The text also addresses the maintenance of public infrastructure like bridges and roads, and the protection of widows and orphans.

This legislative text, issued by King Pippin of the Lombards, establishes administrative and judicial regulations for both Frankish and Lombard populations in Italy. It mandates that bishops and abbots maintain canonical order, defines the roles of local commissioners and advocates in resolving disputes, and outlines procedures for prosecuting crimes such as murder, theft, and adultery. The decree specifically addresses the rights of widows and orphans and establishes protocols for legal testimony and the enforcement of local laws.
topics: Property and protection of the vulnerable

summary: This section of the capitularies establishes procedures for the apprehension of runaway slaves and servants in regions including Austria, Neustria, Emilia, and Tustia. It mandates that local officials (sculdasii, decani, saltarii) must not hide fugitives and must deliver them to the king's representatives. The text also establishes a fine of 60 solidi for the killing of pilgrims traveling to Rome or other holy sites, and issues a decree in the name of King Charles (Karolus) to ensure immediate justice for those long denied it.

The text mandates that judges search for runaway slaves and servants in the regions of Austria, Neustria, Emilia, and Tustia (the coast). It establishes a deadline of fifteen days after Easter for the apprehension of fugitives and the reporting of their capture to the royal court. The passage also provides a fine of 60 solidi for the killing of pilgrims traveling to Rome or other holy sites, and commands bishops and abbots to ensure these laws are enforced under the authority of King Charles (Carolus), King of the Franks and Lombards.

This section of the capitularies addresses the apprehension of runaway slaves and servants in the regions of Austria, Neustria, Emilia, and Tustia. It mandates that local officials (sculdasii, decani, saltarii) must not hide fugitives and must deliver them to the king's representatives. The text also establishes a fine of 60 solidi for the killing of pilgrims traveling to Rome or other holy sites, and issues a decree in the name of King Charles (Karolus) regarding the prompt administration of justice.

This 8th-century Latin ecclesiastical decree, titled Capitulare Mantuanum primum, addresses the internal governance and discipline of the Church under the reign of King Carolus (Charlemagne). The text mandates the organization of churches according to canonical authority and the regulation of monastic life for both men and women. It specifically addresses the conduct of abbots and abbesses, the management of royal monasteries, and the administration of 'senodochiae' for the relief of the poor. The document further establishes regulations regarding the rights of presbyters and deacons, the distribution of tithes, and the prohibition of illicit rewards or 'exenia' during the ordination of clergy. It concludes with protections for baptismal churches against episcopal overreach and the preservation of ancient customs.

This 8th-century medieval Latin text is a legislative decree, the Capitulare Mantuanum, concerning ecclesiastical and civil law. The first section establishes clerical immunity, mandating that clergy be judged by their own bishops rather than secular courts. It details the management of church property, the regulation of tithes, and the specific legal status of laborers, including servi, aldiones, and libellarii. The second section addresses the detention of rebels and those asserting unauthorized authority for trial by state officials. It further specifies the payment of tithes and 'sex solidis' to the church. The text concludes with a royal decree regarding the maintenance of Christian practices until a meeting in mid-October.

This section of the Capitulare Mantuanum establishes legal protections for the clergy, ensuring they are judged by their own bishops rather than secular courts. It outlines procedures for resolving disputes over ecclesiastical property, the management of church lands, and the regulation of labor and tithes. Specific provisions are made for the treatment of laborers (servi, aldiones, libellarii) and the enforcement of tithe payments through the appointment of witnesses and the imposition of penalties for non-compliance.

The text outlines legal procedures for rebels or those asserting unauthorized authority, mandating their detention by state officials until they can be tried for crimes against the count or the public. It specifies that remaining obligations regarding tithes and 'sex solidis' (six solids) are to be satisfied in favor of the church. The final section notes that Christian practices are to be maintained until a meeting in mid-October, where changes may be made if the king commands or if improvements are found.

This 8th-century Latin manuscript, titled 'Pippini Italiae regis capitulare Papiense', contains a series of legal and administrative decrees (capitula) regarding justice and governance within the Italian kingdom. The text explicitly references the authority of King Charles (Carolus) and incorporates elements of his broader capitularies. It addresses specific regulations for clergy, including the movement of monks from France and the requirements for priests moving between parishes. The document also details legal procedures for the handling of cases in the royal palace, the management of roads and bridges, and the oversight of monastic life. Additionally, it contains specific provisions for the rights of 'liberos Langobardos' (free Lombards) and the protection of ecclesiastical immunities.

This 8th-century Latin legal text is a capitularies of the Italian kingdom, issued under the authority of King Charles (Charlemagne). The document outlines various judicial regulations and administrative mandates concerning the governance of the realm. It addresses specific regulations for clergy, including the movement of priests between parishes and the return of monks from France to their respective monasteries. The text also establishes protocols for legal proceedings involving bishops, abbots, and counts, and defines procedures for the legal status of individuals in the Italian territory. Additionally, it contains provisions regarding the maintenance of infrastructure, the status of women with husbands in France, and the rights of the Langobardic people. The document concludes with mandates on the preservation of ecclesiastical immunities and the regulation of legal testimony.

This 8th-century Latin text is a 'capitulare Italicum' containing a series of legal and administrative decrees issued by a king. The document is organized into thematic sections covering ecclesiastical governance, land tenure, and judicial procedures. Specific topics include the management of 'senedochia' (likely a local land tenure term), the oversight of baptismal churches by priests rather than laypeople, and the legal status of 'advocates' for the clergy. It addresses the rights of various groups in Italy, the distribution of fines or 'compositions' to the royal palace, and the management of monastic lands. The text also includes specific provisions regarding the property of a woman, the legal status of slaves, and the restitution of fugitives from Benevento, Spoleto, and Pentapolis. A specific mention of Queen Hildegarda and the city of Placentia (Piacenza) provides local geographical context.

This 8th-century Latin text consists of a series of legal and ecclesiastical instructions (capitula) regarding the identification and punishment of various moral and religious offenses. The document addresses women who took monastic vows but subsequently entered into marriages, as well as men practicing sorcery, divination, or the burning of candles and making vows at altars. It mandates that local authorities or clergy investigate these 'unlawful connections' and separate the individuals involved to undergo penance. Specific cases of incestuous marriages, such as those involving a man's brother-in-law or a father's wife, are identified for immediate separation. The text concludes with a royal decree regarding the punishment of officials who neglect to correct these crimes within their jurisdictions.

A medieval Latin capitularies (capitulare missorum) from the 8th century, likely originating from the Italian region. The text provides administrative and legal instructions for officials regarding the ecclesiastical order, the restoration of churches, and the maintenance of peace among the faithful. It addresses specific legal procedures concerning the 'marca' (march/borderland), the conduct of neighbors, and the status of 'liberi homines' (free men). The document outlines regulations regarding the acceptance of certain individuals by marshals, the qualifications of judges and advocates, and the conditions for military service. It also addresses the status of 'vassis regalibus' and the legal protections for the poor and those in need. The text concludes with specific protocols regarding the seizure of individuals for military service ('exercitali causa') and the authority of royal messengers.

This 9th-century Latin manuscript, titled 'Capitula Italica incerta I', contains a collection of ecclesiastical and legal regulations (capitula) pertaining to the Italian church. The text addresses matters of clerical discipline, the administration of tithes (decimas) from fields and vineyards, and the legal status of serfs and their marriages. It outlines procedures for resolving disputes between clergy members, specifically regarding the jurisdiction of bishops versus secular courts. The document also addresses the maintenance of baptismal churches and the rights of poor laborers (aldiones) working on church lands. The final section discusses the collection of agricultural produce and the obligations of local officials.

This text consists of two distinct legal chapters (capitula) concerning ecclesiastical and secular law. The first section establishes judicial procedures for members of the clergy, specifically prohibiting abbots, priests, deacons, and subdeacons from bringing private disputes before secular courts. It outlines a specific legal process where cases involving ecclesiastical property or persons must be referred to a bishop or, in cases of irreconcilable dispute, to a count or judge. The second section concerns the restoration of 'ecclesiae baptismales' (baptismal churches) and the appointment of church ministers. It includes provisions against the acceptance of bribes by judges and defines the penalties for the illicit granting of church titles or public offices.

This text is a legal fragment, specifically a single chapter (capitulum) from a medieval legal collection or addendum. It addresses the legal status of inheritance following the death of an individual. The text specifies that those who receive an inheritance through the death of the predecessor are not to be compelled to settle the debt through capital or 'dilatura' (extension/prolongation). The document is a legal instruction regarding the rights of heirs in relation to debt obligations.
