This 9th-century Latin text is a collection of legal and ecclesiastical 'capitula' (headings) intended for discussion or deliberation. The document outlines specific legal problems regarding property, inheritance, and the status of individuals within the church and feudal structures. It addresses technical legal issues such as the number of witnesses required for oaths, the status of infants born in utero, and the rights of 'liberti' (freedmen) on church lands. The text mentions specific historical and legal contexts, including the 'preceptum inmunitatis' (precept of immunity) and a reference to the time of King Pippin. The content focuses on the intersection of canon law and secular land tenure, specifically regarding 'res ecclesiasticas' and the rights of those living on church lands.

This 9th-century Latin text, titled 'Capitula de coniurationibus,' is a collection of ecclesiastical and legal regulations concerning conspiracy and the conduct of clergy. The work is structured into numbered chapters, specifically featuring the eighteenth chapter regarding the crime of conspiracy (coniuratio/conspiratio). It cites the Council of Chalcedon as a source of authority. The text outlines specific penalties for clerics and monks found conspiring against bishops or other members of the clergy, noting they are to be punished according to their rank and by imperial sentence. A subsequent section addresses those who have taken sacred oaths but refuse to make peace, prescribing the deposition of clerics and the suspension of laypeople from the Eucharist for one year for perjury.

This text is a collection of ecclesiastical canons or disciplinary rules (capitula) for a church, likely of Italian origin. The document outlines regulations regarding the authority of the bishop over the clergy and the administration of sacraments. It specifically prohibits laypeople or clerics from performing ecclesiastical mysteries or performing duties without the explicit consent of the presiding bishop. The text also addresses the collection of tithes (decimas) and the prohibition of baptisms outside the established church. A disciplinary clause mandates excommunication for any member of the priesthood or clergy who acts without the bishop's permission. The text focuses on themes of episcopal jurisdiction, clerical discipline, and the regulation of sacred rites.

This 9th-century Latin text, titled 'Capitula Italica incerta III', consists of a series of short chapters or regulations concerning ecclesiastical and monastic discipline. The text outlines the administrative organization of churches and monasteries under the authority of bishops, specifically addressing the 'senodochium' and the management of its resources. It provides specific instructions regarding the conduct of monks and nuns, the appointment of abbots and abbesses, and the oversight of those living in solitary habitations. The document also addresses the legal and spiritual status of women in religious habits and the rules regarding communal property. The text is characterized by its focus on 'canonic order' and the disciplinary oversight of the clergy.

This is a brief medieval Latin legal or administrative fragment, possibly a heading or a short record. The text contains two nearly identical lines regarding 'immunitate infracta' (violated immunity). The name 'Karolus Augustus' (Charles Augustus) is repeated twice. The text is too brief to establish a narrative structure or a specific geographical setting. The primary subject matter concerns a breach of legal immunity involving a figure named Carolus.

This medieval Latin theological treatise by Abbaudus abbas defends the doctrine of the 'fraction' (breaking) of the body of Christ in the Eucharist. The work is structured as a systematic defense against the heresy of Berengarius and the positions of several 'labyrinths' of France, specifically Abelard, Peter of Lombardy, Peter of Poitiers, and Gislebert of Porrentrucs. Abbaudus abbas engages in a technical debate with the scholastic Petrus Abaetardus regarding the physical integrity of Christ's body versus its distribution in the sacrament. The text utilizes scriptural evidence from the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, the Psalms, and the Pauline Epistles to argue for the Real Presence. It addresses the paradox of Christ's body being simultaneously whole in heaven and broken on earth, attributing this to divine power and the distinction between human perception and divine reality. The author also critiques minor dialectical arguments concerning the physical appearance of the host.

Abbaudus abbas discusses the theological controversy regarding the 'fraction' (breaking) of the body of Christ in the Eucharist, specifically in response to the heresy of Berengarius. The text compares the positions of the scholastic scholar (identified as Petrus Abaetardus) and the heretic Berengarius, while referencing a work by Walterius abbas Victorinus against four 'labyrinths' of France (Abelard, Peter of Lombardy, Peter of Poitiers, and Gislebert of Porrentrucs). The author concludes by analyzing the scriptural basis for the 'breaking of the bread' in the Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles.

Abbaudus abbas argues that the use of the term 'panis fractionis' (bread of breaking) by the Apostles and the Evangelists is a deliberate choice to emphasize the mystery of the Eucharist. He addresses the theological paradox of how the body of Christ can remain whole and incorruptible in heaven while being physically broken and distributed on earth. The text concludes by asserting that human reason cannot fully comprehend the divine power that allows the physical body of Christ to be both palpable and incorruptible.

Abbaudus abbas defends the doctrine of the Eucharist, arguing that the physical breaking of the bread does not compromise the integrity of Christ's body. He addresses the apparent contradiction in the Gospel of Luke regarding the girl and the mockery of the onlookers by distinguishing between temporal and eternal states. The text concludes by arguing that while human bodies are subject to local division, God's perspective transcends spatial and temporal limitations.

Abbaudus abbas argues for the physical integrity of the body of Christ despite its division in the Eucharist, asserting that the divine substance remains undivided even when the bread is broken. He addresses the theological debate over whether the 'fraction' occurs in the physical body or merely in the sign, and critiques those who argue over the 'whiteness' or 'roundness' of the host. The text mentions the Berengarian heresy, the doubt of Thomas, and identifies Petrus Abaetardus as a key figure in the debate against the 'four labyrinths' of France (Abelard, Peter Lombard, Peter of Poitiers, and Gislebert of Porrentruc).

This is a theological treatise by Thomas Aquinas titled Summa theologiae. The text serves as an introductory prospectus for the work, outlining its pedagogical methodology and structural goals. The author states that the work is intended to instruct both advanced students and those beginning their education in the Catholic faith. Aquinas explicitly aims to avoid the common pitfalls of contemporary theological writings, such as the proliferation of unnecessary questions, repetitive arguments, and disorganized expositions. He intends to present matters of sacred doctrine briefly and clearly, following the natural order of the subject matter. The text references the biblical precedent of 1 Corinthians 3:1 to justify this pedagogical approach.

This collection consists of occasional poems and elegies compiled by Iacobus Grauisius. The work is organized into two primary sections containing funeral laments, dedicatory verses, and dialogues. The first section commemorates the deaths of Hieronymus Mazzarelli (Bishop of Tragurium), Helena Lucia, and Ioannum Pridoevium, while also featuring a dedication to Tranquillus Andreus and a dialogue between Sebastianus and Petrus. The second section contains formal addresses to scholars including Petrus Lucius, Simon Rosam, and Michael Racetinus, as well as a dedication to a grammar teacher in Verona. The texts frequently reference the city of Tragurium, the Muses, and themes of friendship and shared grief.

This collection of occasional poems and elegies commemorates several deaths, including those of Hieronymus Mazzarelli (a bishop of Tragurium), Helena Lucia, and Ioannum Pridoevium. The texts include a dedication to a 'lord' named Tranquillus Andreus, a lament for a sister, and a dialogue between friends (Sebastianus and Petrus) regarding shared grief. The poems frequently invoke the Muses, mention the city of Tragurium, and reference various literary and mythological figures.

This collection of occasional poems and dedications includes a lament for a deceased woman, a series of formal addresses to scholars and peers, and several dedicatory verses. Specific individuals mentioned include Iacobus Grauisius, Petrus Lucius, Simon Rosam, and Michael Racetinus. The text includes a dedication to a teacher of grammar in Verona and a concluding note regarding the identity of the author and the recipient.

This collection, titled Carmina minora ex libro De vita et gestis Christi, consists of a series of Latin poems, dedicatory verses, and formal letters. The work is organized into five sections containing a mixture of literary critique, religious poetry, and personal correspondence. Notable figures include the poet Iacobus Bonus Racusaeus, who is the primary subject of several commendations, and Hieronymus Caluus, who provides a formal critique of Bonus's eloquence. The text includes dedications to Cardinal Augustinus Triuulicius, the priest Aegidius Viterbiensis, and King Henry VII of England. Geographical references include the cities of Viterbo and Racusan. Thematic content focuses on Christian dogma, the Trinity, liturgical themes, and the defense of theology, interspersed with moralizing verses and panegyrics.

This section contains two brief Latin poems (epigrams) addressed to the poet Iacobus Bonus, followed by a lengthy prose letter from Hieronymus Caluus to the same author. The prose portion serves as a formal literary critique and commendation of Bonus's work, praising his mastery of poetic figures, his ability to navigate traditional forms, and his superior eloquence compared to other contemporary writers.

This section contains a collection of Latin poems and dedicatory verses by Iacobus Bonus Racusaeus (Jakov Bunić). It includes a poetic address to a 'vates' (prophet/poet) regarding divine mysteries and the Trinity, followed by a formal dedication to a student or younger cleric regarding a pastoral task or 'lamb' of the Passover. The text concludes with a formal dedication to Cardinal Augustinus Triuulicius.

This section contains a series of laudatory poems and a formal letter addressed to Aegidius Viterbiensis (a priest or official in Viterbo). The text includes panegyrics for Aegidius and other figures like Augustus (Augustinus) and Blasius, and mentions the city of Racusan (Raceres). The final portion is a formal letter regarding the submission of verses and the delay of a meeting until the feast of Christmas.

This section contains a series of short poems, dedications, and epistolary fragments. It includes a personal correspondence involving Iacobus Bonus, a dedication to Henry VII of England regarding his role as king and warrior, and a series of moralizing and religious verses. The text also includes a dedication to a 'Virgin' (possibly a religious site or personage) and a brief address to a 'warrior against the Gaul'.

The text is a laudatory poem addressed to a reader, praising the theological eloquence of Polycarpus of Sibenik (Policarpus Seueritani). It specifically praises the poet Iacobus (Jakov Bunić) of Racusae as a brilliant scholar and defender of Christian dogma, while invoking the Gorgon and Libitina to symbolically cast out impious influences.

This collection contains a series of Latin epigrams and a hexastich addressed to specific individuals in Split (Spalatum). The first epigram is dedicated to Benedictus de Mulla, the praetorian prefect of Split, and Donatus Pasqualitius, an archdeacon of Split. The second piece is a hexastich by Hieronymus Martiniacus addressed to the same Benedictus. The third and fourth entries are addressed to the same individual and involve a composition by Nicolaus Albertus. The texts feature themes of civic duty, legal justice, and the comparison of earthly authority to celestial power. Specific locations mentioned include Spalatum and references to Libya and Venice. The poems utilize classical tropes of wealth, justice, and the role of the praetor.

This collection consists of Latin epigrams and commemorative verses, including funerary inscriptions and panegyrics. The text contains specific epitaphs for individuals such as Paulius Antonius of Cipicius and Petrus Natalis. It features a significant section of praise for the city of Spalatum (Split) and its inhabitants, attributed to Aelius Tolimerius of Sibenice. The collection also includes a poetic tribute to the poet Marullus and references to classical figures such as Plato, Cato, and Apollo. Themes include civic virtue, the preservation of local history, and the celebration of literary and intellectual achievement.

A collection of three Latin epigrams by the author Kabalin. The text features a dialogue or exchange between figures identified as Chrysogonus and Caballinus. The content includes references to classical figures such as Plato, Cicero, Demosthenes, and Laercius, as well as mythological and geographical references like Atlantis, the Indians, and the Pierides. The poems engage with themes of literary merit, the weight of praise, and the comparison of contemporary poets to the ancients. The structure consists of three distinct sections of verse, some of which contain repetitive refrains regarding the moderation of praise.

This work is a collection of nine Latin epitaphs for Marcus Marulus, transcribed by Frano Božićević Natalis. The text is organized into numbered sections, each providing a different poetic tribute to the deceased. The epitaphs feature various contributors and dedications, including Franciscus Martiniacus of Split, Hieronymius Martiniacus, Nicolaus Albertus of Split, Antonius Albertus of Split, and Hieronymius Papalis. The poems employ classical and religious imagery, referencing themes of fame, virtue, and the transition from the physical body to eternal renown. Specific geographical and mythological references include Split (Spalatum), the Hesperian plains, and the Muses' realm (Parnassus).

This work consists of a preface and a collection of letters concerning Dalmatian history and historiography. The first section contains two formal letters from Dominicus Zavoreus: one to Faustus Verantius regarding the compilation of a history of Dalmatia using sources such as those by Marcus Marulus, and a second to Thomas Surichievich in Split regarding the editorial condensation of ten volumes of local history into seven books. The second section contains a letter to a man named Dominicus regarding the collection of diverse works and the difficulties of restoring writings concerning Dalmatian matters. The text includes specific geographical references to Dalmatia and Split. The work concludes with a personal closing and the date July 1602.

The text contains two formal letters from Dominicus Zavoreus. The first is addressed to Faustus Verantius, a bishop and counselor, regarding the compilation of a history of Dalmatia based on various sources, including a work by Marcus Marulus. The second letter is addressed to Thomas Surichievich, an archpriest in Split, and details the author's process of editing and condensing ten volumes of local history into seven books after a period of scholarly seclusion.

The author addresses a man named Dominicus, praising his improved eloquence and the collection of diverse works he has compiled. The author argues that while the task of restoring certain 'writings concerning Dalmatian matters' (rebus Dalmaticis) is difficult, the effort is more praiseworthy because of its complexity. The text concludes with a personal closing and the date July 1602.

The Jura sancti Petri de Gomai is a multi-part legal and ecclesiastical record concerning the property, endowments, and litigation of the monastery of Saint Peter at Gomay. The text documents land acquisitions, vineyard ownership, and the redemption of serfs (seruum) involving figures such as Petrus Zerni, Anna, and various local landowners. It details specific geographical locations including Salona, Masaro, Biaki, and the territory of Saint Maximus. The work includes a detailed inventory of liturgical objects, such as a silver cup, antiphonaries, and vestments. Legal disputes are adjudicated by high-ranking prelates, notably Archbishop Rainerus of Split. The text also incorporates royal confirmations from King Slauis and King Suinimir, and includes a historical list of the 'bans' of Croatia and the Dalmatian coast.
topics: Monastery of Saint Peter of Gomay

summary: Petrus Zerni and his wife Anna record the legal and ecclesiastical proceedings regarding the construction and endowment of a church in honor of Saint Peter at a site called Selle. The text details the acquisition of land and liturgical items (a silver cup, a book of passions, and an antiphonary) from various individuals, including Semianus and Zulo, and documents a legal dispute with Miroslaus over territorial boundaries. The document concludes with a list of witnesses and a personal note from the author regarding his physical infirmity.

This section of the Jura sancti Petri de Gomai records a series of land transactions and property disputes involving the author, Peter, and various local figures. It details specific land acquisitions from individuals such as Iuanizo, Dobrouito, and Bolano, involving locations like Monticellum, Saline, and the territory of Saint Maximus. The text lists numerous witnesses for these transactions, including several priests, deacons, and local figures like Slauzo, Petrus banus, and various members of the Tugarani.

This section of the Jura sancti Petri de Gomai records a series of land and vineyard transactions involving several individuals including Dranegus, Uilcanus, and various local figures. The text details specific payments in grain, salt, and wine for land parcels in locations such as Salona, Durana, and near the 'Arca' above the land of St. Stephen. It also documents a legal dispute over a mill (molendinum) involving the heirs of Uilcanus and a subsequent settlement.

This section of the Jura sancti Petri de Gomai records a series of legal transactions, comparisons, and transfers of serfs (seruum) and land rights. It documents specific agreements involving individuals such as Formino Platimissa, Nycola, and various others, often involving the exchange of 'solidis' (likely a form of payment or security) and the assignment of individuals to the service of the church or specific lords. The text includes details of kinship, witness lists, and the formal redemption of individuals from servitude.

This section of the Jura sancti Petri de Gomai contains a series of land grants and legal confirmations involving the monastery of Saint Peter. It records specific donations of fields, vineyards, and houses by individuals such as Brana, Rusinus, and the sons of Palunduzuli, often for the 'remedy of the soul' (pro remedio animae). The text also documents royal confirmations by King Slauis and King Suinimir regarding territories in Masaro, Salona, and Biaki, and lists numerous witnesses and officials including Duymo, Uilcana, and others.

This section of the Jura sancti Petri de Gomai contains a series of land grants and legal testimonies involving several individuals, including the sons of Uisen (Desizo and Bogdano) and the property of the sons of Tomizay. It records specific land parcels in Mirizo, the territory of Tamali near Mount Grasso, and a vineyard belonging to the daughter of Uilumiro. The text also documents a legal dispute and subsequent settlement regarding the property of Ludinus, involving a list of witnesses such as Dabro, the abbot of St. Stephen, and various local figures.

The text records a legal dispute over land ownership between the monastery of Saint Peter of Gomai and several local claimants (including the 'Adrianiki' and others). It details a formal inquiry and judgment involving the arbitration of Archbishop Rainerus of Split and various other bishops and prelates. The proceedings involve the verification of historical land grants from Rossene Moristicus and the subsequent confirmation of the monastery's rights through a formal charter.
topics: Monastery of Saint Peter of Gomai

summary: The text records a legal judgment by the Archbishop of Split (Spalatum) regarding land disputes between the monastery of St. Peter of Gomay and a claimant named Cirne. It includes a detailed inventory of liturgical books and vestments owned by the monastery, as well as a historical list of the 'bans' (regional leaders) of Croatia and the Dalmatian coast. The final section contains a list of specific liturgical items, including vestments and linens, and a land grant from Peter Cerni and his wife Anna.

This section contains a list of liturgical items and vestments, including various homilies, antiphonaries, and a manual. It records a land donation to the monastery of Saint Peter by Petrus Çerni and Gumay, involving territory in a place called Campo. The text names witnesses such as Petris, Falcus, Iuanus, Benedictus, and Bogdan, and concludes with a note by Dobrona regarding the decree of Pribimirius.

This work is a liturgical collection for the feast of Saint Domnius, provided in an electronic version by Adam Parižanin. The text is organized into three distinct sections containing chants, hagiography, and ritual instructions. The first section contains antiphons, psalms, and a hagiographic narrative (Passio) concerning the Syrian noble Theodosius and his son Dompnius. The second section provides readings, responses, and verses featuring figures such as Antiocenis, Maurilius, and Beatus Petrus, with specific references to the regions of Dalmatia and Salona. The final section contains musical instructions for the Secundis Vesperis, a hymn to the Trinity, and an antiphona for the Magnificat mentioning the 'Corpora sanctorum' and Masarontis.

This text contains a series of liturgical chants, antiphons, and psalms for the feast of Saint Domnius (S. Domnii). It includes a hagiographic narrative (Passio) detailing the life of Theodosius, a Syrian man of noble birth, and his son Dompnius, who is portrayed as a martyr and teacher of the faith.

This section of the liturgical text contains a series of readings (Lectio), responses (Responsorium), and verses (Versiculus) for a feast, likely related to Saint Domnius. It features several specific figures including the figures of Antiochus (Antiocenis), Maurilius, and the 'Blessed Peter' (Beatus Petrus). The text includes liturgical movements involving the cities of Dalmatia and Salon, and references to the martyrdom of a soldier-like figure and the defense of the faith.

This section contains liturgical verses and a musical instruction for the 'Secundis Vesperis'. The text includes a hymn to the 'Sublimi Domino' regarding the Trinity and the crowning of saints, and a specific antiphona for the Magnificat involving the 'Corpora sanctorum' and a reference to 'Masarontis'.

This document is a Latin charter of land and vineyard donation dated 1070. The donor, Radauanus, grants his possessions, which were previously held by his ancestor Ualeco, to the monastery of Saint Chrysogon. The text identifies the reigning authorities as the third Roman Emperor and King Peter of Croatia and Dalmatia. The transaction is recorded in the city of Nona Adamizo. A list of thirteen witnesses is provided, including several individuals with the title 'iupano' and several priests. This collection consists of three hymns and a series of liturgical texts (hymns, antiphons, and prayers) dedicated to the martyr and pontiff Saint Domnius. The work is organized into five parts that detail the liturgical history, hagiography, and translation of the saint's relics in the diocese of Spalatum (Split) and the city of Salona. The content features invocations for protection against the 'monstra Tartari' (Turks) and prayers against disease and famine. The text also includes a hagiographical account involving Saint John of Fulginus and mentions of a figure named Maurilius.

The text begins with a historical and liturgical introduction regarding the translation of the relics of Saint Domnius (S. Domnius) in the diocese of Split (Spalatum) and the celebration of his feast. It notes the history of three previous translations and the establishment of a unified feast day on the Kalends of August. The section concludes with three hymns (Hymni) dedicated to Saint Domnius, featuring poetic praises of his martyrdom, the triumph over paganism, and the celestial glory of the Trinity.

This section contains a series of liturgical hymns, antiphons, and psalms for the feast of a martyr named Domnius (or Domnius). The text includes references to the city of Salona (Solana), the province of Dalmatia, and a specific narrative involving a figure named Maurilius and a conflict with the 'monstra Tartari'.

This section contains liturgical texts (hymns, antiphons, and prayers) for the veneration of Saint Domnius, a martyr and pontiff associated with the city of Spalatum (modern-day Split). The liturgical structure includes sections for Vespers, Matins, and the Easter season.

This section contains liturgical texts (hymns, antiphons, and prayers) for the feast of Saint Domnius, a martyr and bishop (Pontifex) from Salona (modern-day Solin, Croatia). The text includes specific invocations for protection against the Turks, prayers for the remission of diseases and famine, and mentions of the region of Dalmatia.

This section contains liturgical texts for the feast of Saint Domnius, including a hymn and various prayers for the evening and morning offices. It includes a historical and hagiographical account of Saint Domnius and Saint John of Fulginus, mentioning the city of Spalatum (Split) and the island of Diomedes. The text also references the translation of the saints' bodies and the influence of the Benedictine monastery.

This text is a Latin funerary inscription (epitaphium) for a man named Petrus Lucius of Tragurium, identified as a member of the highest noble class (patricius nobilissimus). The work is a modern electronic version composed by Nikolaus Albertus of Spalatum. The poem is structured as a series of rhetorical questions regarding the vanity of worldly status, wealth, and virtue in the face of death. It concludes with a mythological reference to Atropos and a moralizing reflection on the example of the saints. The text mentions the specific locations of Tragurium and Spalatum.

A brief Latin description of the city of Ragusa (modern-day Dubrovnik) authored by Amatus Lusitanus in 1560. The text provides a geographical and demographic overview of the city, noting its location on the Illyrian Sea and its resemblance to Venice. It describes the local climate, specifically the impact of southern winds and winter diseases, and notes the scarcity of fruit and wheat. The work details the social structure of the city, distinguishing between the governing nobility and the merchant class. It concludes by identifying a third, impoverished segment of the population.

This text is a Latin charter of land donation and confirmation (Confirmatio Radovani) dated to the year 770 (indicated as the 70th year of the world/incarnation) during the reign of King Cresimir of the Croatians and Dalmatians. The donor, Radouan, son of Lilicius, cedes a specific plot of land located at Suchouara to the monastery of the Holy Martyrs of Grisogon, under the supervision of Abbot Petrus. The document records a legal dispute with Uekemir (Lucius of Jupanus) and Boleslaus over the ownership of the land, which the donor claims was granted by the king. The text includes a formal royal confirmation by the king, a list of witnesses including several local figures with specific descriptors, and a list of five tribes (Croatin, Zelodrag, Dragouit, Dobrogoi, Negouan). The document concludes with a formal certification by Anastasius, Bishop of the Croatians and royal chancellor, in the city of Nona.

An electronic version of a Latin letter addressed to Iohannus Bonzagnum (John Bonzano), dated March 15, 1529, from Constantinople. The author addresses the recipient as 'reverende domine' and discusses the author's personal circumstances, including a period of illness and a journey from Constantinople to Hungary. The text mentions the 'Regia maiestas' (Royal Majesty) and his movements between Poland and Hungary, as well as the military situation regarding the conquest of provinces and fortresses. Specific individuals mentioned include Ludovicus Gritti, Statilius, and Rincone (identified as the orator of Cupio). The letter concludes with a report on the death of Radul wayvoda and his son.

This Latin work by Tranquillus Dalmata consists of a collection of elegiac and didactic poems. The text is organized into three distinct movements: a formal prayer and lamentation concerning the threat of the Turks and the defense of the empire, a series of meditations on the vanity of earthly power and the inevitability of death, and a polemical exhortation regarding spiritual virtue. The work includes a dedication to Caesar Ferdinandus and references the 'mandata ultima' of Iulius Viennae. Specific dedicatory addresses are made to Nicolaus Olah, Archbishop of Strigon. The content features themes of Christian morality, the transition of the soul to the afterlife, and a critique of those who conflate barbarian tactics with Christian symbols. Notable geographical and historical references include Vienna, Strigon, Europe, and Asia.

The text begins with a formal prayer (Precatio) to God, followed by a lamentation on human vice and the physical dangers of war, specifically referencing the threat of the Turks and the defense of the empire. It includes a dedication or reference to 'Caesaris Ferdinandi' and a 'mandata ultima' (last mandate) of a dying 'Iulii Viennae' attributed to Tranquillus Dalmata. The final section contains a series of poetic reflections on the fleeting nature of power, the loss of military strongholds, and the vanity of earthly glory.

This section contains a series of elegiac and didactic poems concerning the vanity of earthly power, the inevitability of death, and the distinction between material wealth and spiritual virtue. It includes a specific epitaph for a ruler (Caesar) and a formal dedicatory address to Nicolaus Olah, Archbishop of Strigon, regarding the burdens of age and the pursuit of sacred studies.

The text begins with a meditation on death, the liberation of the soul from the body, and the transition to eternal life. It transitions into a polemical address against a 'madman' (possibly a specific contemporary figure) who is accused of being a host to 'Eumenides' (furies) and a threat to the faithful. The passage includes a critique of those who mix barbarian tactics with Christian symbols, mentions the conquest of Europe and Asia, and concludes with a metaphorical warning about the loss of leadership and the dangers of following a 'beast' (cerus) instead of a virtuous leader.

This collection of Latin poems, preserved in the Budapestensis H46 manuscript, is structured into five distinct sections addressing religious, political, and geographical themes. The work opens with a dedicatory address to Pope Pius V and a defense of the Christian faith against the Ottoman Turks, including a specific address to Maximilian regarding the expulsion of the Turks. Subsequent sections detail the military conflict between the Greeks (represented by Millos) and the Turks, while providing a geographical survey of regions such as Pannonia, Dalmatia, Thrace, and the Caucasus. The text incorporates a prayer of the Dalmatian Christians against the 'hostis atrox' and includes a formal invocation featuring Antonio Verantio, Bishop of Agriens. The work concludes with a moralizing reflection on vanity and a petition for mercy, incorporating mythological geography including Olympus and Hyperborea.

This collection of poems includes a dedicatory address to Pope Pius V, a defense of the Christian faith against the Ottoman Turks, and a lament for the fallen. It features a specific address to 'Caesarem Maximilianum' regarding the expulsion of the Turk, a satirical critique of a 'scoundrel' (possibly a reference to a specific contemporary figure), and a moralizing reflection on the decay of old age and the vanity of worldly pleasures.

The text describes a military conflict between 'Millos' (representing the Greeks) and the Turks (referred to as 'Orcus' or 'Orco'). It details the prowess of the warriors, the tactical maneuvers of the Turkish forces, and the geographical scope of their expansion across Europe and Asia. The passage concludes with an exhortation to the Emperor (Caesar) and his allies to unite their forces against the 'barbarian' threat, ending with a prayer to Christ.

The text is a prayer of the Dalmation Christians against the Turks, invoking the supreme God to protect the land and people from the 'hostis atrox' (fierce enemy). It laments the destruction of Christian sites, the desecration of temples, and the loss of territory across the Mediterranean and Near East, specifically mentioning Lycia, Cilicia, Cappadocia, and the Caucasus. The poet describes the physical and spiritual toll of the invasion, contrasting the former sanctity of the land with the current presence of 'Turcorum' (Turks) and their 'prophanus' (profane) actions.

The text describes a geographical and mythological survey of lands including Libya, Thrace, Aemonia, and the regions of the Danube (Pannonia, Dalmatia). It transitions into a series of rhetorical questions and pleas addressed to a divine power (God/Christ) regarding the plight of the Christian people, the destruction of cities, and the preservation of the natural and celestial order.

This section of the poem is a formal prayer or invocation addressed to a divine figure (referred to as 'Sancte pater' and 'dominator Olympi'). It includes a plea for mercy for 'wretched nations' and a confession of sins involving 'vanity' and 'lust.' The text mentions specific figures and places including Antonio Verantio (Bishop of Agriens), the mountains of Olympus, Atlas, and the Hyperborean regions, while referencing mythological elements like the Tithonian sun and the Parnassus.

This Latin text, 'Commentarius rerum actarum Constantinopoli anno 1542', is a diplomatic report and record of negotiations concerning the Ottoman Empire and the Kingdom of Hungary. The work is organized into seven sections detailing the author's journey through Dalmatia and Messia, his meetings with Ottoman officials such as Rustam Bassa, Solimano Bassa, and the eunuch counselor of Sultan Suleiman. It documents specific negotiations regarding the cession of Buda and four fortresses (Strigonium, Vissegrad, Tattam, and Alba Regalis) in exchange for annual payments of 50,000 gold pieces or ducats. The text includes diplomatic exchanges involving the Holy Roman Empire, the Venetian Republic, and the Polish King. Key geographical locations mentioned include Vienna, Galata, Pest, Belgrade, and Adrianople. The narrative also references historical figures such as Maximilian, Ladislaus, and Sigismund, while discussing military movements and the status of various envoys.

The text is a report by a diplomat (likely a representative of the Holy Roman Empire) regarding his journey to Constantinople in 1542. It details the hardships of the journey through Dalmatia and Messia, the observation of the Turkish military's state of exhaustion, and a diplomatic meeting with the eunuch and first counselor of Sultan Suleiman. The author argues for the pursuit of peace over the uncertainty of military victory, citing the fragility of human power.

The text records a diplomatic negotiation regarding the Kingdom of Hungary and the city of Buda. The author, acting as a formal envoy (legatus), argues for the peaceful transfer of Buda and four specific fortresses (Strigonium, Vissegrad, Tattam, and Alba Regalis) from the Emperor to his master. The narrator recounts a diplomatic encounter with the Ottoman officials Mechmet and Usrei, and later with Rustam Bassa, regarding the capture and execution of a servant who was an expert in the Turkish language. The narrative includes specific geographical references to Vienna, Buda, and Galata, and mentions historical figures such as Maximilian, Ladislaus, and Sigismund.

The text contains a diplomatic petition from a royal envoy to the Emperor (referred to as 'V. Imperial Alteza') regarding the Kingdom of Hungary and the city of Buda. The text records a diplomatic exchange between an envoy and Ottoman officials, including Solimani Basse and Rhustan Bassa, regarding the status of a peace negotiation with the Emperor. The text records a diplomatic dialogue between a Venetian envoy and a representative of the Ottoman Empire (likely a Pasha or high official) regarding negotiations with the Polish King. The text describes diplomatic maneuvers and military concerns involving the Ottoman Empire and the defense of the realm. A fragmentary Greek text, likely a medieval manuscript fragment or a collection of notes, containing a mix of liturgical, hagiographic, and perhaps legal or historical references. A fragment of a Greek poetic text, likely of a liturgical or mystical nature given the presence of Orpheus and the mention of 'stones'. A fragmentary Greek text of medieval origin. The passage contains a series of short, highly stylized lines involving abstract imagery and metaphorical language. It details Trajan's reign, his military and civil policies, the construction of public works like baths, and his death; it also describes Hadrian's education in Greek culture, his architectural projects, and his personal character. The text includes specific mentions of the city of Adria, the forum of Trajan, and the names of figures such as Petronius, Nerva, and Sabina.

The text provides biographical accounts of the emperors Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, detailing their reigns, physical ailments, and personal virtues. It mentions specific locations such as the Forum of Trajan and the villa of Lorios, and notes the death of Lucius Annius Verus. The passage also describes the public mourning of Marcus Aurelius and the construction of temples in his honor.

This section provides a chronological succession of Roman emperors, beginning with the reign of Commodus and the assassination of his mistress Marcia. It details the reigns of Pertinax, Didius Julianus, and Septimius Severus, noting Severus's military achievements in Britain and his successors, Bassianus (Caracalla) and Geta. The passage concludes with the brief reigns of Macrinus and Elagabalus (Heliogabalus).

Aurelius Victor provides a chronological succession of Roman emperors and their relatives, including the tragic deaths of Severus Alexander, the rise of Maximinus Thrax, and the reigns of Gordian I and II. The text details the military careers and fates of figures such as Valerian, who was captured by the Sassanid King Shapur, and the local rulers of the late 3rd and early 4th centuries. Specific geographical locations mentioned include Aquileia, Verona, Moesia, and the bridge at Spoleto.

Aurelius Victor provides a chronological succession of Roman emperors, beginning with the reign of Gallienus and his conflicts with Aureolus and the Alamanni. The text details the reigns of Gordianus, Quintillus, Aurelianus, Tacitus, Florianus, Probus, Carus, and Numerian, noting specific military actions, deaths, and personal characteristics. It concludes with the rise of Diocletian, noting his origins and his 25-year reign.

Aurelius Victor records the fates of several late Roman emperors and generals, including the deaths of Galerius (Armentarius), Maxentius, and Maximinus, and the rise of Constantine and Licinius. The text details specific locations of these events, such as the bridge of Mulvius, Tarsus, and the city of Rome, while providing biographical notes on the character and lineage of figures like Galerius and Alexander. It concludes with the growing discord between Constantine and Licinius regarding the governance of the empire.

Aurelius Victor describes the military victory of Constantine over Licinius at the Cibalas, the subsequent execution of Licinius, and the rise of the usurper Magnentius. The text details the division of the empire among the sons of Constantine (Constantinus, Constantius, and Constans) and records the deaths of Constans and Magnentius. It concludes with the military actions of Magnentius in Italy and his eventual death near Lugdunum.

Aurelius Victor provides a biographical account of several late Roman emperors and figures, including the Gallic-born Gallus, the philosopher-soldier Julian (Iulianus), and the farmer-turned-emperor Jovianus. The text details Julian's military campaigns against the Alamanni, his death in the Taurus Mountains, and his personal life, including his marriage to Eusebia. It concludes with the lineage of Valentinianus and the career of his father, Gratianus.

Aurelius Victor provides biographical sketches of the emperors Valentinian, Valens, Gratian, and Theodosius. The text details Valentinian's character and death at Bergentium, Valens's defeat and death against the Goths, Gratian's military actions against the Alamanni and the Huns, and Theodosius's victories over the Huns, Goths, and the usurpers Maximus and Eugenius.

The text describes the character of a ruler (implied to be Theodosius, based on the context of the final lines) as possessing a balanced temperament of mercy, simplicity, and intellectual curiosity. It details his personal conduct, including his aversion to the excesses of past rulers like Sulla and Marius, his practice of reciting the Greek alphabet to calm his anger, and his preference for modest, dignified social gatherings. The passage concludes with his death at Milan after fifty years of rule, the division of the empire between his sons Arcadius and Honorius, and the translation of his body to Constantinople.

This Latin translation of Dares Phrygius's history of the Trojan War, prefaced by Cornelius Nepos, provides a detailed account of the conflict and its preceding myths. The narrative begins with the exploits of Jason and Hercules in Phrygia before transitioning to the specific events leading to the siege of Troy, including the abduction of Helen by Alexander. The text details the military maneuvers of the Achaeans and Trojans, focusing on key figures such as Achilles, Hector, and Agamemnon. It records specific diplomatic negotiations, the deaths of major heroes like Troilus and Memnon, and the internal politics of the Trojan court. The final sections describe the fall of Troy, the betrayal at the Scaean Gate, and the subsequent distribution of spoils and the departure of Aeneas. Key locations include Troy, Cythera, and the Temple of Apollo at Thymbrae.

The text begins with a preface by Cornelius Nepos to Sallustius Crispus, defending the accuracy of his translation of Dares Phrygius's history of the Trojan War. The narrative then recounts the voyage of Jason and the Argonauts to Phrygia, where they are met by King Laomedon and forced to retreat due to his hostility. Following this, Hercules leads an army to Phrygia to avenge the insult, defeats Laomedon, and secures the spoils. The final section describes Priam's return to a fortified Ilium, where he establishes a royal palace and an altar to Jupiter.

Antenor, a Trojan from Dardania and Thymbria, travels to Greece to demand the return of his sister Hesion from the Greeks. He meets with Peleus, Castor, Pollux, and Nestor, who all refuse his request. Priam subsequently gathers his sons and allies—including Hector, Deiphobus, Troilus, and Panthus—to prepare a fleet for a retaliatory expedition to Greece to avenge the wrongs committed against the Trojans.

Alexander, a Trojan commander, sails to the island of Cythera to retrieve Helen and negotiate with Castor and Pollux. After a skirmish at the sanctuary of Helaia, Alexander successfully abducts Helen and returns to Troy, where Priamus marries her to him. The passage concludes with the Greeks, led by Agamemnon, preparing for war against Troy, and provides physical descriptions of key figures including Castor, Pollux, Priam, Hector, Deiphobus, and Helen.

The text provides physical and character descriptions of Greek and Trojan figures, including Troilus, Achilles, Agamemnon, and Briseis. It lists the Greek leaders and the number of ships they brought to the siege of Troy, followed by a consultation at Delphi and a consultation with the oracle. The passage concludes with the Greeks preparing to march toward Troy under the leadership of Philoctetes.

Following the fall of Tenedus, Agamemnon sends ambassadors Diomedes and Vilix to Priam to negotiate the return of Helen and the spoils. Priam rejects the peace, citing past insults and the fate of his family, leading to a formal declaration of war and the assembly of various regional allies. The text then details the military maneuvers of the Greeks, including the arrival of Nauplius, the skirmishes involving Protesilaus and Hector, the death of Patroclus, and the subsequent funeral rites and internal sedition by Palamedes.

The text describes a series of battles between the Achaeans and the Trojans, detailing specific casualties among leaders such as Hector, Aeneas, and Diomedes. It recounts Agamemnon's leadership decisions, including a three-year truce and a subsequent period of intense fighting. The narrative concludes with the specific actions of Hector and Achilles on the battlefield, including the wounding of Sthenelus and the focus of Achilles on Hector.

The narrative describes a battle where Hector kills Polypoetus and is wounded by Achilles, followed by a period of truce where the Greeks and Trojans exchange terms and burial rights. Palamedes takes over command from Agamemnon, who yields leadership to him. The text concludes with a negotiation between Hecuba and Priam regarding the marriage of Polyxena to Achilles, and a subsequent battle where Palamedes defeats Deiphobus.

The text describes a series of battles between the Argives and the Trojans, focusing on the death of Palamedes and the subsequent retreat of the Argivans. It details a council of the Greek leaders, including Agamemnon, Menelaus, Diomedes, and Nestor, who discuss the lack of a successor to Hector and the role of Troilus. The narrative concludes with the negotiation of a six-month truce and the eventual engagement of Achilles' Myrmidons in the conflict.

The text describes a series of battles between the Greeks and Trojans, specifically focusing on the deaths of Troilus and Memnon. It details a conspiracy by Hecuba and Alexander (Paris) to ambush Achilles in the temple of Apollo at Thymbrae, which results in Achilles' death. Following the battle, the Greeks redistribute Achilles' spoils to Ajax and the other leaders, and the narrative concludes with the actions of Diomedes.

Following the burial of Alexander and the arrival of the Amazon leader Penthesilea, the Trojan forces engage in a fierce battle against the Argive army. After the Argivians are driven back to their camp, a council is held in Troy involving Priam, Antenor, Polydamas, Aeneas, and Amphimachus to debate whether to seek peace or continue the war. A conspiracy is formed between Priam and Amphimachus to eliminate the pro-peace faction, while Antenor, Polydamas, Vcalegon, and Dolon secretly plot to seize power by exploiting the king's perceived stubbornness.

Antenor coordinates with Aeneas and Polydamas to facilitate the fall of Troy, involving a secret signal at the Scaean Gate and the betrayal of the city's defenses. Following the fall, Agamemnon distributes spoils, grants freedom to Helen and Cassandra, and later executes Polyxena to appease Neoptolemus. The text concludes with the retreat of the Argive forces and a numerical tally of the casualties from both sides.

Aeneas departs in twenty-two ships, the same vessels previously used by Alexander to travel to Greece. The text lists the number of followers for specific figures: 3,400 men followed the general group, 2,500 followed Antenor, and 1,200 followed Helen and Andromachus.

This 4th-century Latin treatise provides a systematic analysis of physiognomy, correlating physical attributes with internal moral character. The work is organized as a progressive anatomical survey, beginning with the head and eyes before moving to facial features, hair, and the body. The author utilizes the authorities of the physician Loxus, the philosopher Aristotle, and the rhetorician Polemon to establish a framework of masculine and feminine qualities. The text incorporates extensive animal analogies—including lions, pigs, dogs, horses, and roosters—and mythological references to figures such as Thyestes, Tereus, and Oedipus. Ethnographic observations are included regarding Egyptians, Syrians, Germans, and Ethiopians. The work concludes with a classification of human temperaments, a distinction between 'stultitia' and 'malitia', and a case study of a man named Samus.

The author introduces a treatise on physiognomy, citing the works of the physician Loxus, the philosopher Aristotle, and the rhetorician Polemon as sources. The text establishes a system of classification based on the 'masculine' and 'feminine' qualities of both the soul and the physical body. It provides specific physical descriptions for each sex, including hair color, facial features, and body proportions, while noting that certain traits can appear in both sexes.

The text outlines the methodology of physiognomy, beginning with the determination of sex based on the symmetry or asymmetry of body parts (e.g., eyes, hands, genitals) and the orientation of the head. It identifies three historical methods of physiognomy: the identification of ethnic groups (Egyptians, Celts, Thracians), the observation of internal states (anger, contemplation, lust), and the use of animal analogies. The author concludes with a technical guide on how to weigh conflicting signs, prioritizing clarity and potency, and emphasizes the primacy of the eyes as the 'windows' of the soul.

This section of the treatise on physiognomy analyzes the relationship between physical traits and internal character, specifically focusing on how blood volume affects physical vigor and mental acuity. It provides a detailed catalog of hair types, colors, and textures, correlating them with specific personality traits such as boldness, timidity, or lust. The text also includes a series of physical descriptions of the head (caput) and scalp, linking head shape and hair distribution to qualities like wisdom, insolence, and impulsiveness, while referencing the Egyptians, Syrians, and Germans.

This section of a treatise on physiognomy analyzes facial features—specifically the forehead, eyebrows, and eyes—to determine character traits such as courage, intellect, and moral corruption. It uses animal comparisons (bulls, pigs, dogs) and mythological references (Thyestes, Tereus, Oedipus) to categorize human behaviors like impudence, lust, and greed. The text concludes that the eyes are the primary seat of authority in physiognomic judgment.

This section of the treatise on physiognomy analyzes the physical characteristics of the eyes and eyelids to determine moral character and temperament. It distinguishes between various types of eyes—such as 'glauci' (blue/grey), 'cyanei' (blue), and 'haropoi' (bright/sparkling)—correlating their size, movement, and color with traits like courage, greed, intellect, and lust. The text concludes by citing Polemon as an authority who identified a specific criminal based on these physical signs.

This section provides a detailed physiognomic analysis of the eyes, correlating physical attributes such as size, color, moisture, and movement with moral and psychological traits. It categorizes specific eye types to identify traits like madness, lust, wisdom, and deceit, and cites the opinions of Polemon and the philosopher Socrates. The text concludes by attributing specific ocular characteristics to Alexander the Great.

This section analyzes various physical characteristics of the eyes to determine the moral and intellectual character of the individual. It categorizes eyes based on moisture (humidi vs. sicci), size, and movement, specifically discussing the 'dark' eye as a sign of maturity or malice depending on accompanying features. The text cites Polemon's description of Emperor Hadrian's eyes and concludes with a transition from discussing 'closed' (conclusi) eyes to 'open' (patentes) ones.

This section of the treatise on physiognomy details the physical characteristics of the eyes and surrounding facial features as indicators of character, intellect, and moral status. It cites the author Polemon to describe a specific eunuch (identified as Fauorinus) and provides a systematic list of physical traits—such as the shape of the forehead, nose, and limbs—that correlate with specific traits like lust, wisdom, or madness. The text concludes by arguing that while many signs exist, the most significant indicators are those closest to the face, followed by the neck, chest, and limbs, while emphasizing the importance of 'epiprepea' (the overall appearance or manner) as the primary component of physiognomy.

This section of the treatise on physiognomy analyzes facial features—ears, lips, mouth, and nostrils—to determine character traits such as courage, deceit, and intellect. The author compares human facial types to animal archetypes, specifically the lion, bear, horse, and pig, to distinguish between masculine and feminine temperaments. The text also references Aristotle and uses Greek terms (e.g., κυνόδοντας, διηρθρωμένον) to describe specific physical proportions and their corresponding moral implications.

This section of the treatise on physiognomy analyzes physical features such as the chin (mentum), the neck (ceruix), the throat (guttur), and the shoulders (humeri) to determine character traits. It correlates specific physical shapes and textures with moral qualities like boldness, timidity, and intellect, while contrasting 'masculine' and 'feminine' traits. The text also references Greek terms such as θρασύδειλος and the concept of ἐπιπρέπειαν to characterize specific types of behavior.

This section of the treatise on physiognomy analyzes physical traits such as the size and texture of hands, nails, and fingers to determine character traits like greed, intelligence, or malice. It provides specific anatomical evaluations of the chest (pectus), the lower back (metaphrenum), the abdomen (venter), and the hips (ischia), often contrasting 'masculine' (virile) and 'feminine' qualities. The text incorporates Greek terminology to describe physical proportions and refers to animal analogies, such as frogs and wild beasts, to characterize human behavior.

This section of the treatise on physiognomy analyzes physical features such as the skin, hair, and limbs to determine character traits. It cites the opinions of Polemon and Aristotle to interpret the significance of body parts like the calves (κνήμη), feet, and hair distribution. The text concludes by categorizing three types of 'affected' (artificial) bodily movements or poses associated with lust, deception, and social posturing.

The text categorizes physical movements and vocal qualities into four types, distinguishing between natural and artificial behaviors. It provides specific physiognomic interpretations for physical gestures (such as the movement of the head and shoulders) and vocal characteristics (pitch, volume, and resonance), comparing human behaviors to those of animals like lions, horses, and dogs. The final section correlates skin colors and complexions with specific character traits and geographical origins, specifically identifying the inhabitants of the south (Ethiopians, Egyptians) and the north.

This section of the treatise on physiognomy analyzes physical traits such as eye color, shape, and size, as well as facial hair and nose structure, to determine character traits like temperance, lust, and intelligence. The author cites the works of Aristotle (Loxus) and Polemon to categorize these physical signs, comparing human features to animals like lions, dogs, asses, and goats. The text concludes with a discussion on the 'sarcasm' of the face and includes a quotation from Virgil's Bucolics.

This section of the treatise on physiognomy cites Aristotle to describe physical traits associated with specific character types, including the 'unrestrained' (rustici), the 'slow-witted' (tardiores), and the 'idle' (adoleschoi). It details physical markers such as facial hair, skin color (warm vs. cold), and body proportions to indicate traits like lust, stupidity, or effectiveness. The text concludes by noting the consensus between Aristotle, Loxus, and Polemon on these physical indicators.

This section of the treatise on physiognomy provides specific physical descriptions to identify various human character types, including the brave (fortis), the timid (timidus), the intelligent (ingeniosus), the senseless (sine sensu), the impudent (impudens), the temperate (temperatus), the secure (securus), the sad (tristis), and the ironic (Eiron). The author uses physical traits such as hair texture, facial features, and body proportions to categorize these temperaments, occasionally referencing Greek terms like 'ischion' and 'osphys'. The text concludes by beginning a description of those covetous of money.

The text provides a physiognomic analysis of human character based on physical features, distinguishing between 'folly' (stultitia) and 'malice' (malitia). It cites the Greek term μωροβλάπται for certain types of fools and references a specific example from the author Polemon to illustrate a man possessing both extreme folly and malice. The passage concludes with a physical description of the 'inuerecundus' (uncircumcised) and the 'thumoeides' (hot-tempered/spirited) man.

This section of the treatise on physiognomy categorizes human types based on physical traits, linking specific facial features and body proportions to character traits such as 'mercy,' 'passion' (libidinous), and 'loquacity.' The author argues that the ideal 'mean' (medietas) in physical proportions is not a mathematical midpoint but a 'temperament' influenced by the 'excellence' of the form, often referencing the lion as a model for superior proportions. The text concludes by comparing human types to animal archetypes, specifically the horse and the donkey, to illustrate different temperaments.

This section of the treatise on physiognomy describes various animals—including the ox, deer, lion, dog, monkey, goose, wolf, tortoise, serpent, owl, peacock, and rooster—and correlates their physical traits with the character of humans who share their likeness. The text details specific physical features such as head shape, eye size, and facial hair to determine moral qualities like honesty, boldness, or lack of intelligence. It includes specific Greek terms for certain animals, such as 'λχνον' (lamb) and 'φιλεγλῆμον' (lamb/mutton) for the dog, and 'γλαῦξ' (owl) and 'ἀλέκτρυὼν' (rooster).

The author discusses the methodology of physiognomy, specifically how physical traits of various animals are mapped onto human character traits. The text addresses the complexity of a single human possessing traits from multiple animals and notes that human behavior is often masked by social interaction, unlike the 'naked' and 'unprotected' nature of animals. The passage concludes by citing the works of Polemon and Loxus, and provides an example of a man named Samus whose facial features and eyes were interpreted as divine omens.

This late antique Latin treatise, 'De rebus bellicis', provides a technical and administrative examination of military affairs and state policy. The work is structured into six parts, beginning with a rhetorical discourse on 'largitio' and the distribution of state rewards to soldiers and land cultivators. It transitions into a critique of currency debasement under Constantine and the corruption of provincial tax collectors. The middle sections provide detailed technical descriptions of siege engines (ballista quadrortis, ballista fulminalis), weaponry (plumbata, clipeocentrum), and specialized equipment like the 'tichodifrus' and 'currodrepani'. The final sections detail engineering solutions for river crossings, such as the 'liburna' and iron-reinforced bridges, and conclude with tactics against the Persians and a plea for judicial reform.

The author addresses 'sacratissimi principes' (most sacred princes) regarding the utility of 'largitio' (generosity/distribution of wealth) in military and civil contexts. The text argues that true merit stems from natural talent rather than status, and it details specific benefits of state-sponsored rewards for land cultivators, soldiers, and the development of naval and bridge engineering. The author concludes with a warning against excessive, unmeasured distribution of wealth, which could undermine the fiscal stability of the state.

The author critiques the debasement of currency and the resulting economic instability during the reign of Constantine, specifically the substitution of gold with base metal (aes) for military and commercial use. The text denounces the greed of tax collectors and judges in the provinces, who exploit their positions to defraud the state and the public. It concludes with a call for the Emperor to restore fiscal integrity and reform the minting of coins to prevent fraud.

The text addresses military logistics and personnel management, specifically proposing a system of rotating soldiers into retirement or reassignment to reduce the burden of high pay and food costs on the state. It then transitions to a technical description of siege engines and weaponry, including the 'ballista quadrortis', the 'tichodifrus' (a siege device for scaling walls), and the 'clipeocentrum' (a small shield). The final section describes the 'plumbata', a javelin-like weapon thrown by hand.

This section describes various types of military equipment and weaponry, specifically focusing on javelins with lead weights and feathers, and different types of chariots (currodrepani). It details the construction of the 'thoracomachus' (body armor) and the use of inflated leather bladders (utres) to facilitate the crossing of rivers by armies.

The text describes military engineering and tactics, specifically the construction of bridges with iron bars and ropes to facilitate rapid troop movement across rivers. It details two specific machines: the 'liburna' (a ship-like vehicle) powered by wheels and oxen to transport troops across water, and the 'ballista fulminalis,' a heavy siege engine designed for long-range defense. The final section provides tactical advice on troop formation, equipment for cold climates, and the use of light transport vehicles for rapid reinforcements.

The text describes military tactics against the Persians, specifically the use of 'tichodifri' (shield-bearers) to protect soldiers and the deployment of 'machinarum' (siege engines or machines) in narrow passages. It also addresses the construction of border fortifications (limitum munitionibus) and concludes with a legal plea to the Emperor to resolve conflicting laws and judicial inconsistencies.

This 4th-century Latin translation of Dictys Cretensis' 'Ephemeris belli troiani' provides a chronological account of the Trojan War and its aftermath. The text begins with a dedicatory letter to Rufinus regarding the work's discovery at Gnosus and its prior translation for Nero. The narrative details the abduction of Helen, the gathering of Greek forces at Aulidas, and the fall of Troy, including the theft of the Palladium and the construction of the Trojan Horse. Key figures featured include Agamemnon, Achilles, Menelaus, Priam, Diomedes, and the Amazon leader Penthesilea. The text also records the intervention of Memnon and the subsequent fates of heroes such as Neoptolemus, Orestes, and Idomeneus. The final sections include a narrative concerning Vlix and Telegonus, involving the island of Aeaea and the lineage of Vlix.

The text begins with a dedicatory letter to Rufinus regarding the 'Ephemeris belli Troiani' by Dictys of Crete, describing the discovery of the work in a tomb at Gnosus and its subsequent translation into Greek for Emperor Nero. The narrative then transitions to the prologue of the work, detailing the lineage of the Cretan kings, the division of property among figures such as Idomeneus, Merion, and Menelaus, and a description of a sacred temple. The final section mentions a transgression committed by Alexander Phrygius, Aeneas, and others while staying with Menelaus in Sparta.

The text describes the aftermath of the abduction of Helen and the subsequent gathering of Greek forces, including Agamemnon and Nestor, to prepare for a campaign against Troy. It details the diplomatic mission of Palamedes, Vilix, and Menelaus to Troy, where Palamedes argues against the crimes of the Greeks. The passage concludes with the arrival of Menelaus at Troy and a consultation between King Priam and his sons regarding the fate of Helen and the stolen goods.

The text describes a diplomatic negotiation between the Trojans and the Greeks regarding the return of Helen. Alexander (Paris) argues the lineage of the Trojan royal house to Hecuba and the other leaders, while the Greeks, led by Menelaus and Antenor, engage in clandestine maneuvers and internal deliberations. The passage concludes with the Greek leaders, including Aias Telamonius, Teucer, Idomeneus, and Merion, assembling at Argos to prepare for war.

The text lists the Greek leaders and their respective contingents preparing for the Trojan War, including figures such as Nestor, Achilles, Agamemnon, and various regional leaders from Boeotia, Phocis, and Crete. It details the ritual preparations at Aulidas, including a sacrifice to Mars and Concord and the swearing of oaths. The final section provides a detailed inventory of the number of ships and men assigned to specific commanders like Menelaus, Diomedes, and others.

The text describes the preparations of the Greek forces, noting the scarcity of fodder for horses and the division of the army into four parts under leaders including Palamedes, Diomedes, Aias, and Idomeneus. Agamemnon is depicted accidentally killing a sacred goat of Diana, leading to a divine omen and a frantic attempt by the leaders to manage the religious fallout. The narrative also details a secret correspondence between Agamemnon and Clytemnestra regarding the sacrifice of Iphigenia, and the subsequent arrival of a letter from Clytemnestra to Achilles.

Following the sacrifice of a deer and the departure of the Aulidians from Aulis, the Greek forces encounter the Mysian forces under the command of Telephus. The text describes a bloody skirmish where several leaders, including Thessandrus and Teuthranius (brother of Telephus), are killed. Achilles and Ajax Telamionus divide the army to engage the enemy, and Telephus survives a spear wound to the thigh from Achilles.

Following a period of intense fighting and the death of many soldiers, the Greek forces and the forces of Telephus (a kinsman of the Pelopids) reach a truce. Tlepolemus and Antipho Phidippus meet Telephus, who, despite his wounds, offers them hospitality and grants the Greeks permission to withdraw from the war. The passage concludes with the Greek fleet returning to Boeotia for the winter while Agamemnon and Menelaus remain in a state of internal discord regarding the past sacrifice of Iphigenia.

The text describes the Greek preparations for the Trojan War, including the dispatch of envoys to gather allies and the organization of a fleet of fifty ships. It details the arrival of the wounded Trojan prince Telephus at Argos, where he is treated by Achilles, Machaon, and Podalirius. Upon reaching Troy, the Greeks engage in a preliminary skirmish against the forces of Sarpedon and the local forces of Cycnus, during which Protesilaus distinguishes himself in battle.

The text describes the surrender of the city of Neandriens and the subsequent capture of the royal children Cobin, Corian, and Glaucen by the Greeks. It details the siege of Cilla, the sacrifice of 100 victims by the priest Chryses, and the serpent bite of Philoctetes. The narrative follows Achilles' conquests in Lesbus, Scyrum, and Cilicia, and concludes with Aias Telamonius' siege of Cherronesum and the surrender of the city by Polymestor.

The text describes the distribution of spoils and the negotiation of peace between the Greeks and the Trojans. Following the capture of the daughter of the ruler of the Teuthrants, Aiax, Achilles, and others divide the booty, including the capture of Tecmessam and the retention of Hippodamia. Menelaus and Vilix then present a formal plea to Priam and the Trojan elders, arguing that the Greeks seek a peaceful resolution and the return of Helen based on mutual respect and previous treaties.

The text records a diplomatic negotiation between the Trojans and the Greeks regarding the return of Helen and the status of the war. Panthus and Antenor argue against the Greek proposal to trade Helen for Cassandra or Polyxena, while Menelaus reacts with anger to the suggestion of exchanging his spoils for the sake of the enemy. The passage also mentions the figures of Polydorus, Hector, and the Greek leaders, and details the internal deliberations of the Trojan leaders regarding the terms of peace.

The text records a diplomatic exchange between envoys and the Trojans, specifically regarding the fate of Polydorus and the actions of the Greeks. It details the abduction of the girl Io by the Sidonians and the subsequent actions of Aias Telamonius, who plunders several cities (Pitya, Zelea, Gargarum, Arisba, Gergitham, Scepsis, and Larissa) and steals livestock from Mount Ida. The narrative concludes with the priest Chryses seeking ransom for his daughter from Agamemnon, the subsequent plague sent by Apollo, and the leaders seeking Calchanta to address the divine wrath.

Following a consultation with Calchas regarding the wrath of Apollo, Achilles and Agamemnon negotiate the status of the captive Hippodamia and the return of Astynome. The Greek and Trojan armies engage in a fierce battle involving leaders such as Diomedes, Menelaus, Hector, and Sarpedon. After the battle, the Greeks distribute spoils and send a portion to Philoctetes on Lemnus, while Achilles retreats into a state of isolation with Patroclus, Phoenicus, and Automedon.

The text lists the various Trojan allies and leaders, including Pandarus of Lycia, Hippothus of Pylea, and Sarpedon, who are joined by a disorganized mass of followers. It describes a period of stalemate and preparation where the Greeks, led by Menestheus, and the Trojans, led by others, face each other in a divided field. The narrative details the capture and death of the spy Dolon by Diomedes and Vlix, and concludes with a specific skirmish involving Menelaus and the Trojan forces.

The text describes a chaotic battle between the Greeks and Trojans, focusing on the actions of Menelaus, Diomedes, and the archer Pandarus. It details a desperate Trojan counter-offensive led by Hector and later Aias Telamonius, who successfully drives the Trojans back and secures the Greek ships. The passage concludes with the Greek victory, the naming of specific Trojan casualties (including Antiphus, Polites, and others), and the honoring of Aias by Agamemnon.

The leaders of the Greek forces recount their victories over the Phrygian cities and the destruction of the fleet. Rhesus, son of Eione, arrives with a Thracian army and is intercepted by Diomedes and Vilix. The text describes the capture of the Thracian king, the retrieval of his chariot, and the subsequent negotiation of terms with the Thracians. Finally, the Greek leaders, including Aias Telamonius and Agamemnon, deliberate on sending envoys to Achilles to reconcile him with the army.

Agamemnon performs a ritual sacrifice and makes a formal oath regarding the marriage of Hippodamia, which is then reported to Achilles by Patroclus. Achilles delivers a long speech defending his actions and the distribution of spoils, leading to a reconciliation with the other Greek leaders. The text concludes with a description of the Greeks and Trojans practicing military maneuvers and archery at the sanctuary of Apollo Thymbraeus during the winter.

The text describes a clandestine meeting between Achilles and the Trojan women, specifically Polyxena and Cassandra, where Achilles expresses a desire for Polyxena. A negotiation occurs between Achilles and Hector regarding the girl, leading to a tense standoff. The narrative then shifts to a large-scale battle involving Diomedes, Idomeneus, and Hector, featuring the deaths of Pyraechmus and the involvement of Glaucus and Deiphobus.

The text describes the aftermath of the battle involving Patroclus and Sarpedon, detailing the deaths of Sarpedon, the horseman, and the seer Helenus. It lists specific casualties among the sons of Priam, including names like Archemachus and Philenor, and depicts the Greek soldiers returning to their camp to recount Patroclus's deeds. The passage concludes with a subsequent skirmish where several leaders, including Arcesilaus Boeotius and Agapenor, are wounded or killed.

Following the death of Patroclus, the Greek leaders gather to mourn him and perform his funeral rites on Mount Ida, where he is cremated. The text describes the gathering of leaders including Aias, Diomedes, and others, the collection of spoils, and the capture of prisoners like Pisus and Euander. The narrative concludes with the arrival of Penthesilea, queen of the Amazons, and a subsequent ambush by Achilles against her forces.

Following the capture of the Trojan children and the display of Hector's spoils, the Trojan city falls into mourning and chaos. Achilles holds a series of games and competitions for the Greek soldiers, awarding prizes to figures such as Eumelus, Diomedes, Menelaus, and Philoctetus. The section concludes with the distribution of honors to Agamemnon, Nestor, and Idomeneus, and a final scene where a grief-stricken Priam approaches Achilles.

Priam approaches Achilles, who is holding the bones of Patroclus, and pleads for mercy for the bodies of the fallen. Priam argues that the Greeks have violated the laws of war by desecrating Patroclus's corpse and that he seeks only to recover the bodies of his children. Achilles eventually agrees to release the bodies, and the leaders depart to their respective tents.

Priam and Achilles negotiate the return of the body of Patroclius (referred to as the son in the text's context of the exchange). Achilles questions Priam's judgment regarding the continued retention of Helen, while Priam recounts the history of Helen's abduction and the fate of the house of Antenor. The passage concludes with Priam's return to Troy with the body and his retinue, while the Trojans express amazement at the Greeks' unexpected display of mercy.

Following the funeral of Hector, the text describes the arrival of Penthesilea and her Amazons, who are defeated by Achilles in a battle involving various Greek leaders like Menelaus, Diomedes, and Agamemnon. The passage then shifts to the arrival of Memnon from the Caucasus with Indian and Ethiopian troops, and the subsequent actions of Phalas at Rhodes and the cities of Camirum and Ialysum. It concludes with the preparation of the diverse, multi-cultural forces of Memnon for battle against the Trojans.

This section describes a major battle between the Greeks and the Trojans, focusing on the combat between Ajax and Memnon, and the subsequent death of Memnon at the hands of Achilles. It lists specific casualties among the Trojan princes and leaders, including Aretus, Echemmon, and Glaucus. Following the victory, the Greeks celebrate Ajax and Achilles while the Trojans mourn the losses of Sarpedon and Hector. The passage concludes with a final skirmish where the remaining Trojans flee in disorder.

Following the capture of Lycaon and Troilus, a truce is declared for the feast of Apollo Thymbraeus. During this period, Priam sends a message to Achilles regarding Polyxena, leading to a confrontation at a temple where Deiphobus and Alexander are killed by Aias. The passage concludes with the Greeks transporting Achilles' body to their ships and the construction of a funeral pyre for him and his comrades at the site of Patroclus' previous location.

Following the death of Achilles, the Greeks bury his remains and the remains of Patroclus in Sigeum. Neoptolemus (Pyrrhus) arrives at the Greek camp, where he is greeted by Hippodamia and the other leaders, including Ajax, Diomedes, and Menelaus. The text describes a subsequent battle where Eurypylus leads the Trojan forces and is killed by Neoptolemus, causing the remaining Trojans to flee in disorder.

Following the death of the Trojan leader Alexander, the Greek forces and the remaining Trojans engage in a final, intense battle where Philoctetes kills Alexander with a poisoned arrow. The text details the aftermath of the battle, including the burial of Alexander by his wife Oenon, the capture of the Trojan gates, and the final decision by Aeneas and the daughters of Antenor to return the women to Menelaus. Deiphobus marries Helen upon learning of the agreement.

Priam sends Antenor to the Greek camp to negotiate a peace treaty and the return of Helen. Antenor meets with Talthybius and other leaders, and later, Priam delivers a formal speech to the Trojan leaders and allies. In his speech, Priam argues for a peaceful resolution based on the shared history and previous interactions with the Greeks, specifically mentioning the roles of Aeneas, Antenor, and the status of Helen.

The text describes a council of Greek leaders, including Aeneas, Diomedes, and others, negotiating with Antenor and the Trojans. It details the internal deliberations regarding the fate of the city, the status of the Palladium in the Temple of Minerva, and the specific roles of Priam and the fate of the sons of Alexander (Bunomus, Corythus, and Idaeus). The passage concludes with the Greek leaders' negotiations with Antenor regarding the city's defense and the potential removal of the Palladium.

Antenor negotiates with the Greeks, who demand gold, silver, and grain as a ransom for the Palladium. Following a divine omen involving an eagle and a failed sacrifice at the altar of Minerva, the Greeks and Trojans reach a final agreement on the remaining payment. Helenus then reveals the secret theft of the Palladium by Antenor and the subsequent actions of the Greeks.

The text describes the final stages of the Trojan War, focusing on the construction and presentation of the wooden horse as a gift to Minerva.
