The text begins with a lament for a fallen Caesar and the decline of Rome, transitioning into a series of fragmented, partially illegible lines containing various religious and courtly motifs. The latter half of the passage shifts into a formal liturgical and celebratory hymn for a king (referred to as 'Karolus' or 'Rex'), concluding with a Trinitarian doxology.

This section of the collection contains a series of varied poems and fragments, including a sequence of literary references to authors like Maro, Flaccus, Naso, Lucanus, and Ausonius. It features a narrative involving a monk and a bishop discussing a 'sacred order' and an 'ass' (asellus), as well as a series of religious and allegorical verses involving Christ, the Virgin Mary, and the figure Lanfrancus.

This section of the collection contains a series of varied poems and lyrical fragments. The text includes a religious invocation of Christ as king and priest, a pastoral and mythological sequence involving Bacchus, the Rhône river, and the goddess Cynthia, and a concluding series of maritime and philosophical reflections on nature and the limitations of speech.

This section of the poem contains a dramatic dialogue between a young man and an elderly man (referred to as 'vetus' and 'senex'). The text features a personified 'delusor' (deceiver) and a character named Terentius who is addressed as an 'old poet.' The dialogue involves a debate over age, wisdom, and the quality of poetic composition, concluding with a warning against the pride of youth.

This medieval Latin collection from the 9th century consists of various poems and liturgical verses. The first section contains theological meditations on Christ and the Virgin Mary, alongside a maritime-themed exhortation to a traveler. It specifically mentions the figures of Brigita and the saint Colman, and includes dedicatory verses. The second section focuses on liturgical prayers, including a petition for longevity and a reference to the Trinity. It features invocations involving a prelate and the people, and mentions 'Federa bina'. The work alternates between mystical imagery and practical themes of aging and sea travel.

This section contains a series of medieval Latin poems and verses, including a theological meditation on the nature of Christ and the Virgin, a maritime-themed exhortation to a traveler or sailor, and a concluding series of dedicatory verses. The text mentions the figures of Brigit (Brigita), the saint Colman, and the 'Mother Church' (Ecclesie matris). The poems alternate between mystical imagery of light and protection, the physical hardships of aging and sea travel, and expressions of religious devotion.

This passage contains a series of religious and liturgical verses. It includes a prayer for long life and happiness, a reference to the Trinity (three persons, one deity), and a sequence of invocations involving a 'presul' (prelate) and the people. The text also contains a reference to 'Federa bina' (two confederations) and a plea for the fulfillment of prayers.

This 9th-century collection of medieval Latin poems, titled 'aevi Ottonum, suppl. A', is organized into nine distinct sections of lyrical, devotional, and allegorical verse. The work explores the persona of the 'Scolastica' and the Virgin Mary through mystical imagery, celestial motifs, and the figure of Phoebus. It incorporates moralizing allegories attributed to Solomon, utilizing mercantile and weaving metaphors to describe the spiritual life of the Church and the cultivation of scripture. The text features significant theological meditations on Christology, the Fall of Man, and the sacraments, while also incorporating elements of sacred architecture and the physical purification of sanctuary space. Notable figures included in the text are Adam, Eve, Job, Daniel, and Noah, whose roles are interpreted through the lens of eschatology and celestial symbolism. The collection concludes with a scholarly commentary on biblical figures and the creation of the world.

This section contains a series of lyrical and allegorical poems concerning a 'Scolastica' or 'Virgo' (the Virgin). The text alternates between mystical descriptions of a divine bride, a narrative involving a brother and sister (possibly a biblical or allegorical pair) and a dialogue between them, and a series of hymns to the Virgin and the 'Scolastica' involving celestial imagery and the figure of Phoebus.

This section of the collection contains a series of devotional and liturgical poems. It includes a series of invocations to various female figures (including Maria, Sophia, and several names like Atala, Perhtsuuindis, and Odilia), a passage reflecting on the merits of Christ and the Virgin Mary, and a concluding section on the spiritual rewards of the faithful and the condemnation of heretics.

The text presents a series of allegorical and moralizing verses attributed to Solomon, using metaphors of weaving, spinning, and trade to describe the spiritual life of the church. It employs imagery of a 'strong woman' (mulier fortis) and a merchant ship to symbolize the soul's journey toward the heavenly kingdom and the cultivation of the 'vineyard of scripture.' The passage concludes with a transition into a sermon regarding the internal service of the soul within the church.

The text contains a series of allegorical and mystical poems describing a spiritual journey, the virtues of the Church, and the role of the Virgin Mary as the 'bride of Christ.' It features a transition from theological meditations on the sacraments and the scriptures to a more visionary sequence involving a woman in golden garments, the figure of Lucifer, and a dialogue regarding spiritual instruction.

This section of the medieval Latin poems contains a series of allegorical and theological reflections. It includes a narrative of the Fall of Man involving Adam and the serpent, a theological meditation on the resurrection of Christ and the salvation of the soul, and a concluding allegorical sequence involving 'fur' (thieves) and the theft of the fruit.

This section of the carmina contains a series of devotional and allegorical verses centered on the symbolism of the cross, contrasting the 'pagan' world with Christian salvation. It includes a series of poetic descriptions of a paradisiacal landscape, a plea for mercy from the speaker to Christ, and a concluding passage regarding the construction of a temple or monument adorned with gold, stone, and wood.

This section of the poem describes a liturgical and architectural transformation of a sacred space, transitioning from a physical description of a temple's construction to a mystical and spiritual renovation. It features a transition from 'Alleluia' to 'luia', the physical purification of the site, and the sensory experience of the clergy and faithful within the sanctuary. The text concludes with a focus on the presence of Christ and the ritual of the liturgy.

The text contains a series of moralizing and allegorical poems concerning the soul's journey toward spiritual salvation and the dangers of worldly sin. It features a dialogue-like exhortation to a brother to seek 'true light' and 'holy bread' (scripture) over worldly pleasures, followed by a cosmological sequence describing the creation of the world and the elements. The final section includes a mystical passage referencing the Tree of Life and the creation of the heavens.

This section of the poem presents a theological and mythological narrative concerning the Fall of Man, the role of Christ, and the interpretation of biblical figures. It contrasts the actions of the first man (who sought to be like God) with Christ (who suffered for humanity's crimes), and concludes with a scholarly/theological commentary on the marital statuses of Job, Daniel, and Noah as symbols of celestial realms.

This 9th-century medieval Latin collection, titled 'aevi Ottonum, suppl. B', consists of a compilation of varied poems and liturgical fragments. The first section contains a funeral lament for Cunibertus, identified as a consul and 'father of the country,' alongside religious exhortations and prayers involving Christ and the Archangel Michael. These sections also include rhymed verses concerning mortality, the vanity of life, and clerical duties. The second section contains shorter, disparate fragments including a plea for commitment and references to the plan of Genesis and the Day of Judgment. It concludes with nature imagery involving fish, birds, and serpents, and a stanza on mutual affection.

This section contains a series of medieval Latin poems and liturgical fragments. It includes a funeral lament for a man named Cunibertus (described as a 'consul' and 'father of the country'), a series of religious exhortations and prayers involving figures like Christ and the Archangel Michael, and several segments of rhymed verse concerning mortality, the vanity of life, and the duties of the clergy.

This section of the collection contains a series of short, disparate poetic fragments and religious exhortations. The text includes a plea for a promise or commitment, a reference to the 'plan of Genesis' and the 'day of judgment,' and a series of disjointed lines involving nature imagery (fish, birds, serpents), a reference to the 'right hand of Christ,' and a concluding stanza on the endurance of mutual affection.

This 9th-century medieval Latin collection, 'aevi Ottonum, suppl. C', is a multifaceted work containing dialectical meditations, moral poetry, and narrative scenes. The first section provides a syllogistic exploration of human nature and identity, referencing Aristotle, Parmenides, Socrates, Origen, Priscian, Alexander the Great, and Porus. The second section transitions into moral and religious exhortations, referencing Tullius, Varro, and Donatus to discuss rhetoric, grammar, and the virtues of the soul. The third section contains instructional verses on military tactics, game rules involving 'agmina' and 'tabulas', and astronomical calculations of the sun and moon, concluding with a scene of a hunter and a philomela. The final section features a dramatic dialogue between a man named Claudius and a priest regarding stolen coins and a horse. The work is organized into distinct movements ranging from scholastic philosophy to allegorical narrative.

This section of the text is a scholastic and dialectical meditation on the nature of man, distinguishing between the biological 'animal' and the specific 'human' (homo). It employs syllogistic logic to debate identity and essence, referencing figures such as Priscian, Aristotle, Parmenides, Socrates, Origen, and the historical figures Alexander the Great and Porus. The passage concludes by asserting the superiority of dialectic over rhetoric and grammar in distinguishing truth from falsehood.

This section of the collection contains a series of poems or verses that transition from a didactic discussion on rhetoric and grammar to a collection of moral and religious exhortations. It mentions specific figures such as Tullius (Cicero), Varro, and Donatus, and includes a series of moralizing verses regarding temperance, the dangers of avarice, and the virtues of the soul. The final portion contains a series of structured, possibly allegorical or instructional, verses regarding the senses and the nature of the world.

The text contains a series of instructional and descriptive verses concerning a game or competition involving 'agmina' (divisions), 'tabulas' (tables), and 'cursum' (courses). It describes tactical movements, the roles of 'equites' (knights) and 'pedites' (footmen), and includes a section on astronomical calculations involving the moon and the sun. The final portion shifts to a mythological or allegorical scene involving a 'vorax' (predator) and a 'philomela' (nightingale) in a nest, culminating in a scene of a hunter or youth with a spear.

The text describes a dramatic encounter between a man named Claudius and a priest (presbiter) who has ascended a tree. The narrative includes a dialogue between the two, involving a dispute over stolen coins (nummos) and a plea for mercy or the return of a horse. The passage concludes with a meta-commentary addressed to the reader regarding a house written in two parts.

This 9th-century Latin collection, titled 'aevi Ottonum, suppl. D', consists of various poems (carmina varia) likely composed in honor of the Ottonian dynasty. The text contains a series of religious and laudatory verses featuring several specific figures, including the names Otto, Liudger, and Vffingus. The poems blend traditional Christian themes, such as the glory of the cross, the intercession of the Virgin Mary, and the protection of the faithful, with imperial and royal panegyrics. Specific geographical and cultural references include the 'valley of Werdina,' the 'Roman people,' and 'Greece.' The work also contains elements of medieval courtly and religious imagery, such as the 'golden spell of the spheres' and the 'sacred deeds' of the Virgin. The text is structured as a series of distinct poetic units or stanzas, some of which are significantly corrupted or fragmented.

A collection of varied Latin poems (carmina varia) dating to the 9th century, organized into eight distinct sections of varying thematic content. The work contains a mixture of devotional hymns to Christ and the Virgin Mary, hagiographic sequences, and moral narratives. Notable figures mentioned include Notgerus, Deodricus, the philosopher Seneca, Pope Gregory the Great, and the martyr Thrutbert. Geographical references include the Rhine, Bavaria, the Moselle, the Hren, and the city of Verona. The text also features a narrative of a noblewoman from Dieton and a series of prayers addressed to Saint Columba. Themes include the defense against heresy, liturgical order, and the duties of the clergy.

This section contains a series of religious poems and prayers, including a penitential confession addressed to Christ and a series of hymns to the Virgin Mary. It mentions specific figures such as Notgerus (Notker), Deodricus, and the king of the Franks, and references the feast of the Virgin Mary and the lineage of Jesse. The text also includes a passage regarding the clergy, the defense of the faith against heretics, and a reference to the city of Tidericum.

This section of the collection contains a series of religious and celebratory poems. It features a hagiographic and historical sequence including mentions of the Apostle Paul, the philosopher Seneca, and Pope Gregory the Great, followed by a series of shorter verses and a concluding hymn. The text also includes a concluding section with geographical references to France, the rivers Hren (Hron) and Moselle, and a final address to a 'Castor'.

This section of the poem contains a series of short, often disjointed verses and a list of names associated with titles or locations. It mentions specific individuals such as Ercanberte, Thiodolte, Bromagod, Hartwig, and several others (e.g., Otfrido, Wisiriche, Ratoldus) in a sequence that resembles a list of benefactors, saints, or historical figures. The text includes references to religious themes, such as the grace of Christ, the dangers of heresy, and the duties of a priest or scholar.

This section contains a series of hagiographic and commemorative verses concerning several figures, including the martyrs Thrutbert (Truthpert) and the priest/scholar Erchanbaldus (Erchenbaldus). It mentions specific locations such as the Rhine, Bavaria, and Avaricum, and includes a biographical sketch of a pontiff named Emmerammus. The text also includes a personal dedication by Erchanbaldus and a series of poetic praises for the Virgin Mary.

This section of the poem describes a moral and legal drama involving a noblewoman from Dieton who is pregnant as a result of a rape (stuprum). The narrative involves a priest named Emmerammus, a man named Lampertus, and a prince who seeks justice for the woman's dishonor. The text concludes with a transition into a musical or liturgical framework involving eight tones and a plea for divine protection.

This section contains a collection of varied poems and hymns. It includes a technical description of musical or liturgical ordering, a series of devotional hymns to Christ and the Virgin Mary, and a hagiographic list of local saints and figures including Liutharius, Perinhardus, Adalungus, Sarhilo, and Adalpreht. The text also references the land of Hibernia and the city of Bosra.

This section contains a collection of varied poems and dedications featuring several historical and religious figures. It includes references to King Otto of the Franks, the martyr Kilian, and the city of Verona, alongside a specific address to a man named Albert. The text also contains a series of shorter, seemingly unrelated poetic fragments involving themes of scholarly study, religious devotion, and descriptions of physical landscapes.

This section of the collection contains a series of prayers and petitions addressed to Saint Columba (Sancte Columba). The text includes a dialogue or internal monologue involving a 'miser' (wretch) and a 'Petrus' (Peter), involving pleas for mercy, the performance of penance, and the protection of a child. It concludes with a series of mystical or liturgical-style verses concerning the dissolution of the 'knot of sinners' and the salvation of the earth.

This 9th-century Latin manuscript contains a collection of poems structured into three distinct sections blending cosmology, allegory, and nature poetry. The first section provides an astrological and cosmological meditation on celestial bodies such as Arcturus, the Pleiades, and Sirius, juxtaposing these observations with Christian symbols like the Star of David and the influence of comets. The second section transitions into a series of allegorical descriptions of meteorological phenomena, including storms and lightning, while invoking figures from Greek mythology (Titans, Eolus) and the Hebrew Bible (Amos, Job). The final section focuses on the mechanics of timekeeping, contrasting Hebrew and Roman traditions. It details the seasonal cycle and concludes with references to the Roman calendar and ancient punishments.

This section of the text is a cosmological and astrological meditation on the movements of celestial bodies, including the sun, the moon, and specific stars such as Arcturus, the Pleiades, and Sirius. It weaves these astronomical observations with Christian allegory, contrasting the 'light of faith' and the 'star of David' against the 'hostis' (enemy) and the 'pestilent' influence of comets. The text references biblical figures like Solomon and the prophet, and mentions geographical locations such as Latium and the Argives.

This section contains a series of poetic and allegorical descriptions of natural phenomena, specifically focusing on storms, clouds, lightning, and the movement of the heavens. It references mythological figures such as the Titans and the god Eolus, and mentions biblical figures like the prophet Amos and the figure of Job. The text also incorporates astronomical and seasonal observations, including the movement of the sun and the transition of months.

The text describes astronomical and seasonal cycles, contrasting Hebrew and Roman methods of timekeeping. It details the movement of the sun, the transition of seasons (summer, autumn, winter), and the influence of celestial phenomena like thunder and snow. The final lines mention the Roman calendar (Kalends) and the month of April, concluding with a reference to old punishments recorded in books.

This 9th-century Latin work by Cyprianus Cordubensis is a collection of liturgical and devotional texts. The first section contains penitential prayers for the remission of sins, invocations to the Trinity and the Holy Spirit, and a formal exorcism directed at a demon. This exorcism specifically invokes the power of the cross and the presence of the saints. The second section contains a devotional exhortation concerning the holiness of the Lord and the goodness of the mind. It concludes with a specific formula of exorcism directed against 'demonum fantasma' (phantasms of demons) utilizing the sign of the cross. The work focuses on themes of Christology, demonology, and the sacramental power of the cross.

This text is a collection of liturgical or devotional prayers and exorcisms. It includes a penitential prayer for the remission of sins, a series of invocations to the Trinity and the Holy Spirit, and a formal exorcism directed at a demon to flee the presence of the cross and the saints.

This section contains a liturgical or devotional exhortation involving a prayer for the holiness of the Lord and the goodness of the mind. It concludes with a formula of exorcism directed at 'demonum fantasma' (phantasms of demons) using the sign of the cross.

This 9th-century Latin poem, titled 'Cypriani et Samsonis carmina', is a devotional and commemorative work attributed to Cyprianus Cordubensis. The text begins with a dedication to a count named Adulfus, who is credited with providing a collection of books. The poem transitions into a spiritual meditation on the nature of sacred texts, describing them as a 'true testament' that nourishes the spirit rather than the body. It features several specific figures and locations, including the martyr Acisclus, a figure named Vernulus, and a woman named Hermildis. The work incorporates elements of hagiography and sacred geography, referencing a 'sacred gurgite,' a 'Valentinian chamber,' and a marble inscription. The final sections contain a series of poetic verses and a concluding prayer to Christ.

This 9th-century medieval Latin work consists of rhythmic verses and liturgical-style poetry. The first section contains prayers to God regarding his role as creator of light and ruler of the stars, featuring specific petitions for a 'son of Willem' and a 'mother.' It includes structural instructions for the reader and repetitive, rhythmic phrasing. The second section contains moral exhortations addressed to a 'noble boy' and a theological meditation on the creation of man from a virgin. It further includes prayers for the dead, a reference to the feast of Saint Andrew, and a meditation on the equality of the rich and poor in death. The work concludes with a discourse on the virtues of youth.

This section contains a series of prayers and liturgical-style verses addressed to God as the creator of light and the ruler of the stars. It includes specific petitions for a 'son of Willem' (filium Willelmum) and mentions of 'two sons' (mis duo) and a 'mother' (genitrix). The text contains several passages of repetitive, rhythmic phrasing and includes a section of instructions for the reader regarding the structure of the verses.

This section contains a series of rhythmic verses and liturgical-style exhortations. It includes a series of moral instructions to a 'noble boy' (nobilis puer), a sequence of prayers for the dead (including a reference to the feast of Saint Andrew), and a theological meditation on the creation of man from a virgin. The text also contains a moralizing passage on the equality of the rich and poor in death and a concluding section on the virtues of youth.

summary: A short Latin verse composed by Dicuil in the 9th century. The text is addressed to a figure named Hlodvice, identified as a successor to Carolus (Charlemagne). The author presents a series of arguments or 'argumenta' structured around a chronological progression starting in the month of April. The poem contains specific numerical references, including the years 870 and 872, and mentions the month of May. The final section describes agricultural imagery involving stables, herds of cattle, and a weary ploughman. The work functions as a formal address or dedication containing personal and chronological markers.

This collection of Latin verses, titled 'versus inserti,' is integrated into the 'gesta Normannorum' by Dudo Viromandensis. The text is organized into fifteen sections of highly stylized, often repetitive, and occasionally corrupted poetic and liturgical passages. It primarily functions as a series of panegyrics and prophetic exhortations for Norman leaders, specifically Duke Richard (Ricardus), Duke Rollo, and William (Willelme). The content alternates between maritime allegories, theological meditations on the Trinity and Sophia, and historical references to figures such as Scipio, Pompey, and Cato. Geographic locations mentioned include Rouen (Rotome), the Seine (Sequanae), and the lands of the Gauls and Britons. The work concludes with a personal penitential lament and a series of complex, occasionally corrupted, liturgical fragments.

This section contains a series of highly stylized, likely mock-heroic or satirical Latin verses. It includes a series of laudatory exclamations addressed to a 'Ricarde' (Richard), mentions of the 'Northmanni' (Norsemen), and a series of moralizing and rhetorical observations on wisdom, speech, and the dangers of ignorance. The text contains several nonsensical or highly distorted phrases, such as references to 'ginger' and 'nard' and a mention of 'Lazarus'.

This section contains a highly ornate, laudatory Latin poem (likely a panegyric or a formal dedication) praising a figure named Ricardus (Richard) and his predecessor, Duke Huguinus. The text employs dense rhetorical flourishes to extol the virtues of the subjects, referencing historical figures like Scipio, Pompey, and Cato, and mentions the conquest of the Dacians and the establishment of churches.

This section contains a highly stylized, poetic, and likely liturgical or celebratory Latin text. It features a series of repetitive, alliterative descriptors for a ruler or entity, mentions the names of Rollon and William (Willelmus), and references the conquest of lands by the Normans (Nortmanni). The text also includes a list of ethnic groups including Greeks, Indians, Dacians, and Angles, and concludes with a metaphorical description of a long, arduous journey.

This section contains a series of poetic and allegorical verses, including a retelling of the myth of Daedalus and Icarus and a technical passage on musical theory (diatessaron, diapente, and proportions). The text transitions into a series of exhortations and praises directed toward the leaders of the Norman conquest, specifically addressing Rollo and the reconciliation of the 'Dacigenis' and 'Francigenis'.

This section contains a series of poetic and prophetic verses addressed to Duke Rollo, praising his merits and predicting his role as a ruler who will establish laws and peace. The text includes a metaphorical passage comparing a ship's perilous voyage through storms and 'syrtes' (sandbanks) to a state of distress, and mentions the purification of 'leprosy' through a sacred fountain.

The text begins with a poetic, highly metaphorical description of a maritime voyage and a storm, incorporating a biblical narrative of Peter's distress on the water and his interaction with Christ. It transitions into a series of theological and liturgical-style praises for the Trinity and the Holy Spirit. The final section addresses a specific individual, 'Willelme,' and offers a prophetic or celebratory address regarding the future of France and a 'luculentus' leader.

This section of the 'versus inserti' contains a series of laudatory and prophetic verses concerning a leader, specifically identifying him as 'Willelme patrici' (Patrician William) and a 'Northmannis' (Northman). The text employs heavy allegorical and religious imagery to praise his leadership over the 'Regna Gallorum' (Kingdom of the Gauls) and the 'Britones' (Britons), while condemning enemies and 'perfidies'. It includes specific references to the 'Rotome' (Rouen) and the 'Carybdis'.

This section of the text contains a series of poetic and highly stylized eulogies or hagiographic descriptions of noble figures, specifically a 'dux' (duke), 'patricius' (patrician), and 'marchio' (marquis). It includes a list of the Muses and references to a 'Ricardus' (Richard) who is associated with a 'rosea corona' (rose-colored crown). The passage blends religious imagery of martyrdom and divine favor with descriptions of aristocratic titles and virtues.

This section contains a highly stylized, dense, and likely allegorical or mystical Latin text featuring a mix of Christian and Neoplatonic imagery. It mentions Richardus (Richard), the Trinity, the Paraclete, and the figure of Sophia, while incorporating Greek terms such as 'Nous', 'Ousia', and 'Theophanes'. The text moves from a description of a 'sacred' leader to a complex theological meditation on the nature of the divine and the unity of the Trinity.

This section contains a series of highly stylized, repetitive, and arguably corrupted liturgical or laudatory verses. It mentions several names including Richardus, Willelme, and various titles such as 'Patriarcha', 'Dux', and 'Marchio'. The text references geographical locations including Sequana (the Seine), Belgicus, Aquitana, and Gaul, while employing dense, repetitive poetic structures regarding divine praise and religious devotion.

This section contains a highly corrupted and fragmented Latin text, likely a corrupted transcription or a composite of several different liturgical or poetic fragments. It mentions several names including Richardus, Hugo, and Otho, and refers to a 'Rex Haigrolde' and 'Northmanniae' (Normans). The text contains repetitive laudatory epithets for leaders and a list of people including children, old men, and virgins.

This section contains a series of highly stylized, repetitive, and arguably corrupted poetic praises and exhortations directed at a figure named Richard, identified with titles such as 'marchio', 'dux', 'patricius', and 'comes'. The text includes a series of imperative commands to flee or surrender, mentions of the 'Northmanni' (Northmen), and a concluding section of laudatory descriptors for the 'just' and 'holy'.

This section contains a series of highly stylized, repetitive panegyrics and laudations for Duke Richard (Ricardus), described with various titles such as marchio, patricius, and comes. The text includes a long list of synonyms for virtue and physical attributes, and mentions the Seine (Sequanae) and the city of Rouen (Rotome). The author, Dudo Viromandensis, includes a self-deprecating note on his own lack of eloquence while praising the Duke's role as a protector and ruler.

This section of the text contains a highly stylized, likely poetic or liturgical, Latin sequence featuring several references to historical figures such as Leodegarius, Gildebert, and the Duke of Ebroin. The passage includes a transition into a lamentation regarding death and suffering, and concludes with a series of invocations to Christ and the Trinity. The text contains several Greek words (e.g., ΘΕΩΣΙΣ, ΘΕΩΡΙΚΑ) and appears to be a complex, possibly corrupted or highly metaphorical composition.

The text is a prayer or penitential lament addressed to God (Cunctipotens). The author expresses personal distress over past sins and the passage of time, seeking purification and salvation. The final lines contain highly corrupted or corrupted Latin, mentioning 'Almiflui' and 'Coagnus' in a context that is structurally incoherent.

This medieval Latin collection, titled 'reliquiae et fragmenta', consists of liturgical poetry and devotional verses. The work is organized into three sections containing hymns, prayers, and laudatory verses. It features specific addresses to the high-ranking clerics Wulfhelmus and Dunstane (Dunstane). The text includes a series of praises for the 'Pastor apostolicus' and the 'spectator of the people of England.' Themes include Eucharistic imagery, the Trinity, and maritime safety. The final sections contain specific petitions for the English people, the removal of pestilence, and the blessing of children.

This section contains a series of poetic and liturgical verses addressed to a high-ranking cleric, identified as 'Wulfhelmus' and 'Dunstan amande'. The text includes a series of laudatory verses regarding the 'Pastor apostolicus', a section of praise for the 'spectator of the people of England' (speculator gentis Anglorum), and a concluding series of petitions and prayers for protection during a sea voyage.

This section contains a series of poetic and liturgical verses, likely a collection of hymns or a series of prayers. It features several direct addresses to a 'praesul' (prelate) named Dunstane, mentions a figure named Sigeric, and includes a repetitive refrain 'Salve sancta dies'. The text contains several heavily corrupted passages and fragments of what appear to be liturgical chants or religious poems.

This section contains a series of liturgical or devotional verses, including a recurring refrain 'Salve sancta dies' and a specific address to 'Dunstane'. The text includes a hymn to the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit), a prayer for the English people ('gentis Anglicae'), and a plea for the removal of pestilence and the blessing of the church's children.

This 10th-century medieval Latin work, 'ecbasis captivi', is a complex literary exercise characterized by dense allegorical and moralizing poetry. The text is structured into several distinct movements, beginning with a pastoral scene in Vosaginis involving a speaking calf and the deity Jupiter. It transitions through various allegorical cycles featuring recurring animal figures such as the fox (vulpes), leopard (pardus), and a parrot (Psytacus). The narrative incorporates diverse settings, including Rome, the rivers Hrenus and Ticinus, and the regions of Swvarzvvalt and Alemannica. Notable figures and themes include the Passion of Christ, the Queen of Sheb, and the feast of Saint Severinus, alongside references to figures like Catonus, Malchi, and Luter. The work blends pastoral, military, and liturgical imagery with moral philosophy and mystical reflections.

The text is a medieval Latin literary exercise or allegorical poem featuring a narrator reflecting on his past and the craft of poetry. It transitions into a narrative involving a calf (vitulus) in a pastoral setting near Vosaginis, which eventually speaks and addresses Jupiter. The passage includes elements of moral instruction, descriptions of pastoral life, and a dialogue between the calf and a divine figure.

This section contains a series of dense, likely allegorical or poetic verses involving a feast, a journey, and a confrontation. It mentions specific locations like Rome and the river Hrenus, and includes a list of food items (mullus, trutta, etc.) and a reference to the figure of Pluto. The text transitions from a description of a banquet and a master's speech to a scene involving a cave, a struggle against beasts (wasps, hornets), and a warning about sleep and danger.

This section of the 'ecbasis captivi' contains a series of dense, allegorical, and potentially satirical verses involving a variety of imagery: a calf, a fox, a priest (Archicapellanus), and a barbarian guest. It features a transition from pastoral and pastoral-adjacent imagery to a scene of military conflict involving cavalry and infantry, as well as a reference to the biblical figure Esau.

This section of the 'ecbasis captivi' contains a series of allegorical and symbolic exchanges involving figures such as a fox (vulpes), a pard (panther), and a lion. The text features a dialogue regarding a 'medicine of life,' a legal decree (edictum), and a journey involving locations like Rome and the Ticinus river. It concludes with a series of mystical or moralizing statements regarding the 'law of the cross' and the 'climate of the world.'

This section contains a series of disjointed, likely allegorical or satirical verses involving a fox, a prince, and a monk named Malchi. The text shifts between descriptions of a banquet with various foods (bread, beans, fish, and wine), a legalistic warning regarding a 'vicar' and 'senate,' and a description of a garden or orchard. It concludes with a scene of a girl playing a lyre and a house decorated with flowers.

This section contains a series of disconnected, often surrealist or allegorical verses. It features imagery of a palace, a feast involving fish and meat, and a list of animals (leopard, monkey, wolf, deer) interspersed with moralizing statements on prudence, friendship, and the duties of masters and servants. It mentions the poet Catonus, the river Indus, and a cave named 'Teutonice Stensile'.

This section of the text contains a series of allegorical and metaphorical verses involving a fox (vulpes) and a leopard (pardus) in a courtly or royal setting. It includes references to the Queen of Sheba, Solomon, and the biblical figures Gabriel and Emmanuel, alongside a transition into a liturgical or devotional meditation on the Passion of Christ and the Eucharist.

This section contains a series of dramatic and allegorical dialogues, likely from a liturgical or dramatic play, involving a 'Doctor of the Church' and a figure suffering in a state of 'exile' or 'prison.' The text transitions into a symbolic scene featuring a 'Psytacus' (parrot) and a 'Cignus' (swan) interacting with two kings and a military context. It concludes with a reference to the feast of Saint Severinus and a collective movement toward a holy abode.

This section of the text contains a series of poetic and allegorical verses involving a fox (vulpes) and a leopard (pardus) in a narrative involving a king, a feast, and a journey. It includes a sequence of liturgical-style praises, a reference to a 'virgin John' (virgo Iohannes), and a transition to a scene where a leopard leads birds to western parts and writes an epitaph. The text also mentions the 'Swvarzvvalt' and the 'Alemannica' regions.

This section of the 'ecbasis captivi' contains a series of allegorical and moralizing verses involving a fox, a wolf, and a man named Luter. The text includes a dialogue regarding a 'sacred' counsel, a description of a siege or capture of a camp, and a concluding section featuring a mother's address and a reference to a 'sotium' (perhaps a musical instrument or a specific figure).

This passage contains a series of disparate, seemingly disconnected verses or fragments. It mentions a figure named Luther, the deity Bacchus, the biblical figure Herod, and concludes with a religious doxology to Christ. The text also includes a numerical calculation of 1,170 years and a concluding statement of silence.

The ecloga Theoduli is a 9th-century Latin work composed of three sections featuring a dense weave of mythological, biblical, and allegorical imagery. The first section contains a dialogue between Pseustus and Alithia followed by a sequence of figures including Saturn, Cecrops, Licaon, Deucalion, and Ganymede, alongside biblical figures such as Cain, Abel, Abraham, Lot, and Noah. The second section presents cryptic poetic fragments and vignettes featuring Hippolytus, Cadmus, Proserpina, Moses, Samson, Elijah, King Ezechias, Jeremiah, and Achilles, alongside mystical imagery. The final section includes Medea, Proserpina, Mopso, Daniel, and Olofernes, referencing the city of Edessa. The work concludes with a formal hymn praising God as ruler over heaven, earth, sea, and Tartarus.

The text contains a series of disparate mythological, biblical, and allegorical scenes. It features a dialogue between a shepherd named Pseustus and a woman named Alithia, followed by a sequence of mythological figures (Saturn, Cecrops, Licaon, Deucalion, Ganymede), biblical figures (Cain, Abel, Abraham, Lot, Noah), and various mythological entities (the Leviathan, the Cyclopes, and the goddess Cytherea).

This section contains a series of disparate, often cryptic poetic fragments and allegorical vignettes. It features mythological figures such as Hippolytus, Cadmus, and Proserpina, alongside biblical figures including Moses, Samson, and Elijah. The text also references historical or legendary figures like King Ezechias, the prophet Jeremiah, and the hero Achilles (Alcides), interspersed with descriptions of natural phenomena and mystical imagery.

This section of the ecloga contains a series of poetic and allegorical verses featuring mythological figures such as Medea, Proserpina, and Mopso, as well as biblical and historical references to Daniel, Olofernes, and the city of Edessa. The text weaves together themes of divine judgment, the nature of virtue, and the physical world, concluding with a formal hymn of praise to God as the ruler of heaven, earth, sea, and Tartarus.

This Latin medieval text is a hagiographic and dramatic work structured in four parts, focusing on the themes of exorcism, martyrdom, and the power of Christ. The narrative begins with a dialogue in Rome between an exorcist named Peter and a jailer named Artemius regarding the salvation of the jailer's daughter. The subsequent sections depict the miraculous appearances and trials of Saint Peter and the martyr Marcellinus presbyter. These figures are shown performing exorcisms, enduring imprisonment by a 'savage judge,' and facing physical torment. The text includes a miraculous intervention by an angel and the inclusion of specific figures such as the woman Candida, the Roman women Lucilla and Firmina, and the convert Dorotheus. The work concludes with the ritual handling of the martyrs' bodies and the conversion of a former persecutor.

The text recounts a dialogue between a Roman exorcist named Peter and a jailer named Artemius. Peter, who preaches the faith of Christ, attempts to convince Artemius to believe in Christ's power to save Artemius's daughter, who is tormented by a demon. The passage concludes with a description of the jailer's internal conflict and his wife's skepticism regarding the power of Christ.

The text describes a miraculous appearance of Saint Peter and the martyr Marcellinus presbyter. Peter is depicted performing exorcisms and gathering a large crowd of men and women to witness the power of Christ, while Marcellinus is shown in a prison setting defending his faith against a 'savage judge' who attempts to break his resolve through threats of physical torment.

This section depicts a dramatic confrontation between the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter and their captors, including a judge and a crowd. The text describes the martyrs' defiance against their persecutors, the physical binding of the martyrs with chains to tree stumps, and a miraculous intervention involving an angel. It also mentions a woman named Candida and the presence of a crowd of Christians.

The text recounts the martyrdom of saints, specifically mentioning the figures of Marcellinus and Peter, and the Roman women Lucilla and Firmina. It describes the physical suffering of the martyrs, the ritual handling of their bodies by clerics, and the conversion of a man named Dorotheus who had previously persecuted them.

This 9th-century collection of Latin poems by Engelmodus consists of four distinct sections of lyrical and occasional verse. The first part contains a dialogue on friendship and modesty, a passage on the Eucharist and sacred names, and references to the poet Empedocles and the regions of Boeotia and Ismenia. The second and third sections feature dense allegorical and metaphorical praise, utilizing pontifical imagery, sacred objects, and nature motifs to describe piety, the Virgin, and the kingdom of heaven. The final section transitions from descriptions of divine light to the physical suffering of a captive, concluding with a plea for intercession against hell and a reference to Liberius. The work moves from classical and geographical references to highly ornate religious and mystical themes.

This collection of poems contains a series of varied lyrical and occasional verses. The text includes a dialogue on friendship and modesty, a passage referencing the Eucharist and sacred names, and a section featuring mythological and geographical references such as Boeotia, Ismenia, and the poet Empedocles. It also contains a sequence of shorter, more abstract verses involving themes of love, nature, and social status.

This section of the carmina contains a series of highly ornate, metaphorical praises and religious exhortations. The text employs dense allegorical imagery involving sacred objects (mitres, incense, trumpets), celestial and pastoral motifs, and references to religious figures and roles such as the 'holy father' and 'pontiffs'.

This section of the carmina contains a series of highly ornate, allegorical verses describing the virtues of a pious individual, the sanctity of the Virgin, and the spiritual rewards of the kingdom of heaven. The text employs dense metaphorical imagery involving nature (flowers, honey, vines), celestial bodies, and religious symbols to contrast holy devotion with worldly lust and intellectual vanity. It concludes with a series of dense, abstract descriptions of spiritual elevation and the divine order.

The text is a religious poem featuring a transition from a description of divine glory and light to a depiction of the physical suffering of a captive or sinner bound by chains. It concludes with a plea to a holy figure (sancte) to intercede against the perils of hell and a final, somewhat obscure reference to 'Liberius' and a journey toward fields.

This is a Latin funerary inscription (epitaphium) for an individual named Gozlinus. The text identifies Gozlinus as a 'domini praesul' and 'verbique lucerna,' likely a title of local authority or scholarly distinction. The poem employs metaphorical language regarding his transition to the afterlife, mentioning 'aethereis' and 'caelos.' It references his 'virtutum stemmis' and his 'actibus' regarding 'iuris apostolici.' The text includes a specific date of death or transition: the sixth of May and the tenth day before the Kalends. The final lines are a plea for his presence or a traditional exhortation to a traveler.

A Latin funerary inscription (epitaphium) dating to the 9th century, dedicated to a man named Heinricus. The text identifies the deceased as 'magni Francorum germinis alti,' suggesting a high-ranking lineage or status among the Franks. The poem employs complex, possibly alliterative or rhythmic structures, and references a 'triarch' (triarchos) associated with the Saxons, the Francis (Franks), and the Fresonibus. The text contains religious invocations to Christ and the Virgin, and mentions a 'sign of the Lion' (signa Leonis) in relation to justice. The final lines lament the death of the man, shifting from the mourning of his status to the mourning of his personhood.

This 9th-century medieval Latin collection, aevi Karolini by epitaphia varia, consists of a series of funerary inscriptions and epitaphs. The work is organized into three parts, each containing a distinct set of commemorative texts. Part 1 features the figures Armannus of Lauson, Almannus, Reinoldus, Hildegarde, Atanasius, and Fridricus, with references to Lugdunum and Saint Maurice. Part 2 commemorates a prince of France, Egino of Verona, Hrotrohc, Irmingart, and Hildgrimus, focusing on virtues and ecclesiastical roles. Part 3 contains inscriptions for Thidgrim, Geroldus, Abbas (Avo), and Walburg, including mentions of monastery foundations and specific calendar dates.

This collection of funerary inscriptions and epitaphs commemorates several individuals, including Armannus (a bishop of Lauson), Almannus (a scholar), Reinoldus and his sister Hildegarde, the monk Atanasius, and Fridricus. The texts include mentions of specific locations such as Lugdunum (Lyon) and the French territories, and reference religious figures like Saint Maurice and the Pope.

This collection of medieval Latin epitaphs commemorates various figures including a prince of France, a priest named Egino of Verona, a scholar named Hrotrohc, and a woman named Irmingart. The texts include funerary praises for a bishop, a mention of a tomb in a palace, and a specific reference to a man named Hildgrimus. The passages vary in focus from personal virtues and literary skill to the physical state of the remains and the specific dates of death.

This section contains a series of funerary inscriptions and epitaphs for various individuals, including Thidgrim, Geroldus (a Levite), Abbas (named Avo), and Walburg. The texts include prayers for rest, mentions of monastery foundations, and references to specific dates such as the Ides of September and the tenth of May.

This 9th-century Latin text is a collection of funerary inscriptions (epitaphia) and memorial verses. The primary subject is an abbot of the name H. (possibly a placeholder or abbreviation) who is described as a priest, monk, and protector of the Senones. The text includes a specific mention of a figure named Magingodus and a reference to a person named Paul (Paulus). The inscriptions employ standard medieval hagiographic and funerary tropes, including themes of mortality, the fleeting nature of earthly glory, and the hope for eternal rest in the celestial realm. The work contains several distinct segments, some of which appear to be distinct epitaphs or variations on common liturgical and funerary formulas.

A 9th-century collection of medieval Latin funerary inscriptions and commemorative verses. The text is organized into twelve sections, each containing a series of epitaphs for various individuals including royalty, clergy, and nobility. Notable figures mentioned include Queen Gerberga, Emperor Otto III, and various prelates such as Geberhardus and Winfrid. Geographic references include Rome, Cologne, Trier, Fulda, and the city of Danis. The content alternates between biographical notes on titles and lineages, liturgical-style prayers, and poetic laments on mortality. Themes include monastic life, the Benedictine Rule, and the virtues of the deceased.

This collection of funerary inscriptions and epitaphs commemorates several figures, including Otto, a man named by the name of his father Heinrich, and a queen named Gerberga. The texts mention historical and biblical figures such as David, Solomon, Ezechias, and Josiah, while also referencing local figures like the priest Adso and the king Lotharius. The inscriptions describe architectural features, military triumphs, and the virtues of the deceased.

This section contains a series of funerary inscriptions and commemorative verses for several individuals, including Machtilth, Erenfrid, Fredericus, Bernhard, and Liudricus. The text mentions specific roles such as a 'praesul' (prelate), a 'dux' (duke), and a 'monachus' (monk), while referencing religious themes like the Rule of Benedict and the transition from earthly life to divine rest.

This collection of funerary inscriptions and epitaphs commemorates various individuals including the child Durandus, the knight Ratger, the monk Ricfridus (Dodo), the abbot Theitfridus, and the noblewoman Machtildis. The texts record specific dates of death, familial lineages (such as the house of Balduin), and ecclesiastical roles. Notable locations and figures mentioned include the cathedral of Tungren, the city of Danis, and the names of several saints or local figures like Folquinus and Gofrid.

This section contains a collection of funerary inscriptions and commemorative verses for various individuals, including a 'Bruno' (described as peaceful and pious), 'Megengaudus' (married to Gerbirga), and 'Irmindrudis'. The texts include liturgical-style prayers, references to the 'father of the country' (pater patriae), and mentions of specific locations like Cologne and Rome. The entries vary in style, ranging from poetic lamentations on death to formal records of titles and lineage.

This section contains a series of funerary inscriptions and commemorative verses for various individuals, including Drogo, Deodericus, Evrardus, Arnulfus, Sendebaldus, and Wolpertus. The texts mention specific locations such as Metten and the Alps, and reference historical figures like Emperor Charles and the Ottonian dynasty. The passages alternate between praising the virtues of the deceased, describing their roles as priests or leaders, and offering liturgical-style prayers for their souls.

This section contains a collection of funerary inscriptions and memorial verses for various clergy and holy figures, including Winfrid, Liutwinus, Egbertus, Ruothildis, and Willerus. It mentions specific locations such as Fulda and the Diocese of Trier, and records dates of death and specific titles like 'Archimandritae' and 'Presul'. The text also includes a brief mention of a 'Vroldus' as a builder and a reference to the 'Moguntinensis' (Mainz) prelate.

This section contains a series of funerary inscriptions and commemorative verses for various clergy and figures, including the bishops Wilhelm, Geupaldus, and the martyr Kiliane. It mentions specific locations and figures such as the Wormatians, the city of Richgowo, and individuals named Liudolphus, Hildeboldus, and Erchanfridus. The text alternates between elegiac reflections on mortality and specific biographical notes on the offices and deeds of the deceased.

This section contains a series of funerary inscriptions and commemorative verses for several individuals, including the bishop Geberhardus (presul herilis), a monk named Notkerus, and a man named Stephen (Stephani). The text includes liturgical-style praises for the deceased, mentions of specific dates (such as the Ides of November and the month of March), and references to figures like the Virgin Mary and the prophetess Sibyl (Sobeonis).

This section contains a series of funerary inscriptions and commemorative verses for various religious and political figures. It mentions Pope Benedict, King Gonradus, Emperor Otto III, and a figure named Sergius (formerly of Damascus), while also referencing the construction of a monastery and the burial of Landolfus.

This section contains a series of funerary inscriptions and commemorative verses for various individuals, including Crescentius, Theodora, Bonifatius, and others. It mentions specific locations such as Rome, Naples, and Capua, and identifies figures such as the monk Landolfus and the prince of Benevento. The text includes liturgical-style prayers for mercy, descriptions of the deceased's virtues, and genealogical notes.

This section contains a collection of funerary inscriptions and epitaphs for various individuals, including the figures Rofrit, Adelferus, Adalmanus, Hubertus, and Vberto. The texts mention specific locations such as the city of Firmensum and the Diocese of Rome, and include religious invocations, descriptions of the deceased's virtues, and mentions of specific dates and titles.

This section contains a series of funerary inscriptions and epitaphs. It includes a memorial for a man named Fridericus, who lived sixty years and is associated with the suppression of the 'wrath of Pannonia' and the peace of Italy; a passage regarding the establishment of clergy; and a longer, more complex lament or poetic text involving a figure named Vgo (or Vgo. dux) and references to Rome and a marble tomb.

This 9th-century Latin martyrology, attributed to Erchembertus Casinensis, provides a structured calendar of saints' feast days. The text follows a chronological progression through the liturgical year, identifying specific saints associated with the Roman calendar markers such as the Kalends, Nones, and Ides. Notable figures included in the list are Polycarp, Eustatius, Boniface, and various martyrs such as Stephen and Euphimia. The work also incorporates specific local or regional figures like Cuthberth and Wilfrid, as well as mentions of the Virgin Mary and the dedication of churches. The text concludes by noting that the order of these feasts is explicitly set forth by Bede.

This 9th-century Latin devotional and liturgical poem by Ermenricus Elwangensis is structured in two distinct movements. The first part consists of hymns and prayers focused on the Trinity and a plea for divine guidance, concluding with a geographical and mythological survey of the Alps, the Rhine, and the lands of the Tyrrhenians and Sicanians. The second part continues the geographical focus on the Rhine (Rhenus) and the territories of the Franks, Chamaves, and the Hister. It then shifts to a literary defense where the author addresses Homer directly to advocate for a simpler poetic style. The work concludes with a series of classical and mythological references involving the Dardanids, Troy, and the Pelasgians.

The text is a devotional and liturgical poem addressed to God and the saints, featuring a series of hymns and prayers. It includes a theological meditation on the Trinity (trinum specimen, una in personis par tribus), a plea for divine guidance, and a concluding geographical and mythological passage describing the Alps, the Rhine, and the lands of the Tyrrhenians and Sicanians.

The text contains a poetic description of the Rhine River (Rhenus) and its surrounding geography, mentioning the tribes of the Hister, the Rhine, and the lands of the Franks and Chamaves. It transitions into a literary defense of the author's style, where he addresses Homer directly to request a simpler, more accessible form of verse. The passage concludes with a list of mythological and classical references including the Dardanids, Troy, and the Pelasgians.

A medieval Latin carmina (song or poem) attributed to Ermoldus Nigellus. The text is structured as a series of stanzas featuring a recurring refrain regarding a child's instruction and the gathering of gifts. It contains references to historical and geographical figures including King Pippin, the Pope Ebo, and the queen Himiltrud. Geographical locations mentioned include Rome, France, the Rhine (Rhenus), the Seine (Sequana), and the Jordan River. The poem incorporates themes of religious devotion, the passage of time, and the physical construction of holy sites. It also references classical and biblical elements, such as the Muses, the laws of Moses, and the works of Caton.

This 9th-century Latin panegyric by Ermoldus Nigellus is dedicated to the Carolingian ruler Hludowicus (Louis the Pious). The work is structured as a multi-part narrative combining historical praise, military chronicle, and liturgical-style poetry. The initial sections detail the piety of the King and military victories over the Moors and Wascones, featuring figures such as Carolus and Vilhelm in the defense of cities like Barcelona and Cordoba. Middle sections transition into ritualized dialogues and allegorical exhortations involving the priest Stephanus and the monk Benedictus. The final portions incorporate historical and mythological allusions, including Romulus and Remus, alongside descriptions of royal processions and hunting scenes. A secondary layer of the text describes a royal hunt, the distribution of land and vestments to the clergy, a visionary experience involving a priest (possibly Theutrammus), and a poetic address to Judith regarding imperial authority.

This section of the poem is a panegyric for the Carolingian ruler Hludowicus (Louis the Pious). It praises his piety, his military victories over the Moors and the Wascones, and his role as a successor to the Frankish throne. The text also includes a list of classical and medieval authors (Maro, Naso, Cicero, etc.) and references to the geography of the Frankish realm and the Iberian Peninsula.

The text describes a military and political consultation involving King Carolus (Charles), the Duke of Tolosa (Vilhelmus), and the leader Lupus. They discuss military strategy against the Moors, the defense of territories like Aquitaine, and the fortification of cities. The passage also mentions the roles of Bigo and the naming of a figure named Concas.

This section of the poem describes a military conflict involving the forces of King Carolus (Charles) and the character Datus against a Moorish force. It names specific leaders such as Vilhelm, Heripreth, Lihuthard, and Bero (or Bigoque), and mentions the city of Barcelona. The narrative includes a dialogue regarding a horse and a mother, a siege of a fortress, and a call to the Frankish forces to defend the walls.

This section of the poem describes a military confrontation between a Frankish force and a Moorish force (referred to as 'Mauri') at a fortified city. It features specific named figures such as Hilthiberth, Vilhelm, and the leader Zado, and mentions the city of Cordoba. The text depicts a siege involving the defense of walls, the use of siege engines, and the eventual capture of a king.

The text describes a military conflict between the Franks and the Moors, featuring the capture of a Moorish figure named Zado (or Zadun) and the subsequent victory of the Frankish forces. It depicts the siege of a city, the surrender of the Moors, and a subsequent celebration involving King Hludowicus (Ludovicus). The narrative concludes with a series of interactions involving figures such as Carolus, Paulinus, and Pippinus, and the presentation of spoils and captives.

The text contains a series of poetic and liturgical verses concerning the reign of Carolus (Charlemagne) and the transition of power. It mentions specific figures including Pippin, Carolus, Paulinus, and the prophet Heinardus, and references locations such as the river Ligeris and the land of the Franks. The passage describes a scene of royal devotion, the naming of the Frankish kingdom, and a transition of imperial authority.

This section of the poem describes the actions and virtues of King Louis (Hludowicus) and the figure Carolus, including the distribution of wealth to the poor and the church. It features a procession of clergy and people, mentions specific locations such as Paris and the Alps (Olympo), and references figures such as the martyr Stephen (Stephanus) and the virgin Genevefa. The text also depicts a scene of royal reception, the gathering of a council, and the preparation of a religious and civic order.

The text depicts a dialogue and interaction between a figure named Caesar (or a person addressed as Caesar) and a holy man or priest named Stephanus. It contains a series of poetic and liturgical-style exhortations regarding the governance of the Church, the duties of the clergy, and the history of Israel as a model for the current Christian order. The passage includes references to the 'kingdom of the Franks' and the 'kingdom of the blessed polish' (possibly a corruption of 'polus' or 'pauper').

This section of the poem describes a ritualized interaction between a high-ranking figure (referred to as a priest and a king) and a ruler (Caesar). It includes a dialogue regarding the authority of Saint Peter, a formal exchange of gifts and honors involving gold and garments, and a series of invocations to Christ, the apostles, and Mary. The text mentions specific figures such as Peter, Paul, John, and the name 'Irmingart'.

This section of the poem describes the spiritual and administrative life of a holy man named Benedictus, who is characterized as a shepherd, abbot, and teacher. It details the organization of monastic life, the distribution of duties among monks, and the relationship between the monastic order and the secular authority of the Emperor (referred to as Caesar or Hludowicus). The text also mentions a specific location associated with water and a transition of leadership or rule.

The text depicts a dialogue and interaction between characters named Lantpreht (or Lantbertus), Caesar (Hludowicus), and Wichart (or Witchar/Wiccharius) regarding the defense of lands and the state of the Frankish people. It describes a military and political situation involving the defense of borders, the collection of tribute, and a specific encounter between Murman and Wichart in a location characterized by forests and rivers.

This section contains a dialogue between the characters Wicchar and Murman regarding a peace treaty with the Franks. The text includes a formal exchange of demands concerning taxes, territory, and the status of the British kingdom, interspersed with a description of a ritual or feast involving a woman and a man. It concludes with a declaration of the King of the Franks' status.

The text describes a military campaign involving Caesar, who moves through territories including the Loire (Ligeris) and the Rhine (Rheni) to confront the Franks, Saxons, and Suevi. It features a series of direct addresses to individuals such as Matfride, Saepius, and others, and depicts the movement of troops toward cities like Vicus and the defense of churches. The narrative concludes with a commander named Acer preparing for battle and a final address regarding the protection of family and the acquisition of spoils.

This section describes a violent martial encounter between two figures, Murman and Francis (or a Frank), involving a spear (cuspis) and a sword (ensis). The narrative includes a dialogue regarding a 'gift' and a 'promise,' followed by a physical struggle where Murman is struck and his head is severed. The text concludes with the identification of the severed head and the arrival of the 'genus Murmanis' (the kin of Murman) following the death of the combatants.

The text describes a formal ceremony where a leader (referred to as Caesar) receives the oath of office from a figure named Brittonica and rewards his followers. It depicts a legal and military dispute involving a man named Bero, who is accused of seeking royal power and is confronted by a man named Sanilo before a royal court. The narrative concludes with a scene of military preparation and a final act of mercy by Caesar toward a defeated opponent.

This section of the poem contains a series of allegorical and religious exhortations involving figures such as Pippinus, Ebo, and a figure referred to as Caesar. It contrasts Christian faith with pagan worship of Neptune and Jupiter, mentions the conversion of the Franks, and describes a transition from old rituals to new dogmas. The text also references the land of the Britons and the actions of a leader (possibly a king) seeking to secure his kingdom.

This section of the poem describes a military scene involving the leaders Matfrid and Lantpertus, and the figures Pippin and Ebo, who is described as a priest of the northern realms. The narrative then shifts to a religious and allegorical sequence involving the life of Christ, the Virgin Mary, the flight to Egypt, and the construction of a temple near the Rhine. It concludes with a series of biblical and mythological allusions involving the Magi, Herod, and the deeds of Cyrus.

This section of the poem contains a series of historical and mythological allusions, including the founding of Rome by Romulus and Remus, the conquests of Hannibal, and the transition of the Roman capital to Constantinople under Constantine. It transitions into a narrative involving figures named Caesar, Heroldus, and Judith, and includes a religious discourse on the Trinity and the baptism of a figure named Herold. The text also references local and regional elements such as the Rhine river, the lands of the Franks, and the leadership of Pippin and the Carolingian dynasty.

This section of the poem describes a ceremonial procession and feast involving figures such as Caesar, Heroldus, Judith, and Hluttharius. It details the ornate golden and jeweled attire of the participants, the preparation of food and drink (including a reference to Bacchus), and a subsequent hunting expedition through a forest. The text concludes with the sounding of trumpets and the scattering of wild beasts.

This section of the poem describes a royal hunt and subsequent feast involving Caesar (Louis IX) and his retinue, including the character Heroldus. It details the distribution of spoils such as deer, wild boar, and capreolus, and concludes with Caesar granting lands, wine, and sacred vestments to Heroldus and the clergy.

The text describes a mystical or visionary experience involving a priest (possibly Theutrammus) and three men in white robes who appear in a sacred space. It includes a transition from a description of a celestial vision—featuring an altar with gold and gems—to a scene of divine intervention involving thunder and light. The passage concludes with a personal address to 'Caesar' and a concluding stanza by Ermoldus Nigellus regarding the virtues of Christ.

The text contains a poetic address to Judith, who is described as a noble wife holding the heights of the empire by right. The speaker addresses a legal or moral situation involving a crime and a state of exile, calling for the release of a prisoner and the honoring of Judith's status.

This 9th-century Latin poem by Ermoldus Nigellus is a royal panegyric composed in honor of King Pippin. The work is structured into four distinct movements: an opening invocation to the Muse Thalia and a description of a royal procession; a series of laudatory verses incorporating classical and biblical allusions; a moralizing and theological meditation on the Carolingian dynasty; and a concluding personal address to the King and his wife, Irmgart. The text features specific geographical references to the Rhine (Rhenus), Strasbourg (Strazbrum), and the land of Helisaz. It incorporates references to the poets Virgil and Maro, as well as biblical figures such as John, Peter, Paul, Saul, and David.
