The text contains a series of highly alliterative and rhythmic Latin verses, likely a poetic exercise or a collection of moralizing and mystical imagery. It features a speaker addressing 'brothers' regarding the divine, the world's elements, and the dangers of the 'hostis' (enemy). The passage concludes with a reference to the prayer of Wilfrid and a final note to the reader.

A collection of medieval Latin poems and verses by Froumundus, organized into ten distinct sections. The work transitions between pastoral laments, liturgical-style praises, and moral exhortations, featuring a mix of religious and secular themes. Notable figures include the abbot Hartvvicus, the apostle Paul, and local figures such as Liutold, Ellinger, and the Duke Henricus. The text incorporates pastoral allegories, biblical narratives (such as the resurrection of the widow's son), and panegyrics for rulers like Duke Henry and Prince Brono. Specific locations mentioned include Treveris, while the later sections employ martial imagery and hagiographic lists. The collection concludes with a blend of imperial praise, Christology, and polemical critiques of intellectual failings.

This collection of poems and verses includes a pastoral lament, a memorial for a monk named Hartvvicus (the abbot of a local site), and a series of religious and lyrical verses. The text mentions specific figures such as the abbot of Hartvvici, the apostle Paul, and a figure named Liutold, while referencing locations like Treveris. The content shifts between liturgical-style praise, personal devotion, and descriptions of spiritual transformation.

This section of the poems by Froumundus contains a series of varied verses including a dialogue regarding the division of property and the care of the sick, a series of moralizing and religious exhortations, and a pastoral allegory involving a wolf, a shepherd, and a flock of sheep. The text mentions specific figures such as Froumundus, Liutoldo, and a figure identified as Ilisa, and includes a concluding section on the nature of letters and names.

This section of the carmina contains a series of panegyrics and religious invocations, specifically addressing a 'Dux' (Duke) named Henricus. It includes a list of the twelve apostles (Petrus, Paulus, Andreas, Thomas, Iohannes, Philippus, Bartholomei, Mathee, Tadhee, and others) and concludes with a series of poetic exhortations and personal reflections on faith, leadership, and the nature of poetry.

This section of the carmina contains a series of addresses and salutations to various figures, including Duke Henry, Prince Brono, and several named individuals such as Gotahardus, Wigo, Perngerus, and Gotafridus. It features a transition from a satirical or mocking tone regarding a 'servant' and a 'fool' to a formal, laudatory address of rulers and the 'people of Augustus.' The text concludes with a formal closing and a list of greetings to the author's peers and associates.

This section contains a series of poems and religious reflections by Froumundus, including a lament on mortality, a dialogue with a peer (Ellinger), and a series of biblical paraphrases. The text includes a narrative of the resurrection of the widow's son at Nain, a scene involving a Pharisee and a man with an ulcer, and a healing of a man in a bed. It concludes with a personal address to a 'Father Perenger' regarding the composition of verses.
topics: Healing of the Man with an Ulcer

summary: This section of Froumundus's poems contains a series of lyrical and religious verses addressing 'brothers' and 'children' (pueri). It includes a personal address to a brother named George, a lamentation over lost work and 'blind' eyes, and a series of religious invocations involving figures such as David, Herod, and Eudochias. The text concludes with a liturgical-style plea for the forgiveness of sins through the blood of Christ.

This section contains a series of religious and panegyric verses addressed to a 'Caesar' (likely a contemporary ruler), blending themes of Christology, the crucifixion, and imperial praise. It includes specific invocations to Saint Peter, Saint Kilian, and a reference to the 'Ellinger' family or a specific individual named Ellinger. The text concludes with a series of personal prayers and a concluding note regarding the transcription of scripture.

This section of the carmina contains a series of laudatory and didactic verses regarding a religious figure, likely a monk or priest, who is praised for his piety, teaching of scripture, and mastery of grammar. The text transitions into a series of moral exhortations and a sharp, polemical critique of a specific individual's intellectual failings and perceived blasphemy. It mentions specific figures or concepts such as Plato, Labeon, and the goddess Diana.

This section of the poem contains a series of confrontational and polemical verses directed at an unnamed opponent, utilizing imagery of warfare, martial prowess, and divine protection. It features a long list of Christian and hagiographic names, including Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, Paul, Stephen, Kilian, Quirinus, Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine, as well as a reference to the biblical figures David and Jonathan. The text also references mythological figures like Hercules and Pluto, and mentions specific regional or cultural identifiers such as 'Saxconicus' and 'Noricus'.

This section of the carmina contains a series of martial and religious exhortations, utilizing military imagery such as cohorts, spears, and captives. The text transitions from a confrontational, almost aggressive dialogue regarding victory and defeat to a concluding passage invoking the name of the Lord and the planting of a 'divine land'.

A Latin poem by Fulbertus Carnotensis concerning the nightingale (luscinia). The text describes the awakening of nature in spring, specifically the budding of leaves and branches and the fragrance of flowers in the grass. It focuses on the bird Philomela, whose singing is compared to the clarity of a cithara. The poem describes the bird's song captivating a flock of birds and filling the woods and shrubs. The final stanzas contrast the earthly beauty of the bird's melody with the sovereignty of the celestial King who rules all things.

A brief Latin and and verse of praise (versus) composed by Gerwardus. The author identifies himself as a 'supplex famulus' (supplicating servant) and addresses a 'princeps' (prince or ruler). The text contains a formal dedication of praise to the memory of Einhardus Magnus and Karolus (Charlemagne). The poem utilizes a rhyming structure to exalt their names to the stars. The work functions as a commemorative or dedicatory piece of medieval Latin poetry.

This medieval Latin hagiography, composed by Gerardus Suessionensis, recounts the life and sanctity of Romanus, the Bishop of Romagen (Rothomagus). The work is structured into five parts: the first details the holy man's spiritual preparation and official consecration under a Frankish king; the second describes his purification of Rothomagus by destroying a temple of Venus and purging the city of paganism and prostitution. The third section provides poetic verses on the destruction of idols (Jupiter, Apollo, Diana) and describes the liturgical vestments of the episcopacy. The fourth part focuses on mystical and liturgical scenes involving anointing, the Eucharist, and the transition from physical suffering to spiritual exaltation. The final section concludes with a poetic eulogy for Romanus and mentions his successor, Audoenus.

The text describes the life and divine selection of a holy man named Benedict (later identified as the Bishop of Romagen) during the reign of a Frankish king. It details his spiritual preparation, his role as a 'signifer' and 'pastor' of the flock, and the formal process of his election and installation as a prelate. The narrative includes a transition from his personal devotion to his public role as a leader of the Church, culminating in his official investiture and the celebration of his office.

The text describes the spiritual and physical victory of the Bishop of Romans (Romanus) over paganism and moral decay in the city of Rothomagus. It details the destruction of a temple of Venus, the removal of idols, and the purification of the city from 'meretrician' (prostitute) influence. The narrative employs biblical parallels, specifically comparing the Bishop's actions to Joshua's conquest of Jericho and the miracle of the crossing of the Jordan.

This section of the hagiography of Saint Roman of Romagna contains a series of poetic verses describing the destruction of pagan idols (Jupiter, Apollo, Diana) and the establishment of a Christian temple. It further details the liturgical vestments and symbolic attributes of a bishop, including the pallium, the miter, and the crozier, while incorporating scriptural and allegorical imagery regarding the Passion of Christ and the virtues of the clergy.

This section of the hagiography of Roman of Romagna describes a series of liturgical and mystical scenes involving a holy figure (the 'athlete of God') and a 'holy father' (sanctus pater). It depicts ritual actions such as anointing with holy oil, the distribution of sacraments, and a transition from a state of physical suffering or 'pestilence' to spiritual exaltation. The text incorporates heavy metaphorical and poetic imagery regarding the soul's journey, the sanctity of the altar, and the physical sensations of religious devotion.

This section of the hagiography of Romanus of Rothomagus concludes with a poetic and metaphorical eulogy of the saint's life and virtues. It mentions the successor to his pontificate, Audoenus, and concludes with a formal prayer for Romanus to serve as a guide to the heavens. The text employs high-style Latin verse to describe his spiritual integrity, his role as a shepherd, and his transition to the celestial realm.

This 10th-century Latin medieval text, titled 'gesta Apollonii', is a dramatic narrative featuring a mixture of liturgical elements, mythological references, and historical-style conflict. The work is organized into seven sections, beginning with a communal prayer to the Trinity and the Virgin before moving into a courtly drama involving a king named Antiochus and a woman accused of a crime. The narrative follows the character Apollonius, who engages in a series of confrontations with the king, including a scandalous speech regarding a shared past and a common spouse. The setting moves between the cities of Antioch and Tyre, involving military movements, maritime voyages, and diplomatic negotiations involving a messenger named Taliarchus. The final sections incorporate poetic alliteration and mythological figures such as Mars and Saturn, though the concluding passages are significantly corrupted by transcription errors. Key themes include the tension between royal authority and personal accusation, the transition from war to ritual, and the interplay between sacred and profane spaces.

The text begins with a liturgical or communal prayer involving a 'brother' and a 'sodalis' (companion) invoking the Trinity and the Virgin. It then transitions into a narrative involving a king named Antiochus and a woman (a 'virgin' or 'lady') who is accused of a crime involving her father's honor. The narrative describes a confrontation between the woman and a nurse regarding a secret crime, ending with the woman's testimony regarding a king's actions.

This section of the 'gesta Apollonii' contains a series of dramatic and mythological scenes, including a dialogue regarding a 'miserable' death, a description of a king's madness, and a scene involving a figure named Antiochus. It features a military confrontation involving a 'Signifer' and a 'plebs' near a shore, and concludes with a transition to the city of Antioch where a king enters a hall.

The text depicts a tense confrontation between a king named Antiochus and a youth named Apollonius. Apollonius delivers a complex, arguably scandalous speech regarding a shared past and a 'common spouse,' which causes the king to react with visible anger and internal turmoil. Following the exchange, Apollonius addresses a gathering of people and a servant named Taliarchus, while the narrative mentions the city of Tyre and the threat of a Tyrian invasion.

The text describes a dramatic scene involving a prisoner or captive, a figure named Apollonius, and a military movement toward the coast and the port of Tyre. It depicts a transition from a tense confrontation involving threats of poison and swords to a scene of celebration and ritual, followed by a period of mourning and the closing of public spaces like gymnasiums and temples. The narrative includes a specific mention of the king's madness and a voyage involving ships and the sea.

The text depicts a tense diplomatic encounter between a messenger from Antioch, named Taliarchus, and a young man (possibly a ruler or high-ranking official) regarding a potential alliance or peace treaty. The dialogue involves a debate over the history of their respective lands, the sanctity of their ancestors, and the terms of a proposed covenant. The passage concludes with a transition to the people of Syra (Syra/Syracuse) preparing for a collective action or assembly.

The text describes a confrontation between a king and a young man, identified as Apollonius, who is praised for his martial skill and bravery. The king addresses the crowd and the youth, questioning Apollonius's right to life despite his crimes. A respondent defends Apollonius, urging the king to cease his anger and seek peace.

The text contains a series of poetic and highly alliterative verses involving a king's speech, a journey by sea involving the ship Argo, and a dialogue regarding shared danger and the city of Tyre. It includes mythological references to Mars, the kingdom of Saturn, and the goddess Alba (or a similar name). The text is heavily corrupted by transcription errors or complex wordplay, making several lines nearly unintelligible.

This 10th-century Latin work, the 'gesta Berengarii', is a historical narrative and poetic chronicle concerning the deeds of Berengarius II. The text is structured into several sections that blend historical reporting with highly stylized, allusive poetry and military descriptions. It begins with a prologue referencing Homer, Virgil, and the myth of Aeneas before detailing the conquest of Italy and the actions of Charlemagne. The narrative follows Berengarius through various military engagements involving figures such as Wido, Walfredus, and Sinbaldus, and locations including the Rhine, Ticinus, and Latium. Later sections incorporate elements of imperial imagery, religious ritual, and hagiographic references to figures like Eusebius and Constantinus. The work concludes with liturgical-style poetry and a formal prayer.

The text begins with a poetic, highly allusive prologue featuring references to Homer, Virgil, and the myth of Aeneas before transitioning into a historical narrative. It mentions Berengarius (Berengarius II), Charlemagne (Karolus Magnus), and the conquest of Italy. The passage concludes with a series of descriptive verses concerning pastoral scenes, the Rhine, and the Ticinus river, interspersed with mythological references to Paris and the Atridae.

This section contains a series of highly stylized, likely poetic or rhetorical, descriptions of military conflict and leadership. It mentions specific figures such as Rodulfus, Wido, and a 'Poenus' (Punic) king, and references locations like Verona and Latium. The text includes a formal invocation to a deity of the heavens and earth, followed by a sequence of martial imagery involving soldiers, horses, and the spoils of war.

This section of the gesta Berengarii describes a military engagement involving figures such as Wido, Gauslinus, Vbertus, and Vbaldus. It details troop movements, the presence of 3,000 masters, and the actions of Berengarius regarding Latium. The text includes a formal address to the troops and a concluding section describing the aftermath of the battle and the death of a commander.

The text describes a chaotic battle scene involving various figures such as Walfredus, Bernardus, and the leaders Athesinus and Othus. It details military maneuvers, the movement of troops across fields and water, and the specific actions of named individuals like Bonifacus and Erardum. The narrative includes references to locations such as the Rhine and the fields of Latium, and mentions of groups like the 'Hiberis' and 'Gallus' (Galeae).

The text describes a violent battle involving the Ausonians and the Germans, featuring specific figures such as Anscherius, Albricus, and Vmfredus. It depicts a chaotic scene of combat, the death of a horseman, and the subsequent retreat of the Ausonians. The passage concludes with a mention of Arnulf and Berengarius in the context of German law and royal lineage.

This section of the gesta Berengarii describes a military confrontation involving figures such as Sinbaldus, Berengarius, and the Duke Gallicus. It details a siege or defense of a city (Vrbis) involving the movement of troops, the closing of gates, and the actions of a character named Ambrosius. The text includes a dialogue between a king and a young man regarding the defense of the realm and the movement of forces toward the Rhenus.

The text describes a series of military and diplomatic interactions involving figures such as Arnulfus, Lanbertus, and a leader of the Latins. It recounts a confrontation between a 'fearless' leader and a king, the movement of troops toward the Ticinus river, and the death of a figure named Widone. The narrative includes a religious or prophetic lamentation regarding the fate of the land and the transition of power.

The text describes a series of scenes involving a youth (possibly a fallen leader or hero) and the figure of Berengarius. It includes a lament for a fallen youth whose body is prepared for burial, a scene of a king or leader addressing his troops or subjects, and a transition to a tense atmosphere of murmuring and brewing unrest among soldiers. Specific names mentioned include Berengarius, Ludovicus, and references to Latium, Italy, and the people of Rhodes.

The text describes a dramatic scene involving a ruler or 'prince' entering a temple, where he is met by a crowd and potentially confronted by figures like Ludovicus. It contains highly stylized, possibly poetic or allegorical descriptions of imperial power, religious ritual, and the transition of authority. Specific names mentioned include Ludovicus, Johannes, Adalbertus, and references to figures like Peter, Constantinus, and the 'fisherman' (Christ).

The text contains a series of poetic verses describing imperial imagery, the presence of jewels and gold, and the actions of a priest or leader. It mentions specific historical figures including Eusebius, Berengarius, and a figure named Azon, while referencing locations such as Mantua. The passage concludes with a formal prayer for the author and a dedication to a father and a son.

This collection of medieval Latin poetry (carmina) by Giraldus Floriacensis consists of hagiographic verses, liturgical hymns, and narrative poems. The work is organized into sections that transition from local monastic and hagiographic accounts to themes of pilgrimage and miraculous relics. It features the figures of Aigulfus, Leodebodus, and Benedictus, and references the Virgin Mary, as well as biblical figures such as Abraham, Solomon, and Elijah. Geographical locations mentioned include Floriacis, Cenomannensis, Lirinen, Gaul, and Rome. The text incorporates themes of monastic life, the preservation of sacred remains, and the construction of churches. The final sections shift toward liturgical praise, featuring the Virgin Mary as 'Stella maris' and 'mater mundi'.

This section of the carmina contains a series of poetic and hagiographic verses concerning the lives of holy men, specifically mentioning figures such as Leodebodus, Aigulphe, and a figure associated with the name Benedicte. It references specific locations including the land of Floriacis, the city of Cenomannensis, and a 'coenobium' (monastery) in the Lirinen region. The text describes monastic life, the construction of churches, and the transition of leadership and property within a religious order.

The text describes a journey toward Rome and the Basilica of Saint Peter, involving a figure named Aigulfus who is tasked with identifying and illuminating sacred sites. It depicts a dialogue between an older man and a younger companion regarding a divine mission, the discovery of a hidden treasure (theusaurum) containing the remains of saints, and a vision involving the Pope of Rome.

The text contains a series of poetic and hagiographic verses concerning the veneration of the bones of a holy figure, identified as Benedictus. It mentions specific figures such as Aigulfus and a 'Scolastica virgo,' and references locations including the land of Gaul and a site named Nova Villa. The narrative involves a miraculous healing, the distribution of sacred remains, and a dialogue regarding divine favor and the protection of the holy body.

The text describes a miraculous scene involving the movement and preservation of sacred remains, specifically the bones of a prophet or holy figure. It mentions a figure named Mummolus, the presence of a girl, and the location of a basilica. The passage concludes with a series of liturgical-style praises to Christ and the Virgin, referencing the 'holy flame' and the 'kingdom of the just.'

This section of the carmina contains a series of liturgical or hagiographic praises and invocations. It features specific mentions of biblical figures such as Abraham, Isaac, Samuel, Solomon, and Elijah (Helias), as well as the Virgin Mary and the figure of Christ. The text includes a specific address to a 'Benedicte' and mentions of the land of Gaul (Gallia) and the city of Rome.

This section of the carmina contains a series of hymns and prayers dedicated to the Virgin Mary, addressing her as 'Stella maris' and 'mater mundi'. It includes invocations for the people, the clergy, and the 'femineo sexu' (female sex), and references biblical figures such as Christ, David, Gabriel, and Enoch. The text incorporates liturgical imagery of the Eucharist, the celestial spheres, and the triumph of the Virgin.

A Latin hymn or devotional poem attributed to Godescalcus Saxo, dating to the 9th century. The text is a series of invocations and praises directed toward Christ and the Virgin Mary. It employs traditional medieval theological imagery, including the 'light of darkness,' the 'mother of the sea' (Virgin Mary), and the 'conquest of death.' The poem incorporates cosmological and cosmological elements, referencing the stars, the heavens, and the creation of the world. It concludes with a series of benedictions and a focus on the 'weight of love' and the 'scepter of the father.'

This collection of medieval Latin devotional hymns and poems by Godescalcus Saxo is structured into four distinct movements. The opening sections consist of alliterative prayers to Christ as King and Creator, focusing on themes of redemption, sin, and spiritual healing. The second section expands the intercessory scope to include the Virgin Mary, Saint Michael, Saint Peter, and various martyrs, concluding with a rhetorical meditation on exile and the Israelites in Babylon. The third section addresses the Trinity and a 'good doctor,' transitioning into a poetic defense of the author's 'rusticitas' amidst references to the month of August and the constellation Cancer. The final section features theological reflections and addresses to a 'dear friend' and 'noble poet,' mentioning figures such as Augustine, Matcaudo, Ione, and Lupus, while referencing the Palatine and Olympus.

This section of the text is a series of devotional hymns and prayers addressed to Christ, characterized by repetitive, alliterative structures and heavy use of Latinate synonyms. The author petitions Christ as the 'King of Kings,' 'Creator,' and 'Redeemer' to provide spiritual healing, cleanse the speaker's sins, and offer protection from the 'many-faced' dangers of the world. The text includes specific invocations for the 'soul' (alma) and the 'servant' (servus) to find peace and restoration.

This section of the carmina contains a series of penitential prayers and pleas for mercy addressed to Christ, the Virgin Mary, Saint Michael, Saint Peter, and various saints and martyrs. The speaker confesses to living in vanity, neglecting divine law, and seeking redemption from the 'yoke of slavery.' The latter portion of the text shifts into a dialogue or a series of rhetorical questions regarding the necessity of singing and lamenting in exile, referencing the Israelites in Babylon.

This section of the carmina contains a series of religious and lyrical verses featuring a direct address to the Trinity and a 'good doctor' (likely a reference to a teacher or spiritual mentor). The text includes a transition into a more descriptive, poetic mode featuring a reference to the month of August, the constellation Cancer, and a plea for the poet's 'rusticitas' (unpolished style) to be overlooked in favor of the spiritual message.

The text contains a series of poetic addresses and theological reflections, featuring a dialogue or address to a 'dear friend' and a 'noble poet.' It mentions specific figures including Augustine, Matcaudo, Ione, and Lupus, and references the 'Palatine' hall and the 'Olympus' of the ruling. The passage concludes with a series of religious and moral exhortations regarding the redemption of the soul and the protection of the faithful.

This medieval Latin collection of poems by Godescalcus Saxo consists of five parts structured as a series of devotional and liturgical hymns. The work is addressed primarily to the Trinity and Christ, moving from personal penitential pleas to cosmological and biblical meditations. The text includes specific biblical narratives involving the resurrection of Lazarus, the sacrifice of Abel, the Ark of Noah, and the figures of Abraham and Moses. Imagery of the vineyard, the Passion of Christ, and the mythological perils of Syrtis and Charybdis are employed to illustrate divine protection and redemption. The final section concludes with a brief commentary on the use of 'et' and the 'caelicus' chorus.

A penitential poem addressed to the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) in which the speaker confesses sins and pleads for mercy. The speaker describes their spiritual state as dry and hardened like rock, seeking a transformation of the heart and a flow of tears for their transgressions. The text concludes with a reference to the 'prodigal son' and a plea for the father's kindness.

The text is a devotional poem addressed to the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) and Jesus Christ. It features a narrative and prayerful sequence involving the resurrection of Lazarus, the purification of lepers, and the plea of a sinner for mercy and grace. The speaker identifies as a 'servant' and 'brother' seeking redemption from the 'flames' of punishment.

This section of the poem is a series of religious and mystical invocations addressed to Christ and the Trinity. It contains liturgical-style praises of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and uses cosmological imagery involving the sun, stars, and the movement of time to describe divine light and the victory over death and darkness.

This section of the carmina contains a series of liturgical-style prayers and hymns addressed to the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit). The text incorporates biblical and mystical imagery, including the sacrifice of Abel, the Ark of Noah, the figures of Abraham and Moses, and the symbolism of a vineyard. It concludes with a personal lamentation regarding the suffering of Christ on the cross.

This section of the carmina contains a series of liturgical-style prayers and hymns addressed to God and Christ. It includes invocations for protection against the Syrtis and Charybdis, a call for frequent thanksgivings, and a concluding doxology. The text concludes with a brief commentary on the use of 'et' and the 'caelicus' chorus.

This Latin text, attributed to Godescalcus Saxo and dating to the 9th century, is a poetic or liturgical work characterized by a dense, highly stylized rhetorical structure. The content oscillates between theological meditation, moral exhortation, and mystical imagery. It features themes of divine judgment, the fate of the soul, and the distinction between earthly suffering and spiritual grace. Specific references include the 'Tartars,' the 'Pontifices,' and a 'Lord' (Dominus) associated with 'holy offspring.' The text employs a series of antitheses and rhetorical questions regarding the nature of wisdom, the role of the 'elect,' and the transition from mortal life to the afterlife.

A medieval Latin acrostic poem by Gosbertus, likely composed in the 9th century. The text is structured as a series of rhyming couplets and quatrains, featuring a recurring refrain that addresses a figure named Guillelme (William). The poem combines religious imagery, such as the cross, the Eucharist, and the teachings of Paul, with references to ecclesiastical figures and monastic life. It incorporates mythological and biblical motifs, including references to the Troygenes, Gog, and Magog. The work concludes with a list of descriptors and a final signature by the author, Gosbertus. The primary themes involve the crowning of a ruler or holy figure, the virtues of the faith, and the juxtaposition of spiritual and worldly symbols.

This text is a medieval Latin epilogue to a letter addressed to the inhabitants of Augenz (epistula ad Augienses) by Gunzo Novariensis. The work is structured as a series of theological and allegorical verses. It invokes the 'Conditor omnipotens' and addresses themes of divine judgment, the afterlife, and the transition of souls. The text references mythological and geographical markers such as Avernus, Charon, the river Minois, and the figure Heridan. It contrasts the fate of those under the law of Christ with those facing the 'draconis' (dragon) and the 'Averno' (underworld), concluding with a passage on the rewards of the faithful.

A prefatory address to a collection of texts (collectaneum) by the 9th-century author Heiricus Autissiodorensis. The text addresses a figure named Hildebolde and contains a series of poetic and rhetorical flourishes. It mentions two specific individuals, Lupus and Haimo, who are described as companions or students involved in the composition or study of the work. The text alternates between praising the intellectual labor of the author and the companions and invoking religious imagery. The concluding section contains a formal benediction and a prayer for peace and victory in the name of Christ.

This 9th-century Latin hagiography by Heiricus Autissiodorensis chronicles the life and virtues of Bishop Germanus of Autun. The work is structured as a blend of theological meditation, liturgical poetry, and narrative hagiography, characterized by stylized, alliterative Latin and allegorical narratives. It contains extensive geographical references to Gaul, Rome, Britain, the Rhône, the Alps, Mediolanum, and Ravenna. Specific figures mentioned include the priest Julius, Simplicius, Albanus, Cassianus, Placidia, Valentinianus, and Volusianus. The text incorporates diverse motifs such as maritime voyages, military conflicts involving the Britanni, and descriptions of plague and medical treatment. Theological content includes Christology, the hypostatic union, and a technical commentary on numerology and Greek terms like Monas, Dyas, ousia, dynamis, and energeia. A fragmented mythological interlude concerning Dedalus and Icarus is also present.

This text is a highly stylized, dense theological and philosophical meditation on the nature of God, utilizing a mix of Latin and Greek phrases. It explores themes of divine unity, the Trinity, and the paradoxes of the divine essence (such as the 'still motion' and 'unity in plurality') while incorporating references to biblical figures like Moses and the Sinai. The passage concludes with a transition toward a formal liturgical or laudatory address to the author, Germano.

This section of the biography of Bishop Germanus of Autun contains a highly corrupted and fragmented text. It includes a series of disjointed Latin phrases and poetic fragments that mention names such as Germanus, Autissiodorus, and Altiodorus, as well as geographical references to Gaul, Latium, and Rome. The text appears to be a collection of literary fragments or a corrupted transcription of a formal hagiography, featuring themes of legal study, moral conduct, and ecclesiastical status.

This section of the hagiography of Bishop Germanus of Autun employs high-style Latin to describe the virtues, titles, and spiritual authority of the bishop. It lists various Roman and ecclesiastical offices (praetorian, judicial, and pastoral), contrasts the sacred with the profane, and portrays the bishop as a defender against heresy and a guardian of the faith. The text concludes with a formal defense of his status and the divine nature of his office.

This section of the hagiography of Bishop Germanus of Autisiodorens contains a series of highly stylized, likely poetic or rhetorical, passages. It includes a dramatic scene involving a confrontation with a 'prince' or 'leader' (dux) and a 'double-edged sword,' a description of a martyr's preparation for death, and a concluding section of prayers and liturgical-style praise for the saint.

The text describes a formal assembly and the transition of leadership within a religious context, featuring figures such as the bishop (implied by the title), a priest named Julius, and a holy man named Simplicius. It includes a historical/mythological preamble regarding the city of 'Augustidunum' (Augustonum) and its origins. The narrative concludes with a formal proclamation of office and a call to the people to witness the sacraments.

This section of the 'Vita Germani' contains a series of poetic and allegorical verses, likely intended as a moralizing or hagiographic meditation. It features a lion and a shepherd motif, references to the clergy, and a transition into a spiritual defense of the ascetic life. The text concludes with a series of dense, metaphorical lines regarding the rejection of worldly pleasures, the sanctity of the body, and the distinction between physical sustenance and spiritual nourishment.

This section of the hagiography of Germanus of Auxerre contains a highly corrupted and fragmented text, likely containing a mixture of original narrative and unrelated poetic interpolations.
