It interprets the roles of Martha and Mary as symbols of faith and hope, and uses the 'four days' of Lazarus's death to allegorize the four cardinal virtues (prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice) and the stages of the soul's journey from sin to grace.

The text begins with a liturgical-style invocation of the Trinity and the redemption of the faithful. It then transitions into a biblical narrative concerning the patriarch Abraham, his wife Sarah, and the birth of Isaac. The primary focus is the story of Joseph, detailing his dreams of superiority, his betrayal by his brothers, his imprisonment in Egypt, and his subsequent interpretation of Pharaoh's dreams regarding the Nile and the upcoming famine.

This section recounts a narrative based on the biblical story of Joseph and his brothers in Egypt. It describes the brothers' journey to purchase grain during a famine, their interaction with Joseph (who initially hides his identity), the subsequent reunion, and a banquet where they reflect on their past sins against him.

The text recounts the biblical narrative of Joseph and his brothers, specifically the identification of Benjamin and the subsequent reunion of the brothers with their father, Jacob, in Egypt. Following this narrative, the author transitions into a mystical and allegorical meditation on the Passion of Christ, the nature of sin, and the personification of vices such as Pride, Envy, and Discord.

The text begins with a penitential prayer of the author, who seeks forgiveness for his sins and acknowledges the mercy of Christ. It then transitions into a narrative of the Nativity, describing the angelic announcement to the shepherds, the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, and the arrival of the Magi. The passage concludes with the presentation of gold, frankincense, and myrrh to the infant.

The text recounts the biblical narrative of the Magi visiting the infant Christ in Bethlehem and the subsequent slaughter of the innocents by Herod. It transitions into a theological meditation on the nature of charity (caritas) as the highest good and the fulfillment of both the Old and New Testaments. The author concludes with a call for the faithful to love their enemies and remain steadfast in Christ.

This section of the carmina contains a series of religious hymns and poems focusing on the Passion, Resurrection, and life of Christ. It features specific biblical narratives including the Resurrection of the Good Shepherd, the appearance of Mary Magdalene, the fall of Adam, the betrayal of Judas, and the presentation of the infant Jesus in the temple to Simeon.

This section of the carmina contains a series of liturgical and devotional poems centered on the Passion, Resurrection, and the role of the Virgin Mary. It includes specific references to the biblical figures of Moses, Elijah, Jonah, and Mary Magdalene, as well as descriptions of the Eucharist, the triumph over death, and the celebration of the Trinity.

This section of the carmina describes a series of biblical scenes including the appearance of an angel and the women at the tomb, the resurrection of Christ, and the appearance of Jesus to the eleven disciples. It includes a dialogue with Thomas regarding the wounds of Christ and a formal commission of the disciples to preach to the Gentiles. The text concludes with a series of liturgical-style praises to the Trinity and a description of the light of the Gospel and the seven golden candlesticks.

The text contains a series of religious poems or hymns celebrating the figures of Peter and Paul, the Trinity, and the Virgin Mary. It references biblical scenes such as Ezekiel's visions, the martyrdom of saints, and the construction of the Temple of Solomon. The passage concludes with a series of invocations for protection against pestilence and the granting of eternal life through the blood of Christ.

This section of the carmina contains a series of liturgical-style hymns and prayers addressed to the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit). It includes invocations of the Virgin Mary, the Archangels Michael and Gabriel, and the Apostles Peter, Paul, and John, alongside pleas for divine mercy and the calming of natural elements like wind and sea. The text also features specific geographical references to Austria and Africa in a context of seeking favorable weather and agricultural fertility.

This 8th-century Latin poem by Paulinus Aquileiensis is a lamentation and elegiac meditation on the destruction of the city of Aquilegia. The text contrasts the city's former glory as a noble seat of the elite and a center of ecclesiastical life with its ruin following the invasion of Attila the Hun. It describes the physical devastation of the city, the slaughter of its inhabitants, and the desecration of its sacred spaces. The poem transitions from a mourning of lost architecture and urban life to a theological plea for divine mercy and protection. The final section concludes with a traditional hagiographic defense of Saint Peter as the rock of the church and the keeper of the keys of heaven.

This Latin text is a technical grammatical treatise, likely a medieval commentary or manual on the morphology of verbs. It systematically categorizes and describes various 'species' (types) of verb forms, specifically focusing on the nuances of conjugation and the structural properties of syllables. The author analyzes these forms based on their phonetic composition, such as the presence or absence of consonants, the doubling of syllables, and the specific placement of vowels. The text provides numerous illustrative examples of verb pairs (e.g., 'famulavi famulo', 'spondeo spopondi', 'capio cepi') to demonstrate grammatical rules. It also references specific letters of the alphabet (Alpha, Sigma, Iota, Psi) and mentions the scholar Diomedes in a technical context. The work is organized as a systematic progression through numbered forms and conjugations.

This collection of Latin poems by Paulus Diaconus (8th century) comprises a diverse body of religious, allegorical, and occasional verse. The work begins with chronological calculations of biblical history and moralizing allegories, followed by lyrical poems featuring natural imagery and pastoral themes. The text includes several panegyrics and dedicatory verses for contemporary figures such as Karolus (Charlemagne), Pippinus, and Constantius, as well as mentions of the ruler of Benevento and the saint Adalard. Geographical references include the rivers Tiber, Rhine, and Hister, as well as locations like Salerno, Casinum, and the lands of Gaul and Thrace. The collection also features funeral laments, such as that for Hildegard, and various devotional hymns to the Trinity, the Virgin Mary, and the Cross. The final sections contain allegorical beast-fables and exhortations regarding clerical discipline and the nature of the soul.

The text contains a series of poetic verses and calculations of years spanning from the beginning of the world to the era of the Gospel. It mentions specific figures and locations including Abraham, Moses, the city of Babylon, the Virgin Mary (virgo mundi), and the ruler of Benevento. The later sections contain allegorical and moralizing imagery involving themes of judgment, spiritual warfare, and the contrast between piety and deceit.

This collection of poems includes a series of short, often allegorical or moralizing verses. The texts feature imagery of nature (olives, laurel, myrtle, and citrus), celestial bodies, and religious devotion, including a direct address to a 'venerable father' and a plea for protection from a 'pestiferous dragon.' The final section contains a series of short, pithy couplets and quatrains involving themes of love, virtue, and the senses.

This collection of poems by Paulus Diaconus includes a series of religious and lyrical verses. The text features invocations to the Trinity and Christ, a lament for a maiden (possibly a nun or a bride) who died before marriage, and mentions of geographical locations such as the Tiber, Rhine, and Hister rivers. It also contains a personal note from the author regarding the 'unpolished' nature of the poems and a brief mention of a figure named Arichis.

Paulus Diaconus presents a series of poems and reflections characterized by a humble, self-deprecating tone regarding his own literary skills. He references classical and biblical figures such as Homer, Virgil, Tertullus, and Philon the Memphite, while also mentioning the biblical figures Peter and the land of Hebron. The text includes a defense of his poetic ability against critics, a mention of the Norse deities Thonar and Waten, and a concluding section on the nature of the masses.

This section contains a series of miscellaneous poems and verses featuring various themes including lyrical descriptions of nature, mythological references to Cynthius and Phoebus, and a transition into a panegyric. The latter portion specifically names historical figures such as Pippinus, Arnulfus, and Karolus (Charlemagne), and mentions geographical locations like Gallia and Ausonia.

This section contains a series of elegiac and dactylic verses containing funeral laments and a list of ecclesiastical figures. It features a lament for a queen named Hildegard, wife of a king named Carolus, and includes a long list of prelates and clergy members associated with specific titles or locations, such as Peter, Clemens, Victor, and Arnulfus.

This section contains a series of disparate poetic fragments, including a panegyric to King Charles (Carolus) and a mention of the saint Stephen, a description of the rivers Moselle and Rhine, and a tribute to Adalard. The text transitions into a series of allegorical and beast-fables involving a king, a fox, a bear, and a calf, as well as a satirical or moralizing sequence regarding a 'podagra' (gout) and a 'pulix' (flea). The final portion contains a series of short, seemingly disconnected lyrical verses involving hunting imagery and references to Actaeon.

This section contains a collection of diverse religious and occasional poems, including a series of liturgical-style exhortations, a lament for a deceased individual named Benevente, and a formal address to a prince or ruler. The text mentions specific locations such as Salerno and the rivers Siler, Tibris, Ararim, Histrum, and Padum. It also includes a personal correspondence or dedication involving a figure named Benedict and a reference to a 'Petrus'.

This section of the carmina contains a series of poetic addresses and exchanges involving King Charles (Karolus), the monk Paul, and the Virgin Mary. It includes a formal exchange of greetings and prayers, a reference to the mountain of Casinum and the name of Benedict, and a series of lyrical verses concerning divine grace, the nature of the soul, and the virtues of the saints.

This section contains a collection of poems and dedicatory verses by Paulus Diaconus (or a contemporary using his style). It includes a panegyric to a king (likely Charlemagne) praising his mercy and the prosperity of his realm, a series of biblical and historical allusions (Noah, Gideon, David/Goliath), and several personal dedicatory letters to individuals named Peter, Angelbertus, and Angelramus. The text also includes a formal address to a 'pious father' and mentions of geographical locations such as Italy, Gaul, and Thrace.

This section of the carmina contains a series of devotional and exhortative poems. It includes a hymn to the Virgin Mary and the protective power of the Cross, a panegyric for a military leader named Constantius (described as a protector of Italy), and a series of exhortations to clergy and 'great fathers' to maintain spiritual discipline, avoid worldly vanities, and remain vigilant against enemies.

This section of the carmina contains a series of religious and allegorical poems focusing on the role of the shepherd (pastor) and the clergy. It addresses themes of spiritual guidance, the corruption of worldly priests, the judgment of the faithful, and the promise of divine redemption. The text includes references to Christ, the Virgin, and the spiritual rewards of the holy life.

This section of the carmina contains a series of religious and allegorical poems. It includes a passage regarding the Virgin Mary and the Archangel Gabriel, a hymn to the Trinity, and a series of laudatory verses addressed to various figures including a priest, a king, and a 'beloved' father.

A Latin verse by Paulus Diaconus, likely a lyric poem or a personal address. The text addresses a 'libelle' (little lady) and contains elements of courtly love and personal lament. It mentions specific geographical locations, including Beneventum, the Rhône (Rodanus), and regions associated with the Garamantes and India. The poem features a transition from personal address to a description of a journey or geographical movement. The text contains several lacunae and corrupted passages, particularly in the middle section regarding the 'Belgus' waters and the 'tristis' carmina. The final lines shift to a theme of enduring love and the persistence of memory.

This medieval Latin work, attributed to Petrus Neapolitanus, is a collection of devotional and liturgical verses concerning the 'Agnellus sanctus' (Holy Lamb) and associated miracles. The text is organized into two primary sections focusing on themes of divine mercy, Christology, and physical healing. It contains specific petitions for the cure of ailments such as paralysis, tetanus, and madness. Notable geographical and cultural references include 'Parthenope' (Naples) and the 'Tonant' or 'Tonantem' (the Thunderer). The text mentions specific figures including the priest Stephanus, as well as Iohannes and Athanasi. A specific narrative element involves a direct address to a 'paralitica puella' (paralyzed girl).

This text is a series of devotional and liturgical verses concerning the 'Agnellus sanctus' (Holy Lamb) and the 'miracula' (miracles) associated with it. It contains prayers for healing from diseases like paralysis and tetanus, petitions for divine counsel, and a hagiographic focus on the Lamb of God as a source of salvation and purification. The text includes specific references to the 'Tonant' (likely a local or liturgical reference), the 'mira patrans' (miraculous patron), and the 'sacerdos' (priest) Stephanus.

This section of the text contains a series of liturgical or devotional verses concerning the 'miracula' (miracles) of the 'Agnelli' (Lamb). It features specific invocations to the 'Parthenope' (likely referring to the city of Naples), mentions of the 'Tonantem' (the Thunderer), and a series of petitions for healing from ailments such as 'Tetaneos' (tetanus) and 'Insania' (madness). The text includes a direct address to a 'paralitica puella' (paralyzed girl) and mentions figures such as 'Iohannes' (John) and 'Athanasi'.

A collection of Latin poems attributed to Petrus Pisanus, dating to the 8th century. The text functions as a hybrid of devotional praise, academic exhortation, and scholarly commentary on classical and biblical studies. It contains specific references to biblical figures such as Christ, Paul, and Gamaliel, as well as classical authors including Homer, Virgil, Philo, Tertullus, Flaccus, and Tibullus. The work addresses the study of Greek and Hebrew grammars and the instruction of the clergy. Themes include the transition from darkness to light, the power of miracles, and the preservation of sacred knowledge through diverse linguistic traditions.

A Latin funeral lament (planctus) mourning the death of Charlemagne (Karolus). The text is structured as a series of elegiac couplets interspersed with a recurring refrain, 'Heu mihi misero!' (Alas, I wretched one!). It depicts the mourning of the Franks, Romans, and the wider Christian world, specifically mentioning the grief of widows, virgins, and pilgrims. Geographical references include the lands of Aachen (Aquisgrani) and Italy. The poem concludes with a prayer to Christ, the Holy Spirit, and the invocation of Saint Columban to intercede for the deceased. The central theme is the profound loss of a 'most glorious' leader and the resulting universal sorrow.

This medieval Latin work, attributed to Poeta Saxo, is a historical and hagiographic account of the reign and military campaigns of Carolus Magnus. The text is organized chronologically, detailing the conquest of the Saxons, the subjugation of the Lombards under Desiderius, and the expansion of the Frankish realm into Italy and the East. The narrative includes specific geographical locations such as the Rhine, the Danube, the Alps, Aquisgrani, Salerno, and Rome. Notable figures mentioned include Pippinus, the scholar Alcuin, and local leaders Widokindus and Tassilo. The work also chronicles interactions with the Persians, Scots, Moors, and Northmen, alongside the construction of a bridge at Mainz. The final sections transition from military history and the translation of grammar to religious devotion, featuring prophetic verses on the apostles and prayers for the conversion of the Saxons.

The text recounts the military and political actions of Carolus (Charlemagne) and his interactions with the Papacy and the Lombard Kingdom. It mentions the conquest of territories from the Saxons, the submission of the people of Eresburg, and the diplomatic mission of a legate named Petrus to Rome. Specific locations mentioned include Carbonata, Attiniacus, Wormatium, the Rhône (Rhodanus), and the Ticinus (Papia).

The text describes the military campaigns of King Carolus (Charlemagne) against the Saxons, specifically detailing the siege of cities like Frideshlar and the movements toward Ticinum and the Rhine. It mentions specific locations such as Brunesberg, Hlidbeki, and the river Ovaccra, while referencing the role of the Frankish senate and the conversion of the Saxons to Christianity. The narrative includes a transition to a scene involving the king's strategic maneuvers and the eventual infiltration of the Frankish camp.

The text describes the military campaigns of Carolus (Charlemagne) against the Saxons, specifically mentioning the conquest of Eresburg and the submission of the Saxons to Christian baptism. It details the capture of various territories, the naming of locations like the river Lyppia and the city of Pompelone, and the interactions with figures such as the rebel Widokindus and a Saracen named Ibinalarbi. The narrative concludes with a transition toward the conquest of Spanish cities and the crossing of the Pyrenees.

The text describes military movements and conflicts involving the Franks, Saxons, and the King (Carolus). It details the conquest of territories near the Rhine, the destruction of villages and churches, and the submission of the Saxons. Specific locations mentioned include the Pyrenees, the river Lyppia, and the site of Baddanfeldun, while mentioning figures such as the Duke of Spoleto (Hildibrandus) and the King of the Danes, Sigifrid.

The text describes the military campaigns of Charlemagne (Carolus) against the Saxons and the Slavs (Sclavorum). It details the defeat of the Saxons and the deaths of leaders Adalgisus and Geilo, the subsequent suppression of revolts in the Westphalian region, and the movement of troops through locations such as the rivers Albia, Hasa, and the site of Scannigi.

The text describes the movements and military actions of Charlemagne (Carolus) as he secures territories in Italy, specifically mentioning the submission of Desiderius and the Langobards and the conquest of the Duchy of Beneventana. It details his journey through the Alps toward Rome, the fortification of Salerno, and the surrender of local leaders like Rumoldus and Grimoldus. The passage also mentions the conquest of lands in Britain and the subsequent consolidation of his rule over the Frankish realms.

Tassilo sends ambassadors, including Bishop Arnus and Abbot Hunricus, to Pope Adrian to negotiate peace with Charlemagne. The Pope rejects the ambassadors due to their perceived deceit, leading to a breakdown in negotiations. The text then describes military movements involving the Bavarians, the invasion of Italian territories near the Danube and the Brenner Pass, and the actions of figures such as Desiderius and his daughter. The narrative concludes with the mobilization of Carolingian forces against the Bavarians and the defense of Italian cities.

The text describes military maneuvers and territorial conflicts involving King Carolus (Charlemagne), the Saxons, and the Huns. It details the conquest of the Wilti (a Slavic group) near the river Albia, the destruction of their lands by fire and sword, and the subsequent submission of the people. The narrative also mentions the defense of the realm against the Huns and the consolidation of territory in regions like Wormatia.

The text recounts the military campaigns of Charlemagne (Carolus) against the Huns and the subsequent defense of the realm. It describes the movement of troops through Pannonia and along the Danube, the fortification of positions, and the defeat of the Huns. The narrative also includes a theological and legal dispute involving a priest named Felix and the defense of orthodox doctrine against heresy.

The text describes military campaigns and diplomatic maneuvers involving the Saxons, the Huns, and the Franks. It mentions specific locations such as Wisure, the Rhine, the Danube, and Aquasgrani, and names figures including Carolus (Charlemagne), the Pope Adrianus, and the martyr Kilianus. The narrative also touches upon the condemnation of a heresy and the celebration of religious feasts.

The text describes a series of military and diplomatic maneuvers involving the King of the Huns, the Duke of Italy (Pippinus), and the King of the Moors (Abinmage/Abdelle). It details the movement of troops through regions like Aquisgrani and the river Tisan, the capture of banners, and the negotiation of treaties with the Abodrites and the Northalbingi. Specific figures mentioned include Angilbertus, Godescalcus, and the king Hludowicus, while locations such as Oscae and the land of the Carolines are noted.

The text describes a military conflict involving a leader named Thasco of the Abodrites at a place called Suentana, followed by a transition to a narrative involving a king, a priest named Theophilus, and a figure named Sisinnius. It contains a series of disjointed, highly corrupted passages involving a journey to Padarbrunnon, the presence of Carolus, and a sequence of religious and political imagery involving the Pope, the city of Rome, and the defense of territories against pirates.

The text describes the military and political actions of Carolus (Charlemagne), including the submission of the Duke of Brittany and the naming of various figures such as Geroldus and the count of Baioaria. It recounts a journey to Rome where Carolus is received by Pope Leo in the Basilica of Peter, followed by a celebration of the Nativity and the crowning of the king. The passage also mentions the defense of territories, the naming of a Saracen named Azan, and the presence of figures like Pippinus and the count of Mogontiacum.

The text describes a formal ceremony and the establishment of a peace treaty between the Franks and the Saxons under the rule of Charlemagne (Carolus Magnus). It details the transition of the Saxons to the Catholic faith, the abolition of their old rites, and the granting of land, titles, and wealth. The passage concludes by referencing the historical account of these events as recorded by Einhard.

The text describes the movements of a 'praesul apostolicus' (apostolic leader) from Rome toward the Alps and the lands of the Franks. It mentions the defense of the realm against the Sclavi (Slavs) and the actions of Carolus (Charlemagne) in securing territories like Aquitania and the lands of the Saxons and Fresones. The narrative also includes a section on a plague affecting livestock and a description of a vineyard and its fruit.

The text describes the reign and virtues of Pippin (Pippinus) of Italy and the successor of the Frankish throne, comparing their leadership to the virtues of their predecessors and biblical figures like David and Solomon. It details a diplomatic negotiation involving a Greek delegation, the establishment of a treaty (foedus), and the consolidation of the kingdom's defense and faith. The passage concludes with a somber, lyrical lamentation on the hardships of war and the transition of power.

The text is a panegyric for Charlemagne (Carolus), praising his role in the conversion of the Saxons and the eradication of pagan idolatry. It describes his leadership as a 'prince and priest' who protected the faithful, and it lists his lineage, specifically mentioning the names Pippin, Charlemagne, Louis (Hludowicus), and Theodoric. The passage concludes by framing his reign as a period of spiritual victory and a defense of the Christian faith.

The text describes the virtues, lineage, and governance of Charlemagne (Carolus), detailing his expansion of the empire across the Rhine, the Alps, and into Italy, including the conquest of the Saxons and the subjugation of the Aquitanians. It also provides a biographical sketch of a scholar or cleric of Saxon descent who studied under Alcuin and was skilled in grammar, rhetoric, and scripture.

The text describes the lineage and virtues of Carolus (Charles), mentioning his offspring Pippinus and Rhuottrudis, and his relationship with the empire and the city of Constantinople. It details his physical appearance, his habits of hunting and swimming, and his interactions with foreign leaders such as Hadefonsus, the Scots, and the Persians. The final section describes his military actions against the Moors and the Northmen, and mentions specific locations like Centumcellae and Francia.

The text describes the reign and actions of Charlemagne (Carolo), focusing on his military defense of the realm, the construction of a bridge over the Rhine at Mainz (Mogontiace), and the fortification of the kingdom. It details his religious devotion, the funding of churches and the support of the papacy, and his efforts to provide for the poor and maintain diplomatic relations with foreign kings. The passage concludes with his efforts to uphold and correct ancient laws during his rule.

The text describes the intellectual and scholarly activities of Charlemagne (Carolus Magnus), including his collection of books, the translation of grammar into a vernacular, and his military conquests over the Saxons and other peoples. It concludes with a hagiographic and commemorative section detailing his death, the physical signs accompanying his passing, and a prayer for the salvation of his soul and the conversion of the Saxons.

The text contains a series of religious and prophetic verses. It references the apostles Peter, Paul, Andrew, John, and Thomas, associating them with specific regions or groups (Jews, the world, the Achives, Asia, and the Indians). The final section transitions to a prayer or hymn addressed to Christ, mentioning the Saxons and the 'last hour'.

A medieval Latin poetic work by Purchardus Augiensis, titled 'carmen de gestis Witigowonis', structured in five distinct sections. The first part is a lamentation regarding widowhood and the loss of ancestral lands, featuring the figures Augia mater and Ruodmann. The second and third sections transition into a hagiographic and architectural narrative concerning Witigowon, mentioning figures such as Pirminius, Quatinus, and Funginga, and the construction of monastic structures including a chapel for the bones of Ianuarius. The fourth section details liturgical architecture, naming the archangel Michael, saints Peter, Paul, and Bartholomew, alongside the figure Otmaro. The final section concludes with a pastoral and spiritual meditation involving a figure of chastity, a king of Latium, and a figure named Pelagius, ending with a formal blessing.

The text is a poetic work by Purchardus Augiensis dedicated to the memory of a woman named Witigowonis (or a figure associated with the name Witigowo). It features a dialogue or lamentation involving a woman (referred to as 'Augia mater') who addresses a spouse or protector regarding themes of loss, widowhood, and the aftermath of a father's death. The poem mentions specific locations or figures such as Ruodmann and references a state of siege or 'pestilence' following the destruction of ancestral lands.

The text is a poetic or hagiographic account concerning a figure named Witigowon (Witigoth) and his relationship with the author, Purchardus. It mentions several figures including the priest Pirminius, a man named Quatinus, and a person named Funginga, while referencing locations such as Rome and the royal court. The narrative describes themes of religious devotion, the transition of titles or lands, and the physical restoration of church structures.

The text describes the architectural and decorative features of a monastery, specifically the construction of cells, a chapel, and a gate. It mentions the construction of a chapel for the bones of a saint named Ianuarius and the painting of icons, including the evangelist Mark. The passage also references the deeds of Witigowon, a predecessor who oversaw these works and the defense of the site.

This section describes the architectural and liturgical details of a temple or church, specifically mentioning the construction of a high altar, a sanctuary, and a garden. It names the archangel Michael, the saints Peter and Paul, and the saint Bartholomew, while also referencing a figure named Witigowon and a person named Otmaro. The text concludes with a series of theological reflections on the sacraments, the afterlife, and the divine nature of the Trinity.

The text concludes a poetic narrative involving a pastoral figure (pastor herilis) and a woman of chastity (castae) who is described as being sealed with a gospel heart. It contains a transition from a historical or legendary scene involving a king of Latium and a figure named Pelagius to a spiritual meditation on patience, martyrdom, and the redemption of a soul. The passage concludes with a formal blessing of the 'patient' (patientum) and a reference to the kingdoms of the heavens.

This collection of Latin poetry by Radbertus Corbeiensis consists of two distinct movements. The first part is a funeral lament for a deceased priest or monk, aged eighty, structured as a dialogue between a sister and a daughter. This section incorporates biblical imagery from the Book of Isaiah and addresses the transition from pagan to Christian worship. The second part shifts from lamentation to lyrical and allegorical verse concerning Christology, the Virgin Mary, and divine love. It describes celestial rewards, the sacraments, and mystical mysteries. The text explicitly mentions the author, Abbas Radbertus, and includes references to Galathea and the Muse.

A funeral lament (carmina) for a deceased priest or monk, likely a 'patronus' or 'senior' who was eighty years old. The text features a dialogue between a 'soror' (sister) and a 'filia' (daughter) regarding the deceased, incorporating biblical imagery from Isaiah and references to the transition from pagan to Christian worship.

This section of Radbertus's poetry contains a series of lyrical and allegorical verses concerning the virtues of Christ, the Virgin Mary, and the concept of divine love. It features a transition from a lamentation on mortality to a celebratory description of celestial rewards, the sacraments, and the mystical mysteries of the faith. The text includes a specific reference to the author, Abbas Radbertus, and mentions figures such as Galathea and the Muse.

A collection of medieval Latin poems (carmina) by Radbodus Traiectensis. The work is organized into four distinct sections transitioning from liturgical and martial themes to allegorical and philosophical meditations. The first part contains prayers to Christ and a priest named Martin, followed by a narrative of a military conflict involving the Danes and Gauls near the Seine, Loire, and Tournai. The second part features a hymn to Christ and the saint Swidbertus, incorporating mythological imagery and celestial cosmology. The third section focuses on the missionary Lebuinus, the geography of the Rhine and the British Isles, and allegories of agriculture and the soul. The final section employs antitheses to contrast human reason with the laws of nature and creation.

The text contains a series of prayers and lamentations addressed to Christ and a priest named Martin (Martine), followed by a narrative of a military conflict involving the Danes (Danus) and the Gauls. It mentions specific locations such as the Seine (Sequanae), the Loire (Ligerisque), and the city of Tournai (Turonos). The passage describes the siege of these lands, the suffering of the people, and the desperate pleas of the populace to their clergy.

The text contains a series of religious and martial poems. The first section features a hymn to Christ and the saints, including a specific mention of 'Swidbertus' (Swithbert) and his role in converting the Franks, English, and Saxons. The second section employs mythological imagery (Cyclopes, Harpies, Mars) and celestial descriptions to praise the power of Christ and the celestial harmonies of the spheres.

This section of the carmina contains a series of poetic and allegorical verses concerning the figure of Lebuinus (a missionary to the Anglo-Saxons) and his spiritual journey. The text includes a prayer for the holy one, references to the geography of the Rhine (Hreni) and the British Isles, and a series of allegories involving vineyards, agriculture, and the transformation of the soul. It concludes with a transition into a more complex, perhaps esoteric, meditation on nature, geometry, and the 'art' of the body.

The poet employs a series of antitheses comparing a human observer (the 'you') with the speaker (the 'I') in relation to nature, fate, and creation. The text moves from a description of weather elements (rain, wind, frost) to a philosophical meditation on the limits of human reason versus the predetermined laws of nature and the act of creation.

A technical manual of late antique date calculation and calendrical science. The work is organized into six parts, beginning with the mathematical reconciliation of the Julian and Hebrew calendars to determine the dates of Pascha and Quadragesima. Subsequent sections provide detailed calculations for the lunar and solar cycles, including the determination of epacts, embolisms, and the placement of equinoxes and solstices. The text includes specific instructions for the 'computator' regarding the 'tricesima' and the 'Madius' calendar. The final sections transition from technical calculation to a Christianized allegory of the zodiac and a chronological timeline of history. This timeline includes figures such as Noah, Abraham, Moses, Ninus, Semiramis, and the Emperor Tiberius, concluding with eschatological references.

This text provides a technical manual for calculating the date of Easter (Pascha) and the date of the 'Quadragesima' (Lent) by reconciling the Julian and Hebrew calendars. It details specific mathematical operations involving the 'indiction' cycle, the 'epact' (lunar cycles), and the conversion of Hebrew months like Nisan and Adar into the Christian calendar.

This section provides technical instructions for calculating the lunar cycle, the solar cycle, and the determination of the date of Easter (Pascha). It details specific mathematical operations involving divisions by nine, ten, and seventy, and addresses the calculation of 'epacts' and the inclusion of intercalary months (embolisms) in the calendar.

This section provides a technical calculation of the lunar and solar calendars, specifically addressing the intercalation of leap years (bissextus) and the determination of equinoxes and solstices. It details the mathematical division of the year into parts, the movement of the moon through the zodiac, and the specific placement of dates for the months of March, May, July, and August. The text concludes with a moralizing exhortation to the 'computator' (calculator) to maintain diligence and avoid mental sloth when studying the ancient rules of the fathers.

This section provides a technical calculation of the 'embolismus' (intercalary days) in the lunar calendar, specifically addressing the positioning of the moon's phases (the 'tricesima' or thirteenth day) across various months including December, January, May, and July. It details the mathematical adjustments required for the lunar cycle to align with the solar year, specifically addressing the 'novenis' and 'denis' (ninth and tenth) positions. The text includes a specific warning to the 'calculator' regarding the correct counting of the 'tricesima' and the 'novena' and 'vicena' in the context of the 'Madius' and the 'puerili' (children's) calendar.

The text provides a Christianized interpretation of the zodiac, systematically reinterpreting each astrological sign as a religious allegory. It addresses the calculation of lunar months and the 'leap' of the moon, identifies the sign of Taurus as the Lamb of God, and interprets the remaining signs (Gemini, Leo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, and Capricorn) as symbols of spiritual victory over paganism and sin.

The text contains a series of cryptic, possibly astrological or numerological calculations involving the signs of the zodiac (Aquarius, Pisces), the movements of the moon, and a chronological timeline of history. It lists specific dates and durations associated with figures such as Noah, Abraham, Moses, Ninus, Semiramis, and the Roman Emperor Tiberius, concluding with a reference to the unknown date of the end of the world.

A Latin funerary or commemorative text concerning the death of a man named Hug (Hludovicus). The work mentions the names Hug, Karli, and Insons, and references the historical figures Hludovicus (the emperor) and King Pipinus. The text contains a narrative element regarding Pipinus's reaction to seeing the deceased, and mentions a priest and a monk. The structure includes repetitive refrains regarding the benefit of the deceased's actions and a declaration of the absence of crime or robbery. The text is characterized by a mix of eulogy and specific historical references.

This late antique Latin work, composed in a style resembling spoken prose, contains a mixture of hagiographic fragments, liturgical poetry, and historical narrative. The first section features commemorative verses and funeral elegies mentioning figures such as the confessor Damianus, the saint Thomas, and King Cuningpert, while referencing Liguria, Athens, and the cathedral of Ticinensis. The second section provides a historical account of the Lombard kings, specifically the reign of Cunincperct (Conrad I) and his efforts to resolve schisms. This narrative details a synod involving Pope Sergius, Bishop Theodoaldo, and the bishops of Aquilei, while referencing earlier rulers such as Liutprand, Audoald, and Haribertus. The final section contains liturgical lines praising Christ and a petition for eternal life. The text concludes with a specific comparison involving the name Cunincpertus.

This section contains a series of liturgical or commemorative verses and hagiographic fragments. It mentions specific figures such as the confessor Damianus, the saint Thomas, and the king Cuningpert, while referencing locations like Liguria, Athens, and the cathedral of Ticinensis. The text includes funeral elegies, descriptions of sacred spaces, and a formal address to a student named Theodota.

The text recounts the history of the Lombard kings, specifically focusing on the reign of Cunincperct (Conrad I) and his efforts to unify the church and eliminate schismatics. It details a synod involving the Pope Sergius, the bishop Theodoaldo, and the Aquilei bishops to resolve divisions. The narrative also mentions earlier rulers like Liutprand, Audoald, and Haribertus, and concludes with a formal appeal to the king regarding the judgment of schismatics.

The author notes the composition of the text in prose as if in speech. The passage contains a series of liturgical or celebratory lines praising the 'king of kings' and invoking the protection of Christ. It mentions the name Cunincpertus in a comparison regarding a right hand and concludes with a petition for eternal life.

This 6th-century Latin collection, 'Merovingici et Karolini by rhythmi antiquiores,' is a compilation of liturgical-style poetry, hagiography, and biblical narratives. The work is organized into distinct movements beginning with a history of salvation and Old Testament cycles featuring Holofernes, Nebuchadnezzar, and the defense of the Hebrew God at Bethulia. It contains Christological and Marian devotion, including the Nativity, the Passion, and the life of the Virgin Mary. Hagiographic elements include the life of Medardus and an account of Bishop Zeno performing an exorcism on a 'daughter of the empire.' The text transitions into mystical visions and martyrdom accounts involving Eustasius, Placidus, and Alexander. The final sections provide a geographical and ethnographic survey of the known world, mentioning the Saxones, Burgundiones, Taprobane, Parthia, and the Rhine, concluding with an eschatological and theological reflection on Creation.

The text begins with a series of poetic, highly metaphorical verses and a prayer for a holy figure, likely a bishop or saint named Medardus. It transitions into a biblical narrative featuring the historical figures of Nebuchadnezzar, Holofernes, and Achior. The narrative depicts Holofernes' military campaign against the Jews at Bethulia and a subsequent confrontation where Achior defends the power of the Hebrew God.

The text begins with a narrative of the biblical heroine Judith and the defeat of Holofernes, followed by a series of repetitive liturgical-style praises ('Mirabilia fecit deus') and a numbered list of religious symbols and figures including the prophet Josiah, the Virgin Eulalia, and the twelve apostles. The final section is a series of hymns and liturgical verses concerning the Virgin Mary, the Nativity of Christ, the Magi, and the role of the Holy Spirit.

This liturgical or poetic text is a series of hymns and refrains celebrating the Virgin Mary and the birth of Christ. It recounts biblical narratives including the visit of the Magi, the flight to Egypt, the baptism of John in the Jordan, and the miracle at the wedding at Cana. The text also references specific figures such as Herod, Zacchaeus, and the prophet Isaiah, while incorporating traditional tropes of the Nativity and the Passion.

This section contains a series of liturgical or devotional verses detailing the life of Christ, including his baptism in the Jordan, the wedding at Cana, the resurrection of Lazarus, and his passion and resurrection. The text transitions into a series of moral exhortations and instructions for monks, emphasizing humility, the avoidance of worldly praise, and the rejection of sensual pleasures. It concludes with a penitential prayer seeking divine mercy for sins committed through disobedience to God.

This section contains a series of penitential prayers and lamentations, likely intended for use in a monastic or liturgical context. The text features a speaker (a 'miser' or 'humile') confessing specific sins, such as the consumption of 'Falerna' and 'pocula', and seeking divine mercy and 'restitution' from Christ and the 'Redemptor vitae'. It includes a recurring refrain, 'Iesus clementer tribulantes subveni', and concludes with a plea for the forgiveness of sins and the granting of patience.

This section contains a series of liturgical hymns and prayers addressed to Christ and the Trinity, featuring repetitive refrains and invocations for mercy, the forgiveness of sins, and protection from evil. The text includes specific references to biblical figures such as David, Peter, Mary, and the prophet Enoch, as well as a concluding prophetic section regarding the Antichrist, the Day of Judgment, and the persecution of martyrs.

This section contains a series of apocalyptic and eschatological descriptions concerning the Day of Judgment, the defeat of a beast by the angel Michael, and the subsequent creation of a new heaven and earth. The text transitions into a moralizing exhortation against lust and the pursuit of worldly glory, warning the listener of their mortality and the vanity of human praise.

This section contains a series of rhythmic, repetitive exhortations and a narrative of the Passion of Christ. It features a recurring refrain regarding the mortality of man ('Adtende homo, quia de terra factus es') and concludes with a detailed, albeit stylistically irregular, account of the crucifixion involving figures such as Pilate, Judas, Simon, and Barrabban.

This section contains a series of liturgical hymns or poetic praises centered on the resurrection of Christ and his role as 'Salvator mundi' (Savior of the world). The text employs extensive Christological imagery, identifying Christ as the 'Lamb and Lion,' 'Bread of Heaven,' and 'Son of God,' while referencing biblical figures such as Peter, David, and Abraham.

This section of the text describes the Last Judgment, detailing the celestial spectacle of the sun, moon, and stars, and the separation of the righteous from the wicked. It features a dialogue between Christ and the condemned, who are rebuked for their lack of charity toward the poor and the sick. The final portion describes the rewards of the blessed in the heavenly Jerusalem and the eternal punishments of the damned in Gehenna.

This section contains a series of liturgical hymns or antiphons centered on the theme of the 'perennial day of the sabbath' (in perennis die sabbati). The text features a series of Marian and Christological praises, including references to the lineage of Abraham, the victory over the 'king of darkness,' and the role of Mary as the mother of Christ and the 'lily among thorns.'

This section contains a series of Marian and Christological hymns, beginning with a prayer to Mary to obtain the forgiveness of sins. It is followed by a long series of repetitive refrains honoring Saint John the Baptist, who is described as the precursor of the sun, the prophet of the Most High, and the one who prepared the way for Christ. The text includes references to the Virgin Mary, the Archangel Gabriel, and the prophet Isaiah.

This section contains a series of liturgical or devotional hymns and prayers centered on the theme of the Last Judgment and the glorification of Christ. It features a long descriptive passage of the apocalypse, including the resurrection of the dead and the judgment of the wicked, followed by a series of short, repetitive refrains ('Benedictus dominus, Christus dei filius') that recount biblical scenes involving figures such as Abraham, Daniel, Susanna, David, Elijah, Jonah, Joseph, Martha, Mary, Lazarus, Moses, and Noah.

This section contains a series of liturgical or devotional hymns and narrative passages concerning the life, miracles, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. It includes specific biblical scenes such as the healing of a paralytic, the feeding of the five thousand, the woman at the well, the miraculous catch of fish at Tiberias, and the appearance of Christ to the women and the disciples after the resurrection. The text also includes a formal doxology and a concluding narrative regarding the presence of the apostle Didymus.

This section contains a series of liturgical or devotional verses including a narrative of the Doubting Thomas, a doxology to the Trinity, and a moralizing discourse on the contrast between the wealthy man and Lazarus. It features specific mentions of the figures of Christ, Simon Peter, Didymus (Thomas), and the martyr Victor, while concluding with a depiction of the rich man's punishment in the afterlife.

This section contains a moralizing discourse on the avarice of the greedy, contrasting the behavior of the wealthy with the suffering of the poor. It transitions into a historical and theological narrative concerning the Jewish people, the siege of Jerusalem by Titus, and the destruction of the Temple. The text concludes with a series of vivid, repetitive descriptions of the suffering of the captives and the judgment of those who opposed Christ.

The text begins with a lamentation on famine and the slaughter of the weak, featuring a recurring refrain about princes seeking vengeance. It transitions into a geographical and mythological survey of the known world, naming locations such as Taprobane, Parthia, Armenia, and various regions of Europe. The final section describes the fierce and hardy nature of the Germanic tribes near the Rhine.

The text provides a geographical and ethnographic survey of Europe and Africa, naming various tribes (Tolerantes, Quadi, Marcomanni, Saxones, Burgundiones) and regions (Gallia Belgica, Aquitania, Septimania, Spania, Mauritania, Ethiopia). It describes natural features like the Danube, Rhône, and Tagus rivers, and concludes with a theological section on the creation of the world, the fall of Adam and Eve, and the first murder by Cain.

This section of the text presents a chronological and theological narrative of salvation history, moving from the biblical patriarchs (Cain, Lamech, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Lot) to the era of Moses and the Babylonian exile. It concludes with a series of liturgical-style verses detailing the life, miracles, and passion of Jesus Christ, including specific references to the feeding of the five thousand and the calling of Peter and Andrew.

This section contains a series of liturgical or poetic verses recounting the Passion, Resurrection, and appearances of Christ. It includes specific narratives regarding the flight into Egypt, the resurrection in Jerusalem, the appearance of Christ to the disciples at Emmaus, and the subsequent celebration of the Paschal feast.

This section contains a series of liturgical or devotional hymns and prayers centered on the life of Christ, the Nativity, and the Passion. It features specific narratives including the visit of the Magi, the flight to Egypt, the betrayal by Judas, and various biblical scenes such as the baptism of John, the miracle of the loaves and fishes, and Peter walking on water. The text concludes with a series of petitions for protection and forgiveness.

This section contains a series of liturgical-style prayers and a hagiographic narrative concerning Bishop Zeno (Zeno episcopus). The text describes Zeno as a 'confessor of the Lord' and 'shepherd of the people' who performs exorcisms against a demon and protects a 'daughter of the empire' (imperii filia) from demonic possession. The narrative includes a dialogue with a demon and concludes with a series of invocations and warnings against the 'accuser' and 'Judas'.

The text begins with a series of liturgical-style prayers and a series of 'Beatus homo' (Blessed is the man) and 'Est maledictus' (Cursed is he) antitheses regarding spiritual virtues and vices. It then transitions into a narrative based on the Book of Esther, featuring the characters of King Ahasuerus (Assuerus), Mordecai (Mardocheus), and Haman (Aman), and the Queen Hester. The narrative describes the royal court at Susa, the plot of Haman against Mordecai, and the decree against the Jews.

The text contains a narrative and liturgical sequence beginning with a retelling of the biblical story of Mordecai, Haman, and Esther, followed by a series of hymns and prayers. It includes a section of celebratory verses for a figure named 'Libero' associated with wine and the 'Andechavis' people, and concludes with a series of petitions for divine mercy and a concluding narrative about a hunter and a white deer.

The text recounts a mystical vision of a deer with a cross on its horns, leading to the conversion and baptism of a man named Placidus and his family. It follows the subsequent life of Eustasius, who survives a period of persecution and travels to Egypt, where he is eventually recognized by soldiers as the military commander Placidus. The narrative concludes with Eustasius being rewarded by the Emperor with wealth and titles.

The text recounts the military actions of Eustasius and the liberation of the Pannonian borders by the general Placidas. It follows a narrative of a mother and her two sons, who were separated and captured by barbarians, and their subsequent reunion and martyrdom. The final section shifts to a legendary account of a figure named Alexander who traveled the world and encountered various beasts.

This section contains a series of penitential hymns and prayers addressed to Christ, featuring themes of judgment, the end of the world, and the purification of the soul. It includes descriptions of the apocalypse, such as the darkening of the sun and moon, the judgment of the just and the wicked, and the physical punishments of the damned. The text also contains personal pleas for mercy from a sinner who confesses to lust, greed, and the worship of idols.

This section contains a series of liturgical or devotional hymns and prayers addressed to Christ. The text includes a repetitive plea for mercy and the forgiveness of sins, descriptions of the Passion and Resurrection, and a concluding hymn praising the Trinity and the divinity of Christ.

This section contains a series of liturgical-style hymns and prayers centered on the figure of Christ, including references to the Trinity, the Passion, and the Resurrection. A significant portion of the text is dedicated to a repetitive refrain, 'Abicite vana loqui' (Cast away vain words), interspersed with descriptions of a peacock (pavo) and warnings against the 'gifts of the enemy.'

This passage contains a series of liturgical prayers and a Marian hymn. It includes a petition for deliverance from evil and a doxology to Christ as the protector of all, followed by a repetitive series of praises to the Virgin Mary as the mother of God and the bearer of the Lord.

A late antique Latin hymn or panegyric addressed to a ruler named Odo. The text is structured as a series of exhortations and comparisons, invoking biblical figures and historical figures to illustrate the virtues of the prince. The first section lists biblical figures including Abel, Samuel, Daniel, Nathanael, Enoch, Sadoc, Jacob, Job, Abraham, Balaam, Jeroboam, Joatam, Solomon, Samson, Absalom, and Gideon. The second section introduces historical figures, including Julius, David, Judas, Alexander Maximus, and Pompeius. The concluding section shifts to a geographical and celebratory mode, mentioning Gaul, Burgundy, Wasconia, and Teutonia. The work employs a repetitive 'Sis' (May you be) construction to attribute specific qualities to Odo.

This 6th-century Latin collection, titled 'ex variis codicibus collecti by rhythmi antiquiores,' is a compilation of liturgical poetry, devotional hymns, and theological meditations. The work is organized into nine distinct sections that move from mystical and allegorical descriptions of Christ, the Virgin Mary, and the Trinity to extensive biblical narratives and hagiography. It features prominent biblical figures such as Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, and the prophets Isaiah and Jeremiah. Notable geographical and symbolic references include the New Jerusalem, the mountains of Lebanon, and the city of Damascus. The text also incorporates moralizing exhortations against gluttony, avarice, and acedia, and includes a specific historical reference to a monastery founded by a pontiff named Frodomundus during the reign of Theodoric. The collection concludes with a transition from apocalyptic imagery to practical moral and pedagogical themes.

This text is a collection of liturgical or devotional hymns and prayers. It contains a series of petitions for protection against physical dangers (sea, fire, enemies), a series of praises for the Virgin Mary and Christ, and a mystical description of the New Jerusalem and the sacraments of death and baptism.

This section contains a series of mystical and allegorical descriptions of Christ, the Church, and the Virgin Mary, utilizing biblical imagery such as the city of Jerusalem, the mountains of Lebanon, and the figures of the three archangels (Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael). It employs elaborate symbolic associations, such as the 'tower of Lebanon' representing the virgin's purity and 'Damascus' representing prudence, while describing the liturgy of the saints and the hierarchy of angels.

This section contains a series of hagiographic and biblical vignettes structured by a recurring refrain regarding the names of saints. It recounts the lives and deeds of figures including Adam, Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Aaron, Phinehas, Joshua (referred to as 'Iesus Nave'), Caleb, Samuel, David, Nathan, Solomon, and Elijah.

This section contains a series of liturgical or devotional verses and hymns featuring biblical figures and events. It includes references to the prophet Isaiah, King Hezekiah, King Josiah, and the prophet Jeremiah, alongside a dramatic dialogue between the Devil (Infer) and Satan regarding the imprisonment of the 'Prince of Death' (Christ). The final portion recounts the biblical narrative of the brothers of Joseph and their conspiracy against him.

The text recounts the biblical narrative of Joseph being sold by his brothers, his imprisonment in Egypt, and his trial before Potiphar's wife. It transitions into an apocalyptic prophecy concerning the Antichrist, the judgment of nations, and the final glory of Jerusalem. The passage concludes with a warning against the damned and a call to imitate the virtues of the saints.

This section contains a series of liturgical or devotional hymns and prayers concerning the apocalypse, the judgment of the world, and the creation of the cosmos. It features specific references to the Trinity, the fall of man (Eve and the serpent), the Great Flood, and the biblical figures of Abraham, Moses, and Noah. The text concludes with a series of theological descriptions of the Trinity and the creation of the world in six days.

This section contains a collection of liturgical and devotional texts, including a hymn to the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, a narrative of the Pentecost, and a series of historical/genealogical verses. It mentions biblical figures such as Isaiah, Enoch, Abraham, and Sarah, and includes a specific reference to a monastery founded by a pontiff named Frodomundus in the sixth year of the reign of Theodoric in France. The text also includes a list of diverse nations (Arabs, Medes, Scythians, etc.) and a concluding section on the creation and history of humanity.

This section contains a collection of varied liturgical, educational, and moralizing verses. It includes a Marian hymn (the Ave Maria), a series of instructional verses for students and teachers, a section on the dangers of gluttony and avarice, and a concluding passage on the spiritual dangers of acedia.

This section contains a series of moralizing and theological exhortations against pride, vanity, and worldly desires, interspersed with liturgical-style reflections on the Eucharist and the Apocalypse. It references biblical figures such as Ezekiel and the lineage of David, and includes a passage regarding the counting of sheep and the role of a shepherd. The text concludes with a plea for spiritual guidance and a mention of the 'venal grammar' (grammaticam venalem).

This medieval Latin text is a collection of liturgical or devotional hymns and prayers, likely intended for use in a liturgical cycle or as a private devotional book. The work contains several distinct sections: a series of apocalyptic and eschatological verses concerning the judgment of the world, a narrative of the resurrection of Christ, and a series of 'Miserere' petitions. It features specific references to the city of Rome, the location of Bethlehem, and the figure of Mary Magdalene. The text emphasizes themes of divine judgment, the suffering and triumph of Christ, and the necessity of penance. The structure moves from a general warning of the end times to specific biblical narratives and concludes with repetitive pleas for mercy.

This 9th-century Latin collection of carmina consists of five distinct sections blending theological meditation, moral exhortation, and elegiac poetry. The work opens with a Christological meditation on the Trinity and a formal address to a high-ranking cleric regarding a prologue. Subsequent sections provide moral reflections on civil strife and the dangers of internal division, incorporating biblical history involving King Josiah and the tribes of Israel. The text features several prominent biblical and ecclesiastical figures, including Paul, Samuel, Daniel, Jerome, and the prophet Jeremiah. The final sections transition into elegiac laments for a deceased brother and a lyrical appeal for consolation following physical suffering. The work is characterized by its movement from formal ecclesiastical doctrine to personal mourning and spiritual guidance.

The text begins with a theological meditation on the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) and the unity of substance in the diversity of persons. It transitions into a formal address to a high-ranking cleric (referred to as 'presul' and 'vicarie Christi') regarding a literary work or prologue. The latter half contains a series of moral and theological reflections, including a reference to 'Doctor Gregorius' and a lamentation over the state of the Church and the 'plebeian' masses.

The text contains a series of moral and religious poems concerning civil strife, the dangers of internal division, and the consequences of disobeying divine law. It references biblical figures and groups, including Paul, the tribes of Israel (Ammon, Madian, Moab, Amalech, Philistines, and Judah), and the king Josiah. The final section describes the biblical king Josiah's actions in restoring the temple and the law.

The text contains a series of moral and spiritual exhortations, referencing biblical figures such as Samuel, Daniel, and Jerome. It features a dialogue or internal monologue regarding a ruler's governance, the hardships of a traveler or a woman in distress, and a concluding prayer for a brother. The passage also includes a section on the distribution of divine gifts and the duties of a spiritual guide.

This section of the carmina contains a series of elegiac and didactic verses centered on themes of mourning, brotherhood, and religious devotion. It references biblical figures such as Adam, Eve, Seth, Jacob, Joseph, and Benjamin, as well as the prophet Jeremiah and the figure of Lazarus. The text includes a lament for a deceased brother, a reference to the 'preesul' (prelate), and a concluding appeal for the remembrance of a brother's death.

The text is a lyrical address involving two speakers (or a collective 'we') appealing to a third party for assistance and comfort. The speaker describes a moment of suffering involving a 'recent wound' (plaga recentem) and a subsequent lamentation, concluding with a request for the listener to provide a transition from weeping to joy.

A medieval Latin carmina (song or poem) attributed to Sedulius Scotus. The text is structured as a lyrical dialogue or mystical vision involving a male figure and a female figure (referred to as 'virgo'). The poem contains heavy allegorical and mystical imagery, including references to 'sophia' (Greek wisdom) and 'sapientia' (Roman wisdom), as well as celestial and physical descriptions such as 'lumina' (lights), 'astra' (stars), and 'radientia fronte' (radiant foreheads). It incorporates religious and moral themes, mentioning 'dei' (God), 'pietate' (piety), and 'alms'. The text also contains specific geographical or cultural references such as 'Europae', 'Graece', and 'Romae'. The poem concludes with a description of 'candida progenies' and 'patria pauperibus'.

This 9th-century Latin poem by Sedulius Scotus is a moral and theological panegyric concerning the virtues of kingship and divine governance. The work is organized into four movements that move from the qualities of a just ruler to the nature of the Creator. It utilizes allegorical comparisons between earthly leadership and the cosmos, featuring biblical figures such as Christ, David, Abraham, and the land of Israel. The text contrasts the virtues of prudence and law with the vices of pride and worldly corruption, specifically citing Antiochus, Pharaoh, Herod, and Pilate as cautionary examples. Later sections meditate on the 'medicine' of peace, the defeat of Goliath, and the role of the Good Shepherd. The work concludes with a vision of an ideal Christian ruler who governs through equity and divine mandate.

This section of the poem is a panegyric and moral exhortation regarding the virtues of kingship, governance, and divine authority. It features a series of allegorical comparisons between the rule of a just monarch and the governance of the cosmos, referencing biblical figures such as Christ, David, and Abraham, and the land of Israel. The text emphasizes the necessity of 'art' (skill/craft) in leadership, the importance of chastity and prudence in the ruler, and the stability provided by law and discipline.

The text presents a series of moral and religious allegories regarding the contrast between the virtues of a righteous ruler and the corruption of worldly kings. It specifically names historical figures such as Antiochus, Pharoah, Herod, and Pilate as examples of those who suffer the consequences of pride. The final section transitions into a theological description of the creation of the world and the divine attributes of the Creator.

This section of the poem uses a series of allegorical and metaphorical comparisons to contrast the virtues of peace and spiritual devotion with the perils of pride and military might. It features a lengthy meditation on the 'medicine' of peace, the dangers of relying on personal strength, and a concluding theological reflection on the divine nature of the creator. The text incorporates biblical imagery, including the defeat of Goliath and the role of the Good Shepherd.

The text describes the qualities of an ideal Christian ruler who governs through equity, divine favor, and the fear of God. It contrasts the true glory of a ruler who upholds the laws and order of the land with the deceptive, 'honeyed' words of those who harbor hidden malice. The passage concludes with a vision of a peaceful state where the public is blessed and the ruler is honored with trophies.

This medieval Latin collection of poems by Sedulius Scotus consists of panegyric, pastoral poetry, and religious allegory. The work is organized into cycles that alternate between the praise of the Carolingian dynasty and the use of classical mythological imagery to illustrate Christian themes. Notable figures praised include Carolus (Charlemagne), Ludewicus, Lothar, and the noblewoman Ermingard. The text incorporates botanical and celestial imagery, such as trees, flowers, and topaz, to symbolize the Eucharist and spiritual virtues. Specific allegorical segments include a dialogue between a rose and a lily, the figure of the Cherub of the law, and the inclusion of the Muses alongside biblical figures like Moses and the Magi. The geography mentioned includes the Rhine, the Moselle, Rome, and biblical sites such as Sion, the Jordan, and the Nile. The work also mentions specific individuals including Hildwinus, Berta, and Guntharius.

This section of the poem contains a series of laudatory verses addressed to a high-ranking prelate, likely a bishop or abbot, referred to as 'praesul' and 'pastor'. The text includes specific references to the 'Francigenis' (Franks), 'Scottigenis' (Scots), and the name 'Lantbertus'. The poet employs classical and mythological imagery, including references to Apollo, Tithona, and the winds (Boreas, Eurus, Zephyrus), while praising the subject's eloquence, wisdom, and spiritual leadership.

The text is a pastoral and allegorical poem addressed to a 'good shepherd' (bonus pastor) and a 'father' (pater), likely a high-ranking cleric. It contains a series of invocations and praises involving religious imagery, the city of Rome, and the landscape of Italy. The poem incorporates classical and biblical references, including the names of the Musae, the prophet Daniel, and the figure of Hannibal, while utilizing metaphors of gems (beryllus, zaphirus) and nature (cedrus, olive trees).

The text contains a series of lyrical and allegorical verses involving figures such as Moses, Orpheus, and Calliope, set against a backdrop of pastoral and celestial imagery. It mentions specific locations including Rome, Mantua, and the Hesperides, and references historical or semi-historical figures such as Caesar, the Frankish leader Lothar, and the priest Hartgarius. The narrative shifts between mythological scenes of musical performance and a formal, quasi-ecclesiastical address regarding the leadership of the Church and the state.

The text contains a series of poetic addresses and allegories involving figures such as Maron, Calliope, and the shepherd. It features a transition from classical and mythological imagery (Pegasus, the Muses, the Nile, and the beast of the desert) to Christian themes, specifically the birth of the Messiah, the role of Joseph, and the journey from Egypt.

This section of the poem contains a series of laudatory verses celebrating the virtues, lineage, and divine favor of a ruler named Carolus (Charles), specifically identified as a 'new Carolus' and a 'prince of Europe.' The text weaves together biblical imagery (Sion, the Magi, the Virgin Mary, and the shepherd), references to historical figures like Croesus and Darius, and a series of panegyrics regarding his military prowess and role as a protector of the Church. It also includes a section of mystical or liturgical-style praise involving the number seven and the 'sacred Sophia.'

This section of the poem contains a series of laudatory verses and religious exhortations. It features specific mentions of historical and biblical figures such as Charlemagne (Karolus), Louis (Ludewicus), and the biblical figures of the Daughter of Zion and the Shepherd. The text also includes a personal dedication to the author's peers, including a mention of a 'Lantberti' and a 'Vulfengus', while incorporating standard liturgical and celebratory imagery of the Church.

This section of the poem is a panegyric addressed to Ermingard, a noblewoman of the Frankish court, and a celebration of the Carolingian dynasty. It features a series of laudatory verses describing her physical beauty and virtues, followed by a hagiographic and allegorical narrative involving biblical figures such as Peter, Paul, and Cornelius. The text concludes with a formal praise of the Frankish realm, the lineage of Lothar, and the new ruler, Carolus (Charlemagne).

This section of the poem contains a series of laudatory verses and martial imagery, likely celebrating a ruler or military leader (referred to as Caesar or a 'nobile sidus'). It includes specific references to the defense of the realm against Moors and Saracens, the mention of the names Lothar and Ermengardis, and a concluding section of religious and poetic praise.

This section of the poem is a panegyric for a ruler named Ludewicus (Louis), identified as the successor to the Carolingian dynasty (Karoli). The text utilizes heavy celestial and biblical imagery, comparing the king to Solomon and David, and praises his role as the protector of France and the leader of the Franks. It mentions specific geographical and cultural entities including Europe, Africa, the Alps, the Jordan, and the Jews and Greeks.

This section of the carmina contains a series of celebratory and exhortative verses addressing a ruler or leader, likely in a military or political context involving the Rhine, the Franks, and the Scots. It transitions into a panegyric for a 'Medicinae matris' (Mother of Medicine) and a description of a multi-colored cross (Iris) and its symbolic colors. The final portion concludes with a drinking song or toast, referencing the Falernus wine and the 'Bachicus' measure.

This section of Sedulius's poetry contains a series of elegiac and celebratory verses addressing various figures and themes. It includes a series of addresses to individuals such as Franconus, Fergus, Blanda, Marcum, Beuchellem, and others, while referencing figures like Moses, Christ, and the Muses. The text also contains a lament for a deceased youth, a reference to the 'Sons of Eberharde and Gisla,' and a concluding passage regarding a 'Ludewicus' and the 'image of a father.'

This section of Sedulius's poetry contains a series of distinct, often disjointed segments. It includes a panegyric to a youth named Eberhard (or a figure addressed as such) for his military success against the Moors and Saracens, a transition to a pastoral/mythological lament regarding a horned beast (possibly a bull or ram) and the goddess Lucina, and a concluding scene of a military skirmish involving a 'magnanimous leader' and a 'bold cohort.'

This section of the poem describes a dramatic confrontation in a forest involving a figure named Hartgarius, who identifies himself as a 'praesul' (leader) and a 'dux gregis' (leader of the flock). The narrative includes a dialogue regarding a 'sacrificial' lamb, a transition to a sacred space (a house or temple) dedicated to the Virgin Mary and the name of Hartgarius, and concludes with a series of liturgical-style praises for the 'Conditor' and the 'clerical order'.

This section of the poem contains a series of religious and allegorical sequences, including a narrative of the Nativity, the journey of the Magi, and the flight into Egypt. It features specific mentions of figures such as Christ, Mary, Joseph, Simeon, and the archangel Gabriel, as well as the saints Peter and Paul. The text also includes a transition into a pastoral and celestial scene involving the seasons, the river Moselle, and a concluding section on the judgment of nations and the deeds of warriors.

This section of the poem contains a series of allegorical and martial descriptions involving a trumpet, a chariot, and an elephant, followed by a series of praises and invocations directed at a 'prelate' or 'leader' named Robert. The text includes a list of names including Francis, David, Solomon, and Moses, and concludes with a defense of the author's 'hard words' against the threat of being stoned.

This section of the poem contains a series of panegyrics and religious invocations, specifically praising a ruler named Lothari (a descendant of Carolus/Charlemagne) and his lineage. It incorporates heavy allegorical and biblical imagery, referencing the River Jordan, the Mount of Zion, and the city of Siloam, while also mentioning specific figures like Hartgarius and the queen/mother Ermingardis. The text blends Christian devotion with imperial praise, utilizing traditional tropes of the 'peaceful prince' and the 'holy feast'.

This section of the poem contains a series of laudatory verses and allegorical descriptions, likely for a religious or ceremonial occasion. It mentions specific figures such as Leutbertus (Lantberti), Everhardus, and the 'Francigenas' (Franks), while referencing geographical locations like Rome, Italy, Africa, and the Alps. The text weaves together celestial imagery, biblical references (Jacob, Gideon, the Garden of Eden), and military metaphors involving the 'lorica fidei' and the 'scutum' of Italy.

This section of Sedulius's poetry contains a series of highly ornate, allegorical verses blending Christian and classical imagery. It mentions specific figures such as Sedulius, Peter (Cephas), and the martyr Bonifacius, while referencing geographical locations like the Jordan (Geon, Fison, Euphrates, Tigris), the Rhine, and the city of Solima. The text weaves together biblical themes of the tree of life and the fountain of Siloam with classical references to Muses, Bacchus, and the river Pactolus.

This section of the poem contains a series of laudatory verses and allegorical descriptions. It features specific mentions of the figures Christ, Mary, and the Muses, as well as the names Hildwinus, Berta, and the location of Cologne (Colonia). The text employs heavy metaphorical imagery involving botanical symbols (trees, flowers, fruit), celestial bodies, and precious stones like topaz to describe virtues and spiritual rewards.

The text features a series of allegorical and symbolic poems involving a 'sacred bridegroom' (Christ), a 'rose' (representing a virgin or martyr), and a 'lily'. It includes a dialogue between the rose and the lily, a description of the Cherub of the law, and a concluding section that identifies Guntharius and mentions the river Moselle.

This medieval Latin poem by Sedulius Scotus is a liturgical and celebratory work organized into two distinct sections. The first part contains hymns praising Christ as the ruler of the cosmos and redeemer of humanity, incorporating celestial imagery and references to the Passion. It includes specific geographical and historical references to Rome, Latium, and Caesar Augustus, and contains a direct address to Sofride. The second part shifts toward ecclesiastical and local themes, featuring a series of benedictions and liturgical praises. It addresses a pastor and a duke named Leodfride, while invoking the names of Angelbertus, Ambrosius, and Tado. The text also mentions the gathering of Scottigenas and concludes with a formal address to the 'optime ductor' regarding the elements of earth and sea.

This section of the poem contains a series of liturgical and celebratory verses praising Christ as the ruler of the cosmos and the redeemer of humanity. It includes a direct address to a figure named Sofride, mentions of the city of Rome, and a concluding prayer to the Holy Trinity. The text incorporates celestial imagery, references to the Passion, and a brief mention of Caesar Augustus and the land of Latium.

This section contains a series of celebratory and liturgical verses addressed to a 'pastor' (shepherd) and a 'dux' (duke) named Leodfride. It includes invocations of figures such as Angelbertus, Ambrosius, and Tado, and mentions the gathering of 'Scottigenas' (Scots). The text concludes with a series of benedictions and a formal address to the 'optime ductor' (best guide) involving the elements of earth and sea.

This medieval Latin pastoral poem by Sedulius Scotus is structured in two parts focusing on the duties and spiritual status of the clergy. The first section provides a series of exhortations to a priest (sacer) regarding pastoral care, the study of scripture, and the administration of the sacraments, specifically baptism, mass, and confession. It emphasizes the moral requirements for entering heaven and the spiritual significance of the Eucharist. The second section focuses on the role of the presbyter, addressing his status in marriage, his authority to bind and loose, and his role as a mediator. It concludes with descriptions of liturgical actions at the altar and the specific customs regarding the priest's death and burial.

This section of the pastoral poem contains a series of exhortations and warnings addressed to a priest (sacer).
