It covers themes of pastoral care, the importance of diligent study and scripture, the duties of the clergy in the sacraments (baptism, mass, and confession), and the moral requirements for entering the kingdom of heaven. The text also includes instructions on communal life, the avoidance of worldly distractions, and the spiritual significance of the Eucharist.

The text describes the roles, duties, and spiritual status of a priest (presbyter) in relation to his marriage, his role as a mediator and legislator in the church, and his liturgical actions. It details the priest's authority to bind and loose, his conduct at the altar, and his transition from life to death, including his specific burial customs.

The *sequentiae Sangallenses* is a medieval Latin liturgical collection containing a series of hymns, prayers, and chants. The work is organized into nine distinct sections, beginning with the martyrdom of Saint Stephen and the role of the Holy Spirit, followed by a cycle of sacraments including Baptism and the Eucharist. It features hagiographical cycles for Saint Blaise, Gordianus, Epimachus, and Martin of Tours, the latter of whom is associated with miracles in Gaul and Italy. The text incorporates specific geographical references to Lugdunum, Vienna, the Rhine, Cassino, and the Retian region, as well as mentions of India, Hibernia, and Germany. Notable figures included are the Virgin Mary (as Theotocos), the apostles Paul and Columban, and saints such as Otmar, Michael, Mauricius, and Heimrammus. The collection concludes with a series of doxologies and petitions focused on the unity of the Holy Trinity.

This text is a liturgical chant or hymn for the feast of Saint Stephen (Stephane), the first martyr (protomartyr). It recounts the martyrdom of Stephen, describing his trial before the authorities, his intercession for his persecutors, and the subsequent recognition of his sanctity by the Church. The passage also includes references to Christ as the 'Levite' and 'Lord of Hosts,' and mentions the biblical figure Saul (Paul) and the role of the Holy Spirit.

This section of the medieval liturgy contains a series of hymns and prayers focused on the life of Christ, the Virgin Mary, and the sacraments of Baptism and the Holy Spirit. It includes specific references to the infancy of Christ, the role of the Virgin, and the martyrdom of saints. The text also incorporates traditional liturgical elements such as the 'Levamus praecordia' and a concluding call for the world to celebrate the day.

This section of the medieval liturgical text contains a series of hymns and prayers focused on the sacraments of baptism and the Eucharist, as well as the feast of Saint Blaise (Blasi). It includes specific references to the Trinity, the Virgin Mary, and the role of the Holy Spirit, while incorporating traditional tropes of redemption and the transition from the Old Law to the New Covenant.

This section of the *sequentiae* contains a series of liturgical chants and hymns celebrating the martyrdom of Gordianus and Epimachus. The text includes references to the triumph of Christ over death, the suffering of the martyrs under persecution, and a series of invocations to the saints and the divine. It mentions specific historical/hagiographical figures such as Gordianus, Epimachus, and the apostle Paul.

This section of the medieval Latin text contains a series of fragmented, often cryptic liturgical or devotional phrases. It mentions specific names such as Desiderius, Helias, Zezabelis, Margareta, and several locations including Lugdunum and Vienna. The text includes references to Christ, the Virgin, and various religious concepts like the Eucharist, the sacraments, and the struggle against the flesh.

This section of the medieval Latin text contains a series of liturgical or devotional verses. It features a Marian hymn celebrating the Virgin Mary as the 'Theotocos' and the 'seed of Jesse,' followed by a series of invocations to saints, specifically naming Michael, Mauricius, and Heimrammus. The text concludes with a series of religious exhortations and mentions of geographical locations such as India, Hibernia, Gaul, and Germany.

This section of the liturgical text contains a series of hymns and prayers dedicated to Saint Martin of Tours, emphasizing his role as a confessor and his miraculous deeds, such as clothing a leper and raising the dead. It includes specific geographical references to Gaul, Italy, and Pannonia, and mentions the 'medicines' of the saint which are said to cure fevers and paralysis. The text also references the 'Svevia' and 'Otmarum' in a liturgical context.

This section of the *sequentiae* contains liturgical chants and invocations for a feast, specifically mentioning the saint Otmar and the saint Columban. It includes a series of 'Alleluia' verses involving natural elements (birds, mountains, seas) and a concluding trinitarian hymn. The text references specific locations such as the Rhine, Cassino, and the region of the Retians.

This liturgical text contains a series of hymns or prayers focused on the Holy Trinity (Pater, Filius, Spiritus Sanctus) and the unity of the divine essence. It includes a series of doxologies and petitions for protection, redemption, and purification of the people. The text emphasizes the attributes of the Trinity, such as their shared substance and the distinction of their persons.

This Latin text is a collection of funeral hymns and a commemorative inscription (rhythmi) composed by Sigloardus Remensis in the 9th century. The first section is a funeral lament for a high-ranking prelate named Fulco, characterized by praise for his eloquence, wisdom, and service to the church. The text includes a dramatic narrative regarding a villainous figure, identified as Guinemarus, who is portrayed as a treacherous 'serpent' and 'glass-maker' who betrayed the deceased. The second section functions as a hagiographic and commemorative text for Saint Remigius (Remigius), detailing his transition to the heavenly realm and his role as a healer of the blind and lame. The work mentions specific historical and ecclesiastical figures, including the King Carolus (Charles) and Prince Richard, and concludes with a formal dedication of the tomb.

This 9th-century Latin collection of poems by Smaragdus combines didactic, allegorical, and devotional modes. The work opens with a treatise on cosmology, the creation of the world, and the nature of the Holy Spirit, followed by a technical exploration of number theory and the hierarchy of names. The second section shifts to a study of Latin grammar and rhetoric, utilizing a nautical metaphor and botanical imagery to describe the mastery of language. The third section provides moralizing verses on the monastic life, employing metaphors of musical harmony and the refining of gold to describe the spiritual pilgrimage toward the celestial kingdom. The final section is a devotional poem and liturgical-style hymn addressed to Christ, concluding with a mystical vision of the heavenly Jerusalem and an angelic host.

The text is a collection of poems or didactic verses concerning theology, cosmology, and mathematics. It contains a section on the creation of the world and the nature of the Holy Spirit, followed by a dense allegorical and technical treatise on the properties of numbers (specifically the distinction between 'unus' and 'vinius' or similar numerical concepts) and the hierarchy of names.

This section of the poem explores the technical and aesthetic construction of Latin grammar and rhetoric, specifically focusing on the relationship between words, cases, and figures of speech. It employs an extended nautical metaphor, describing the navigation of a ship through 'seas of words' and the 'taming' of language. The text also includes a list of botanical imagery (lilies, violets, cinnamon, rose) and a series of rhetorical variations of verbs.

This section of Smaragdus's carmina contains a series of allegorical and moralizing verses concerning the spiritual journey of the monk toward the celestial kingdom. It employs heavy metaphorical imagery involving musical harmony, the refining of the soul like gold, and the navigation of a 'sacred path' (via regia) to achieve divine favor. The text concludes with a series of exhortations on virtues such as humility, patience, and the study of sacred figures.

The text is a devotional poem and prayer addressed to Christ, characterized by a transition from the author's personal invocation of divine inspiration to a series of liturgical-style praises. It includes a formal hymn of praise to Christ as the source of light and truth, followed by a mystical description of the spiritual nourishment of the faithful and a concluding celestial scene involving the 'superna' Jerusalem and a host of angels singing 'Alleluia'.

A Latin hymn or poetic text attributed to Smaragdus, likely part of a medieval psalter or liturgical collection. The work describes the physical and spiritual qualities of a sacred book, contrasting its external ornamentation with its internal mystical content. It references the 'dogma of the holy fathers' and the 'sacred' tradition of the past. The text specifically mentions the Psalms of David and the author's own name, Smaragdus, in a metaphorical context regarding the discernment of 'gems' (gemmas) within the text. The structure moves from a description of the book's physical casing to the spiritual significance of the words contained within.

This 9th-century Latin text by Smaragdus is a formal exhortation and moral instruction addressed to the son of Louis the Pious. The first section focuses on the virtues of kingship, specifically justice, prudence, and the rejection of greed as divine requirements for governance. It employs allegorical and poetic imagery to describe the rewards of a righteous reign, such as the 'treasure of heaven' and the 'crown of wisdom.' The second section transitions into a prayer and hymn of praise addressed to Christ. This portion contains a cosmological description of the creation of the heavens, the placement of stars, and the elements of the sea and sky. The work concludes with a declaration of Christ's power and includes Eucharistic imagery.

This text is a formal exhortation and moral instruction addressed to a prince (the son of Louis the Pious). It emphasizes the virtues of a ruler, including justice, prudence, and the rejection of greed, while framing these qualities as divine requirements for the governance of the kingdom. The passage also contains a series of allegorical and poetic descriptions of the rewards of a righteous reign, such as the 'treasure of heaven' and the 'crown of wisdom.'

This passage is a prayer and hymn of praise addressed to Christ, characterized by a transition from a petition for celestial protection to a description of the cosmos. It describes the creation of the heavens, the placement of stars, and the natural elements of the sea and sky, concluding with a declaration of Christ's power.

This text is a collection of excerpts from the life of Saint Landbert, attributed to Stephanus Leodiensis. The passage contains a series of poetic and theological reflections, beginning with a rejection of pagan entities such as the Dryads and the Nymphs. It features a meditation on the nature of truth, the distinction between substance and existence, and the spiritual state of the individual. The narrative includes a dialogue involving a figure addressed as a hero, who responds to a lament regarding madness. The text concludes with a cosmological description of the sun moving toward the stars and the flight of Aurora from the darkness.

This 9th-century Latin sylloge is a multi-thematic compendium organized into five distinct sections. The opening portion features descriptive poetry concerning fauna, gemstones, and botany, followed by a nautical passage involving the winds Eurus, Boreas, Vulturnus, Zephyrus, Austris, and Aquilon. The second and third sections transition into a dense meditation on sacred geometry, the Trinity, Christology, and the musical and mathematical proportions of the cosmos, including the movements of the seven planets and human anatomy. The fourth section provides technical astronomical calculations regarding the orbits of celestial bodies and the measurement of 'ortus' and 'occasus'. The final section concludes with a geographical survey of the Iberian Peninsula, specifically mentioning Hispania, Aquitania, the Tagus River, and Gaditanus.

This section contains a series of poetic and descriptive verses featuring a variety of animals (birds, beasts, and sea creatures), precious stones, and botanical elements. It includes a nautical passage describing a ship navigating through various winds (Eurus, Boreas, Vulturnus, Zephyrus, Austris, Aquilon) and a concluding architectural description of a temple or building.

This section of the text describes a physical and symbolic architectural space, detailing a portico, altar, and various vessels (patenae, urcei, calices) used in a ritual or liturgical context. The latter half of the passage transitions into a dense numerological and theological meditation on the Trinity, the dual nature of Christ, and the division of the world into triads, diads, and various mathematical proportions.

This section of the text explores the mathematical and musical proportions of the cosmos, specifically focusing on the relationships between numbers like six, eight, nine, and twelve. It links these numerical harmonies to the creation of the world, the movements of the seven planets, and the physical structure of the human body. The passage concludes with a discussion on the harmony of musical intervals and the inherent order of the universe.

This section of the text describes astronomical and cosmological calculations, specifically the movements of the sun, moon, and planets within a system of spheres and orbits. It details the measurement of celestial distances, the division of the year into seasons, and the geometric properties of the cosmos, including the use of various units of measurement and the calculation of 'ortus' (rising) and 'occasus' (setting).

The text describes the geography of the Iberian Peninsula and surrounding regions. It mentions the fertility of the land, the proximity of Asia and Africa, and specific locations including Gaditanus (Gades), the Tyrrhenian Sea, Spain (Hispania), the Tagus River, and Aquitania.

This 9th-century Latin sylloge is a diverse collection of liturgical texts, hagiographical prose, and technical treatises. The first half of the work consists of prayers, hymns, and a martyrology featuring figures such as the Magi, Saint Lawrence, Saint Otmar, and Saint Gall. It includes a narrative of the Nativity and a specific hagiographical account of the virgin Hildigarda, daughter of King Hludowicus and sister of Charlemagne. The latter half of the manuscript shifts toward disparate subjects, including a description of the temple of Beretha, a discourse on geometry and astronomy (mentioning Mars, Mercury, and the Moon), and a technical commentary on the translation of the Vulgate from Hebrew and Greek. The text concludes with a blessing for a prelate and a doxology.

This liturgical text contains a series of prayers and hymns for a feast, beginning with a call to spiritual purification and the contemplation of mystical words. It includes a narrative section concerning the Nativity of Christ, the adoration of the Magi, and the subsequent slaughter of infants by King Herod. The text concludes with a long list of saints, including the apostles, martyrs, and confessors, invoked for protection and intercession.

This section contains a series of liturgical hymns and prayers, including a litany of female martyrs (Felicitas, Eulalia, Verena, etc.) and a series of petitions to Christ and the Virgin Mary. It includes specific invocations to saints such as Otmar, Lawrence, John the Baptist, and Peter and Paul, as well as a concluding section of praise for Rome and the German land.

This section contains a series of liturgical prayers and hymns addressed to Christ, the Virgin Mary, and various saints, including Saint Gall, Saint Peter, Saint Paul, and Saint Stephen. It includes specific petitions for the forgiveness of sins, the protection of the faithful, and the celebration of holy days. The text concludes with a series of invocations and a list of geographic regions and peoples, including Noricum, Saxony, Spain, and Gaul, addressed to a king or ruler.

This section of the sylloge contains a series of liturgical or devotional verses and prayers. It mentions King Carol (Charles), the abbot Otmarus, and the apostle Peter, while invoking the Trinity and the protection of the apostles. The text includes invocations for mercy, the forgiveness of sins, and the celebration of the divine nature of Christ.

This section contains a series of liturgical prayers, hymns, and hagiographical prose. It includes a prayer for the martyrs and saints, a sequence of liturgical chants (including a 'Kirieleison' and a 'Carmina' section), and a biographical passage concerning a virgin named Hildigarda, daughter of King Hludowicus, and her sister, a sister of Charlemagne.

This section of the sylloge contains a series of disparate fragments including a description of a temple (Beretha) with architectural details, a liturgical scene involving the clergy and the 'virgins of Christ', and a series of mystical or allegorical verses. It features several proper names and locations, including the figures Felix and Regula, the locations of Vranikos and Albisum, and the city of Memphis. The latter half of the text shifts into a dense, abstract discourse on geometry, astronomy, and the movement of celestial bodies like Mars, Mercury, and the Moon.

The text begins with a poetic description of music and the arts before transitioning into a technical commentary on biblical translation and the production of the Vulgate. It discusses the differences between Hebrew, Greek, and Latin versions of the scriptures, specifically mentioning the work of Jerome (Hieronimus). The final section contains a series of liturgical or celebratory verses, including a blessing for a prelate (presul) and a concluding doxology.

This medieval Latin collection of enigmas, attributed to Tatwinus, consists of two primary sections of riddles and allegorical verse. The first section contains twenty-one riddles employing metaphorical language to describe entities such as a figure 'wiser than Solomon,' a queen with a shining throne, a twin born of one mother, and a 'son of Lucifer.' The second section contains twenty-two riddles utilizing wordplay and imagery related to royalty, warfare, and celestial bodies. These riddles likely personify physical objects such as crowns, swords, or stars. The work is characterized by dense allegorical construction and mythological references.

This collection of medieval Latin enigmas (riddles) describes various entities through metaphorical and allegorical language. The texts feature a series of riddles concerning a person or object that is 'wiser than Solomon,' a 'queen' whose throne shines, a 'twin' born of a single mother, and a 'son of Lucifer.' The riddles utilize dense, metaphorical imagery involving physical attributes, celestial bodies, and mythological references.

This section of the 'enigmata' consists of a series of riddles and allegorical verses. The text employs heavy wordplay and metaphorical imagery involving themes of birth, royalty, warfare, and celestial bodies, likely personifying objects such as a crown, a sword, or a star.

A Latin carmina (poem) by Theodulfus Aurelianensis, likely dating to the 8th century. The text is structured as a series of cryptic, allegorical verses involving mystical and symbolic imagery. It features themes of spiritual initiation, the nature of divine revelation, and the transition from earthly to celestial realms. Specific motifs include the 'five mothers' (mammas quinque), the 'six leaves' (sex foliis), and the 'path of Christ' (semita Christi). The poem employs complex metaphors involving celestial bodies, botanical growth, and the duality of silence and speech. It concludes with a transition from the 'heart of heaven' to the earthly field.

This collection of 8th-century Latin carmina by Theodulfus Aurelianensis constitutes a didactic and moralizing corpus blending sacred poetry, moral philosophy, and allegorical meditations. The work is structured into several movements, beginning with meditations on vices such as anger, pride, avarice, and gluttony, followed by allegories concerning the soul, the liberal arts, and the nature of justice. The text incorporates biblical figures including Job, David, Solomon, and the prophet Ephraim, alongside mythological references to the Styx, Phlegethon, and the Gorgon. Geographical references include the Rhine, Rhone, Seine, and the cities of Rome, Paris, and Aureliana, as well as the regions of Gaul, Iberia, and the East. The poems include royal dedications to figures such as Queen Fastrada, King Hluderic, and Queen Ermengardis, and address contemporary figures like the priest Martinus. The final sections feature complex alliterative verse, a critique of judicial corruption and perjury, and a systematic summary of the Old and New Testaments.

The text is a moral and theological meditation on the nature of anger (ira) and hatred (odium), contrasting them with virtues such as patience (patientia) and reason (ratio). It utilizes allegorical imagery, including mythological references to the Styx, Phlegethon, and the Gorgon, to describe the psychological degradation caused by uncontrolled passions. The poet argues that while anger may be fleeting, hatred is a persistent and heavy state that leads to spiritual ruin.

The text presents a moral and theological meditation on the nature of pride (Superbia) and its spiritual consequences. It utilizes the biblical figure of Job to illustrate the contrast between the trials of the faithful and the spiritual ruin of the proud, specifically addressing the Pharisees. The passage concludes with a warning against the 'swelling' of the heart and the resulting fall from grace.

This section of the carmina contains a series of allegorical and didactic verses. It features a medical allegory where a physician treats various ailments (avarice, envy, and lust) with 'contrary' remedies, followed by a theological and moral comparison between the 'old' woman of sin and the 'new' virgin of Christ. The text concludes with a series of instructional verses regarding the duties of a rector and the spiritual preparation of a practitioner.

The text is a collection of poems or verses by Theodulf of Orleans, beginning with a reference to the prophet Isaiah. It contains a series of moral and allegorical reflections on the roles of shepherds, the distinction between the soul and the flesh, and the contrast between the lives of the pious and the wicked. The passage also includes a section on the duties of the clergy and the spiritual state of the faithful.

The text contains a series of moral and ecclesiastical allegories, beginning with a critique of 'shepherds' who neglect their flock and a description of the spiritual burdens of those in leadership. It references biblical figures such as Moses and David, and concludes with a series of liturgical-style exhortations regarding the purity of the soul, the weight of office, and the distinction between divine grace and human vanity.

The text contains a series of poetic verses and a list of geographical locations including Iberia, Gaul, Britain, and the East (Assyria, Ophir, India). It features biblical and mythological figures such as David, Jeremiah, and the god-king, while contrasting the spiritual state of the righteous with the 'wicked' who possess worldly wealth. The passage concludes with a direct address to God regarding the prosperity of sinners.

The text contains a series of poetic and theological reflections on the Passion of Christ, the role of the martyrs, and the contrast between true faith and worldly folly. It references biblical figures such as Job, Peter, and Judas, and mentions the Styx and Phlegethon as symbolic boundaries. The passage also includes a critique of those who follow 'wicked' paths and a defense of the sacraments and the divine nature of the Church.

The text contains a series of allegorical and moralizing verses concerning the spiritual life, the nature of faith, and the contrast between virtue and vice. It utilizes symbolic imagery—such as bread (love), fish (faith), and an egg (hope)—to illustrate theological concepts, while also contrasting the 'just' and 'pious' with the 'wicked.' The passage concludes with a meditation on the divine order and the grace of God.

The text contains a series of poetic and allegorical verses contrasting true piety with worldly deception. It features a symbolic numerical and geometric analysis of 'good' and 'evil' (using figures like 100, 60, and 30), and describes the physical and spiritual distinctions between holy figures (virgins, martyrs, and priests) and those who wear the 'garments' of faith as a disguise.

The text contains a series of religious and allegorical poems concerning the distinction between the present life (left) and the eternal life (right) in Christ. It includes a section on the three states of the church, a passage on the biblical figure Job, and a prophetic calculation of the 'three and a half years' of tribulation based on the Book of Daniel. The final section describes the movement of Christ from the Mount of Olives to the temple.

This section of the carmina contains a series of allegorical and biblical verses concerning the transition from the Old Law to the New Covenant. It lists numerous biblical figures including Adam, Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Lot, Moses, David, Solomon, Josiah, Elijah, Jonah, Ezekiel, Zorobabel, Nehemiah, Haggai, Esther, Mardochek, Judith, and Peter. The text also references the destruction of Sodom and the rebuilding of the Temple.

This section of Theodulfus's carmina contains a series of religious and celebratory verses. It includes a formal dedication of the poems to a king (noted as a descendant of David), mentions the queen Fastrada, and includes a list of rivers (Mosa, Rhenus, Arar, Rodanus, Tiberis, Padus). The text also features a hymn to Christ and a description of the physical attributes of a holy figure or saint.

The text is a series of laudatory and descriptive verses featuring a royal court setting. It mentions specific figures such as Carolus (Charles), Ludoich, Riculfus, and several women including Berta, Chrodtrudh, Gisla, and Leutgardis. The passage includes geographical references to the Euphrates, the Ganges, and Cordoba, while describing a scene of royal feast, musical performance, and the presence of a figure named Flaccus.

The text contains a series of complex, allegorical, and highly alliterative Latin verses. It mentions several figures including Ercambaldus, Osulfus, Nardus, and the Pope, and references a 'Theodulfica Musa' (Theodulfic Muse). The passage contains dense wordplay regarding letters, musical notes, and a transition from a description of a feast or courtly scene to a personal address to a Pope regarding the loss of a parent.

The text contains a series of complex, allegorical, and potentially satirical verses involving biblical figures (David, Nehemiah, Solomon, Elijah), mythological figures (Apollo/Phoebus, Tityrus, Polyphemius), and various animals (ravens, peacocks, geese). It features a dense interweaving of religious imagery, classical allusions, and seemingly nonsensical or surrealist descriptions of feasts, landscapes, and physical attributes.

The text contains a series of moral and religious exhortations, featuring a transition from allegorical warnings about sin and the path to heaven to specific biblical and historical figures like Moses, Samuel, and Josiah. The latter half of the passage shifts to a geographical and political description of territories, naming rivers such as the Sequana, Garonna, and Hister, and regions like Aquitaine and Toulouse, while mentioning the figure Laidradus.

The text describes a geographical and spiritual journey through various regions including Noricum, Lugdunum, Narbonne, and Massilia, mentioning specific figures like Madalona, Sextatius, and the hero Alcides. It transitions into a mystical or allegorical dialogue involving a 'minister' and a 'vessel' of old age, followed by a scene of dispute between brothers over inheritance and property. The passage concludes with a description of contrasting items, such as white and red objects.

This section of the carmina contains a moralizing and didactic discourse on the corruption of justice, specifically addressing the influence of bribery and greed on judges and officials. The poet uses a series of metaphors involving physical goods (wool, grain, meat), geographical locations (the Ganges, Syria), and allegorical figures to contrast the 'bitter pestilence' of avarice with the integrity of the law. The text concludes with a call for moderation and the establishment of firm foundations in public service.

The text is a didactic and moralizing poem concerning the dangers of luxury, gluttony, and the loss of intellectual clarity. It warns against the 'poison' of excessive food and wine, contrasting the 'noble' man with those who become dull and 'muddled' by physical indulgence. The passage concludes with a series of rhetorical warnings regarding the preservation of spiritual order and the avoidance of base, 'plebeian' behaviors.

This section of the carmina contains a series of allegorical and moralizing verses concerning the duality of the soul and the body, the transition from earthly to celestial life, and the judgment of the deceased. It features a dialogue or internal monologue regarding the 'burden' of the flesh versus the 'light' of the spirit, incorporates a reference to the biblical figure Job, and concludes with a cryptic warning regarding maternal deceit.

The text contains a series of complex, allegorical, and didactic verses concerning moral conduct, legal proceedings, and interpersonal interactions. It features specific references to Solomon, Scylla, and various figures such as a child, a nurse, and a servant, while employing metaphors involving legal disputes, physical attributes, and pastoral imagery.

This section of the carmina contains a series of didactic and moralizing verses concerning the legal and ethical implications of perjury and the role of witnesses in a judicial setting. It contrasts the 'wicked' witness with the 'good' one, warns against the dangers of false testimony, and concludes with a reflection on the presence of Christ in the judgment and the severity of legal punishments.

The text is a moral and legalistic poem concerning the distinction between the actions of the just and the wicked. It contrasts the 'cruel acts' of the wealthy and the 'merit' of the poor, while referencing the 'law' (lex) as a standard of judgment. The passage concludes with a series of warnings regarding crime, punishment, and the physical consequences of transgression.

The text contains a series of poetic verses and exhortations involving religious and moral themes, including the 'law of the ancients' and the 'new law.' It mentions specific figures such as Teudulfus, Benedictus, and Maximinus, and references locations like the city of Aureliana. The passage concludes with a series of invocations and descriptions of spiritual growth, the 'scent of ambrosial nectar,' and the presence of a 'blessed multitude.'

The text contains a series of laudatory verses addressed to a king, likely a Carolingian ruler, praising his role as a protector of the church and the people. It mentions specific names including Attila, Clarinus, Teutfredus, and Leubila, and references the Pope Leo. The latter half of the passage shifts into an allegorical or metaphorical hunt involving various animals such as hares, bears, and deer, concluding with a reflection on the lack of profit from the hunt.

This section of Theodulfus's poems contains a series of panegyrics and allegorical verses, notably addressing Charlemagne (Karle) and praising his role as a protector of the faith and a ruler of the realm. The text incorporates references to biblical and historical figures such as the Pharisees, the Achaemenids, and the Geryon myth, while utilizing a complex, often cryptic allegorical style. It concludes with a series of laudatory attributes describing a ruler as wise, moderate, and a defender of the Church.

This section of the carmina contains a series of laudatory verses and prayers addressed to various rulers, including the Carolingian monarchs (Carolus, Ludovicus) and a figure named Hludoroic. It features specific mentions of local figures such as the abbot Fulradus and the hero Helmengaldus, while invoking themes of divine protection, imperial expansion against Moors and Arabs, and the sanctity of the church. The text includes a formal benediction for the deceased and a concluding prayer for the peace of the grave.

The text provides a systematic summary of the Old and New Testaments, listing specific books and figures such as Genesis, Leviticus, Numbers, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and the Gospels. It identifies specific biblical figures like Ruth, Saul, and the prophets Obadiah, Nahum, and Haggai, while concluding with a sequence of Pauline epistles including Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, and Philemon.

The text is a didactic poem providing instructions and exhortations to a reader or student of sacred scripture. It emphasizes the importance of internalizing the Word of God through meditation, the superiority of action over mere speech, and the cultivation of a humble, prudent heart. The author uses metaphors of paths, light, and nourishment to describe the spiritual journey and the transition from worldly knowledge to divine truth.

Theodulf of Orleans provides a concluding series of poems and a formal dedication to his work, which he describes as a 'small body' containing great spiritual treasures. He addresses the reader directly, offering a blessing for the soul, and includes a specific address to a woman named Gisla, offering her a spiritual and domestic blessing. The text concludes with a final address to his brothers, praising their efforts and distinguishing his work as a sacred 'carmina' rather than a secular lyric.

Theodulfus addresses a group of students or peers, specifically mentioning Vulfinus, Donatus, and the poet Sedulius, while praising the works of Gregory, Augustine, and Pope Leo. He distinguishes between the 'true' style of the holy fathers and the 'false' style of secular poets, and provides a detailed allegorical personification of the Liberal Arts, specifically Grammatica, Rhetorica, Dialectica, and Logica. The text concludes by distinguishing Logic from Ethics and the role of Prudentia in the sacred life.

The text describes a series of allegorical figures and symbols representing virtues (Justitia, Moderatio) and the liberal arts (Physica, Musica, Geometrica). It incorporates a detailed astronomical and astrological sequence, listing the zodiac signs and celestial bodies (Sol, Luna, Mars, Iovis, Cytherea, Saturne). The final section transitions into a moralizing exhortation regarding the 'tree of life' and the 'double duty' of the bishop, Theodulfus, in providing both spiritual and physical sustenance.

The text contains a series of poetic fragments and allegories involving a city of hospitality, a journey toward the Rhine, and a pastoral setting. It mentions specific figures and locations including the prophet Ephraim, the city of Rome, the river Rhine, and the names Dordonia, Mencius, and Rotharius. The imagery shifts between religious devotion, descriptions of nature (fields, vineyards, and horses), and a narrative involving a 'predator' and a 'sacred' task.

This section of Teudulfus's carmina contains a series of religious and liturgical poems. The text includes a plea for intercession, a description of the victory of Christ over death and the Tartars, a series of instructions for liturgical performance (including the 'Praesul ave' and the blessing of wine), and a concluding address to the clergy and people of the realm.

This section of Theodulfus's poems contains a series of liturgical and celebratory hymns addressed to Christ as King and Redeemer. It features specific invocations of saints and locations, including mentions of Rome, Libya, the land of the Franks, and specific figures such as John the Baptist, St. Martin, St. Maurice, and St. Sergius. The text concludes with a personal address to a priest named Aiulfus, noting Theodulfus's own status as an exile.

The text contains a series of poetic addresses and exhortations, likely directed at a high-ranking cleric or 'praesul' (prelate). It includes a specific dialogue or instruction for a person named Erato (or a similar name) who is returning from a 'carceris antro' (prison cave) and a direct address to a 'frater' (brother) regarding shared spiritual struggles and the duties of leadership.

The text contains a series of poetic and allegorical verses concerning the spread of illness, the nature of law and justice, and the observation of natural phenomena. It mentions specific geographical locations such as the rivers Sarta, Meduana, and Hiericunta, and references historical or mythological figures like Leander, the king Hludovic, and the tribe of the Caturci. The final section describes a military or diplomatic standoff between the Poeni and the Quiriti.

The text describes a violent battle between birds (avians) and a subsequent scene of carnage and death. It mentions specific locations such as Tolosa, the Rhone (Rodanus), and the city of Rome, and names individuals including the priest Arlardus, the poet Naso, and the scholar Severinus. The final section contains a personal address from Theodulphus regarding the difficulties of poetic composition and the risks of literary criticism.

The text contains a series of poetic and allegorical verses featuring historical and biblical figures such as Virgil, Seneca, John, and Peter. It transitions from a lamentation on the fate of the persecuted and the corruption of the clergy to a pastoral description of a garden (the 'paradise' of Helisius) and concludes with a moralizing meditation on the transience of the flesh versus the immortality of the soul.

This section of the carmina contains a series of mystical and theological meditations on the nature of the flesh versus the spirit, the enduring nature of Christ's words, and the virtues of the clergy. It includes a specific address to a 'blessed king' (rex benedite) and a 'pontiff' (pontificum), identifying them as models of spiritual nourishment and leadership. The text also features a brief, possibly liturgical or celebratory, address to 'Hludowice' (Hlodovikus) and a reference to the 'Innocents'.

This section contains a series of laudatory poems and addresses directed at several figures, including a king (Hluderic/Hlothari), a queen (Ermengardis), and a priest (Martinus). The text includes specific mentions of the city of Paris (Vrbs nostra), the region of Gaul, and names such as Albinus, Prudens, Galindo, and Gondacharus. The poems alternate between religious exhortations, praise for the rulers' piety and lineage, and a concluding section of poetic exchange among a group of poets.

The poet uses a nautical metaphor, describing a ship filled with poets to carry a heavy weight. The text then shifts to a metaphorical description of a beast or entity that consumes without being satisfied, characterized by a frantic appetite and a state of 'rest' covered in dung.

This text is a Latin funerary inscription (epitaphium) composed by Theodulf of Orleans (Theodulfus Aurelianensis) in the 8th century. The poem commemorates a deceased individual who served as both a leader (praesul) and an abbot (abbas) within a monastic context. It describes the deceased as a man of high virtue, described as 'sublimis' and 'pius,' who was born in the West (Hesperia) but nurtured in Gaul. The text references the reign of Charlemagne (Carolo Magno) and the transition of the deceased from a worldly life to a spiritual one. The final section contains a direct address or prayer, including a specific invocation of Christ and a plea for mercy. The poem utilizes traditional elegiac tropes regarding exile, the sanctity of the grave, and the judgment of the soul.

This 10th-century Latin hagiography, composed in a rhythmic style, recounts the life and devotion of the virgin Liutrudis. The narrative begins in Pertensis with the pious life of Sigmarus and his wife, who provide for seven daughters, including Liutrudis, under the instruction of the priest Eugenius. The text follows Liutrudis through her consecration to virginity, her spiritual journey toward Rome and Ravenna, and her role in collecting relics. It includes accounts of miraculous healings, the ascetic practices of Liutrudis (modeled on John the Baptist), and the deathbed of her sister Pusinna. The work concludes with the death of Liutrudis, a miracle involving anointing oil, and a formal doxology. Key figures include Sigmarus, Eugenius, and Alpinus Cathalaunensis, while notable locations include Mount Sigmarus and the city of Ravenna.

The text recounts the pious life of Sigmarus and his wife in the region of Pertensis, who lived in devotion and shared their wealth with the poor. They had seven daughters—Imma, Othildis, Liudtrudis, Pusinna, Francula, Libere, and Magethildis—who were instructed in the scriptures, psalms, and spiritual hymns by a priest named Eugenius. The passage concludes by mentioning the ecclesiastical authority of Alpinus Cathalaunensis.

The text describes a priest, Sigmarus, who consecrates seven daughters to a life of virginity and religious devotion. It details the blessing of these women, the establishment of a secluded site in a mountain (referred to as Mount Sigmarus), and the subsequent life of a virgin named Liutrudis. The narrative includes a prayer of dedication to God and a transition of property and spiritual legacy following the death of a father.

The text describes a spiritual journey and vision involving the virgin Liudtrudis and a priest named Eugenius. It recounts a divine message from an angel to Liudtrudis regarding her pilgrimage to Rome and the collection of relics, followed by a narrative involving a girl and her parents in a state of distress. The passage also mentions the city of Ravenna and a transition of a girl into the care of a mistress.

The text describes a miraculous healing of a girl named Liudtrude, who is restored to health and consciousness after a period of illness. A man, possibly a priest or guardian, prays to Christ and a figure identified as 'Plasmator' for her recovery, during which she offers thanks and a vow of virginity. The narrative concludes with the girl being taken to a hospice under the care of a man named Georgius and the subsequent establishment of a church and cell dedicated to Saint Maurice.

The text describes the ascetic life of the virgin Liudtrudis, who is portrayed as imitating the life of John the Baptist through fasting, wearing hairshirts, and seclusion. It then recounts the illness of her sister, Pusinna, and the arrival of Liudtrudis to provide comfort. The passage concludes with a dialogue between the sisters and the death of Pusinna, who expresses gratitude to God before her soul departs.

This section of the hagiography of Liudtrudis (Liudtrudis) praises her as a holy virgin and model of chastity who achieved a 'perfect martyrdom' through the mortification of carnal desires. It recounts her death in a church she built, her burial in a known location, and a miracle involving an overflowing vessel of oil used for anointing. The text concludes with a formal doxology to the Holy Trinity and a call for other virgins and Christians to imitate her life.
The text consists of a single line of liturgical or poetic formula. It expresses a wish or declaration of duration 'forever into the ages of ages.'

A collection of Latin funerary inscriptions (epitaphia) from the Italian region, likely dating to the 9th century. The text contains two distinct memorial sections: one for a man named Adelbertus (Adalbert), identified as a 'dux' (duke) and a member of the 'Tile' lineage, and another for a woman, the daughter of Lotharius and granddaughter of Carolus (Charlemagne). The inscriptions mention specific historical figures including King Lotharius and King Carolus, and reference territories such as Germany, France, Corsica, Sardinia, Greece, and Italy. The text employs standard hagiographic and funerary tropes, including descriptions of the deceased's virtues, their roles in governance, and pleas for divine mercy. The final section includes a traditional Christian prayer for perpetual light.

An epitaph from Lunense (Lucca) dating to the 9th century. The text is a funerary inscription containing fragmented lines and significant lacunae. It mentions the construction of a 'dochium aula' (hall or courtyard) by a 'Martini praesule Christo' and references the 'Olympiads' and 'lustrum' in a chronological context. The text contains references to 'tutamina vite' (vineyard stores), 'idola' (idols), and 'carmina' (songs/chants). The final lines mention 'Aistulfi', likely referring to the Carolingian King Aistulf.

This 9th-century Latin collection of epitaphs from Milan (Mediolanum) contains a series of funerary inscriptions for various individuals. The text identifies several specific figures, including Anspertus, Landulfus, Petrus, Benedictus, Arnulfus, and Hilderamnus, as well as a woman named Sagintruda. The inscriptions detail the virtues of the deceased, such as their roles as judges, their dedication to religious vows, and their contributions to the construction of sacred buildings and houses. The text also mentions specific locations and figures like the house of Stilichon and the figure of Satyrus. The latter portion of the text is heavily fragmented and corrupted, making the specific details of the final entries difficult to determine.

This 8th-century Latin collection, tituli metrici I, consists of funeral elegies, commemorative verses, and liturgical inscriptions. The work is organized into four sections containing eulogies for various figures including the priest Petrus, the man Thomas, the priest Rotgangus, and the figures Aggiardus and Arichius. Notable geographical locations mentioned include Rome, Noviomense, Benevento, and Pannonia. The text features specific religious and historical figures such as King Liutprand, Saint Columban, Carolus, Romuald, and Hadrianus. Themes include the virtues of the deceased, the feast of Saint Michael, and the establishment of religious orders. Architectural descriptions include a marble-clad loculus and imagery of Christ.

This section contains a series of funeral elegies and commemorative verses for various individuals, including a 'doctor' and a 'pastor' (referred to as Petrus). It features several laudatory descriptions of the deceased's virtues, mentions of the feast of Saint Michael, and a list of ethnic groups including the Angles, Getae, Waeses, Burgundians, Greeks, and Hibernians.

This section contains a series of laudatory verses and commemorative inscriptions for several figures, including a man named Thomas, the King Liutprand, and a priest named Rotgangus. It mentions the city of Rome, the saint Columban, and the construction of a marble tomb or shrine. The text includes references to the Gospel of John and the establishment of a religious order.

This section contains a series of funeral elegies and commemorative verses for various figures, including a prefect in a city, a man named Aggiardus, and a figure identified as Arichius. It mentions specific locations such as Noviomense (Nimeguen), Benevento, and Rome, and references historical or literary figures like Carolus, Romuald, and Hadrianus. The text alternates between personal laments for fathers and sons and formal praises of clergy and rulers.

This section contains a series of liturgical or commemorative verses, including a prayer to the 'holy Father' and a reference to the 'love of Peter.' It mentions the names Silverius, Geroldi, and Abbot Gautus, and references the location of Pannonia. The text describes architectural features such as a marble-clad niche (loculus) and a painting of Christ's image.

This 9th-century Latin collection of 'tituli metrici' consists of commemorative and liturgical verses, likely intended for inscriptions or funerary monuments. The text contains several distinct sections: a panegyric for a prince named Arichus (or Arichus's successor) and a warrior named Romoald; a section concerning the defense of Benevento against the Gauls; and a series of hagiographic and dedicatory verses. Notable figures mentioned include the martyr Albanius, the cleric Riculfus, and the prince Carolus. The work features a transition from secular heroic praise to religious devotion, specifically mentioning the construction of a hall or temple. The final sections include a formal dedication and a plea for the soul of a brother, likely a cleric or monk.

This 9th-century Latin text consists of a collection of metric titles (tituli metrici) likely serving as dedicatory inscriptions or liturgical headers. The text mentions several specific figures, including Gaugericus (a bishop or prelate), Autbertus, Audomarus, and the priest Adalhuno. It references geographical locations such as Moguntiacensis (Mainz) and the figure of the Roman priest Gregory. The content shifts between hagiographic elements, such as the martyrdom of Dionysius, and descriptions of ecclesiastical architecture and construction. The latter portion of the text contains more lyrical, poetic passages concerning the Virgin Mary, the heavens, and the celestial order.

This 9th-century Latin collection of tituli metrici consists of liturgical and commemorative inscriptions organized into three distinct sections. The first section contains inscriptions concerning figures such as Phoebus, Jove, Sergius, Demetrius, and Pope Leo, while referencing sacred spaces like a temple, an aula compared to Sinai, and the city of Iohannipolis. The second section provides funerary inscriptions for a series of popes and saints, specifically naming Benedict, Nicholas, Stephen, Boniface, Sergius, John, Anastasius, and Christopher, and notes a period of exile lasting twenty-seven years. The final section concludes with a single line of devotional instruction regarding prayer and divine rest. The work combines hagiography, sacred architecture, and funerary commemoration.

This collection of liturgical or commemorative inscriptions (tituli metrici) mentions several saints and figures including Phoebus, Jove, Sergius, Demetrius, and Pope Leo. The texts describe sacred spaces such as a temple, a hall (aula) compared to Sinai, and the city of Iohannipolis, while offering prayers for the deceased and the protection of the faithful.

This section contains a series of funerary inscriptions (tituli metrici) for various popes and saints, including Benedict, Nicholas, Stephen, Boniface, Sergius, John, and Anastasius. The text describes their virtues, roles in the apostolic see, and the physical location of their remains within the sacred space. It also includes a brief mention of the saint Christopher and a reference to the exile of a figure for twenty-seven years.
The text contains a single line of liturgical or devotional instruction. It exhorts the reader to petition God with their heart in order to obtain rest.

This 9th-century Latin collection of metric titles and liturgical verses is organized into three distinct sections of devotional and ceremonial poetry. The first section contains prayers and hymns for Saint Martin, Saint Andrew, and the Trinity, alongside a narrative of the Passion and Resurrection of Christ and descriptions of sacred objects like a biform ivory and silver body. The second section features hagiographic fragments concerning the disciples, Saint Peter, and the healing of Cornelius, followed by local dedicatory inscriptions involving Herardus, Abbot Autacher, and the city of Mogontiacum. The final section consists of liturgical verses and invocations to the 'Virgo parens Christi' and the 'supreme creator.' Notable figures mentioned throughout include King Pippinus, King Arnulphus, Abbot Adalpert, Boso, Hemma, Plectrudis, and Grimoaldus.

This collection of liturgical and devotional verses includes several distinct sections: a series of prayers and hymns for the saints Martin, Andrew, and the Trinity; a narrative of the Passion and Resurrection of Christ; and several dedicatory inscriptions for altars and buildings. Specific figures mentioned include the King Pippinus, the abbot Adalpert, and the donor Agalsius. The text also contains a sequence of poetic descriptions of sacred objects, such as a 'biform' body of ivory and silver, and a section on the betrayal of Christ by Judas.

This section contains a series of Latin verse fragments, likely from a liturgical or hagiographic collection, featuring a narrative involving the disciples of Christ, the figure of Peter, and the healing of a man named Cornelius. This 9th-century Latin hagiography recounts the life and miracles of the saint Martinus.
