The passage concludes by posing a rhetorical question regarding the creation of man in the image of God.

The text explores the theological distinction between the 'image' (eikōn) and the 'original' (prōtotupon) of God in human nature. It references the theologian Gregory (the Theologian) and the prophet Daniel to argue that while humans share a rational and intelligible nature with angels, they possess a unique status as the image of God. The author defends the consistency of these doctrines against potential accusations of heresy or confusion regarding the hierarchy of beings.

The text provides a theological and philological analysis of the term 'κατ' εἰκὸνα' (in the image) regarding the creation of man and the incarnation of the Word. It cites the writings of Gregory (likely Gregory of Nazianzus or Gregory of the Theologian) to distinguish between the 'image' (εἰκὼν) and the 'original' (πρωτότυπον). The author argues against certain interpretations that conflate the human nature with the divine nature, emphasizing the distinction between the Word's pre-existent nature and his incarnation.

The text presents a theological defense of the Incarnation, arguing that Christ took on human form to reconcile the divine and human natures without compromising the integrity of either. It addresses and refutes charges of anthropomorphism and 'passions' in Christ, while also critiquing Jewish 'myths' regarding the nature of the Trinity and the Holy Spirit. The final section reconciles the Old Testament law of 'an eye for an eye' with the New Testament's call to mercy by distinguishing between human and divine responses.

The text presents a theological defense of the omnipresence of the Word (Logos) and the incarnation of the Son in human flesh. It argues against the notion of a 'partitioned' divinity, asserting that the divine nature is not localized or divided by the limitations of the human body. The passage also addresses the nature of the physical body as a vessel for the soul and the theological implications of the Trinity and the suffering of Christ.

The text contains a theological and exegetical commentary on the nature of the divine presence (presence in all places) versus the limitations of the material world. It features a specific scholarly defense of the biblical genealogy in Genesis, specifically regarding the naming of the sons of Rachel and the lineage of Benjamin. The author argues for the distinction between the 'first cause' of a lineage and the immediate biological parentage in sacred texts.

The text examines the biblical concept of 'brotherhood' in relation to the sons of Aaron, the sons of Uzziel, and the distinction between biological kin and spiritual fellowship. It then transitions to a detailed exegetical analysis of the Exodus, specifically the miracle of the Nile turning to blood. The author argues for a precise interpretation of the scriptural text, distinguishing between the water of the river and the general waters of Egypt, and addressing the specific roles of the Nile's branches and the physical objects within the river.

The text analyzes the miracle of the Nile and Egyptian waters turning into blood during the Exodus, specifically debating the theological and physical implications of the transformation. It discusses the role of Moses and Aaron, the perceived 'sorcery' of the Egyptians, and compares the miracle to the actions of magicians. The passage also cites and compares different Greek and Hebrew translations (including those of Aquila and Theodotus) regarding the description of the water's transformation.

The text provides a theological commentary on the biblical narrative of the Exodus, specifically focusing on the plagues of Egypt and the hardening of Pharaoh's heart. It argues that the various ways the biblical text describes God's actions—such as 'giving over' or 'hardening'—are linguistically and theologically equivalent expressions of divine judgment. The author defends the consistency of these scriptural variations against potential accusations of inconsistency.

The text provides a theological commentary on the biblical passage in Isaiah regarding God's wrath and human sin. It argues against interpretations that attribute the 'turning away' of God's face to the power of sin itself, asserting instead that it is a result of human transgression. The author defends the integrity of the sacred scriptures and the consistency of the prophetic message against potential misinterpretations.

The text presents a theological and rhetorical analysis of the relationship between divine wrath, human sin, and the role of grace. It examines the nuances of the phrase 'You were angry, and we also sinned,' debating how divine judgment is mediated through 'Old Doctrines' and the distinction between sin committed out of boldness versus sin that precedes the movement of wrath. The passage also references the 'sacred words' and the 'work of Atticus' in the context of scholarly or rhetorical defense.

The author analyzes the scriptural phrase 'You were angry, and we have sinned' (Psalm 103:10), arguing that it is a specific confession of the nation of Israel rather than a general human plea. The text examines the distinction between the unique covenantal privileges of Israel—such as the manna, the pillar of fire, and the parting of the sea—and the general human condition of sin. It concludes that the specific phrasing of the Psalm reflects the unique relationship between God and the Israelites, who were granted exceptional provisions and divine care.

The text examines the theological distinction between two types of Israelites: those who are 'grateful' and those who are 'ungrateful' (ignorant of God). It analyzes the liturgical and scriptural use of the confession of sins and the specific formula of baptism in the name of 'the Lord Jesus Christ' as a practical and pastoral choice for the early church. The author argues that the omission of the Trinity in the baptismal formula was a matter of expediency and clarity for the multitude.

The text defends the doctrine of adoption and the Trinity against a critic who argues that the disciples' understanding of the 'mystery' was flawed. It cites the baptism of the Gentiles by Paul at Ephesus and the baptism of Cornelius as evidence of the divine authority of the apostolic mission. The author argues that the distinction between the 'law of salvation' and the 'opinion of the disciples' is clear, and that the sacred command to baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is beyond human judgment.

The text is a polemical theological treatise concerning the validity of baptism and the interpretation of sacred mysteries. It argues against those who introduce 'other voices' or 'different doctrines' into the ritual of baptism, specifically criticizing those who deviate from the 'Lord's' command or the 'unmixed' tradition. The author cites the conversion of Paul (referred to as the 'transgressor') and the role of Ananias as examples of proper sacred practice versus the 'ridiculous' innovations of opponents.

The text explores the theological significance of baptism, contrasting the 'word of rebirth' with the physical elements of the rite. It argues that while the ritual symbols (water, names, and words) are diverse, they collectively signify the death and resurrection of Christ and the restoration of the 'old Adam.' The passage also references the biblical account of Ananias and the baptism of the Israelites in the Jordan River.

The text provides a theological defense of the use of the name 'Christ' in baptismal formulas, arguing that the name signifies the full mystery of the Word made flesh and the doctrine of the Trinity. It contrasts the early persecutor Saul with the apostle Paul, asserting that the name of Christ is not a 'small' or 'common' term but a profound proclamation of the Savior's identity as the Son of God. The author addresses a potential conflict regarding the specific phrasing of baptismal formulas, defending the theological depth of the name Christ as a vehicle for the entire mystery of salvation.

The text explores the theological nuances of the Trinity, the incarnation of the Word, and the specific role of the Apostle Paul in proclaiming these mysteries. It argues for the unity of the Trinity in the proclamation of the Gospel and defends the distinction between various types of discourse. The passage concludes by affirming the authority of Paul's writings and the consistency of his preaching regarding the divinity of Christ and the Holy Spirit.

The text discusses the theological significance of baptism in the name of Jesus Christ, contrasting the 'name' (ὄνομα) with 'faith' (πίστις) as a means of salvation and the 'mystery of godliness.' It recounts a scene in Judea where a man was healed and proclaimed to have risen in the name of Christ, and describes the subsequent reactions of the Jewish people and the actions of the apostles, specifically Paul and Peter. The passage concludes with a theological defense of the apostolic practice of baptizing in the name of Christ.

The text is a polemical defense of the traditional trinitarian baptismal formula against those who perform baptisms in a 'different' or 'new' manner. The author argues that those who deviate from the established doctrine of the 'Teacher' (Christ) and the 'Savior' are acting out of malice and have forgotten the original commandments. The passage specifically addresses the validity of the baptismal rite, the role of the apostles, and the necessity of the trinitarian formula as a symbol of Christ's death and resurrection.

The text provides a theological defense of the phrase 'baptized into Christ' and 'baptized into his death,' arguing that these are not innovations but core mysteries of the faith. The author defends the apostolic tradition against those who allegedly misinterpret these terms or deviate from the established baptismal formulas. The passage concludes by referencing the ritual of anointing and the distinction between the spiritual meaning of words and their phonetic forms.

The text provides a moral and allegorical exhortation on the virtue of mercy (eleos) and the spiritual significance of anointing with oil. It contrasts true spiritual charity, which stems from the 'head' (wisdom and divine guidance), with worldly actions that are merely 'treatments' for the body or self-interest. The passage concludes with a scriptural meditation on keeping one's eyes fixed on Christ as the head to avoid the snares of the enemy.

The text provides a theological commentary on biblical passages, specifically interpreting the 'oil' and 'perfume' as symbols of the Holy Spirit's grace and the 'white garments' as the purity of virtue. It addresses the interpretation of the words 'Who is my mother?' in the context of Christ's relationship to his mother and the rejection of worldly desires. The author argues against those who interpret these scriptures through a lens of physical lust or 'fleshly' desires, defending the spiritual integrity of the scriptures.

The text provides a theological defense of the words of Jesus regarding his mother and brothers, arguing that his statements were not a slight against his family but a prioritization of spiritual salvation over biological kinship. It addresses and refutes accusations of blasphemy or disrespect toward his mother, asserting that his teaching was intended to offer a higher spiritual 'marriage' to the divine. The passage also addresses the specific context of the women and brothers appearing at the door, interpreting the scene as a moment of spiritual transition rather than a breach of social etiquette.

The text provides a theological and rhetorical analysis of a biblical scene involving a 'Savior' (Christ) and a woman identified as a mother. The author examines the nuances of the Greek text regarding the 'motherly' relationship, the distinction between natural and divine actions, and the specific phrasing of the words 'What is mine and yours' (Τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοὶ). The passage argues that the miraculous transformation of water into wine and the specific interactions with the woman were intended to honor her status while distinguishing between human nature and divine power.

The text presents a theological and legalistic defense of the harmony between the law of retribution (lex talionis) and the virtue of mercy. It argues that a judge who chooses mercy over punishment does not contradict the law but rather fulfills a higher spiritual standard, while a criminal who seeks only punishment is acting out of malice. The passage concludes with a mystical and poetic transition, referencing the 'spirit of salvation' and the 'Spirit of God' in a context of spiritual birth.

The text presents a theological polemic regarding the identity of the 'father of the devil' and the spiritual status of the Jews. The author argues that while some interpret the devil as the 'father of the Jews' due to their adherence to law and ancient traditions, the Jews are actually 'sons of the devil' because of their deeds, such as slander, envy, and plotting against the Savior. The passage also addresses the distinction between the devil as a murderer from the beginning and the specific titles attributed to him in scripture.

The text critiques the role of the devil in the fall of man, specifically regarding the 'first transgression' and the introduction of death. It addresses the theological status of the devil as the 'father of the Jews' and critiques the literary and theological differences between the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke. The passage concludes by analyzing specific biblical narratives, including the Transfiguration, the feeding of the five thousand, and the timeline of the Passion.
topics: Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke

summary: The text provides a theological commentary on three distinct instances of anointing with perfume in the Gospels: the woman who loved the Lord (sister of Lazarus and Martha), the woman who anointed Jesus' feet (the 'sinful woman'), and the woman who anointed his head. It analyzes the motivations of the participants, including the reactions of Simon the Sinner, Judas Iscariot, and the disciples, while contrasting the actions of the women with the greed of Judas and the lack of spiritual insight in Simon.

The text provides a theological and exegetical commentary on the Gospel narratives of the woman anointing Jesus' feet, the woman with the issue of blood, and the raising of Lazarus. It analyzes the specific reactions of the Pharisee, Judas Iscariot, and the other disciples to these events, contrasting the 'mercy' of the Teacher with the 'judgment' of the observers. The passage also discusses the different ways the Gospel accounts of Luke, Matthew, and Mark present the forgiveness of sins and the rewards of these specific acts of devotion.

The text analyzes the internal motivations of the disciples during the anointing of Jesus by the woman with the issue of flux, contrasting the greed of Judas with the compassion of the other disciples. It provides a theological defense of the Holy Spirit's role in the forgiveness of sins and the 'new birth' (regeneration), arguing that blasphemy against the Spirit precludes any hope of pardon. The passage concludes by discussing the dual nature of Christ, specifically the indwelling of the divine in human nature.

The text presents a polemical critique of a specific individual (likely a contemporary heretic or a specific religious figure) who is accused of blasphemy against the Son of Man and the Holy Spirit. The author argues that this person has witnessed divine works—such as the healing of the blind, the lame, and the resurrection of the dead—yet chooses to interpret these events as demonic or to justify his own errors. The passage concludes by condemning the individual's actions on the Sabbath and his perceived alliance with death and 'Beelzebul'.

The text provides a theological and exegetical commentary on the Gospel of Mark, specifically addressing the interpretation of the 'unforgivable sin' of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. It analyzes the distinction between the punishment of blasphemers in the present age versus the future, and examines the relationship between the words of Jesus and the accounts of the Evangelists Mark and Luke. The author also discusses the nature of the Holy Spirit's actions and the distinction between the 'Old' and 'New' covenants regarding the forgiveness of sins.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Gospel narrative of Jesus' ministry, specifically addressing the 'Exalted' (ἐξεστή) status and the actions of those who sought to restrain him. It contrasts the 'brothers' (disciples) with the 'wicked' Jews who accused him of madness and blasphemy. The author concludes with a meditation on the limitations of human intellect and the necessity of divine grace and the 'promise of the Most High' in understanding the mysteries of the Word.

The text presents a theological defense of the creation of Paradise and the subsequent fall of Adam. It argues that the existence of Paradise was necessary to provide a sphere of immortality and a means of repenting for the 'first citizen' (Adam), while also serving as a foretelling of the future restoration of the cosmos. The author contends that the loss of Paradise was not a failure of divine economy but a necessary component of the human experience of sin and the subsequent redemption.

The text provides a theological and exegetical commentary on the New Testament passage regarding 'heaping coals' on the heads of enemies. It analyzes the dual meanings of the word 'σωρεύσεις' (heaping) and the metaphorical nature of 'coals' as both divine punishment and the transformative power of kindness. The author references the Apostle Paul, the 'Melodist' (likely a reference to a hymn or specific liturgical tradition), and the concept of the 'forefather' (Christ) in relation to the creation and the judgment of the world.

The text provides a moral and theological exhortation on the practice of loving and serving one's enemies through acts of hospitality, such as providing food and drink. It utilizes a biblical typology comparing the roles of Moses and Aaron in the wilderness and the plagues of Egypt to illustrate the transmission of divine authority and the performance of miracles. The final section interprets Pauline scripture regarding the 'freedom' of the believer, contrasting the slavery of the flesh with the service of one another through love.

The text contains a theological and polemical discourse regarding the interpretation of the Gospel and the role of women in sacred acts, specifically referencing the 'work of a woman' and the 'sacred service.' It addresses the tension between the 'law' and 'love,' the practice of circumcision, and the defense of a woman's actions against accusations of immorality. The passage includes several fragments of liturgical or scriptural-style formulas and a concluding section on the difficulty of comprehending certain divine mysteries.

The text provides a theological and philological analysis of scriptural passages, specifically comparing the phrasing of David's lamentations with other biblical texts. It examines the nuances of divine judgment and mercy in the cases of David and Pharaoh, arguing that the specific phrasing of the scriptures reflects a consistent theological logic. The author defends the integrity of the prophetic tradition against perceived inconsistencies in interpretation.

The text analyzes the biblical narrative of David, contrasting his grave sins (adultery and murder) with the divine mercy and 'foreknowledge' shown toward him. It argues that the scriptural account of David's repentance and the subsequent divine rewards provide a consistent theological model for the relationship between human transgression and divine grace. The passage concludes with a theological reflection on the institution of baptism, mentioning John the Baptist and the disciples as witnesses to the divinity of Christ.

The text contains a theological discourse on the distinction between the baptism of John and the baptism of the disciples of Christ, emphasizing the gift of the Holy Spirit and the forgiveness of sins. It transitions into a detailed allegorical interpretation of biblical narratives involving Abraham, Isaac, and the wells of the wilderness, specifically referencing the 'Well of the Oath' and the actions of the Philistines. The final section provides a moral and practical exhortation regarding the completion of a 'house' or work, warning against negligence and the risks of unfinished construction.

The text presents a theological defense of Christ's actions regarding the Sabbath and the Law, arguing that the Savior's actions are superior to the mere observance of human laws. It addresses the criticism of the disciples regarding the Sabbath, asserting that Christ as the Son of Man is the true Lord of the Sabbath. The passage also includes a comparison between the 'old' and 'new' ways of salvation, emphasizing the superiority of divine work over human tradition.

The text argues that the Savior's actions, such as healing a leper and performing miracles, were not mere violations of the Sabbath but were intended to demonstrate his authority as the true Lawgiver. It contrasts the 'works of his hands' with the 'works of the word' and argues that the Mosaic Law was a preparatory stage that he fulfilled and superseded. The author defends the Savior against accusations of lawlessness by comparing his role to a king who establishes laws for his subjects while remaining above them.

Following the internal divisions and the flight of Eudoxius, the narrative shifts to a military account of the siege of Nisibis (also called Antioch Mygdonia) by the Persians. The text describes the defense of the city by Bishop James and the specific engineering of the Mygdonius river during the siege.

Theodoretus describes a siege where a commander named Sabor is repulsed by a wall built through divine intervention and the miraculous appearance of a royal garment and a vision of a king. The narrative shifts to the aftermath of the Persian war, where the church of Antioch is left without a leader until Meletius is chosen to lead. The text concludes with a formal assembly in Antioch where Meletius, supported by figures like George of Laodicea and Achaeus of Caesarea, defends apostolic doctrine against heretical views.

The text describes the internal division of a church community in a city called Palaia, where a group following Arian and Euzeus (an advocate of Arian doctrine) was separated from the apostolic church. It recounts a confrontation between the priest Eusebius and the Emperor Constantius regarding a document of confession; Eusebius refused to hand it over despite threats of mutilation. The passage concludes with a list of chapter headings covering the reign of Julian, the actions of Constantius, and various local incidents involving martyrs and local events in Antioch and Carrhae.

Theodoretus describes Julian's transition from a youth who shared in the 'godly doctrine' to a ruler who sought out diviners and soothsayers in Greece. He recounts a specific encounter where Julian was led to a pagan temple and confronted by 'demons' who were repelled by the sign of the cross. The text concludes with the ecclesiastical reorganization following Constantius's death, specifically noting the return of Meletius to Antioch and Athanasius to Alexandria, and the internal divisions within the Antioch church.

Theodoretus describes the internal divisions and conflicts within the church at Antioch following the exile of Meletius, specifically involving the factions of Eustatius and the followers of Lucifer. The text details the actions of Lucifer in Antioch and Sardis, the subsequent rise of Alexander to lead the Antiochian church, and the persecution of Christians under the reign of Julian. Specific instances of pagan desecration and the martyrdom of figures like Cyril in Heliopolis and Aemilianus in Dorostol are recorded.

The text recounts the physical abuse and mockery of a Christian martyr by captors, who mocked his endurance and his use of scripture. It then transitions to the persecution of Athanasius by the Roman official Julian, who sought to execute him. The narrative concludes with the relocation of the remains of martyrs (including one named Babylon) and the subsequent arrest of those who participated in a celebratory procession.

Theodoretus recounts the martyrdom of a young man named Theodorus, who was punished by a king for his devotion to Christ. The text describes the physical suffering of Theodorus, the actions of a local official named Julian (governor of Euboea) and a treasurer named Felix, and the subsequent execution of Felix. The narrative concludes with a woman and a young man (a priest's son) seeking refuge and fleeing the persecution of the king.

Theodoretus recounts the conversion of Julian's father and a youth named Melitios (or Meletius) following a festival at Daphne. The narrative describes the capture of Melitius by a man of God, his subsequent imprisonment, and his eventual conversion and leadership. The text concludes with the actions of Julian in Antioch, where he addresses the concerns of soldiers regarding the pollution of sacred sites and the subsequent recognition of martyrs Joventinus and Maximinus.

Theodoretus recounts the story of a soldier named Valentian who was promoted to a high rank and later a kingdom, and the subsequent actions of a tyrant who attempted to corrupt Christians with gold and ritualistic offerings. The text describes a group of Christians who, upon discovering the corruption, were martyred, and the subsequent actions of Artemius, a commander in Egypt. The narrative concludes with the mention of a woman named Publia and her association with a priest named John in Antioch.

Theodoretus recounts a narrative involving a man (possibly a pagan priest or leader) who is confronted by a woman and a choir, and later by a group of Jews who are shown to be following Christ. The text describes a miraculous destruction of a pagan site involving earthquakes, fire, and a vision of the Cross, which leads to the conversion of local Jews. The passage concludes with a critique of a pagan oracle's false prophecy regarding a war against the 'Galileans' (Christians) and mentions a confrontation in Berea.

Theodoretus recounts a narrative involving a man of great reputation and his son, who was cast out for falling into wickedness. The text then shifts to a scene in Antioch involving a man named Libanius, a renowned sophist, and a confrontation regarding the identity of the 'son of the carpenter' and the power of the 'speaking' tongue. The final section describes a military leader who, after crossing a river into Persian territory, burned his ships and was later found dead in the wilderness, followed by a description of a man named Julian (referred to as the 'Syrian Sabbath') and his prayers.

The text describes a sorcerer in Carrhae who performed a ritual involving blood and a 'gall-bearer' who identified a victory over the Persians through a liver. It then recounts the discovery of sacred relics and bodies in Antioch, followed by a list of ecclesiastical topics and historical figures including Athanasius, Valens, and various monks. The final section lists specific theological and historical subjects, including the siege of Antioch, the actions of Bishop Barzus, and the military campaigns of Valens against the Goths.

Following the death of Julian, the army elects Jovian as emperor, who is described as a man of great stature and piety who refuses to rule over the 'wicked' troops of Julian. Jovian subsequently issues a decree restoring bishops from exile and commissions Athanasius to write on the orthodox faith. The text concludes with a formal defense of the Nicene Creed against Arianism, specifically refuting the claims of Arius regarding the nature of the Son of God.

Theodoretus defends the Nicene Creed against Arian and semi-Arian interpretations, specifically regarding the nature of the Son and the Holy Spirit. He lists numerous geographical regions and their respective churches that adhere to the Nicene faith. The text concludes with a historical narrative of the death of Emperor Constantine the Great at Dadasthas and the subsequent transition of power to his successor, mentioning the actions of Julian and Valentinian.

The text describes the aftermath of the death of Bishop Ausentius in Mediolanum and the subsequent selection of Ambrosius as his successor. It details a dialogue between the Emperor and the bishops regarding the legitimacy of Ambrosius's appointment and the distinction between civil and religious authority. The passage concludes with a defense of the clergy's adherence to divine law versus the imperial laws, specifically citing the principle of 'Render unto Caesar'.

Theodoretus records a formal correspondence regarding the doctrine of the Trinity (homoousios) and the nature of Christ's pre-existence. The text names several local figures—Amigetus, Cicero, Damasus, Lampon, and Brenthasius—and mentions the bishops of Illyricum and the provinces of Asia, Phrygia, Carophrygia, and Pacataea. The passage includes a specific theological defense against those who claim the Son was not present before his birth, and concludes with a formal greeting and a call to unity in the faith.

Theodoretus identifies and condemns several individuals—Polychronus, Telemachus, Faustus, Asclepiades, Amantius, and Cleopatra—as Arian-leaning heretics who do not affirm the full Trinity. He describes the rise of the Messalians (also called 'Enthusiasts'), who claim to experience the Holy Spirit through visions but are accused of practicing illicit behaviors and seeking illicit wealth. The text concludes with a narrative of three leaders—Leto, Amphilochus, and Flavius—who identify and purge these 'diseased' elements from their respective regions of Melitene, Lycaon, and Antioch.

Theodoretus describes a spiritual transformation of a man (referred to as Flavius) who experiences a divine presence and liberation from worldly passions. The narrative then shifts to a historical account of the spread of a 'disease' (heresy) from Syria to Pamphylia, and the subsequent actions of leaders like Valus, Eudoxius, Meletius, and Eusebius. The text concludes with a scene of a shepherd (or leader) being mourned by followers near the Euphrates river as he prepares to move toward Zeugma.

Theodoretus recounts the actions of the heretic Eunomius (referred to as 'the shepherd') and his successor Lucius, who is described as a 'wolf' among the flock. The text details a specific incident at a bathhouse in a city where Eunomius shared water with a crowd, and later describes the appointment of Antiochus as his successor. The narrative concludes with the movements of the bishop Eusebius, who traveled to Oxyrhynchus in Egypt and is associated with a miraculous healing site in Arad.

Theodoretus describes a confrontation in Edessa where a military commander (Modestus) encounters a woman carrying a child who claims to seek a 'holy death.' The commander reports her to the king, leading to a tense dialogue with a man named Eulogios, who is eventually sent away with eighty others to Thrace. The narrative then shifts to the education of a group of youths under Protogenes, who teaches them scripture and music, and a miraculous healing of a sick youth.

The narrative describes a series of interactions involving a holy man (referred to as the 'divine man' or 'great King' in the text) and several figures including a man named Protogenes, a ruler named Valens, and a man named Balus. It recounts a confrontation in the city of Caesarea where a ruler's son is ill, and the holy man is initially threatened but later respected. The text also features a brief exchange with a servant named Demosthenes, who is rebuked for his lack of theological depth.

The text describes a series of miraculous events and persecutions involving figures named Peter, Lucius, and Euzoeus in Alexandria and beyond. It recounts the expulsion of a group of idol worshippers to an island, where a girl possessed by a spirit (likened to the spirit of Python) speaks to the Christians. The passage concludes with the conversion of these idol worshippers to Christianity and a subsequent public gathering in a city where the crowd reacts to the actions of Lucius.

Theodoretus recounts the actions of Lucius, who allowed a group of men into caves, and the subsequent behavior of a man named Palladius, a local leader accused of promoting idolatry and opposing Christ. The text describes a scene of ritualistic desecration involving the 'holy virgins' and the presence of Euzoeus, a figure associated with the destruction of a church in Berytus. The author defends his harsh rhetoric against these 'tyrants' and 'godless' individuals who have compromised the sanctity of the church.

Theodoretus describes a legal and theological confrontation between a group of Christians and a man named Magnus (a 'bitter and savage satrap') who is accused of being an Arian. The text details the interrogation of nineteen elders and ministers, some over eighty years old, who are forced to defend their faith against the Arian doctrine of the Son's relationship to the Father. The passage concludes with the Christians being condemned to exile from Alexandria to Heliopolis in Phoenicia, where they are sent to a harbor and ordered to sail away.

Theodoretus describes the mourning of a city following a massacre of Christians, where some victims were sold into mines at Phennese and others were executed. He recounts the arrival of a servant from Damasus, Bishop of Rome, and the subsequent persecution of eleven bishops from Egypt in the city of Diocesarea. The text concludes by mentioning a gathering of clergy in Antioch and the preparation of a residence in Neocaesarea.

Theodoretus describes the conflict between the orthodox and the heretical 'unholy assembly' in Alexandria and Antioch. He recounts the actions of Flavius and Diodorus, who defended the faith against the teachings of the heretic Valus (referred to as Valus/Bally) and the influence of the priestess. The narrative concludes with the martyrdom of the heretics in a ship fire near Constantinople and the subsequent defense of the faith by Flavius and Diodorus against the teachings of Arius.

Theodoretus describes the movements of a holy man (implied to be a shepherd) and the geography of the Orontes river near a royal palace. He recounts a dialogue between this man and a king regarding his role as a protector of 'divine sheep' and a subsequent encounter with a merchant who died after consuming frogs in hot water. The text also mentions the movements of Julius, Flavius, Diodorus, and Athanasius, and lists several ascetics—including Abitus, Marcian, and Acephemus—in various regions such as the Chaldean wilderness and the land of Apameon.

Theodoretus records the names and locations of various Christian figures, including the martyrs Peter the Galatian, the Syrian, the Roman, Seirus, Zeno, Moses, and Malchus, as well as the theologians Ephraim of Edessa and Didymus of Alexandria. The text describes the intellectual and spiritual activities of these figures, specifically Didymus's use of Greek philosophy as a defense against heresy. The narrative concludes with a military and political allegory involving a general named Trajan, a leader named Balak, and others like Arinthos and Victor, who navigate a conflict involving the Goths and the Bosporus.

The text recounts a conflict between a ruler and a group of 'barbarians' (Goths) involving a failed negotiation and a subsequent military engagement near a village. It details the actions of Betranius, a high priest in Scythia, and the diplomatic maneuvers of Eudoxius and Valens to reconcile the Goths with the imperial government. The final section is a list of chapter headings covering the piety of various emperors (Gratian, Theodosius, Arcadius), the actions of bishops (Amphilochius, Marcellus, Theophilus, Flavian), and the destruction of pagan temples.

The text begins with a list of chapter headings covering the Scythians, Marcionists, and various bishops including Alexander of Antioch and Theodotus of Antioch. It then transitions to a historical narrative concerning the reign of Gratian and his policies regarding the church, specifically the restoration of property to those who shared in the 'Damascus' fellowship. The narrative focuses on a theological and jurisdictional dispute in Antioch between Paul (of the Damascus faction) and Apollinarius, regarding the nature of Christ and the status of the clergy.

Theodoretus records a theological dispute between a man and Apollinarius regarding the Trinity and the nature of Christ, specifically referencing the writings of Damasus. The text then details the ecclesiastical appointments and movements of several figures, including Meletius, Paulinus, Diodorus, John, and Eusebius, across locations such as Tarsus, Antioch, and Edessa. It concludes with the transition of Gratian to Pannonia and the activities of Theodosius in Spain.

Theodoretus describes a military victory over barbarians in Thrace and the subsequent appointment of a commander who receives a divine vision of Meletius of Antioch. The text then details the internal ecclesiastical divisions following the death of Constantine and the subsequent leadership of Meletius in Constantinople. It concludes with a list of specific bishops and clergy associated with various regions and the mention of Timotheus of Alexandria.

Theodoretus describes a gathering of bishops in the East, including figures such as Gregory, Peter, and Cyrillus of Jerusalem, who deliberate on internal discord and the appointment of Nectarius as bishop of a major city while condemning Maximus. The text then transitions to a formal letter from the bishops of Constantinople to those in Rome, detailing their sufferings under Arian persecution and the restoration of their churches. The correspondence mentions specific figures like Damasus and Ambrose and addresses the ongoing struggle against 'wolves' (heretics) who disrupt the peace of the assemblies.

Theodoretus addresses the clergy at Rome and other regions, emphasizing the unity of the faith and the shared experience of past persecutions. He lists specific bishops—Nectarius of Constantinople, Flavian of Antioch, and Cyrillus of Jerusalem—while affirming their orthodoxy against the heresies of Sabellius, Eunomius, and Apollinaris. The text concludes by citing apostolic authority to condemn various heterodoxies, including those of Paul the Samosite and Marcellus.

Theodoretus records a letter from Damasus, Bishop of Rome, to Paul of Thessalonica, which addresses the condemnation of the heretic Apollinarius and his disciple Timothy. The text includes a formal confession of faith (homologia) condemning various heresies, including those of Sabellius, Arius, Eumonius, and Photienus. It concludes with a series of anathemas regarding the nature of the Trinity, the incarnation, and the status of the Holy Spirit.

The text begins with a series of anathemas regarding Christological and Trinitarian dogmas, specifically concerning the nature of the Trinity, the role of the Holy Spirit, and the unity of the Godhead. It transitions into a historical narrative concerning the death of the Emperor Valentinian and the subsequent rule of his brother, Maximus, who is depicted as being influenced by his mother Justina's Arian leanings. The passage concludes with a confrontation between Maximus and a preacher of the truth, involving a refusal to surrender the preacher to 'wolves' and a subsequent military movement toward Mediolanum.

Theodoretus recounts a narrative involving a king, a tyrant, and a youth, and the subsequent actions of the 'wonderful' figures Amphilochius and Ambrosius. The text describes a legal and moral conflict regarding the punishment of rebels and the desecration of a sacred space. It concludes with a theological defense of the sanctity of the body as the vessel of the 'common master' (God) and a rebuke of the king's actions.

The passage depicts a dialogue between a king, a man named Rufinus, and the high priest Ambrosius regarding the king's imprisonment and the legal process of his release. The king expresses his distress over his situation and the spiritual implications of his actions, while Rufinus attempts to mediate between the king and the high priest. The text concludes with the king's formal submission to the high priest's legal procedures and a description of his ritualistic display of repentance.

The text describes a dialogue between a king and a high priest regarding sacred mysteries and the king's education in Constantinople. It recounts the life of the king's wife, who served the sick and the poor, and the subsequent unrest in Antioch following the removal of a bronze statue of the queen, Placilla. The narrative concludes with a pious Macedonian man intervening to de-escalate a conflict between the king and his officers, advising them to treat the king as a man as well as a ruler.

Theodoretus recounts a theological argument regarding the distinction between the 'image' of God in humans versus inanimate idols, followed by a narrative of the destruction of pagan temples. The text names several rulers, including Constantine, Julian, Jovian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, and describes the actions of a priest named Marcellus in the city of Apamea. The final section describes a specific, miraculous method used to dismantle a massive stone structure, involving a laborer and a ritualistic confrontation with a demonic force.

Theodoretus describes a miracle involving a priest who uses water and a cross to repel a demon and destroy a pagan temple dedicated to Serapis. The text then transitions to a historical account of ecclesiastical disputes in Antioch and Rome involving figures such as Meletius, Flavius, and Evagrius. The passage concludes with a dialogue between Flavius and a king regarding the validity of Flavius's priesthood.

Theodoretus describes a dispute over the leadership of the church in Antioch and the subsequent reconciliation of several eastern and western sees, including Euboea, Asia, Pontus, and Thrace. The text details the role of Bishop Acacius of Beroea in resolving a seventeen-year schism and the subsequent actions of the Emperor (Constantine) as he moved toward Europe. The narrative concludes with a visionary account of the Emperor's military preparations, where he receives a vision of two riders, identified as John the Evangelist and Philip the Apostle, before engaging the forces of the tyrant.

Theodoretus describes a military victory where a king's forces overcome a numerically superior enemy aided by a divine wind and dust. The text then transitions to a series of hagiographic accounts of bishops and leaders, including Flavius of Antioch, Elpidius of Laodicea, and John the Great, who are noted for their governance of regions such as Thrace, Asia, and Pontus. The passage concludes with the expulsion of idolaters from Phoenicia.

Theodoretus describes a leader (implied to be a Christian figure) who organized a community of elders and ministers to convert the Scythians near the Hystrus river and communicated with Leontius, the bishop of Anchora. The narrative then shifts to a confrontation between a Scythian commander named Gainas and a man named John (referred to as 'the great' or 'the teacher of the world'), who rebukes Gainas for his luxury and tyranny. The passage concludes with the actions of a leader moving toward Thrace and the author's admission of confusion regarding the specific historical context of the final section.

Theodoretus describes a legal dispute and subsequent exile of a group of 'adversaries' (δυσμενεῖς) to a remote area in Armenia called Kukkos, near the border of Pontus. He recounts the actions of several bishops, including Cyril of Alexandria, John of Jerusalem, and Alexander of Antioch, and mentions their interactions with figures such as Porphyrius, Eustatius, and Evagrius. The text concludes with a description of a large public gathering and musical performance that caused distress among Jews and those following the teachings of Arius.

Theodoretus recounts the actions of a faithful king who protected a sacred treasure, showed mercy to those who sinned in ignorance, and oversaw the removal of pagan idols. The text transitions into a series of historical and biblical parallels, including the defeat of the Scythian leader Roilas, the defense of a city by a high priest named Eunomius (or Hermione), and a confrontation with a blaspheming king. The passage concludes with a list of successions of Roman bishops and a mention of Praulius in Jerusalem.

The text describes the leadership of Theodotus at Antioch following the tenure of Alexander, and the subsequent persecution of Christians by the Persian King Istigerdes (Istigerides) following a conflict over a 'fire' (pyreion). It details the martyrdom of several Christians, including Hormisdes (Hormisdes), and concludes with the narrative of Saen (Saehn) and his wife's refusal to abandon the truth.

Theodoretus recounts the story of a servant named Benjamin, who was imprisoned for teaching Christian doctrine and later released by a king who was unaware of the specifics. The text transitions into a list of bishops and leaders in major cities including Rome, Antioch, Alexandria, Jerusalem, and Constantinople, distinguishing between those labeled as orthodox and those labeled as heretical. The author concludes by noting the historical scope of his work and the names of specific figures like Theodorus of Mopsuestus and Gregory of Nazianzus.

This 5th-century Greek theological commentary by Hesychius Hierosolymitanus provides a systematic allegorical and typological interpretation of the Psalms and the Prophet Malachi. The work is structured to transition from Old Testament types, such as the Law of Moses and the Davidic throne, to New Testament fulfillments in Christology, including the Incarnation, the Passion, and the role of the Good Shepherd. The author integrates extensive scriptural citations from the Pauline Epistles, the Gospels (Matthew, Luke, and John), and the writings of Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Daniel. Specific figures discussed include David, Moses, Solomon, Peter, Pilate, and Judas Iscariot, alongside references to the works of Josephus and Ambacum. The text employs allegorical interpretations of physical imagery and sacred sites, including Jerusalem, Zion, Bethlehem, Golgotha, Mount Tabor, Mount Hermon, and Beersheba. Key theological themes include the transition from the Old to the New Covenant, the role of the Holy Spirit, the sacraments of Baptism and the Eucharist, and the distinction between the 'synagogue' and the 'New Covenant.'

Hesychius provides a theological commentary on the Prophet Malachi and the Psalms, interpreting the 'Sun of Righteousness' as a prefiguration of Christ. He critiques previous scribal traditions regarding the authorship of the Psalms, specifically questioning the inclusion of works attributed to Moses and Solomon. The text argues for the primacy of Davidic authorship and discusses the distinction between the 'hidden' wisdom of the Old Testament and its revelation in the New.

The author provides a systematic interpretation of the names and titles found in the headings of the Psalms, such as David, the sons of Korah, Asaph, and Ethan. He argues that these names are not merely identifiers of authorship but are allegorical; for example, 'David' may signify the 'weakened' or the 'beloved' (the chosen people), while 'Korah' may refer to the 'bald' or the 'pure of heart.' The text also addresses the inclusion of figures like Solomon and Moses in the Hebrew scriptures and the specific roles of the Levites and the sons of Korah as psalmists.

Hesychius examines the authorship and interpretation of the Psalms, specifically addressing the names 'Aetham' (interpreted as 'High') and 'Israel' (interpreted as 'Seed of God') as references to Christ. He argues that the names of Solomon and Moses in the titles are allegorical, and he defends the attribution of certain 'unnamed' psalms to David by citing the testimony of the apostle Peter and the martyr Stephen. The text also addresses the 'Alleluia' and the inclusion of psalms not traditionally associated with the Hebrew people due to their unbelief.

Hesychius provides a theological commentary on the first eight Psalms, addressing the identity of anonymous authors, the role of Asaph, and the distinction between musicians and teachers. He interprets specific phrases such as 'Alleluia' and 'bones' as metaphors for spiritual virtues and the state of the soul. The text also includes a defense of the authorship of the Psalms by David and a distinction between those engaged in high theology and those navigating the practicalities of life.

This section of the commentary on the Psalms provides exegetical notes on Psalms 8, 12, 13, and 15. The text interprets biblical imagery regarding the 'beasts' and 'sinners,' the role of the Christ as the savior of both, and the spiritual warfare against demons. It also addresses the nature of confession, the distinction between the words of the heart and the tongue, and the theological significance of the 'inheritance' of the Church.

The text provides a commentary on Psalms 17, 52, 111, 114, and 115. It interprets the psalms through a Christological lens, identifying the 'serpent' as the devil, the 'judgment' as the divine response to sin, and the 'suffering' of Christ as a triumph over the devil. Specific figures mentioned include David, the prophet Zechariah, Judas, and the people of Israel.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, specifically interpreting the sufferings of Christ through the lens of the prophet Isaiah and the Gospel accounts. It addresses the distinction between the legalistic Sabbath and the 'Sabbath' of Christ's passion, the nature of his physical suffering as a representation of human sin, and the specific theological nuances of his silence before the High Priest.

The text provides a commentary on the Psalms and the Gospels, specifically analyzing the lamentations and actions of Christ. It interprets the distinction between the 'friends' (Jews) and the 'apostles' in the Gospels, the significance of the Passover, and the silence of Christ before his accusers. The author also discusses the prayer of Christ for the apostles and the symbolic washing of the disciples' feet.

The text provides a commentary on the Psalms, specifically focusing on the themes of Christ's suffering, the rejection of his ministry by the Jews, and the interpretation of Paul's writings regarding the 'new Adam' and the role of the Church as a bride. It analyzes specific biblical phrases regarding the 'pain of sin,' the 'law of the law,' and the distinction between the preaching of righteousness and the personal conduct of the teacher.

The text provides a theological commentary on Psalms 103, 104, and 105. It discusses the role of the Church as a vessel for high doctrine, the prophetic fulfillment of Christ in the Old Testament (referencing David, Hezekiah, and Hoshea), and the spiritual transformation of the soul through mercy and the cross. The author also interprets specific imagery, such as the 'sword' as the cross and the distinction between 'heavenly' and 'earthly' thoughts.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, specifically addressing the distinction between the 'faithful' of the Old Covenant who performed ritual sacrifices and the 'faithful' of the New Covenant who offer a sacrifice of praise. It interprets the transition from the physical temple and animal sacrifices to the spiritual reality of the Church, and it analyzes Psalm 51 (referred to as Psalm 10 in the text's numbering) in the context of King David's sin with Bathsheba and his subsequent repentance. The author discusses the nature of sin, the necessity of sincere repentance, and the distinction between a single lapse and habitual lawlessness.

The text provides a theological commentary on the nature of sin, repentance, and the role of the Holy Spirit. It references biblical figures including David, Nathan, Paul, and Job to argue that while sin causes spiritual 'blindness' and 'death,' sincere repentance restores the soul's joy and the ability to praise God. The author also discusses the distinction between the 'living Spirit' and the 'Spirit of God' as a source of divine guidance.

The text provides a theological commentary on Psalms 113 and 114, contrasting the repentance of the sinner with the betrayal of Judas Iscariot and the denial of Peter. It cites Paul's Epistle to the Ephesians regarding the mystery of Christ's incarnation and discusses the distinction between the 'affliction' of Christ and the 'madness' of idolaters. The passage also addresses the concept of divine judgment and the distinction between those who are justified by grace and those who are lost in transgression.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, specifically focusing on the distinction between true faith and the fear of men or worldly power. It addresses the behavior of Jewish teachers who, according to the author, prioritized worldly safety and material gain over the law of God. The commentary also explores the nature of prayer as a spiritual weapon and the role of the 'sacrificial' heart in worship, referencing the apostle Paul and the concept of 'joyful' offering.

The text provides a theological commentary on the prayers of Christ and the actions of his enemies, specifically naming Caiaphas and Judas. It interprets biblical imagery, such as the 'walls' of Jerusalem and the 'darkness' of the cross, as metaphors for the priesthood and the spiritual state of the faithful. The passage also addresses the distinction between the 'lawlessness' of the Jewish leadership and the 'virtues' of the Christian community.

The text provides a theological commentary on the contrast between the betrayal of Judas and the repentance of Peter, using the distinction between an error of action and an error of will. It analyzes the 'prophetic' warnings against Judas, the nature of human life as a 'sojourn,' and the interpretation of specific biblical phrases regarding the Eucharist and the passion of Christ. The author also discusses the nature of prayer and the distinction between the roles of the disciples in the face of divine judgment.

The text provides a theological commentary on Psalm 144 (referenced as Psalm 142 in the Greek numbering), interpreting its imagery regarding the 'hidden' people and the 'enemy' as a dual reference to the Gentiles and the demonic forces. It interprets the location 'Gath' as a wilderness and links the text to the ministry of Paul and the prophecy of Isaiah. The author argues that the psalmist's descriptions of being trampled and the 'shaking of tears' refer to the spiritual warfare of the faithful against Satan and the historical rejection of the Gospel by the Jews.

The text provides a commentary on Psalms 14, 15, 16, 17, and 18. It includes a discussion on the return from Babylon and the rebuilding of Jerusalem, a reference to Josephus's account of Mordecai and the Jews at Shush, and a theological exploration of Christ as the 'Way' and the 'Sun of Righteousness.' The passage also addresses the concept of the 'home church' (κατ’ οἶκον συναγωγή) and the spiritual significance of baptism.

The text provides a commentary on the Passion of Christ, specifically addressing the abandonment of the disciples, the identification of Christ as a 'stranger' to the Jews, and the significance of his suffering for the human race. It incorporates scriptural references to the trial of Jesus, the prophecy of Simeon, and the distinction between natural and spiritual worship. The author also addresses the spiritual warfare against demons and the role of the Church in offering 'rational' praise.

The text provides a commentary on the Psalms, focusing on the role of Christ as a protector and savior against demons and the temptations of the flesh. It includes a discussion on the nature of sin and the spiritual state of the 'poor' and 'needy' people, and references the writings of Ambacum. The passage also addresses the doctrine of the Incarnation, the naming of the twelve apostles, and the proclamation of Christ's glory in both public and private spaces.

The text provides a commentary on the Psalms, specifically addressing the themes of spiritual warfare, the distinction between the righteous and the sinful, and the consequences of falling into error. It features a dialogue with a person named Genoetus regarding the interpretation of scripture, and references the Proverbs to contrast the behavior of the 'fool' with the 'wise.' The author analyzes the spiritual state of those who are 'deceived' by the world and the internal purification of the heart.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, interpreting scriptural imagery regarding the 'sword' of faith, the nature of the Trinity, and the distinction between the human soul, mind, and spirit. It addresses the history of the Fall in Paradise, the role of Christ in overcoming sin (the 'head of serpents'), and the distinction between the 'spirit' and the 'mind' in prayer. The passage concludes with a meditation on the works of God in creation and the judgment of the righteous and the wicked.

The text provides a theological commentary on Psalm 107, interpreting the prophet's use of 'parables' and 'riddles' as a means of revealing God's power and the fulfillment of prophecy. It draws parallels between the physical rods of Moses and Aaron and the cross of Christ, and identifies specific biblical figures such as Job, David, Daniel, and the three sons (the sons of Job) as witnesses to divine wonders. The passage concludes by linking the physical manifestations of God in the Old Testament, such as the wrestling of Jacob, to the incarnation of Christ.

The text discusses the interpretation of the Law as a means for the Gentiles to become 'sons' through the belief in Christ. It contrasts the actions of the scribes and Pharisees with the faithful, and references the prophet Hosea's address to Ephraim and Manasseh. The passage concludes with a comparison between the antiquity of Hebron and Tanis, recounting the miraculous crossing of the sea and the guidance of the Israelites through the wilderness.

The text provides a theological commentary on the miracles of Moses in the wilderness, specifically the provision of a pillar of fire and the striking of a rock to produce water at Horeb and Kadesh. It argues against the notion that the people's later complaints for food were a matter of necessity, characterizing their actions as a deliberate temptation of God and a rejection of his providence. The passage concludes by identifying the 'salvation' mentioned in the scriptures as Christ, whom both the prophets and Simeon recognized.

The text provides a theological commentary on the manna and the events in the wilderness, interpreting the 'bread of angels' as a divine provision not made by human hands. It addresses the sin of the Israelites who, despite receiving miracles, failed to believe and were punished for their lack of faith and improper supplications. The author concludes by contrasting true devotion with the superficial worship of the Jews, citing Isaiah to condemn those who worship with the tongue while their hearts remain distant from God's covenant.

The text explores the nature of Christ's mercy and his role as the mediator of the covenant, contrasting his divine nature with his human experience of weakness and temptation. It references Paul's writings on the Son's obedience and Isaiah's prophecies regarding the 'Holy One' and the 'Seed' left for the Jews. The passage also addresses the miracles of Moses in Egypt and the wilderness, specifically the turning of waters into blood and the signs in the plain of Tanis, to establish God as the ruler of all elements.

The text provides a commentary on the plagues of Egypt and the Exodus, analyzing the specific symbolism of the locusts, frogs, and the destruction of crops and livestock. It argues that the psalmist uses these events to illustrate divine judgment against the Egyptians and the subsequent liberation of the Israelites. The author also discusses the theological significance of the 'firstborn' and the 'tents of Ham' as a reference to the Egyptian people.

Hesychius interprets the promise to Abraham and the crossing of the Red Sea as a movement toward the 'mountain of sanctification,' identifying the 'ark' as the physical Ark of the Covenant and the 'second ark' as the body of Christ. He argues that the Jews' failure to keep the covenant led to the abandonment of the tabernacle of Shiloh and the loss of their spiritual strength. The text concludes by distinguishing between the physical loss of the people's strength and the spiritual 'enemy of the mind' that captured their inner beauty.

Hesychius interprets the prophetic imagery of Isaiah and Micah regarding the destruction of the old Jerusalem and the establishment of a new sanctuary. He argues that the 'tabernacle' and 'Zion' refer to the Church and the internal spiritual life of the believer rather than physical locations. The text addresses the fate of the Jews, the distinction between physical and spiritual circumcision, and the transition from the Old Covenant to the New.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, specifically addressing the distinction between the 'many' rituals of the Jews and the 'one' faith and baptism of the Church. It interprets the role of David as a shepherd of the flock and a prefiguration of Christ, while addressing the transition of the covenant from the Jews to the Gentiles. The author argues that the destruction of the Jerusalem temple and the subsequent occupation by Assyrians, Macedonians, and Romans served to reveal the impurity of the old worship and establish the new order.

The text provides a commentary on the Book of Psalms and the Prophet Ezekiel, focusing on the destruction of Jerusalem and the judgment of those who 'are flesh.' It incorporates scriptural citations from the Gospels and the Epistles of Paul to argue for the role of Christ as the mediator of atonement for both Jews and Gentiles. The author discusses the distinction between the 'holy' and the 'unholy,' the mercy of God, and the transition of the covenant to the Gentiles.

The text provides a theological commentary on the destruction of idols and the role of the Cross in the salvation of the Jews and the Gentiles. It interprets the 'sevenfold' punishment of demons as a just retribution for their rebellion and identifies the 'good shepherd' as Christ. The author argues that the Incarnation was necessary for the salvation of humanity, specifically addressing the transition from servitude to freedom.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms and prophetic imagery, specifically regarding the 'Jewish vine' (the people of Israel) and the role of the Law as a 'shadow' of things to come. It interprets various metaphors, such as 'sea' as baptism and 'rivers' as partial purifications, while referencing figures like Moses, Isaiah, and Paul. The passage also discusses the transition from the era of the prophets to the manifestation of Christ as the 'bread of life'.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, specifically interpreting the imagery of the 'broken fence' and the 'vineyard' as metaphors for the Jewish people and the transition from the Law to Christ. It incorporates and interprets scriptural references from the Gospels (Matthew, John), the Prophets (Isaiah), and the Psalms (David), focusing on the role of Christ as the 'Son of Man' and the 'cornerstone.' The author argues against the current state of the Jewish people (the 'synagogue') and emphasizes the divine authority and presence of Christ as the mediator of signs and wonders.

The text provides a theological commentary on Psalm 119 (referred to as Psalm 10 in the text's numbering), interpreting the 'trumpets' and 'new moons' as symbols of the Gospel and the feast of the Passover. It argues that the Old Testament types, specifically the figures of Joseph and the 'God of Jacob' (Christ), find their fulfillment in the New Covenant. The author discusses the relationship between the Old and New Testaments, specifically the transition from the law to the gospel, and mentions the names of the figures Joseph, Jacob, and the apostle Paul.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, specifically contrasting the figures of Joseph and Christ. It argues that Joseph served as a 'type' or 'witness' of Christ, detailing their shared experiences in Egypt and their roles as 'servants' in the sense of bearing the burden of sin. The passage also incorporates scriptural citations from Exodus and Isaiah to discuss the identity of God, the nature of the Incarnation, and the rejection of the Israelites.

Hesychius provides a commentary on the Psalms, specifically addressing the spiritual blindness of the Jews and the distinction between those who hold sacred offices and those who abuse them. He cites Isaiah and Paul to discuss the judgment of the 'enemies of the cross' and interprets the 'fire' and 'honey' of the Psalms as symbols of the Law and the prophets. The text concludes by contrasting the judgment of the righteous (prophets and priests) with the judgment of the orphan and the poor.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms and the nature of sin, contrasting the plight of the poor and elderly with the behavior of the 'sinner' who acts without shame or awareness. It incorporates scriptural references to Paul's letters, the fall of man in Genesis, and the role of the Messiah as the one who delivers humanity from 'beasts.' The author also analyzes the linguistic nuances of the Psalms, specifically the distinction between 'who' and 'he' in the context of God's uniqueness and the future economy of the Monogenēs (Only-Begotten).

The text provides a commentary on the Psalms, specifically regarding the behavior of sinners who act as enemies of God and his people. It identifies specific groups as enemies, including the Edomites, Ishmaelites, Moabites, Ammonites, Amalekites, and the Hagrites, while tracing their lineage to Abraham and Lot. The passage concludes with a reference to the military victories of Gideon over the Midianites and the defeat of enemies at the Kishon and Endor.

The text provides a commentary on the fall of Sisera and the subsequent judgment of those who sought to plunder the sanctuary and sell sacred vessels, specifically referencing Simon the Zealot. It contrasts the current state of the ungodly, who are currently tolerated by God's patience, with their future state of forced confession and confusion during the final judgment. The passage concludes with a note on the identity of the sons of Korah as psalmists and prophets.

The text provides a mystical and allegorical commentary on the Psalms, specifically focusing on the concept of 'tabernacles' as both physical sacred spaces and the indwelling of Christ and the faithful. It references the writings of John the Theologian and the figure of Epinicius, while interpreting the 'altars of God' as spiritual refuges for the soul. The passage concludes with a theological meditation on the progression of virtues—humility, gentleness, and mercy—leading to the vision of God in Zion.

The text provides a commentary on the Psalms, specifically focusing on the transition from the Old Testament to the New Covenant. It discusses the prophet's transition from the 'law' to the 'Christ' and the 'Spirit,' and interprets the 'captivity of Jacob' as the state of the Jews. The author argues that the 'medicine' of the physician is a metaphor for the forgiveness of sins through Christ's mercy.

Hesychius provides a commentary on the Psalms, specifically addressing the distinction between 'transgression' (Judaean) and 'sin' (Gentile) in the context of the Law of Moses. He analyzes the theme of God's 'turning' from wrath to mercy, interpreting the prophetic character of the psalmist as a foretelling of Christ's incarnation and the inclusion of the Gentiles. The text concludes by discussing the 'tabernacling' of God's glory in the human form and the resulting adoption of the Gentiles as children of God.

Hesychius provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, focusing on the incarnation of the Word (Logos) and the union of divinity and humanity in Christ. He interprets specific phrases regarding 'mercy,' 'truth,' and 'righteousness' as attributes of the Word made flesh, and analyzes the petitions of David as representative of the universal human condition of poverty and sin.

The text provides a commentary on the Psalms, focusing on the theology of prayer as a means of protection and the distinction between the divine and the human. It argues that the 'gods' mentioned in certain psalms refer to holy men and saints rather than idols, and it explores the themes of confession, the mercy of God, and the spiritual rewards of repentance. The passage also addresses the nature of worship, specifically regarding the Eucharist and the distinction between true worship and the worship of idols.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, specifically focusing on the identification of Christ in prophetic imagery. It interprets the 'synagogue of rulers' as those who oppose the law, and identifies the 'holy mountains' as physical locations of Christ's ministry: Bethlehem, Golgotha, Tabor, and the site of the Transfiguration. The author also interprets 'Rahab' and 'Babylon' as symbols of harlotry and confusion, respectively, while discussing the transition of the Word to the Gentiles.

The author interprets the figures of Rahab and Babylon as symbols for the Gentiles, who are 'born' into the faith through baptism. The text explores the mystery of Christ's dual nature as both man (for the flesh) and the Most High (for the deity) and his role as the true interpreter of the scriptures. It concludes by analyzing the Psalms of the sons of Korah, specifically the prayer of Christ in Gethsemane and the role of the apostles as rulers in Zion.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Passion of Christ, interpreting the physical and spiritual sufferings of Jesus as a fulfillment of prophetic scripture and a voluntary assumption of the 'punishment' of the human race. It analyzes specific biblical passages from the Gospels (Luke) and the Prophets (Jeremiah) to explain the significance of the cross, the betrayal by Peter, and the physical 'wounds' of the savior. The author argues that Christ's physical suffering and his presence in the 'pit' of death were necessary to fulfill the mystery of the economy of salvation.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Passion of Christ, interpreting the High Priest's actions and the events of the Passion as a fulfillment of the economy of suffering. It analyzes specific biblical passages regarding the descent into Hades, the role of the prophets, and the relationship between Christ and the Father. The commentary also identifies specific figures, including Peter, the apostles, and Pilate, while addressing the theological significance of the cross and the distinction between the 'mystery' of the cross and the human capacity to understand it.

The text provides a commentary on the Psalms, specifically addressing the names Aiman and Aetham and their shared identity as Israelites. It interprets the themes of mercy, truth, and the 'New Covenant' through the lens of the Gospels, the writings of Paul to the Romans, and the prophecy of Daniel. The author also analyzes the distinction between the role of angels and the 'likeness' of saints in the presence of God, referencing the Acts of the Apostles and the ministry of Barnabas and Paul.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, focusing on the nature of God's power, the distinction between the Father and the Son, and the interpretation of geographical and physical imagery. It discusses the transformation of Christ at Mount Tabor and Mount Hermon, the role of the prophet Isaiah, and the 'foolishness' of the cross as described by Paul. Specific locations mentioned include the mountains of Zion, Tabor, and Hermon, and the biblical book of Numbers.

Hesychius provides a commentary on the Psalms, specifically interpreting the role of Christ as the 'power of God' and the 'chosen one' from the people. He argues that Christ's exaltation on the cross serves as the means of salvation for the Gentiles and the fulfillment of the mystery of the divine plan. The text also explores the distinction between the Jews' reliance on Moses and Abraham versus the Gentiles' reliance on Christ, and addresses the themes of mercy, truth, and the transition from slavery to sonship.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, focusing on the identity of Christ as the 'Good Shepherd' and the 'Savior' who overcomes the powers of darkness. It interprets scriptural imagery regarding the 'hand' and 'arm' of God, the 'anointing' of the Gentiles, and the distinction between the faithful and the 'man of lawlessness' (Antichrist). The passage also addresses the role of the Holy Spirit, the covenant of God, and the distinction between the Jewish and Gentile recipients of divine promises.

The text provides a commentary on Psalm 132, analyzing the distinction between the 'law' of Moses and the 'covenant' of the Gospel. It discusses the role of Christ as the 'true' successor to David's throne, the interpretation of 'moon' as a symbol of the current age's obscured glory, and the distinction between those who are persecuted and those who are exalted. The author also addresses the transition from prophetic speech to personal petition in the final verses.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, specifically addressing the transition from the Jewish people to the Gentiles. It argues that Christ's arrival and the establishment of the New Covenant (baptism) superseded the old Jewish rites and laws, which the author characterizes as 'broken' or 'shortened.' The commentary cites scripture to contrast the 'shortened' time of the Jewish state with the universal mission of the Gospel.

Hesychius provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, specifically focusing on the transition from Old Testament prophecy to the New Testament. He analyzes the 'reproach' of the prophets and the Church, the role of David and Isaiah in foretelling Christ, and the concept of the 'mystery' revealed to the Gentiles. The text concludes by discussing the structure of the Psalter and the specific role of Moses as a man of God.

The text provides a theological commentary on Psalm 90, focusing on the distinction between the 'present' life and the 'future' life. It analyzes the role of Moses as a man of God, the creation of the world, and the nature of divine patience and judgment. The author interprets specific metaphors of grass and flowers as symbols of the fleeting nature of human glory and the certainty of divine justice.

This section of the commentary on the Psalms analyzes the Greek text of Psalm 10, focusing on the distinction between 'wrath' (thumos) and 'discipline' (paideia). The author interprets the 'judgment' of the psalmist as a spiritual exercise in rectifying the soul and explores the role of Christ as the 'right hand' of God and the 'middle way' between height and humility. The text also addresses the brevity of human life, the role of the apostles as ambassadors of salvation, and the concept of divine mercy.

Hesychius provides a commentary on the Psalms, specifically addressing the themes of divine mercy, the transition from the Old Covenant to the New, and the spiritual life of the believer. He interprets the psalmist's transition from lamenting slavery to idols to celebrating the 'good works' of the faithful, and discusses the role of the Holy Spirit and the 'law and the prophets.' The text also addresses the distinction between the physical and spiritual realms and the protection of the believer against demonic influences.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, focusing on the spiritual warfare against demonic forces and the superiority of faith in God over worldly idols. It cites the Apostle Paul and the prophet Jeremiah to argue that the 'truth' of Christ serves as a weapon against the 'fear of the night' (carnal desires) and 'arrows of the day' (pride). The passage concludes by contrasting the refuge found in God with the destruction of those who rely on worldly powers.

The text provides a theological commentary on the protection of the believer, contrasting the 'scourging' of the sinner with the divine protection of the one who takes refuge in God. It references Paul's writings, the role of angels as guardians and guides, and the authority given to believers to overcome spiritual enemies. The final section addresses the authorship of a specific psalm, noting it is not anonymous but rather lacks a specific personal attribution like David or Asaph, while still functioning as a prophetic utterance.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, focusing on the virtue of confession to God and the distinction between the 'law' and 'gospel' as represented by the instruments of the harp and the ten-stringed psaltery. It cites the works of Solomon (Ecclesiastes), the prophet Isaiah, and the Apostle Paul to argue that God's actions are governed by wisdom and that the pride of sinners leads to their destruction. The author interprets the 'sunrise' as a metaphor for the fleeting nature of sin compared to the eternal nature of God.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms and Pauline epistles, focusing on the distinction between current partial knowledge and future perfect revelation. It interprets scriptural imagery, such as the 'one horn' of Christ, the 'fig tree' (φοῖνιξ), and the 'cedars of Lebanon' as symbols of the righteous and the transformation of the faithful. The author argues that the righteous will only fully manifest their virtues in the eschaton, and that the Church is the 'house of God' where these truths are realized.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, specifically focusing on the incarnation of Christ and the role of the Law and the Spirit. It interprets the 'house of God' as the Law and the Church, and discusses the 'rivers' as the gifts of the Spirit. The author addresses the nature of Christ's humanity, the fulfillment of prophecy, and the distinction between the Old Testament's promises and the New Testament's fulfillment.

Hesychius comments on the spiritual gifts of the Holy Spirit and the distinction between the 'depths' of divine mysteries and the 'humble' nature of the Spirit's glory. He addresses the behavior of those who exploit the vulnerable (widows, orphans, and strangers) and the judgment of those who believe they can evade divine justice. The text also explores the concept of natural law, arguing that humans possess an innate ability to distinguish good from evil provided by God.
