The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, specifically focusing on the distinction between divine discipline (paideia) and judicial punishment (timōrēsis). It analyzes the role of the prophet as a mediator of mercy and discusses the spiritual warfare against demonic powers (archai, exousiai, kosmokratōres) and the specific instance of David's repentance after the transgression at Beersheba.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms and the nature of divine justice, contrasting the rewards of the righteous with the punishments of the lawless. It discusses the role of conscience as a witness in judgment, the distinction between the 'throne of iniquity' (associated with the devil) and the 'crown' of the faithful, and the specific fate of those who persecute the righteous. The passage concludes with a brief note on a specific psalm and a reference to David.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, specifically addressing the inclusion of a doxology and the transition from confession to praise. It argues that the 'victory' over enemies and the 'forgiveness' of sins are the divine works that justify the psalmist's joyful shouting. The author interprets the 'greatness' of God through the lens of the Old Testament, citing Isaiah and the distinction between the knowledge of the righteous and the ungodly. The passage concludes with a meditation on Christ as the Good Shepherd who feeds his flock through his humanity, referencing Paul's exhortation to the Hebrews regarding the urgency of 'Today'.

The author provides a commentary on the Psalms, specifically addressing the behavior of the Israelites in the wilderness and their rejection of God's signs. He cites Paul's letters to warn against tempting the Lord and discusses the distinction between the 'rest' of the present age and the 'rest' of the world to come. The text also analyzes the authorship and interpretation of a psalm attributed to David, contrasting the physical temple with the 'house of the flesh' and the incarnation of Christ.

The text analyzes the 'New Song' (Καινὸν ᾆσμα) in the Psalms, arguing that it refers to the New Covenant and the global scope of the Gospel rather than a localized Judean context. It cites Isaiah, the Gospel of Luke, and the Great Commission to argue that the 'New Song' is a revelation of the Trinity and the universal mission to the Gentiles. The author also addresses the nature of 'gods' in the scriptures, identifying them as demons, and concludes with a theological distinction between the fallen spirits and the sanctified saints in heaven.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, focusing on the themes of confession, the holiness of the divine, and the inclusion of the Gentiles. It interprets specific scriptural phrases regarding the 'new song,' the 'holy court' as the universal Church, and the role of baptism in the mystery of the Monogenes (the Only-Begotten). The author argues that the worship of the Gentiles is a spiritual offering of praise rather than physical sacrifice, and notes the transition from Old Testament law to the new covenant in Christ.

The text provides a theological commentary on a Psalm attributed to David, interpreting its imagery of 'the earth' and 'the sea' as references to the physical world and the spiritual realm. It distinguishes between Christ's first coming (to save) and second coming (to judge), and interprets 'the trees of the forest' as the ungodly or 'fruitless' ones. The commentary also addresses the role of the Church (the 'islands') and the distinction between the 'earth' and the 'inhabited world' (the cosmos).

The text provides a theological commentary on the visions of Daniel and the nature of the apostles, who are described as 'mountains' and 'light' of the world. It interprets the 'daughters of Judah' as the Gentile churches and discusses the distinction between the worship of God and the worship of angels. The author argues that the apostles' authority and the 'judgment' of God are manifested through the Holy Spirit and the revelation of the 'Monogenes' (the Only-Begotten).

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, specifically focusing on the exaltation of Christ as the 'One' (Monogenos) and the 'Sun of Righteousness.' It argues that Christ's suffering on the cross revealed God's power over false gods and provides a means for the redemption of sinners. The author incorporates scriptural citations from Isaiah, David, and the Epistle of James to contrast the 'love of the world' with the 'pure love' of God.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, specifically focusing on the revelation of Christ as the Savior and the fulfillment of Old Testament prophecies regarding the transition from the Old Covenant to the New. It interprets the 'harp' as the Old Covenant and the 'trumpet' as the Gospel, while discussing the role of the prophets, the inclusion of the Gentiles, and the spiritual significance of the 'mystery' of the flesh.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Psalms, specifically addressing the nature of Christ's presence, the distinction between his earthly ministry and his role as Judge, and the significance of his holy name. It references biblical figures such as Peter, Moses, and Pilate, and mentions the geography of the Jordan, Zion, and the land of the Jews. The author argues that the 'fearful' nature of Christ's name serves as a source of sanctification for the faithful and a warning to demons.

The text provides a theological commentary on Psalm 99, focusing on the distinction between the holiness of Christ and the holiness of Old Testament figures like Moses, Aaron, and Samuel. It interprets the 'footstool' as Golgotha, where Christ's humanity was subjected to the cross, and discusses the 'holy mountain' as the site of his sacrifice. The author also references the Gospel of John (Thomas) and the writings of Paul to argue for the efficacy of Christ's suffering and his role as the mediator of divine justice.

The text analyzes Psalm 100, discussing the anonymity of the psalmist and the theological significance of the 'thanksgiving' and 'praise' contained within. It references the interpretations of Aquila and the writings of Paul to argue for the unity of Christ as Lord and God. The author also addresses and refutes heretical views on the Trinity, emphasizing the necessity of confession before praise and the eternal mercy of Christ.

This Greek letter, written by Amphilochius of Iconium in the 4th century, is a synodal epistle addressed to a group of clergy or peers. The first section establishes the theological framework of the text by affirming the Nicene orthodoxy regarding the Trinity while explicitly rejecting Arianism, Sabellianism, and Pneumatomachianism. The author cites the Great Commission and the baptismal formula as foundational scriptural proofs for Christology. The second section shifts to an exhortation on ecclesiastical unity and the spiritual dangers of division. It warns against the influence of 'wolves' and the sin of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit associated with Arian communion. The work concludes with a prayer for the purity of the church until the final judgment.

Amphilochius of Iconium addresses a group of clergy or peers, acknowledging their piety and the shared faith established at the Council of Nicaea. The text defends the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity against Arianism, Sabellianism, and Pneumatomachianism by citing the Great Commission and the baptismal formula. The author concludes by stating that a detailed theological defense is omitted from the letter due to its length, trusting the recipients' existing knowledge.

Amphilochius exhorts the recipients to remain 'children of peace' and maintain unity of mind to fulfill the apostolic command, specifically by sharing in the sufferings of Christ. He warns against allowing the 'evil one' to sever their bonds or making them vulnerable to 'wolves' through division. The text warns against the sin of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit associated with those seeking communion with Arians, and concludes with a prayer for the church to remain undefiled until the day of judgment.

Eusebius's Historia Ecclesiastica is a foundational work of early Christian historiography that traces the history of the Church from the Old Testament to the late fourth century. The narrative is structured chronologically, beginning with a theological defense of the Logos and the continuity of Hebrew tradition, followed by the history of the apostles and the early episcopate. The text incorporates extensive scriptural analysis and citations from external sources such as Josephus, Philo, and Hegesippus. It documents the martyrdom of Christians under various Roman emperors, including Nero, Domitian, Trajan, and Decius, and identifies heretical movements such as those of Marcion, Valentinus, and the Ebionites. Key figures mentioned include the apostles Peter and Paul, early bishops like Polycarp of Smyrna and Clement of Rome, and scholars such as Origen and Irenaeus. The work concludes by documenting the transition from imperial persecution to the era of Constantine, detailing the establishment of church property and the defense of orthodoxy.

Eusebius introduces his history of the church, focusing on the succession of the apostles, the deeds of those who led the assembly in prominent places, and the distinction between true doctrine and the 'innovations' of false teachers. He establishes a theological framework for his narrative, beginning with the pre-existent Word (Logos) and the creation of man, before transitioning to the historical figures of Moses and Abraham. The text concludes with the specific account of Abraham's encounter with the divine at the bush of Mambres.

Eusebius argues that the physical appearances of God in Scripture, such as the 'form of a man' seen by Moses and Jacob, do not alter the unchangeable essence of the Almighty. He identifies these appearances as the 'Logos' (Word of God) and 'Wisdom' acting as a mediator, citing the Psalms and the Book of Proverbs. The text also recounts the encounter between Joshua and the commander of the Lord's army at Jericho, and describes the fallen state of humanity after the fall of the first man.

Eusebius describes the revelation of the names 'Jesus' and 'Christ' to the prophets of old, specifically highlighting Moses as the first to receive the title of Christ and the high priesthood. The text incorporates a series of scriptural citations from Daniel, Jeremiah, and the Psalms to illustrate the messianic role of Christ as the savior of both Jews and Gentiles. It concludes by detailing the prophetic promises of Christ's eternal kingdom and the inclusion of the nations in his inheritance.

Eusebius argues that Christ is the only true High Priest, King, and Prophet, surpassing the types and symbols of the Old Testament. He contrasts the physical anointing of the Hebrew priests and kings with the spiritual, divine anointing of Christ, who is identified with the eternal priesthood of Melchizedek. The text concludes by asserting that Christ's teachings are not new or foreign, but are the eternal words of the Word of God.

Eusebius argues that the Christian movement is not a new religion but a continuation of the ancient piety of the Hebrews, specifically the lineage of Abraham. He asserts that Christians share the same core virtues of the Old Testament figures, such as faith and righteousness, while fulfilling the biblical promises regarding the blessing of all nations. The passage concludes with a transition into the historical narrative, beginning with the reign of Augustus and the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem.

Eusebius cites Josephus to describe the census of Cyrene and the rebellion of Judas the Galilean (also called Gamaliel), a Pharisee and Sadducee. He argues that the appointment of non-traditional high priests by Herod and Archelaus, and the subsequent Roman takeover, fulfilled the biblical prophecy that no ruler from the line of David would remain until the arrival of Christ. The text concludes by linking the 'seven times' in the Book of Daniel to the era of Christ's birth and the fulfillment of the prophetic timeline.

Eusebius addresses the discrepancy between the genealogies of Matthew and Luke, citing a letter from a man named Aphrianus (referred to as 'the African' in the text) to Aristeides. He argues that both accounts are true but differ in focus: Matthew follows the lineage of the physical seed (nature), while Luke follows the legal lineage (law). The text provides a detailed genealogical reconciliation involving the figures of Mattan, Melchi, and the brothers Jacob and Eli, and concludes with a historical anecdote regarding Herod, the city of Ascalon, and the ransoming of Hyrcanus.

Eusebius discusses the genealogy of Joseph and Mary, citing a specific tradition regarding their shared lineage and the legal requirements of the Law of Moses. He recounts the narrative of the Magi and the birth of Christ in Bethlehem, contrasting the actions of Herod with the fulfillment of prophecy. The text concludes with a detailed, medicalized description of the physical ailments and eventual death of Herod, referencing the 'Jewish Antiquities' of Josephus.

Eusebius recounts the final moments of Herod the Great, including his interactions with his sister Salome and his final actions involving a third son and a piece of fruit. The text then transitions to a chronological defense of the timeline of Jesus' ministry, comparing the dates of the high priesthoods of Annas and Caiaphas with the reigns of Tiberius and Pontius Pilate. It concludes by calculating the duration of Christ's teaching based on the successive terms of high priests.

Eusebius discusses the roles of the twelve apostles and the seventy disciples, mentioning specific names such as Barnabas, Sosthenes, Matthias, and Thaddaeus. He incorporates testimony from Josephus regarding the life and martyrdom of John the Baptist and the actions of Herod. The text also references the appearances of Christ to Cephas (Peter), the twelve, and five hundred brothers, while citing the writings of Clement.

Eusebius recounts the story of Abgar, a ruler of a people beyond the Euphrates, who suffered from a severe physical ailment and sought healing from Jesus. He describes the exchange of letters between Abgar and Jesus, and the subsequent arrival of the apostle Thaddaeus (also called Thomas) to perform miracles and heal the ruler. The text includes a transcription of the letters in the Syriac tongue and describes a vision experienced by Abgar during the apostle's visit.

The text records a dialogue between the man Abgar and the apostle Thaddaeus, during which Thaddaeus heals Abgar and a man named Abaddus (son of Abaddus) and promises to preach the gospel to Abgar's people. Following this, the narrative transitions into a theological and historical commentary on the selection of the apostles, the martyrdom of Stephen, and the distinction between two men named James. The passage concludes with a mention of a covenant with the king of the Hosrians and the mission of Thomas, the son of Thaddaeus.

Eusebius recounts the mission of the disciples, specifically highlighting the ministry of Stephen, the preaching of Philip in Samaria, and the conversion of an Ethiopian eunuch. He transitions to a defense of the doctrine of the incarnation and the divinity of Christ, citing the writings of Tertullian to argue against the Roman legal view that a god could not be manifested in human form. The text concludes by addressing the legal risks faced by Christians under the Roman Senate and the Emperor Tiberius.

Eusebius describes the spread of the Gospel across the world through the preaching of apostles and the conversion of the Gentiles, specifically mentioning Cornelius in Caesarea and the growth of the church in Antioch. He then transitions to a historical account of the Jewish people under the reigns of Tiberius and Gaius (Caesar Augustus), citing the works of Josephus and the writings of Philon of Alexandria. The text details the persecution of Jews who opposed Christ and the specific actions of Pilate and Gaius in the region of Judea.

Eusebius recounts the history of the Jewish people under the leadership of Caius (Galba) and the subsequent persecutions under Tiberius Pilate, who is described as a self-executing instrument of divine judgment. The text details the desecration of the Temple, the siege of Jerusalem, and the execution of James the brother of John by Herod. It also describes the miraculous escape of Peter from prison and the subsequent appearance of a divine messenger in Caesarea.

Eusebius cites Josephus to describe a ruler (likely a local king or tetrarch) who performed a public spectacle in a city called Caesarea and was subsequently confronted by an angel who declared him doomed. The text then transitions to a passage from the Acts of the Apostles concerning the rebel Theudas, who led a multitude to the Jordan, and a famine in Judea where Queen Helen distributed grain from Egypt. Finally, the author mentions the apostle Justin and the activities of Simon, who is accused of practicing divination and spreading error.

Eusebius quotes a letter addressed to Antony regarding the heretic Simon the Sorcerer and his associate Helen. The text details Simon's activities in Rome, his use of magic, and the subsequent confrontation with the Apostle Peter. It also mentions the role of Irenaeus in documenting the heresy and the role of Mark in recording the Gospel.

Eusebius describes Mark as the first to preach the gospel in Egypt and establish a church in Alexandria. He recounts a tradition of Mark traveling to Rome to meet Peter and discusses the writings of Philo, who is depicted as a scholar of the scriptures and the lives of the apostles. The text details the ascetic practices of the early Christians, including their communal living, the distribution of property, and their use of allegorical interpretations of scripture.

Eusebius quotes and analyzes the writings of Philon of Alexandria, specifically regarding his interpretations of scripture and his views on ascetic practices like fasting and the distinction between physical and spiritual nourishment. The text details Philon's extensive works on various subjects including the Ten Commandments, the Tabernacle, the nature of dreams, and the distinction between the first and second covenants. Eusebius notes that Philon's work is characterized by a sophisticated, allegorical approach to the sacred texts.

Eusebius cites and compares the accounts of Josephus regarding the unrest in Jerusalem, specifically the slaughter of three thousand Jews at the Temple during Passover and the rebellion of the Egyptian false prophet. He notes the similarities between Josephus's records and the Acts of the Apostles, specifically regarding the actions of Paul, the Roman officials Felix and Festus, and the presence of figures like Aquila, Priscilla, and Aristarchus.

Eusebius discusses the writings of Paul, specifically the second epistle to Timothy, and the role of Luke in recording Paul's journey to Rome. He recounts the martyrdom of James, the brother of the Lord, and provides a detailed description of his life and character based on the writings of Hegesippus. The text concludes with a narrative of the scribes and Pharisees confronting James at the temple and the gathering of tribes for the Passover.

The text recounts the martyrdom of James, the brother of Jesus, who was stoned and struck by a priest named Ananus (referred to as Hannibal in the translation) near the temple. It includes a narrative of the Jewish leaders' conspiracy against him, the subsequent siege of Jerusalem, and the appointment of a high priest named Jesus, son of Damnaeus. The final section transitions to a critique of Nero's actions and the persecution of Christians, citing Tertullian and the historian Josephus.

Eusebius provides evidence of the martyrdom of Peter and Paul in Rome, citing a letter from Bishop Dionysius of Corinth and a report from Bishop Caius regarding the location of their 'trophies' (relics). He quotes the historian Josephus regarding the Jewish War and the destruction of Jerusalem under Nero. The text concludes by cataloging the status of various apostolic writings, specifically identifying one authentic epistle of Peter and fourteen of Paul, while noting the controversial status of the Epistle to the Hebrews and the Shepherd of Hermas.

Eusebius details the missionary activities of Paul and Peter, specifically noting Paul's work among the Gentiles up to Illyricum and Peter's ministry to the circumcised in regions including Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia. He identifies specific figures such as Timothy in Ephesus, Titus in Crete, Crispus in Gaul, Linus in Rome, and Dionysius in Athens. The text concludes by describing the Jewish persecutions under the Roman Empire, the evacuation of Christians to Pella, and the hardships of the Jewish people during the siege of Jerusalem.

Eusebius recounts a tragic account of a siege and famine, likely referencing a narrative from Josephus. The text describes the desperate actions of the besieged, including the consumption of infants and the elderly, and the subsequent desecration of bodies by those who entered the city. The passage concludes with the Roman commander Titus witnessing the carnage and a man expressing his inability to speak before the magnitude of the suffering.

Eusebius describes the extreme conditions of the siege of Jerusalem, detailing the horrors of famine, the looting of homes, and the desperate acts of a woman named Mary from the village of Beth-zur who, driven by hunger, killed and partially consumed her own child. The text concludes with a statistical summary of the casualties, including those killed by famine and sword, those executed as rebels, and those sent to Egypt or the provinces as captives.

Eusebius recounts the fulfillment of Christ's prophecies regarding the siege and destruction of Jerusalem during the reign of Vespasian. He cites specific scriptural warnings concerning the city's desolation and the capture of the Jewish people. The text concludes with a narrative of a man named Jesus, son of Anania, who performed prophetic acts and was subsequently scourged by Roman authorities.

Eusebius discusses the writings of Josephus, a priest from Jerusalem who fought against the Romans and was later honored in Rome. He details the structure of Josephus's works, including twenty books on Jewish history and seven on the Jewish wars, and mentions his defense against Appion the grammarian. The text also mentions the writings of Justus of Tiberias and the actions of King Agrippa and Titus regarding the publication of these records.

Eusebius recounts the gathering of apostles and disciples following the fall of Jerusalem and the subsequent Roman persecution under Domitian. He details the succession of bishops in Rome and Alexandria, specifically naming Linus, Anicetus, Clement, and Abilius. The text also includes a passage from Hegesippus regarding the interrogation of two men of the royal lineage of David by the Emperor, who were questioned on their wealth and their beliefs regarding the second coming of Christ.

Eusebius recounts the history of the early Church, specifically the transition of leadership and the fate of figures like Domitian and the apostle John. He cites Hegesippus and Tertullian regarding the persecution under Domitian and the subsequent restoration of property under Nero. The text details the leadership of figures such as Linus, Anicetus, Euodius, and Ignatius in Asia, and concludes with a narrative regarding the transmission of a commission from John to a successor in Ephesus.

Eusebius recounts a narrative of a man's conversion and subsequent imprisonment, where he is confronted by a man identified as John (John the Baptist) who offers him spiritual comfort and a promise of life. The text then transitions into a theological and historical defense of the Gospels, specifically distinguishing the roles and contents of the writings of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. It concludes by comparing the introductory accounts of the first three evangelists regarding the imprisonment of John and the ministry of Jesus.

Eusebius evaluates the canonical status of the Gospels and Epistles, distinguishing between the writings of John, Matthew, Luke, and Mark. He addresses disputed texts such as the Apocalypse of Peter, the Letter of Barnabas, and the Didachai, while warning against works that deviate from orthodox tradition. The passage concludes with a critique of Simon the Sorcerer, who is described as a Samaritan who used magic and baptism to teach false doctrines regarding immortality.

Eusebius recounts the history of several heretical groups, beginning with the sorcery of Manander at Antioch and the subsequent rise of the Ebionites who practiced a law-based faith. He details the teachings of Cerinthus, who promoted an earthly kingdom and was later identified by Irenaeus as a fraud. The passage concludes with the brief emergence of the Nicolaitans, associated with Nicolaus and the practice of sexual immorality.

Eusebius provides biographical details and locations of martyrdom for the apostles, specifically mentioning Peter, Philip, and John. He cites various sources, including a letter from Victor of Rome to Polycrates, and records the status of Philip's daughters. The text also recounts the trial and martyrdom of Simon the son of Clopas under Trajan, and mentions the survival of a group of brothers of the Savior named Judas.

Eusebius recounts the history of the early Church and the transition from the era of the apostles to the rise of heretical teachings. He cites a report regarding the persecution of Christians under Trajan and the specific actions of Pliny the Younger. The text concludes with a list of early bishops, including Clement of Rome, Polycarp of Smyrna, and Ignatius of Antioch, and mentions their correspondence and travels.

Eusebius records a series of quotations from the letters of Ignatius of Antioch and Clement of Rome, specifically mentioning his correspondence with the churches at Smyrna and Philadelphia. He identifies Polycarp as the leader of the Smyrnaean church and notes his role in the Antiochian flock. The text also mentions the successor of Ignatius, Heros, and the prophet Codratus, while concluding with a discussion on the authorship and translation of Clement's letter to the Hebrews.

Eusebius evaluates the writings of Papias, noting his role as a student of the elder John and Aristion rather than an apostle. He discusses the distinction between the two 'Johns' (the Evangelist and the Elder) and details the specific roles of Mark as an interpreter of Peter and Matthew as a writer in a Hebrew dialect. The text also mentions the accounts of the apostles Philip and Matthias, and the selection of Matthias to replace Judas.

Eusebius records the succession of bishops in Rome and Alexandria, specifically naming Amphius, Xystus, Telesphorus, and Eumenes. He details a Jewish rebellion in Egypt and Cyrene during the reign of Trajan, involving the commander Lucius and the intervention of Marcius Turbo. The text also lists fifteen successive Jewish bishops in Jerusalem from the apostolic age until the siege under Hadrian, and mentions the writings of Codratus and the defense of Aristides.

Eusebius describes the Jewish rebellion against the Roman Empire, specifically the siege of the city of Bithyra (near Jerusalem) in the 18th year of Hadrian's reign, and the subsequent renaming of the site to Ramah. The text then transitions to a polemic against heretical movements, specifically naming the leaders of the sects of Simon, Saturninus, and Basilides. It concludes with a critique of the practices of Carpocrates and the 'mysteries' of the Gnostics.

Eusebius presents a defense of the Christian faith against accusations of deviance, contrasting the enduring 'truth' of the church with the fleeting innovations of its enemies. He cites the writings of Agesippus and Justin Martyr to provide historical context, specifically mentioning the persecution under Emperor Hadrian and the execution of Antinous. The text includes a Latin translation of a letter from Serennius to Minucius Fundanus, which argues that Christians should only be punished if they are caught in a clear, punishable crime.

Eusebius records the succession of Roman bishops, specifically naming Hyginus, Pius, and Anicetus, while identifying heretical figures such as Valentinus and Cerdon. He cites Irenaeus's descriptions of their doctrines and mentions the philosopher Justin Martyr's defense of the faith before Emperor Antoninus. The text concludes with a series of formal titles and addresses regarding the imperial administration and the status of Christians in the eyes of the law.

Eusebius records the testimony of Melitus of Sardis regarding the persecution of Christians and the defense of the faith before Emperor Verus. The text provides a detailed account of the life and martyrdom of Polycarp of Smyrna, including his interactions with Marcion and Cerinthus. It concludes with a description of Polycarp's physical suffering during his execution and his final letters to the churches in Smyrna and Philomelus.

Eusebius recounts the trial and martyrdom of Polycarp, a Christian elder who remained steadfast before his accusers and the Roman authorities. The text details his interactions with a Phrygian named Cato (or Koiton), his refusal to renounce Christ despite the threat of execution, and his final words in the stadium. The narrative includes a divine voice from heaven and Polycarp's declaration of his 86-year service to Christ.

Eusebius recounts the martyrdom of Polycarp, the bishop of Smyrna, who is interrogated by an accuser and subsequently condemned by a crowd of Jews and Gentiles. The text describes Polycarp's prayer before being burned at the stake, the miraculous preservation of his body from the flames, and the subsequent attempt by the accuser to seize his body for worship. The passage also mentions the involvement of a local official named Philip and a man named Nicias.

Eusebius recounts the martyrdom of Polycarp at Smyrna alongside twelve others from Philadelphia, and mentions the martyrdom of Metrodorus. The text lists other martyrs in Pergamum, including Carpus, Papylus, and Agathonic, before transitioning to a defense of Justin Martyr. Justin's writings are cited regarding his interactions with the philosopher Criscus and the subsequent condemnation of Tatian.

Eusebius recounts the conversion and legal trials of a man and his wife, who were persecuted for the crime of being Christians. The text details the man's interactions with a centurion and a judge named Urbicus, who is challenged by a Christian named Lucius regarding the legality of punishing a man for mere confession of faith. The passage concludes with a list of works by Justin Martyr, including his addresses to the Romans, the Greeks, and Tryphon of Ephesus.

Eusebius recounts the defense of the Church against Tryphon, specifically regarding the status of the apostles and the integrity of the scriptures. He lists several early Christian leaders and bishops, including Irenaeus, Hegesippus, and the successor of the See of Rome, Soter. The text also lists various Jewish sects and heretical groups such as the Marcionites and Valentinians, while noting the use of Solomon's proverbs and the distinction between Hebrew and Syrian traditions.

Eusebius details the activities and correspondence of Dionysius of the Areopagus, including his letters to the Lacedaemonians, Athenians, Nicomedes, and the communities of Gortyna, Amastris, and Pinytus. He records Dionysius's opposition to Marcion and his instructions regarding marriage and chastity. The text concludes with a brief mention of Theophilus of Antioch and his defense against Marcionite teachings, followed by the introduction of Maximinus.

Eusebius identifies several bishops, including Philip of Gortyne, Irenaeus, Modestus, Meliton of Sardis, and Apollinarius of Hierapolis, who defended the faith against Marcionism. The text lists specific theological treatises and a letter from Meliton to Onesimus that catalogs the books of the Old Testament. It also includes a formal petition to the Emperor Antoninus, referencing the patronage of previous emperors like Hadrian and the governor Pundanus.

Eusebius lists and describes the works of several figures associated with various heresies, including Meliton, Apollinarius, and the heretic Tatian, who is noted for his 'Eloquence to the Greeks.' He cites Irenaeus's account of the 'Egretae' (followers of Saturninus and Marcion) and mentions the Syrian scholar Bardesanes and his dialogues against Marcion. The passage concludes by transitioning from the history of these figures to the narrative of martyrs, specifically mentioning the bishop Sotir of Rome and his successor Eleutherus during the persecution of Antoninus.

Eusebius provides a narrative of Christian martyrs in the regions of Asia and Phrygia, specifically mentioning the cities of Lugodunus and Vienna in the land of Gaul (identified by the author as Galilee). The text recounts the trial of these believers before a governor, highlighting the defense of a young man named Vettus Epagatus and the subsequent martyrdom of several others. It also mentions a gathering of local people who, fearing the punishments witnessed by the saints, were influenced by Satan.

Eusebius recounts the martyrdom of several Christians, specifically naming the servant from Vienne, the warrior Maturos, the man from Pergamus named Attalus, and the woman Blandina. The text describes their endurance of physical tortures, their refusal to yield their names or origins to the Romans, and the specific actions of the executioners who eventually used fire and heavy weights. It concludes with the deaths of several young men in custody and the spiritual triumph of the martyrs over their physical suffering.

Eusebius recounts the martyrdom of Pothenos, a bishop of Lundus who, despite advanced age and physical frailty, endured severe beatings and spears from the crowd and authorities. The text then describes the trials of other martyrs, including the names Maturos, Saktos, Blandina, and Attalus, who faced beasts and physical punishment in a public arena. The narrative emphasizes the spiritual triumph and 'crown of immortality' won by these individuals through their endurance of physical suffering.

Eusebius recounts the martyrdom of Christians in a theater, specifically naming the martyr Attalus and the physician Alexander (a Phrygian). The text describes the execution of these individuals and others, including a woman named Blundina and a young Pontic boy, under the judgment of a Roman governor. The narrative details their final words, their endurance of various tortures (beasts, scourges, and a pit), and the subsequent reaction of the surrounding crowd.

Eusebius describes the treatment of the bodies of Christian martyrs, which were left in the camp, mutilated, and eventually cast into the river Jordan. He recounts the mockery of the persecutors who mocked the martyrs' lack of divine intervention and the subsequent inclusion of a letter (Nic. IV, 18) detailing the martyrs' courage, their imitation of Christ, and their peaceful conduct before death. The passage concludes with a reflection on the spiritual rewards of the martyrs and the distinction between their peaceful departure and the lack of mercy shown by their persecutors.

Eusebius recounts the conversion of the apostate Alcibiades and the subsequent condemnation of the heretic Atalus. The text transitions into a defense of the faith involving Irenaeus of Lugdunum, the martyrdom of Christians in Phrygia and Gaul, and a miraculous account of a Roman army saved from thirst in Germany. It concludes with a list of Roman bishops, specifically mentioning Linus and Polycarp.

Eusebius lists the early bishops of Rome, including Clement, Evaristus, Alexander, Xystus, Theophilus, Hyginus, Pius, Aniketus, and Eleutherus. He quotes Irenaeus to discuss the nature of spiritual gifts, the resurrection of the dead, and the authenticity of the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. The text concludes with a discussion on the Revelation of John, the reign of Domitian, and the distinction between divine truth and corruption.

Eusebius recounts the history of biblical translation and interpretation, specifically the work of Ptolemy of Alexandria in translating the scriptures into Greek with the assistance of seventy Jewish elders. He mentions the influence of Marcion, Justin Martyr, and Ignatius, and critiques certain interpretations of the scriptures regarding the virgin birth. The text concludes with a list of early Christian figures and teachers, including Pantheus, Clemes, and the mention of the prophet Ezra.

Eusebius records the lineage of bishops in Jerusalem, identifying Narcissus as the fifteenth successor since the siege of Hadrian and listing his predecessors including Cassius, Publius, and others. The text then details various heretical movements, specifically focusing on the writings of Tatian and the figure of Rhodes, as well as the activities of Montanus, his wives Priscilla and Maximilla, and the leaders Florinus and Blastus in Rome. The passage concludes with a report on Apollinarius of Hierapolis and a letter regarding the sect of the Miltiades.

Eusebius describes a conflict in the church at Pontus involving a man named Montanus and a woman named Maximilla, whom he identifies as false prophets. He recounts their activities in a village in Mysia called Ardabaeus and details the subsequent condemnation and expulsion of their followers from the assembly. The text also mentions a man named Theodotus and a specific instance where the spirit of Maximilla was tested by bishops Zotikos of Komana and Julian of Apamea.

Eusebius critiques the 'Phrygian' heresy (Montanism) by citing the works of Miltiades and Apollonius. He refutes the claims of Montanist 'prophets' such as Themison and the prophetess Priscus, accusing them of greed, fraudulent offerings, and leading the faithful into luxury. The text also mentions the figures of Caius, Alexander, and the locations of Apameia and the cities of Pepus and Tymium.

Eusebius examines the criteria for identifying true prophets, citing a list of behaviors (such as wealth, involvement in gambling, or lending money) to expose false ones. He cites specific cases involving the 'New Prophecy' heresy, mentioning figures like the prophetess Zoticus, the bishop Maximinus of Antioch, and the letter of Irenaeus to Florinus regarding the doctrines of Polycarp and the apostolic tradition.

Eusebius recounts a personal testimony regarding the teachings of Polycarp in Asia Minor, specifically his proximity to the tradition of the apostles and his interactions with those who knew the Lord. The text transitions to a historical account of the Roman Empire under Commodus, detailing the persecution of Christians, including the trial of Apollonius and the martyrdom of a witness before the judge Perennius. The final section lists specific bishops and locations, such as Victor in Rome, Theophilus in Caesarea, and Irenaeus in Gaul, while addressing the ecclesiastical dispute over the timing of the Eucharist and the observance of the Passover.

Eusebius records a dispute regarding the observance of the date and duration of the fast preceding the Pascha. He cites a letter from Polycrates of Asia, which lists several martyrs and elders—including Polycarp of Smyrna, John, and Meliton—who observed the fourteenth day. The text details a reconciliation between the factions of those who observed the traditional fast and those who did not, mediated by the efforts of Victor and Irenaeus.

Eusebius recounts the correspondence between the bishops of Palestine (Narcissus, Theophilus, Cassius, and Clarus) and those in Alexandria regarding the Paschal tradition. He lists several theological works and authors, including Irenaeus, Meliton, and the writings of Marcion, while refuting the claims of those who supported the heretic Victor. The text concludes with a report on the deception of a man named Natalias by the followers of Theodorus the Scythian, who were subsequently condemned by Bishop Victor.

Eusebius describes the martyrdom of Christians under the persecutions of Seberus, specifically highlighting the execution of Leonidas (father of Origenes) in Egypt. The text transitions into a defense of the scriptures against heretical interpretations, citing specific works by authors like Hermophilus and Apollonius. It concludes with a biographical sketch of the young Origenes, noting his early endurance during the persecutions in Alexandria.

Eusebius recounts the early life and education of Origen, detailing his devotion to scripture and his father's role in his upbringing. The text mentions his interactions with others in Alexandria, including Plutarch and his brother Heracles, and describes his role in ministering to both Christians and Gentiles during periods of persecution. It concludes by noting his bold defense of the faith and the divine grace that protected him.

Eusebius describes the intense persecution of a Christian leader (implied to be a local figure) who was sought by the authorities due to the large number of followers attending his teachings. The text details the ascetic lifestyle of this leader, his devotion to scripture, and the subsequent martyrdom of several followers: Plutarch, Serenus, Hercules, Heron, and a second Serenus. It concludes with the account of Basileides and the woman Potamiane, who was condemned by a judge named Akylas and executed by soldiers.

Eusebius records the martyrdom of a man named Basil, who was forced to confess his faith as a Christian and was subsequently beheaded. The text then transitions to the activities of Origen in Alexandria, including his interactions with Demetrius and the mention of his scholarly works and the tenure of Emperor Severus. The final section recounts a miracle involving Narcissus, who transformed water into oil during a Passover vigil.

Eusebius recounts the persecution of the bishop Narcissus by three accusers who were punished by fire, disease, and blindness. The text then details the succession of bishops in the region, naming Zeus, Gordius, and Alexander, and includes a letter from Alexander to the Antiochian church regarding the appointment of Asclepiades. The final section mentions the fall of Domninius to Jewish practices and the production of a discourse by Sarrapion regarding the Gospel of Peter.

Eusebius discusses the writings of Clement of Alexandria, specifically the 'Stromateis' and 'Hypotyposes', and the works of Panthenus. He identifies specific texts such as the 'Sermon to the Greeks', 'The One who is Saved is Rich', and a discourse on the Passover. The text also mentions the authorship of the Epistle to the Hebrews, the role of Mark in recording Peter's preaching in Rome, and the distinction between the 'gospel of the body' and the 'gospel of the Spirit'.

Eusebius recounts the scholarly activities of Origen, who organized students into two groups to study sacred scriptures and mastered the Hebrew language to study original texts and translations by Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotus. He describes Origen's extensive engagement with Greek philosophy, geometry, and mathematics, and his reputation among Greek philosophers. The passage concludes by mentioning Porphyrius in Sicily, who is accused of using Origen's interpretations to attempt to undermine Christian doctrine.

Eusebius presents a defense of Origen against accusations of heresy and hypocrisy, contrasting his scholarly life with that of the philosopher Ammonius. The text details Origen's travels between Alexandria and Arabia, his interactions with figures like Pantheus and Heracles, and his defense against the writings of Porphyry. It concludes by listing specific instances of bishops and their associates preaching to the people in locations such as Lardus, Iconium, and Synnades.

Eusebius records the activities of several early Christian figures, including the youth Demetrius, the bishop Beryllus of Bostra, and the scholar Hippolytus, who authored works on the Passover and various other theological themes. The text details the scholarly activities of Origen under the patronage of Ambrosius, and mentions the leadership of several bishops in Rome and Antioch. It concludes with a technical note on the preservation of specific volumes of the Gospels and the Psalms.

Eusebius quotes a text (likely a defense or scholarly commentary) that lists the twenty-two books of the Old Testament and distinguishes the four Gospels and various apostolic epistles. The text addresses the authorship of the Epistle to the Hebrews and the role of the author as a transmitter of the teacher's words. The narrative then shifts to the late 3rd century, detailing the movements of Origen from Alexandria to Caesarea, the tenure of Bishop Demetrius of Alexandria, and the persecution of Christians under the Emperor Maximinus.

Eusebius records the succession of bishops in Rome (Antrius, Fabius) and Alexandria (Heracles, Dionysius) during the reign of Gordian. He details the scholarly activities of Origen and his students, including Theodorus, Athenodorus, and the writings of Africanus regarding the genealogies of Matthew and Luke. The passage concludes with a condemnation of the heretic Beryllus of Bostros and a mention of the records preserved by Pamphilus.

Eusebius records the transition of Roman power from Gordian to Philip and the subsequent appointment of Dionysius as bishop of Alexandria. The text details the activities of Origen, including his collection of writings, his defense against accusations of heresy (specifically the 'Elkesaites'), and his interactions with figures like the Emperor Philip and the bishop Fabius. The passage concludes with a detailed account of the persecutions suffered by Origen and the defense of Dionysius in a letter to Germaus.

Dionysius recounts his escape from a group of robbers who, after being alerted by a local, captured him and his companions. The text details the specific identities of his companions—Caius, Phaestus, Peter, and Paul—and describes their subsequent imprisonment and treatment. The narrative shifts to a report by Antiochus regarding the persecution in Alexandria, detailing the violent execution of a woman named Mithras and a martyr named Koitane, as well as the destruction of local shrines.

Eusebius describes the persecution of Christians in a city, detailing the varied reactions of the faithful to the threat of execution and the temptation of pagan sacrifices. He names specific martyrs including Julian (a man with a physical disability), the soldier Vesa, the Libyan Macar, the elderly woman Mercurius, and the youth Dioskoros. The text also recounts the experiences of the Egyptian Nemesion and a group of soldiers—Ammon, Zeno, Ptolemy, Ingenes, and Theophilus—who stood firm before the tribunal.

Eusebius recounts the plight of Christians in the desert and mountains, specifically those captured by the Saracens and the case of Cheremon, a bishop of a city near the Nile who disappeared in the Arabian mountains. The text describes a council in Rome involving sixty bishops and many elders to decide how to treat these 'fallen' brothers who had repented. It details a conflict involving a man named Noah (a presbyter) and a deceptive bishop who attempted to seize authority through fraud and violence before eventually repenting.

Eusebius recounts a dispute involving a man (implied to be a cleric) who was accused of cowardice and worldly ambition for refusing to serve as an elder during a time of persecution. The text includes a list of church officials and a report from a letter from Dionysius of Alexandria to Cornelius Fabius of Antioch. The narrative concludes with a personal anecdote regarding the final moments of a faithful elder named Serapion.

Dionysius of Alexandria provides a series of letters and testimonies regarding the aftermath of the Novatianist schism. He addresses Novatus and other leaders (such as those in Egypt, Armenia, and Rome) regarding repentance, the reconciliation of the 'fallen' members, and the specific issue of whether those returning from heresy should be purified by bathing. The text also includes a brief historical note on the Roman Emperor Gallus and a dispute with Stephanas regarding the practice of baptism.

Eusebius quotes a letter from Dionysius of Alexandria to Philemon in Rome regarding the status of heretics and the practice of baptism. The text names several bishops, including Demetrius of Antioch, Theoctistus of Caesarea, and Marinus of Tyre, and discusses the handling of those who had been 'purged' from the church. It also addresses the specific heresy of Sabellius and the actions of a bishop named Stephanas.

Eusebius recounts a letter from a man (implied to be a former Christian) to Bishop Xystus of Rome, in which the man confesses his fall into heresy and his subsequent repentance after being confronted by Xystus. The text then transitions to a letter from Dionysius of Cerinthus regarding the Emperor Valerian, who is described as having been misled by a sorcerer from Egypt into practicing magic and pagan rituals. The passage concludes with a theological reflection on Valerian's actions as a violation of divine law regarding the transmission of sin to offspring.

The text records a dialogue between the author (likely a Christian leader) and Aemilianus regarding the persecution of Christians and the distinction between worshipping the one God versus local deities. It details a meeting involving several individuals, including Dionysius, Faustus, Maximus, Marcellus, and Chaeremon, and describes a relocation to a place called Cephro in Libya. The passage concludes with the author's personal account of traveling to Cephro and his subsequent legal predicament.

Eusebius records a letter from a Christian leader (likely Dionysius) regarding the persecution of believers in Egypt and Syria. The text names several figures including the martyrs Priscus, Malchus, and Alexander in Caesarea, and mentions the leaders Faustinus, Aquila, and the bishop Eusebius. It concludes with a reference to the reign of Gallienus and a decree regarding the distribution of a written text to avoid harassment by authorities.

Eusebius records the leadership of various bishops in the East, including Xystus in Rome, Demetrianus in Antioch, and several others in the regions of Pontus and Palestine. He recounts the martyrdom of Marinus at Caesarea, who was executed for his faith, and the martyrdom of Astyrius at the site of a miraculous spring at the Caesarea of Philip. The text concludes with a description of bronze statues of a woman and a man (representing Christ) located near a site associated with the woman with the issue of blood.

Eusebius recounts the leadership of James, the first bishop of the Jerusalem church, and the subsequent correspondence of Dionysius of Alexandria regarding the Passover and the management of the church during persecution. The text includes a lengthy, poetic lament by Hierachius, bishop of Egypt, who describes a devastating plague in Alexandria and reflects on the suffering of martyrs. The passage concludes with a comparison between the current suffering of the Christians and the biblical plagues of the Egyptians.

Eusebius recounts the experiences of Christians during a plague, contrasting their care for the sick with the abandonment of the sick by the Gentiles. He mentions a letter regarding a feast and the subsequent correspondence with Hermogenes and the brethren in Egypt concerning the aftermath of the persecution under Decius and the peace in Galilee. The text concludes with a scholarly defense of the writings of Nepotus regarding the Revelation of John and the promises of the scriptures.

Eusebius presents a defense of the authorship of the Book of Revelation, addressing a specific controversy involving a leader named Coracian and a sect associated with Cerinthus. He argues that while the author is a holy, inspired man, he distinguishes between the 'John' who wrote the Apocalypse and the Apostle John, son of Zebedee. The text details a communal examination of the scripture where the author's identity is weighed against the possibility of it being a forgery or a work by the Cerinthians.

Eusebius analyzes the authorship and literary characteristics of the Book of Revelation, distinguishing it from the Gospel and the Pauline epistles. He identifies several men named John, including the Apostle John and a 'John' mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles, while noting the unique style and 'barbarian' elements of the Revelation's Greek. The passage concludes by listing several letters written by Dionysius to various recipients such as Sabellius, Ammon, and Telesphorus.

Eusebius describes the writings of Dionysius of Alexandria and the subsequent leadership of Paul of Samos at Antioch. The text details a synod of bishops, including Phirmilianus of Cappadocia, Helen of Tarsus, and others, who gathered to address the heresy of Paul. It concludes with the formal condemnation of Paul's teachings and the subsequent actions of Phirmilianus in confronting him.

Eusebius recounts the condemnation of the heretic Phimilianus, who traveled toward Antioch and was accused of luxury, pride, and consorting with women. The text details his specific transgressions, including the use of a high throne and the performance of 'theatrical' acts during the Passover. Following his removal, Domnus is appointed as the bishop of Antioch to succeed him.

Eusebius describes the actions of Emperor Aurelian and the subsequent successions of Probus, Carus, and Diocletian, while noting the leadership of bishops like Dionysius and Felix in Rome. The text transitions to a condemnation of Manichaeism, describing it as a demonic, Persian-influenced heresy. It concludes with a detailed account of the siege of Alexandria, highlighting the virtues of the scholar Anatolius and the actions of Eusebius during the Roman alliance.

Eusebius describes a military siege where a leader persuades the council to evacuate the non-combatants and those in 'women's clothing' to safety, while a physician named Eusebius cares for the survivors. The text then transitions into a scholarly commentary on the Jewish feast of Passover, citing the works of Philon, Josephus, and Aristobulus to discuss astronomical calculations regarding the equinox and the moon. It concludes by mentioning the appointment of Theothenes as bishop of Caesarea and the presence of Eusebius among the Laodiceans.

Eusebius records the succession of bishops in Palestine and Alexandria, specifically naming the figures of Anatolius, Stephanus, Theodorus, Agapius, Pamphilus, Pierius, Meletius, Maximin, Theon, Peter, Hymenaeus, and Hermogenes. The text details their roles, the length of their tenures, and their personal virtues, such as the medical and spiritual service of Theodorus and the scholarly reputation of Meletius. The passage concludes with a transition to a new section regarding the proclamation of the Gospel among Greeks and barbarians before the persecution.

Eusebius describes the internal divisions and conflicts within the Christian community during the period of persecution, contrasting the 'softness' of the believers with the 'fierce' judgments of God. He recounts the destruction of churches and sacred texts, and the subsequent persecution of clergy and laypeople under the reign of Diocletian. The text concludes by categorizing the responses of Christians to these trials, ranging from heroic endurance to cowardice and the use of deception to avoid sacrifice.

Eusebius describes the martyrdom of the royal sons of Dorotheus, specifically one named Peter, who was subjected to scourging, salt-rubbing, and fire. The text also mentions the persecution of Christians in the military camps and the actions of a high-ranking official in Nicomedia. The narrative concludes by mentioning the martyrdoms of Dorotheus and Gorgonius.

Eusebius describes the martyrdom of Antymon and a multitude of others in Nicomedia, where some were beheaded and others burned. The text details the persecution in Melitene and Syria, and recounts the specific trials of Christians in Tyre, Phoenicia, and Egypt. It describes the physical sufferings of these martyrs, including scourging, being cast into the sea, and enduring wild beasts.

Eusebius describes the various forms of physical torture endured by Christian martyrs, including being bound to trees, scourged with whips and rods, and being stretched on frames. He highlights the contrast between the 'fearless' and 'joyful' endurance of those of high social standing, such as the philosopher Philo-romus of Alexandria and the bishop Philo of Thmythoi, who prioritized their faith over physical safety. The text concludes by noting that these accounts serve as evidence of the martyrs' devotion to Christ and the divine scriptures.

Eusebius describes the martyrdom of Christians in Phrygia, including a man named Adaustus, and recounts the varied methods of execution in Arabia, Cappadocia, and Alexandria. He specifically details the martyrdom of a virtuous woman from Antioch who, along with her daughters, chose suicide over the threat of prostitution or the enslavement of their souls. The passage concludes with the women reaching a river while attempting to flee their captors.

Eusebius describes the martyrdom of a noble virgin in Antioch and various others subjected to brutal tortures, including mutilation and execution by fire. He lists specific martyrs and their titles across several regions, including Antioch, Phoenicia, Palestine, and Egypt, naming individuals such as Anthimus, Lucian, Zenobius, Sylvanus, and Peter of Alexandria. The passage concludes with a transition toward recounting the history of the Christian persecution under Roman rule.

Eusebius describes the transition of power from the peaceful and pious Emperor Constantius to his son Constantine, contrasting their virtuous reigns with the tyranny of Maximinus and the rule of Licinius. The text details the atrocities of the tyrant in Rome, including the persecution of Christians, the practice of sorcery, and the exploitation of the populace. It also mentions the eastern tyrant Maximinus and his involvement in pagan rituals and magic.

Eusebius describes the intensified persecution under Maximinus and Maxentius, detailing the seizure of property, the appointment of high priests in provinces, and the use of severe punishments like fire and wild beasts. He highlights the specific cases of a woman in Alexandria and a noblewoman in Rome who remained steadfast in their faith. The passage concludes by noting the end of the persecution after ten years and the subsequent periods of famine and pestilence.

Eusebius describes a period of divine favor and the subsequent leniency of Roman magistrates toward Christians, contrasting their actions with the 'wicked' behavior of those who persecuted them. The text includes a detailed medical description of a severe physical ailment (likely a severe infection or gangrene) and a list of imperial titles for Galerius, Constantine, and Licinius. It concludes with a translation of a Roman decree regarding the legal status and treatment of Christians, followed by a note on a man who found relief from pain after a confession.

Eusebius recounts the history of the persecution of Christians, identifying four distinct periods or types of rulers who persecuted them. He highlights the reign of Constantius, whom he describes as a pious and just ruler who protected the churches and the faithful. The text then transitions to the reign of Maximinus, a tyrant in the East who ignored previous edicts of tolerance and ordered a renewed persecution. A letter from Sabinus is quoted, detailing the imperial decree to release Christians from mines and the subsequent actions of provincial governors.

Eusebius describes the aftermath of a period of persecution where Christians were celebrated in public and the 'true God' was glorified. He identifies a specific 'tyrant' (likely a local ruler in the East) who, despite his malice, eventually issued decrees that eased the persecution and allowed Christians to reside in their own homes. The text mentions the city of Antioch, the commander of a garrison in Damascus (Phoenicia), and the bishop Sylvanus, who was martyred in the city of Hemis.

Eusebius describes the actions of Peter of Alexandria and Lucian of Antioch during the persecution of Maximinus, noting their roles and the preparation of a defense against the emperor. The text includes a lengthy, ornate rhetorical passage—likely a formal decree or proclamation—that uses highly stylized language to contrast the 'piety' of the Christians with the 'folly' of the pagan world. It mentions the city of Antioch, the city of Tyrus, and the names of Jesus and Pilate.

Eusebius describes the suffering of Christians during a period of famine, pestilence, and war against the Armenians. He details the desperate measures taken by the faithful, including the consumption of grass and the abandonment of property, and depicts the horrific scenes of death in public squares and markets. The text also mentions the specific plight of noble women and the eventual death of rulers and magistrates under these conditions.

Eusebius describes the Christian response to a plague and famine, noting their distribution of bread and care for the dying. He then recounts the military victory of Constantine and Licinius over the 'impious' Maxentius at a river crossing, comparing Maxentius's defeat to the drowning of Pharaoh's army in the Red Sea. The text concludes with Constantine's triumphal entry into Rome, where he is welcomed by the youth, women, and the Senate.

Eusebius describes Constantine and Licinius issuing a decree for Christians in Rome, featuring an inscription regarding the 'saving sign' of the cross and the liberation of the city from the 'tyrant.' The text then includes a lengthy, partially corrupted excerpt from a letter attributed to the tyrant Maximinus, which details his interactions with local officials and the management of Christian populations in the East and Nicomedia. The passage concludes by noting that Maximinus, though forced to issue certain concessions, did not permit the Christians to hold public assemblies or build houses of worship.

Eusebius describes the downfall of a tyrant who, despite a treaty with Licinius, abandoned his allies and was defeated by a multitude of soldiers. The text includes a transition to a decree issued in the name of Emperor Galerius (referred to as 'Caesar Gaius' and 'Maximinus' in a corrupted or complex title) regarding the legal status of Christians. This decree, translated from Latin into Greek, aims to provide a formal legal framework for Christian worship and assembly following the period of persecution.

Eusebius describes the execution of a Christian martyr who, despite being mocked as an impious man by the tyrant Maximinus, endured extreme physical torture including fire and wild beasts before dying in a state of confession. The text details the fall of Maximinus and the subsequent disgrace of his associates, specifically naming Peucetius and Coelianus. It concludes with the identification of a sorcerer named Theotes in Antioch, whose 'deceitful' magic was exposed during his interrogation.

Eusebius describes the execution of the sons of Maximinus and his kinsmen, who were condemned for refusing to follow the 'sacred' exhortations of the state. He contrasts their fate with the 'purification' of the Christians under the reigns of Constantius and Licinius, who are depicted as establishing laws and honors for the faithful. The text concludes with a celebratory description of the post-persecution era, featuring the unification of the Church, the distribution of royal honors to bishops, and the fulfillment of prophetic promises of harmony.

The text contains a panegyric attributed to Paul of Tyre regarding the construction of churches. It features a sermon delivered by a bishop in Tyre to a gathering of clergy, utilizing scriptural allusions to Bezaleel, Solomon, and Zerubbabel to praise the spiritual architecture of the Church. The passage concludes with a series of doxologies and a theological defense of Christ as the supreme physician and savior of humanity.

Eusebius offers a high-style theological defense of Christ as the supreme King, Physician, and High Priest who has conquered the powers of darkness and the 'beasts' of paganism. He contrasts the enduring, universal authority of Christ's laws and kingdom with the fleeting, 'barbaric' rituals of the past. The passage concludes by identifying the role of the high priesthood and the lineage of Melchizedek in the governance of the faithful.

Eusebius presents a theological defense of the Church's continuity, comparing the current Christian community to the biblical wilderness and the sanctuary of God. He utilizes a series of scriptural parallels, specifically citing Isaiah, to contrast the 'desolate' state of the persecuted church with the 'blossoming' of the faith through the sacrament of baptism. The text also addresses the fate of those who 'warred against God,' specifically mentioning the destruction of their 'images' and 'names' in the city.

Eusebius describes the architectural expansion and beautification of the Temple, specifically the transition from the older structures to the newer, more magnificent ones. He mentions the figure of Zorobabel (Zebedee/Zebedee-like figure) and the construction of the sanctuary by Solomon, who is described as the most peaceful of our time. The text details the physical layout of the gates, porticoes, and the marble courtyard, concluding that the current glory of the house surpasses the former.

Eusebius describes the spiritual transformation of the Church from a 'widow' and 'desolate' state to a 'bride' adorned with the garments of salvation and the crown of beauty. He incorporates extensive scriptural quotations from Isaiah to illustrate the restoration of the Church's dignity and the removal of its 'shame.' The passage concludes by contrasting the divine nature of the 'heavenly bride' with the spiritual decay caused by the 'envy and jealousy' of demonic forces.

Eusebius describes the spiritual purification of the faithful and the establishment of the Church as a terrestrial image of the heavenly Jerusalem. He uses architectural metaphors to describe the organization of the clergy and the spiritual hierarchy, culminating in a description of the celestial city and the worship of the Trinity. The text includes a quotation of a biblical prophecy regarding the construction of a city of stone and gold.

The passage begins with a liturgical prayer of praise to Christ, followed by a formal citation of a royal decree from the emperors Constantius and Licinius at Mediolanum. The decree addresses the legal status of Christian worship, specifically granting religious freedom and the right to private interpretation. The latter half of the text details legal provisions for the acquisition and restoration of physical meeting places (locations) for Christian assemblies, ensuring these properties are returned to the community without dispute.

Eusebius includes several imperial letters (royal decrees) from Constantine to various bishops, including Anylinus of Africa and Christ of Syracuse. These documents address the resolution of schisms, the coordination of synods in Rome and Arles (Arelates), and the distribution of imperial gifts to the churches. The text mentions specific figures such as Caecilianus of Carthage, Miltiades, Marcus, Rheticus, Maternius, Marinus, and the prefect Latronianus.

Eusebius includes a letter from Constantius to the bishop of Carthage, Caecilianus, regarding the distribution of funds to those serving the church in Africa, Numidia, and Mauritania. The text also contains a royal decree regarding the exemption of certain clergy from civil duties and a narrative concerning the political tensions and conspiracies involving Licinius and the actions of the Emperor Constantius.

Eusebius describes the actions of Licinius, who is depicted as a lawless and impious ruler who persecuted Christians and their leaders. The text details his specific decrees, including the denial of food to prisoners, the forced conversion of soldiers, and the seizure of lands and gold. The passage concludes with the intervention of God and the victory of Constantine over the persecutors.

Eusebius describes the transition from the reign of a 'tyrant' to the reign of Constantine and his son Crispus, characterizing the latter as a friend of God who replaced old cruelties with acts of mercy and piety. The text contrasts the fate of the ungodly Lycinnius, who fell into ruin, with the 'victory' of Constantine, who established a kingdom of laws and festivals. The passage concludes by describing the spiritual and physical renewal of the empire under Constantine's rule.

This Greek work by Eusebius provides a concise account of Christian martyrdom in Palestine during the persecutions of Diocletian and Maximinus. The text is organized chronologically and geographically, detailing the trials and executions of specific individuals in locations such as Caesarea, Gaza, Tyre, and Ascalon. Notable martyrs recorded include Procopio, Alpheus, Zacchaeus, Appianus, and the virgin Theodosia. The narrative documents various forms of execution, including beheading, wild beasts, and fire, while also noting the physical suffering of women and children. The work concludes with a broad geographical survey of Christian persecution across the Roman Empire, including Egypt, Syria, and Gaul, and ends with a theological reflection on the ministry of Paul.

Eusebius records the martyrdom of Christians in Palestine during the reign of Diocletian, beginning with the execution of Procopio, who refused to sacrifice to idols and was beheaded. The text details the trials of Alpheus and Zacchaeus in Caesarea, and the martyrdom of a man named Palaitinos, a former servant of the temple at Caesarea. It concludes with the mention of Timothy in Gaza, who was executed after a royal decree ordered universal sacrifice to idols.

Eusebius recounts the martyrdom of several Christians, including Agapius, Dionysius, and others from regions such as Pontus, Phoenicia, and Gaza, who faced wild beasts. The text transitions to the reign of Maximinus Caesar, characterized by increased persecution, and introduces the martyr Appianus. Appianus, a youth from Lycia who studied in Berytus, is praised for his piety and courage before his execution in the city of Caesar.

Eusebius describes the martyrdom of a Christian in Caesarea during the persecution of Maximinus, detailing his endurance of physical torture, including scourging and the branding of his face and neck. The text recounts a miraculous event where a great earthquake and a sea surge occurred at the moment of his execution, and it concludes by mentioning the martyrdom of Ulpian in Tyre and the brother of Aedes in Alexandria.

Eusebius describes the martyrdom of Agapius, who was condemned to be thrown into the sea after a trial in Caesarea, and the martyrdom of the virgin Theodosia from Tyre. The text also details the sentencing of Domninus to fire and the torture of Urban, who was forced to offer sacrifices. The passage concludes by mentioning the impending divine judgment against the judge and his soldiers who persecuted the martyrs, including Pamphilus.

Eusebius describes the persecution of Christians in Palestine under the emperor Maximinus, detailing the mutilation and execution of a group of 100 believers, including women and children. He recounts the specific martyrdom of two women, one from the Gaza region and one named Valentina from the Caesarea region, who were tortured and executed by a judge. The passage concludes with a theological reflection on the ministry of Paul, who prayed for the conversion of Jews, Samaritans, and Gentiles before his execution.

Eusebius describes the execution of a man (possibly a local official) and the subsequent persecution of Christians in Egypt and Palestine under Maximinus. The text details the arrest of three men—Antony (Zebina), a man named German, and a woman named Ennachas—and the brutal actions of a commander named Maxys. It concludes with a description of the gruesome remains of victims and a supernatural atmospheric change in the air.

Eusebius describes the martyrdom of several Christians, including the men named Aris (or Armus), Promus, and Elias in Ascalon, and a woman named Aspelamos in the vicinity of Caesarea. He recounts the interrogation of five individuals by Egyptian authorities at the gates of the city and the subsequent trial before a judge. The text also provides a biographical sketch of two martyrs, Pamphilus and Valus, and mentions a third, Paul, while concluding with a narrative of a man's conflicting testimony regarding the location of Jerusalem.

Eusebius recounts the final persecutions and executions of the Christians Pamphilus and Porphyrius. The text describes the interrogation of Pamphilus by a brutal official, the martyrdom of Porphyrius who remained composed and prayed to Christ, and the subsequent martyrdom of Seleucus and Theodulus. The narrative highlights the physical sufferings of the martyrs and the contrast between their spiritual resolve and the cruelty of their tormentors.

The text recounts the martyrdom of the twelfth witness, Julian, who was burned at the stake after being captured by officers and brought before Phimilianus. It details the execution of Adrianus and Eubulus, who were punished with wild beasts and the sword, and mentions the actions of the ungodly leader Phimilianus. The narrative concludes with the relocation of many confessors to Cyprus, Lebanon, and other parts of Palestine, and the arrival of Sylvanus to oversee those remaining in their own lands.

Eusebius describes a martyr who, despite being blind and enduring a gruesome execution where his foot was burned, was praised for his superior spiritual intellect and prophetic manner. The text identifies a specific martyr named John from Egypt who was esteemed for his virtue. The narrative concludes by detailing the geographical scope of the persecutions across Palestine, Egypt, Syria, Libya, Italy, Sicily, Gaul, Spain, and Mauritania, noting a period of peace in some regions while others endured the trials of the early Christian era.

This 3rd-century Greek treatise by Origenes provides a systematic theological and allegorical analysis of Christian prayer, with a specific focus on the Lord's Prayer. The work is organized into eighteen sections that transition from the ontological necessity of divine grace to the mechanics of petition and the internal transformation of the soul. Origenes distinguishes between the terms 'proseuche' and 'euchē' and examines the roles of the Holy Spirit and Christ as mediators. The text features extensive scriptural exegesis of the Gospels, Pauline Epistles, Psalms, and the Book of Job, including references to figures such as David, Moses, and Hannah. Technical and polemical critiques are directed at the teachings of Tatian and the interpretation of the Lord's Prayer. The work concludes with a structural analysis of prayer components, including doxology, thanksgiving, confession, and petition, addressed to his students, Ambrose and Tatian.

Origenes discusses the impossibility of the human mind grasping divine mysteries without the intervention of God's grace through Christ and the Holy Spirit. He cites scriptural passages regarding the 'hidden' nature of the heavens and the necessity of the Spirit for knowing the things of God. The text concludes with a technical distinction regarding prayer, contrasting the content of a petition with the 'how' (καθὸ δεῖ) of its delivery, and addresses the audience of Ambrose and Tatian.

Origenes analyzes the nature of prayer, distinguishing between the 'groans' of the Spirit and the conscious prayers of the mind. He examines the role of the Spirit as a mediator for the saints and discusses the limitations of human speech in the face of divine mystery. The text also examines specific scriptural instances of prayer, including the prayers of Hannah, David, Moses, and the petition of Jacob, while addressing the linguistic nuances of the word 'prayer' in the Old Testament.

Origenes analyzes the linguistic distinction between 'proseuche' (prayer) and 'euchē' (vow/solemn petition) by examining various biblical passages. He cites the plagues of Egypt, the vows of Hannah and Jephthah, and the laws of the Nazirite to distinguish between common prayer and formal, binding vows. The text also addresses the legal and ritual implications of these vows in the books of Leviticus and Numbers.

Origenes addresses the theological paradox of prayer in relation to divine foreknowledge and providence. He argues that while God's decrees are immutable and his foreknowledge absolute, prayer is not 'vain' because it is not a means to change God's mind but a means for the petitioner to participate in the divine order. The text cites biblical figures including Jacob, Esau, Moses, and Judas, and references the Epistle to the Ephesians to contrast the status of the predestined with those who act in error.

Origenes analyzes the nature of motion, distinguishing between the movements of the soul, animals, and rational beings. He argues that human actions are not merely external movements but are internal responses to divine foreknowledge and providence. The text concludes with a theological defense of divine foreknowledge, asserting that God ordains both the actions of the righteous and the fall of the wicked (exemplified by the figures of Josiah and Judas) according to a pre-established plan.

Origenes discusses the nature of prayer, arguing that it requires internal purification from anger and worldly distractions to achieve a state of communion with God. He contrasts the mental state of the male and female worshippers, citing Paul's instructions to Timothy regarding modest dress and inner piety. The text also includes a cosmological reflection on the celestial bodies (sun, moon, and stars) as part of the divine order and their role in the cosmic liturgy.

Origenes analyzes the structure of prayer by examining the Psalms of David, the prophetic warnings of Jeremiah regarding internal malice, and the role of the High Priest (Christ) as an intercessor. He incorporates scriptural examples from the Book of Job, the Gospel of Matthew (the master of the feast), and the deuterocanonical account of the angel Raphael and the healing of Tobias and Sarah.

Origenes discusses the spiritual power of the saints' prayers, arguing that they are bolstered by the cooperation of angels and the active participation of the Holy Spirit. He uses a medical analogy of a physician and a wealthy man's charity to illustrate how God provides for the needy through the means of others. The text concludes by interpreting the command to 'pray without ceasing' as the sanctification of one's entire life, referencing the prophet Daniel.
