Origenes provides a series of scriptural examples of successful prayer, including the instances of Peter, Silas, and Jesus, and the historical figures of Hannah, Hezekiah, Mordecai, Esther, Judith, and Daniel. He argues that these figures achieved spiritual victory over enemies and physical dangers through persistent prayer and the guidance of the Holy Spirit. The text concludes by distinguishing between earthly petitions and the 'mysteries' of spiritual life, emphasizing the necessity of spiritual growth over physical desires.

Origenes analyzes the distinction between four types of prayer (deesis, proseuche, enteuxis, and eucharistia) as listed in 1 Timothy. He provides scriptural examples for each, including the prayers of Zechariah, Moses, Azariah, and the prayer of Tobit. The text also explores the spiritual significance of 'great' and 'heavenly' requests, using the figures of Samuel and Elijah to illustrate the power of prayer in obtaining divine favor.

Origenes analyzes the nature of prayer, distinguishing between the 'prayer' of the faithful and the 'intercession' of the Spirit and Christ. He cites the Book of Jonah, the words of Jesus at Gibeah, and the cry of Samson to illustrate instances of intercession. The text concludes with a technical argument on the proper object of prayer, asserting that while saints and Christ may be invoked as mediators, the ultimate petition must be directed to the Father.

Origenes argues that the faithful should pray to God through Christ as High Priest, emphasizing the distinction between spiritual gifts and their material 'shadows.' He utilizes biblical examples, including David, Hannah, Samuel, Hezekiah, Esther, Mordecai, and Daniel, to illustrate the superiority of spiritual blessings over physical ones. The text concludes by asserting that material wealth is a mere shadow compared to the eternal wisdom and spiritual riches of God.

Origenes compares the physical health of the body to the spiritual health of the soul, arguing that the soul's true beauty is found in the divine rather than in physical forms. He analyzes the Lord's Prayer as recorded by Matthew and Luke, noting the slight variations in wording and the shared core of the prayer. The text concludes by condemning the hypocrisy of performing religious acts for public recognition, emphasizing that the Father already knows the needs of the faithful.

Origenes contrasts the 'synagogue' (public, worldly worship) with the 'church' (private, spiritual worship), arguing that those seeking human praise in public spaces like streets and squares are seeking earthly rewards rather than divine ones. He critiques those who pray for bodily needs or worldly matters as 'speaking in vain' (βαττολογουμέν), likening such prayers to the petitions of the Gentiles. The text concludes by distinguishing the 'narrow way' of Christ from the 'broad road' of worldly pleasure.

Origenes analyzes the theological implications of the term 'Our Father' in the Lord's Prayer, distinguishing between the 'sonship' of the faithful and the nature of God. He argues that while the Old Testament contains instances of the term 'Father,' the New Testament provides the specific 'spirit of adoption' through Christ. The text concludes by contrasting the 'image of God' in the saints with the 'seed of the devil' in those who commit sin.

Origenes defends the doctrine of the omnipresence of God against literalist interpretations of Scripture that suggest God is confined to a physical location. He argues that phrases like 'in the heavens' or 'in the garden' refer to the spiritual realm or the presence of the saints, rather than a physical space. The text specifically addresses the nature of Christ's incarnation, the meaning of the 'seed' of the devil, and the distinction between the physical and spiritual dimensions of the Gospel of John.

Origenes analyzes the use of the imperative mood in the phrase 'Thy name be sanctified' and other scriptural commands, distinguishing between commands and petitions. He discusses the nature of 'the name' of God as a designation of divine attributes and addresses the theological implications of the 'overflow of godliness.' The text also critiques the teachings of Tatian regarding the creation of light and the interpretation of the Psalms.

Origenes analyzes the petitions of the Lord's Prayer, specifically 'Let your kingdom come' and 'Let your will be done.' He argues that the 'Kingdom of God' is an internal reality of the soul's communion with Christ, contrasting it with the 'kingdom of sin' and the rule of the 'prince of this world.' He concludes by examining the phrase 'as in heaven and on earth' as a means of seeking the perfection of the soul and the realization of divine will in the believer's life.

Origenes analyzes the phrase 'Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven' by interpreting 'earth' as the Church and 'heaven' as the realm of the spiritual. He argues that the 'will of the Father' is fulfilled in the Church through the mediation of Christ, who possesses authority over both realms. The text concludes by addressing the 'bread' in the Lord's Prayer, distinguishing between the physical bread of the body and the spiritual 'bread' of heavenly things.

Origenes analyzes the metaphor of 'bread' in the Gospels, specifically comparing the physical bread of the miracle at Capernaum with the 'true bread' of Christ's flesh. He examines the distinction between 'milk' and 'solid food' in the letters to the Corinthians and Hebrews to argue that spiritual nourishment depends on the believer's level of maturity. The text concludes with a philological note on the term 'epiousion,' noting its unique usage in the Gospels and by Hebrew interpreters.

Origenes analyzes the term 'epiousion' (living) bread as a metaphor for the spiritual nourishment of the soul, identifying it with the 'tree of life' and the 'wisdom of God.' He argues that this spiritual food is shared by both humans and angels, and he clarifies that scriptural references to 'eating the food of angels' or the 'bread of the fathers' refer to intellectual and spiritual sustenance rather than physical matter. The text concludes by linking this spiritual communion to the feast of the Last Supper and the shared meal of Christ.

Origenes analyzes the distinction between the 'bread of life' and the 'serpent' in the context of the spiritual nourishment of the faithful. He examines the biblical use of the word 'today' (σήμερον) in the Gospels and Epistles, arguing that it often signifies the eternal present of the age to come. The text concludes with a reconciliation of the Pauline passages regarding the 'fullness of ages' (συντελείᾳ τῶν αἰώνων) and the revelation of Christ's grace.

Origenes analyzes the concept of 'debt' (ὀφειλή) in the context of the Lord's Prayer and the relationship between the believer and God. He argues that believers owe a debt of worship, obedience, and love to God, the Holy Spirit, and the community of believers, including fellow Christians, neighbors, and the wider world. The text concludes by interpreting the biblical command for husbands and wives to repay each other's debts as a metaphor for mutual fulfillment in the spiritual life.

Origenes examines the nature of debt and forgiveness, distinguishing between human debts (social, familial, and civic) and spiritual debts before God. He analyzes the authority of the apostles to forgive sins in the Gospels and contrasts this with the limitations of the Old Testament priesthood, specifically regarding sins against God. The text concludes by referencing the Lord's Prayer and the specific limitations of the Levitical priests in cases of high-level transgressions.

Origenes examines the nature of 'temptation' (peirasmos) and 'trial' (peiraterion) in the life of the believer, citing the Book of Job, Psalm 17, and the letters of Paul to the Corinthians. He argues that while the faithful are subject to trials, they are not 'overtaken' by the power of temptation, and he contrasts the spiritual struggles of the apostles with the risks of worldly wealth and poverty. The text concludes with a warning against the spiritual dangers of physical illness and the necessity of guarding the heart against impure thoughts.

Origenes examines the nature of temptation (peirasmos) and the distinction between the 'trial' of life and the 'fall' into sin. He critiques those who have abandoned orthodox doctrine for heretical views on the nature of the Trinity and the distinction between the Father and the Son. The text concludes by arguing that God provides every rational soul with the capacity for either ascent toward the ultimate good or descent into various forms of evil.

Origenes analyzes the Israelites' desire for meat in the wilderness as a metaphor for the soul's lingering lusts and the danger of partial satisfaction. He argues that God's delay in granting their request was a pedagogical measure to ensure they would eventually hate the 'pleasures of the flesh' and seek only heavenly nourishment. The text concludes by contrasting the 'purifying fire' of divine judgment for the faithful with the hardening of Pharaoh's heart.

Origenes analyzes the nature of divine testing (peirasmos) and the distinction between being 'afflicted' (thlibesthai) and 'distressed' (stenochōrēsthai). He examines the moral failings of figures such as Eve, Cain, Noah, Esau, and Joseph to illustrate how trials reveal internal character. The text also includes a commentary on the words of Luke, the Psalms, and the book of Job regarding God's protection from the evil one.

Origenes analyzes the theology of the book of Job, specifically the dialogue between the accuser and Job regarding the suffering of the righteous and the 'three battles' of the Savior. He transitions into a treatise on the physical and spiritual requirements of prayer, discussing the significance of posture (standing, sitting, kneeling), the role of the body as a reflection of the soul, and the symbolic meaning of physical gestures like the 'kneeling' of the heavenly bodies.

Origenes examines the spiritual significance of the 'place' of prayer, arguing that while any location is suitable for the faithful, the specific location of a prayer must not be chosen to evade divine oversight. He discusses the presence of angelic and spiritual powers in the assembly of believers, contrasting the 'double' presence of holy men and angels with the 'double' presence of ungodly men and demons. The passage concludes with a symbolic interpretation of the four cardinal directions, specifically the East as a symbol of the soul's orientation toward the true light.

Origenes provides a structural analysis of the components of a formal prayer, identifying four specific movements: doxology (glorification), thanksgiving, confession of sins, and petition. He provides scriptural examples for each section, citing the Psalms and the Second Book of Kings. The passage concludes with a formal address to his students, Ambrose and Tatian, regarding the theological structure of prayer as presented in the Gospels.

This text is a Polish medieval devotional hymn or prayer, identified as the 'Bogurodzica' (Mother of God). It is structured as a series of numbered stanzas and sub-sections (1-13) containing invocations to the Virgin Mary, the Holy Trinity, and various saints. The content includes traditional liturgical themes such as the resurrection of Christ, the protection of the faithful against the devil, and the seeking of divine mercy. Specific figures invoked include Jesus Christ, Saint Catherine, Saint Stanislaus, Saint Florian, Saint Francis, and Saint Anne. The text concludes with a petition for protection from evil and a final doxology.

This 14th-century Polish sermon, likely composed for the Feast of St. Michael, is structured in three distinct movements. The first section presents a Christological allegory of 'kings' (the Savior, the Poor, and the Humble) supported by biblical narratives involving King David, the siege of Hezekiah against the Assyrians, and the protection of holy angels. The second section consists of a series of exhortations addressed to a woman named Catherine, utilizing the command 'Arise' to describe spiritual states, and incorporates the Canticle of Simeon and visions of the Christ child. The final section provides a theological commentary on the Epiphany, interpreting the gifts of the Magi—gold, frankincense, and myrrh—as symbols of Christ's attributes. The text references specific biblical locations such as Corrozaim and Gilead, as well as the prophets Ezekiel and Habakkuk.

This sermon, likely for St. Michael's Day, presents a series of 'kings' (the Savior, the Poor, the Humble) as spiritual promises to the faithful. It incorporates biblical narratives, including the prophet David, the siege of Hezekiah against the Assyrians, and the role of holy angels in divine protection. The text also references the city of Corrozaim and the land of Gilead as symbolic locations of spiritual struggle or judgment.

The text contains a series of exhortations and biblical reflections addressed to a woman named Catherine, using the command 'Arise' (vstań) to describe the spiritual states of those who are sitting, lying, sleeping, and dead. It incorporates scriptural references to the Gospel of Luke, the prophet Ezekiel, and the prophet Habakkuk (referred to as Habraham), while also featuring the Nunc Dimittis (Canticle of Simeon) and a list of five visions of the Christ child.

The text provides a theological commentary on the Epiphany, specifically interpreting the gifts of the three pagan kings (gold, frankincense, and myrrh) as symbols of the attributes of Christ. The author interprets the 'king' as the 'king of the Jews' and the 'heavenly prince,' using a threefold structure to explain his mercy, power, and the spiritual significance of the offerings. The passage also references the journey of the Magi and the specific number of days following the birth of Christ.

This work is a scholarly analysis of the 'Domostroy' (House-building) manual, specifically the edition edited by the priest Sylvester. The text is organized into three parts: a comparative study of the 'Domostroy''s structure against monastic rules and Western European royal instructions; a linguistic and stylistic analysis of the text's folk idioms and household management instructions; and a narrative analysis of a specific scene involving a merchant, a 'kunka', and a woman. The author references several Western figures, including Platina Cremonesi, Andrea Piccolomini, Joannis Ludovici Vivis, Del Caza, and Castiglione. The study also examines the socio-economic structure of the 'podvorye' and the influence of Zlatoust and Izmaragd. The final section explores Novgorod folklore and the 19th-century reception of the text by the Russian intelligentsia.

The text analyzes the 'Domostroy' as a manual for family life and social order, comparing its structure to monastic rules and the works of Zlatoust and Izmaragd. It examines the socio-economic structure of the 'podvorye' (enclosed courtyard) and its relationship to the state and the church. The author provides a comparative study of the 'Domostroy' genre, citing Western European and Italian examples such as the works of Platina Cremonesi, Andrea Piccolomini, and various French and Spanish royal instructions.

The text provides a scholarly analysis of the 'Domostroy' (House-building) and its various editions, specifically the one edited by the priest Sylvester. It compares the Russian text to Western works on etiquette and domesticity by authors such as Joannis Ludovici Vivis, Del Caza, and Castiglione. The passage also analyzes the linguistic style of the Domostroy, noting its use of folk idioms, direct speech, and specific instructions for household management and social conduct.

The text contains a narrative involving a woman (referred to as 'baba') who interacts with a merchant and a 'kunka' (lady) regarding a delivery. The narrative describes a situation involving a feast, a nurse, and a woman's attempt to reach a mistress to entice her toward marital infidelity. The concluding commentary analyzes the literary style of the text, comparing it to Novgorod folklore and discussing the historical reception of the Domostroy by the 19th-century Russian intelligentsia.

Following a serpent bite, the Prince seeks medical treatment from Fevronia in Murom, leading to a series of mystical dialogues and negotiations regarding her role. The narrative includes a moral discourse on the Oka River concerning the nature of womanhood and the unity of the feminine. The final section details the couple's pious rule, their deaths, and the subsequent veneration of their relics in the Cathedral of the Nativity of the Virgin.

summary: This 12th-century Russian epic poem recounts the military campaign of Prince Igor Svyatslavich against the Polovtsians near the Don River. The narrative begins with a prologue invoking the poet Boyan to recount the history of the Rus' lands and the deeds of princes Yaroslav, Mstislav, and Svyatislav. The text follows Igor's movements through Kiev, Novograd, and Putivl, and includes a dialogue with his brother Vsevolod. Subsequent sections detail the aftermath of the battle, the devastation of the Russian lands, and the defense against Polovtsian and Lithuanian forces. The work features the lamentations of Yaroslavna in Putivl and includes a personified dialogue between the Donets River and Igor. Key figures mentioned include Svyatoslav, Rurik, and David, while locations include Chernigov, Polotsk, and the Danube.

The text begins with a prologue invoking the poet Boyan to recount the history of the Rus' lands, specifically the deeds of Yaroslav, Mstislav, and Svyatislav. The narrative includes a dialogue between Igor and his brother Vsevolod (called Buy Tur), the movement of their troops through various lands (Kiev, Novograd, Putivl), and a description of the battle and the subsequent capture of Polovtsian wealth.

The text describes the military campaigns and subsequent losses of Princes Igor and Svyatoslav, specifically focusing on the aftermath of their battles against the Polovtsians. It mentions specific locations such as Kiev, Chernigov, and the river Kayala, and laments the internal strife (usobitsa) among the princes. The narrative includes a lament for the fallen warriors and a description of the devastation of the Russian land.

The text describes the aftermath of a battle involving Prince Igor and the defense of Russian lands against Polovtsian and Lithuanian forces. It names several princes and figures including Yaroslav, Svitoslavich, Svyatoslav, and the legendary figures Rurik and David. The narrative mentions specific locations such as Kiev, Polotsk, the Danube, and the city of Nemiga, while lamenting the losses and the 'wounds of Igor'.

The text describes the lamentations of Yaroslavna in Putivl, followed by a depiction of Prince Igor's journey through the lands of the Polovtsians. It includes a dialogue between the river Donets and Igor, and a scene where Gzakh and Konchak discuss a falcon. The passage concludes with a series of invocations and praises for Igor, Vladimir, and the Christian host.

summary: A 15th-century Russian travelogue by Afanasy Nikitin detailing a maritime and overland journey to India and the lands of the East. The narrative follows Nikitin's experiences as a merchant, documenting his travels through regions such as Derbent, Baku, and the Indian subcontinent. The text provides detailed accounts of trade in spices, silk, and precious stones, alongside descriptions of local customs and geography in cities like Gurmuz and Beder. It records specific military logistics, including troop counts and the use of elephants in warfare by the Sultan and various Khans. The work also documents Nikitin's personal spiritual struggles, his encounters with Buddhism and Islam, and his observations of diverse religious practices. The final sections include a geographical survey of the Black Sea region and a series of Arabic-influenced religious invocations.

He details the customs of the local people, the geography of the Indian Mountains, and a specific encounter in the city of Chuner where a Khan offers him gold and a horse in exchange for conversion to Islam. The narrator is ultimately saved from conversion on the feast of Easter by the intervention of a local host named Mahmet Horosanes.

Claudius Salmasius's 'De modo usurarum' is a scholarly treatise examining the history, philology, and legal frameworks of usury, debt, and property in Greek and Roman contexts. The work is organized into technical investigations of interest rates (triens, sextans, nauticum foenus), the etymology of financial terms, and the distinctions between security types such as pignus, hypotheca, and fiducia. Salmasius engages in philological debates regarding Hebrew and Greek influences, citing authorities including Scaliger, Aristotle, the Septuagint, Cicero, Seneca, and Justinian. The text provides detailed analyses of maritime law (Lex Rhodia), contract law (chirographa and syngraphae), and the transition of laws into the Byzantine and ecclesiastical periods. Specific legal concepts discussed include the lex commifloria, marital property (dos and res uxoria), and the evolution of debt slavery (nexum). The work also addresses criminal procedure, currency systems (drachma, stater, denarius), and concludes with sections of corrupted text containing fragmented Greek characters and measurements.

Claudius Salmasius provides a preface to his work 'De modo usurarum', addressing the scope of his treatise on usury. He defends the depth of his research against potential critics, references the scholarly works of others (such as the 'Epiphio' and 'Prosatio'), and addresses the methodology of his inquiry. The text also includes a section on the importance of thorough investigation and the distinction between mere rhetoric and substantial knowledge.

Salmasius provides a methodological defense of his work, explaining his decision to include specific legal distinctions between public and private law and the origins of various types of usury (such as *affes*, *femijes*, *trientes*, and *uncia*) in Roman and Attic contexts. He addresses potential criticisms regarding his scholarly choices, defends his authorship against accusations of sycophancy, and concludes with a philosophical reflection on the pursuit of fame versus the pursuit of truth in scholarly writing.

Salmasius critiques a group of individuals who prioritize their own opinions over the truth and are accused of being 'sycophants' rather than 'ingenui' (honest/noble) men. He argues that the defense of truth, even in minor matters, is a duty of the Christian faith. The text also contains a lengthy, corrupted section involving a discussion of biblical texts (Matthew, Mark, Luke) and a specific, poorly legible passage regarding a 'title' and a 'table' (tabella) that appears to be a transcription of a corrupted or poorly printed source.

Salmasius discusses the linguistic and theological implications of the term 'Hellenistic' (Hellenisticus) in relation to Hebrew and Syrian influences in the Greek language. He analyzes the usage of the term in the Septuagint and the works of Arisiarchus, specifically regarding the translation of Hebrew terms like 'Baar' and 'tentoria'. The text also addresses the distinction between 'barbarisms' and 'solecisms' in Greek literature and the historical context of the term 'Gentiles' (Gentilis) in Christian writings.

Salmasius engages in a scholarly debate regarding the distinction between 'Hellenists' and 'Jews' (Iudaei) in historical and biblical texts, specifically addressing the terminology used by Scaliger. He cites Sozomenus, the Septuagint, and the Epistle to the Hebrews to argue that certain groups were identified as Hellenists because they were ignorant of Hebrew. The text also references the works of Prosatius and the 'Emendatione temporum' to discuss the linguistic nuances of Hebrew and Greek influences in religious texts.

Salmasius examines the linguistic and cultural distinctions between Jews, Greeks, and Syrians, specifically addressing the terminology used by Arisiarchus and the distinction between 'Hellenis' and 'Hebrais'. He references the works of Scaliger and the history of the Septuagint to argue against the conflation of distinct ethnic identities in religious texts. The passage concludes with a scholarly defense of his own methodology, inviting correction from peers to ensure the pursuit of truth over personal glory.

The author defends his intellectual integrity and the quality of his work against potential critics, specifically addressing those who might accuse him of error or lack of merit. He distinguishes between his private friendships and public reputation, arguing that his critics are often motivated by malice or lack of understanding. He asserts that his work is intended for the learned and that his modest approach is a deliberate choice to avoid the pitfalls of vanity and the 'rabies' of slander.

Salmasius defends his legal arguments regarding 'res fungibiles' (fungible goods) and the distinction between 'usufructus' and 'dominium' in the context of loans and usury. He addresses criticisms from 'jurisconsulti' and 'critici' regarding his terminology, specifically defending his use of the word 'culina' over 'latrina' in a technical context. He references the works of Theophilus, Arnobius, and the Digest of Justinian to support his legal positions.

Salmasius provides a technical and philological analysis of the term 'usury' (usurarum), distinguishing between Greek and Latin terminology. He examines specific financial practices, such as 'Attic' usury and 'mathematical' calculations involving perfect numbers, while referencing figures such as Plato, Aristotle, and Vitruvius. The text also addresses the legal and historical variations of interest rates under Roman rule and the linguistic nuances of technical terms like 'sextans' and 'septuaginta'.

Salmasius analyzes the legal and economic variations in interest rates (usurarum) based on the identity of the parties involved, the nature of the goods, and the location of the transaction. He distinguishes between private and public lenders, and between land-based and maritime (nauticum) commerce. The text also references the distinction between the sale of goods by owners versus professional merchants and the impact of currency scarcity on interest rates.

Salmasius argues that the rate of usury is determined by the degree of risk (periculum) involved in the transaction, specifically distinguishing between common lending and maritime lending (foenus nauticum). He cites the laws of Solon and the practices of Athens to illustrate how tacit consent and market conditions dictate interest rates in the absence of specific legal limits. The text also examines the impact of the scarcity or abundance of currency (scarcitas/copia nummarum) on the legality and feasibility of high interest rates in both ancient and Roman contexts.

Salmasius analyzes the terminology of interest rates (usury) in ancient Greek and Roman law, specifically distinguishing between 'sextantalis' and 'sextantalis Graeca'. He cites Plato's Laws, Pollux's Oeconomica, and Hesychius to clarify technical distinctions between different types of interest calculations (such as the 'Attic' versus 'Mathematical' systems). The text also examines the legal nuances of 'good faith' (bona fide) in lending and the specific naming conventions for various types of interest.

Salmasius analyzes the terminology of interest rates (usury) and the Greek mathematical systems used to express them. He cites authors such as Agellius, Pollux, and Aristophanes to distinguish between 'Attic' and 'Mathematic' systems of fractions, specifically regarding the 'trientale' and 'sextentale' rates. The text concludes by examining the specific Greek terms for fractional parts, such as 'sesquialterum' and 'quintarium', in the context of monthly versus annual interest calculations.

Salmasius analyzes historical Greek practices regarding usury and interest rates, specifically focusing on the distinction between monthly and annual interest. He cites Aristotle's 'Economics', Xenophon, and Demosthenes to discuss the 'triobolum' (three-day wage) and the 'minae' (minas) paid by citizens. The text also references the legal and social implications of interest in Athens and the specific calculations of revenue for the state.

Salmasius analyzes the calculation of interest rates (usury) in Greek and Roman contexts, specifically comparing the 'triens' and 'sextans' rates. He cites Aristophanes, Demosthenes, and Xenophon to discuss the fiscal administration of Athens, including the census of Attica and the conversion of currency units like the drachma and mina. The text also addresses a specific error in the interpretation of Harpocration's words regarding interest calculations.

Salmasius analyzes the calculation of interest rates (usura) and currency conversions, specifically comparing Greek and Roman systems. He critiques and corrects errors made by Scaliger regarding the conversion of drachmas to denarii and the specific denominations of gold coins used by the Cyrenaeans. The text also references Harpocration, Diogenes Laertius, and the distinction between annual, monthly, and daily interest payments.

Salmasius analyzes various types of usury (interest) in Greek and Roman contexts, specifically discussing 'hebdomadariis' (weekly) and 'quinta' (fifth) rates. He cites Aristotle's Rhetoric and Plutarch to discuss the moral implications of high interest rates, specifically the distinction between 'probitas' and 'improbitas' in lending. The text includes a lengthy scholarly note on a corrupted Greek passage regarding the name 'Merochles' (or 'Merochles') and the specific percentage of interest deemed 'malum' (evil) versus 'minime malis' (minor evil).

Salmasius analyzes the terminology of interest rates, specifically the distinction between 'triens' (one-third) and 'dextans' (one-tenth) in Roman and Greek contexts. He argues that 'dextans' is a mathematical error when used to mean one-tenth, as it technically refers to a different proportion in certain systems. The text also references Aristotle's 'Oeconomica' and the practice of monthly interest payments for long-term loans.

Salmasius analyzes the distinction between annual and monthly interest rates (usurarum) in Roman and Greek financial practices. He examines specific Greek terms for interest, such as 'sexta pars' (one-sixth) and 'drachma,' and argues against the conflation of annual payments with monthly ones. The text references the works of Xenophon and the practices of the Greeks to clarify technical terminology regarding the 'drachma' and 'obol' in lending.

Claudius Salmasius analyzes historical interest rates (usury) in Athens, specifically comparing 'menstrua' (monthly) and 'annua' (annual) rates. He cites a specific legal oratory regarding the case of Eschines and the Socratic defense to illustrate the differences between 'gravissima' (heavy) and 'levissima' (light) interest rates. The text also references the 'Graculi' (money-lenders) and the specific calculations of drachmas and obols used in ancient Greek finance.

Salmasius analyzes the mathematical and legal distinctions between daily, monthly, and annual interest rates (usury) in ancient Greek and Roman contexts. Salmasius examines the etymology and physical nature of 'axes' (axiones) in the context of the laws of Solon and the writings of Plutarch. Salmasius analyzes the distinction between public and private judgments (judicia publica and judicia privata) in Roman and Greek law. Salmasius examines the legal distinctions between public and private accusations (accusatio) in Athenian law, specifically regarding the crime of usury. Salmasius examines the legal distinctions between public and private crimes in Athens and Rome, specifically regarding the 'modum' (method) of usury. Salmasius analyzes the legal and historical definitions of 'dos' (dowry) versus 'peculium' (private property) in Roman and Greek law. Salmasius analyzes the linguistic and legal distinctions between 'donum' (gift) and 'dos' (dowry), citing Homeric and biblical examples like the marriage of Sychem and Dinah. The text examines the legal evolution of 'donatio ante nuptias' (dowry gifts) and 'dotaria' under Roman law, specifically how these were regulated by various emperors and legal scholars like Anthemius and Judinianus. Salmasius analyzes the calculation of usury and dowries, specifically contrasting 'large' and 'small' dowries (minima). Salmasius analyzes the legal distinction between 'usura' (interest) and 'alimenta' (sustenance) in Athenian law. Salmasius analyzes legal and literary texts concerning inheritance and the status of women, specifically addressing the legal rights of a widow (mulier nupta) and the transition of property to a son. Salmasius examines the legal concept of 'res uxoria' (property of a wife) and the 'dos' (dowry) in both Roman and Greek law. Salmasius analyzes the legal evolution of the 'actio rei uxoriae' (the action of the wife) and its replacement by the 'actio ex stipulatu' in Justinian's legal reforms. Salmasius analyzes the legal regulations regarding usury on dowries (dotium) and the differences between Roman and Greek laws. Salmasius analyzes the legal distinctions between 'nautica' (maritime) and 'maritima' usury, citing the laws of Athens, Rhodes, and Rome. Salmasius analyzes the legal distinctions between 'maritima' and 'nautica' usury, specifically regarding the risks of sea travel. Salmasius analyzes the legal distinction between 'commune' (common) and 'nauticum' (maritime) usury, citing a Novella of Justinian regarding the risks of sea voyages. Salmasius analyzes the legal and linguistic distinctions of 'nauticum foenus' (maritime interest) by citing Demosthenes' speeches against Aphobus and Phormion. Salmasius analyzes the legal concept of 'periculum' (risk) in maritime law, specifically regarding the 'Lex Rhodia' and the liability of carriers for goods lost at sea. Salmasius examines the legal status of shipwrecks and the rights of 'publicani' (public collectors) under the Rhodian Law. Salmasius analyzes the legal status of shipwrecks, specifically comparing the 'Lex Rhodia' (Rhodian Law) with Roman law and the reforms of Emperor Antoninus Pius. Salmasius analyzes the legal and economic terms of maritime loans and interest rates in ancient Greek commerce. Salmasius analyzes the terminology of usury and currency, specifically comparing Roman and Greek systems. Salmasius analyzes the terminology and weights of ancient currencies, specifically comparing the Siculus, the Attic obol, and the Roman denarius. Salmasius analyzes the distinction between 'maritima' (maritime) and 'commune' (common) interest rates, noting that common rates were historically more stable and common. Salmasius analyzes the technical terminology of interest rates (usurarum) in Roman and Greek systems, specifically comparing the 'centesima' (hundredth) and 'semesima' (half). Salmasius analyzes the linguistic evolution of the term 'aes grave' (heavy bronze) in Roman law and literature, specifically its transition from a unit of weight to a unit of count. Salmasius analyzes the historical evolution of weights and measures, specifically the transition from the 'libra' (pound) to smaller units like the 'uncia' (ounce) and 'sextans'. Salmasius analyzes the historical weights and values of various coins, specifically comparing the Roman denarius and the Sicilian 'Siculus' (or 'libella'). Salmasius analyzes the linguistic and numerical discrepancies between Latin and Greek terms for currency and weights, specifically focusing on the 'denarius' and 'talent'. Salmasius examines the etymology and usage of fractional terms like 'sextans' and 'triens' in the context of 'De modo usurarum'. Salmasius analyzes the linguistic and mathematical nuances of Greek currency terms, specifically the distinction between 'triens' (one-third) and 'sextans' (one-sixth) in the context of the 'obol'. Salmasius analyzes the term 'centesima' (the hundredth) in the context of usury, comparing Greek and Roman practices. Salmasius examines the term 'semissim' (or 'semissim' usury) in the context of Roman law and ancient inscriptions. Salmasius analyzes the distinction between 'usura' (usury) and 'frugum usura' (the usury of fruit/produce) in ecclesiastical and legal contexts. Salmasius examines the legal and ecclesiastical regulations regarding usury (usurarum) in the Church, specifically comparing the canons of the Councils of Nicæa and Laodicea. Salmasius analyzes the linguistic and mathematical nuances of Latin and Greek numerical terms, specifically focusing on 'sescuplum' (sixfold) and 'sesquitertium' (fourfold). Salmasius analyzes the legal and historical calculations of usury (interest) in Roman and Byzantine law, specifically comparing the 'double' (duplum) and 'sextuple' (sescuplum) rates. Salmasius analyzes the legal and economic complexities of lending grain and wine versus lending money, specifically addressing the risks of fluctuating market prices. Salmasius analyzes the legal distinctions between 'frutum' (agricultural products) and 'pecunia' (money) in the context of usury laws. Salmasius analyzes the legal distinction between 'nauticum foenus' (maritime interest) and 'trajecticiae usurae' (transportation interest) in the context of risk and contract law. Salmasius analyzes the legal distinction between 'penalties' and 'risks' (periculum) in contracts, specifically regarding the 'Scavola' law. Salmasius analyzes the legal distinction between 'nudum pactum' (bare agreement) and 'stipulatio' regarding the payment of interest (usury). Salmasius analyzes legal distinctions in maritime loans (traiecticia) regarding the calculation of interest and the duration of risk for the creditor. It details the *exercitoria* action, used when a master places a son, slave, or pupil on a ship, and the *tributoria* action, employed when creditors feel they have not received a proportional share of assets. The excerpt also touches upon an action *in rem* arising when a transaction involving a son or slave negatively impacts the *pater* or *dominus*, and includes a corrupted formula fragment. The text's focus on legal procedure and the intricacies of Roman family law provides valuable insight into the educational curriculum of the time.

Subsequent, fragmentary sections address the inheritance of property when a woman is compelled to contribute to the *decimae*, a communal fund, though these passages are significantly corrupted and their precise meaning remains obscure. The text appears to grapple with the interplay of legal formulas, customary inheritance practices, and the relationships between freedmen, centenarians, and patrons. The overall focus is on clarifying the conditions under which individuals, even those not considered heirs, might acquire property rights.

summary: CLA 8 1034 is a fragmentary Latin legal treatise, likely from the classical period, dealing with inheritance law and the status of relatives in succession. The surviving text discusses the derivation of property from intestate estates, specifically addressing the inclusion of various family members – parents, mothers, grandmothers, nephews, sisters, and nieces – and the role of tutors. A significant portion of the text appears to concern the legal standing of *pagani* (pagans), with a marginal Greek gloss providing a brief explanation relating to their potential military status and movement. The treatise’s organization is unclear due to the extensive lacunae, but it seems to present a legal argument or exposition, punctuated by the Greek marginalia which offer commentary or perhaps alternative interpretations. The identity of the author remains unknown, and the text’s condition is severely compromised, rendering a complete understanding impossible. The late antique marginalia, written in Greek, are datable to the 6th century CE.

source: papyri.info DCLP TM 64986 (cla;8;1035); Fundort: Egypt; Schreibort:; 450 - 533
summary: CLA 8 1035 is a fragmentary Latin legal treatise, likely originating from the late antique period, tentatively dated to the 5th century CE. The surviving text appears to address inheritance law, specifically concerning the status of a deceased individual’s paternal lineage and the potential for legal challenges. A key element of the discussion involves the interpretation of names and their extension, possibly in the context of adoption or familial relationships. The text references a legal decision (*crinit*) and uses the Latin term *rectitās* (rightness, justice), suggesting a focus on legal propriety. A single Greek word, *ὁμοίως κατ*, is present, indicating possible interaction with Greek legal or rhetorical traditions. Due to the significant lacunae, the precise scope and arguments of the treatise remain obscure, but the fragments point to a sophisticated legal discussion.

source: papyri.info DCLP TM 65155 (tm;;65155); Fundort: Arsinoites ?, Egypt; 500 - 533
summary: This fragmentary Latin legal text, designated Wessely, Schrifttafeln 24, likely originates from the late antique period, tentatively dated to the 6th century CE. The text is preserved on a series of inscribed tablets, and exhibits marginalia written in Latin, suggesting a process of annotation or commentary. The surviving portions address legal procedures, specifically concerning the detention of individuals and the presentation of accusers before a *praeses* and a 'prince'. A key passage details the conditions under which a person should be bound, distinguishing between suspected and non-suspected individuals. The text's condition is severely compromised, rendering much of its content illegible; the fragmentary nature makes definitive interpretation challenging, but the references to a *praeses* and a 'prince' suggest a provincial Roman or early Byzantine legal context.

source: papyri.info DCLP TM 66487 (p.herc;;1067); Fundort: Herculaneum (Campania, Italy) - 1752; Schreibort: Italy; Anfang 100 v.Chr. - 79
summary: CLA 3 386 represents a severely damaged portion of what is believed to be a work by Seneca the Elder, likely from his *Histories*. The surviving fragments, written in Latin, appear to recount events related to the Gallic Wars, potentially involving figures like Cn(aeus) Ledarussus and referencing Augustus. The text is highly corrupt, rendering much of the narrative unintelligible; it is difficult to discern a clear chronological or thematic structure. Scattered phrases suggest discussions of military campaigns, political maneuvering, and personal relationships, interspersed with what seem to be moral reflections and pronouncements. The presence of Greek words and phrases indicates a degree of Hellenistic influence, consistent with Seneca the Elder's known style and interests. The concluding lines mention a civic duty and a reference to Ennius, hinting at a broader commentary on Roman values and historical memory.

source: papyri.info DCLP TM 66488 (p.herc;;1475); Fundort: Herculaneum (Campania, Italy); Schreibort: Italy; 30 v.Chr. - 20
summary: CLA 3 387 is a fragmentary Latin commentary, likely composed in the 1st century CE. The text is severely damaged, rendering a coherent narrative impossible; however, discernible phrases suggest a discussion of legal or rhetorical matters, potentially related to a trial or public accusation. References to 'saevissima conc...' (most savage assembly) and 'civitate' (citizenship) hint at political or legal proceedings. The text also contains allusions to military service ('stipendia', 'armour'), and mentions of ancestors ('maiores'), suggesting a discussion of lineage or tradition. Scattered references to clothing ('vestem', 'scorti') and illness ('morbus') appear alongside passages concerning piety and the actions of birds, indicating a complex and disjointed argumentation. The concluding lines suggest a possible connection to a commentary on legal or rhetorical works, marked by the abbreviation 'L Pr...'.

CLA 7 886 comprises fragmentary Latin imperial constitutions, likely dating to the 5th century CE. The surviving text concerns the regulation of access to civic and military offices, specifically addressing the required *originis propria* – a proper lineage or birthright – for holding such positions. References to *curiales* (city council members) and *militiae* (military service) suggest a focus on the administration of urban centers and the army. The text also mentions *diginitatis praetextu* (under the guise of rank) and *honoris cinguli* (the belt of honor), indicating a discussion of ceremonial or symbolic aspects of office. The fragment is heavily damaged, rendering much of the argument and context obscure; phrases like “with zeal” and “with ambiguity” offer glimpses into the tone of the original legal reasoning, but the overall structure and intended scope remain unclear. The mention of punishments (*poenas*) and conspiracies (*coniventiae*) suggests a concern with maintaining order and preventing corruption within the ruling class.

C.Lat.Text.Pap. 4 no. IV.49–50 presents a fragmentary section of Papinian’s *Responsa*, likely from Book 1, accompanied by Latin marginalia. The text concerns legal questions, specifically addressing issues of criminal accusation, Roman citizenship, and the obligations of freedmen. A significant portion deals with the exemption of *fisc vectigalium redemptores* (those who redeem the revenues of the fisc) from civil duties, contrasting their status with those engaged in commerce. The passage also mentions the duties of sons returning to their homeland and the inheritance of allowances by freedmen, referencing a legal precedent known as the *ius aureorum anullorum* (law of golden rings). The fragmentary nature of the text makes definitive conclusions about its scope difficult, but it clearly demonstrates Papinian’s expertise in imperial law and its application to various social classes.

C.Lat.Text.Pap. 5 no. V.67 is a fragmentary Latin legal text likely originating from the 5th century CE, as indicated by its paleography. The text is written on papyrus and exhibits marginalia, suggesting it may have been used for annotation or study. Due to significant lacunae and corruption, the precise nature of the legal matter is obscure; discernible phrases suggest a discussion of property or inheritance, referencing 'public affairs' and a mention of 'good wine,' which may be part of an inventory or valuation. The presence of Greek words (μ, καθ, κυα) interspersed within the Latin text indicates a bilingual or Greek-influenced legal context, potentially from a region with a significant Greek-speaking population. The text is organized in a loose, prose format, with sentences broken and incomplete, making reconstruction difficult. The fragmentary nature prevents identification of specific legal figures or locations.

This fragment originates from the *Digesta*, a component of the *Corpus Juris Civilis* commissioned by the Byzantine Emperor Justinian in the 6th century CE. The text appears to concern the legal status of *superficies*, a right allowing the construction and use of structures on another’s land in exchange for a stipulated payment. The passage references a legal precedent found in the writings of Publicianus and cites Paulus, specifically mentioning his *Liber Vigesimus* (Book Twenty) concerning edicts. The argument presented involves a scenario where a landowner had conveyed property via letter and subsequently leased it back, raising the question of whether the recipient’s right to possess the land should be considered equivalent to acquisition through a *colonia* (a form of Roman land grant). The text is fragmentary, with significant lacunae obscuring the full context and conclusion of the legal discussion. The fragment's location within the *Digesta* suggests it was intended as part of a systematic compilation of Roman law.

source: papyri.info DCLP TM 942312 (p.herc;;371); Fundort: Herculaneum (Campania, Italy); Schreibort: Italy; 199 v.Chr. - 79
summary: This fragmentary Latin text, published in *Aegyptus* 7 (1926) on page 209, appears to be a portion of either an oration or a comedy, likely composed during the 1st century BCE. The surviving lines suggest a scene involving a reference to specific Ides (a Roman calendar term), a courtyard (*atrium*), and a description of a mother being described as 'threatening' (*minari*). The text also mentions someone 'illustrious' (*illustr*) and another individual, indicated by 'another' (*alio*). Due to the significant lacunae and corruption, the precise context and narrative purpose remain obscure; it is impossible to determine the speaker, audience, or overall argument. The fragment's brevity and damaged state preclude any definitive identification of genre or author.

source: papyri.info DCLP TM 942316 (p.herc;;1059); Fundort: Herculaneum (Campania, Italy); Schreibort: Italy; 100 v.Chr. - 79
summary: This fragmentary Latin prose text, appearing in *Aegyptus* 7 (1926), p. 210, is of uncertain provenance and likely dates to the 1st century BCE, though definitive dating is impossible given the text’s condition. The surviving lines suggest a narrative or rhetorical passage, possibly dealing with the contemplation of ruins and the encouragement of a person (

This fragmentary Latin letter, designated 1447 in *Année épigraphique* 2021, originates from Qasr Ibrim, a Roman-period settlement in Upper Nubia. The text is severely damaged, rendering a complete understanding of its content difficult; extant portions suggest a personal correspondence, likely between a superior and a subordinate. The letter concerns matters of estate management, specifically a 'reli[g]...esium col[...]' (likely a religious estate or property), and the provisioning of soldiers with food ('milites ed[...]crum fecisti'). References to Cotta, a person whose role is unclear from the fragment, and a 'cunegiun ae[...]' (possibly a hunting lodge or similar structure) are also present. The closing contains a paternal address ('fili') and a customary farewell, indicating a familial or close relationship between the correspondents.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 10014 (c.epist.lat;;226); Philadelphia? (Arsinoites); 1. Apr. 340 - 31. März 342
summary: This fragmentary Latin text, designated P.Lond. 2 p. XXXIX no. 447 Ro descr., appears to be an official dispatch or petition, likely originating from the late 4th century CE. It details the movement and resettlement of Blemmyes refugees from the Thebaid province to Constantinople, under the authority of the emperors Constantius and Constantina. The document references Senecio, a former limit commander, and Vala[cio], a companion, and mentions the vexillation of Parthusagittarii stationed in Diospolis. The text outlines a process of promotion and transfer within the military, involving the ala Dionysiados of the province of Aegyptus, and concludes with a plea for daily sustenance and expressions of gratitude to the imperial power. The organization is somewhat disjointed, suggesting a partial or interrupted communication.

P.Gen. 1 45 is a Latin letter, likely an official dispatch, composed in the late antique period, tentatively dated to the 4th century CE. The letter is addressed from Flavius Valacius to Abinneo, and concerns the transfer of responsibility for a military cohort and its associated regalia. The text details the handover of 'signa dominica' (sacred standards) and 'solidamque inarmationem' (solid arming), alongside instructions for maintaining public order and preventing errors among the troops. The letter concludes with a farewell and the signatures of Flavius Leontius, Praetorian Prefect, and Flavius Sallustius, Master of Foot Soldiers, both identified as 'viri clarissimi' (most illustrious men), and consuls. The letter's content suggests a context of military administration and the formal transfer of authority within the Roman army.

This document is a land declaration, likely a legal record produced in Roman Egypt during the late antique period, specifically the 3rd century CE. It details the acquisition of land by an individual, Aurelius Isidoros Ptolemy, from the village of Karanis in the Arsinoite nome. The declaration meticulously lists the boundaries of the land, including measurements of individual plots (arouras), and names numerous witnesses and officials involved in the surveying process, such as geometers (Aphrodisios and Paulinos), land surveyors (Kopre, Herōn, Apolloniōn), and a boundary marker (Pannos). The text references the authority of Roman emperors Diocletian, Maximian, Constantius, and Maximian, indicating the document’s legitimacy under imperial rule. The presence of Greek alongside Latin elements suggests a bilingual administrative environment characteristic of Roman Egypt.

This fragmentary Latin text, likely originating from Egypt in the late 4th century CE, is a *Declaration of Persons* (Latin: *instrumentum personarum*), a standard document used for census or tax registration. The declaration is dated by the consulate of Valerius Licinianus Licinius and Flavius Valerius Constantinus, placing it in the late 350s or early 360s CE. It details the household of Aurelius Isidorus, a citizen of Heptanomia, within the Arsinoite nome, including his son Peon and a sworn oath to the gods and the rulers. The document was recorded before Ulpius Alexander, the census official for Heptanomia, and signed by him, as Isidorus was illiterate. The text reveals aspects of Roman administrative practice and the persistence of traditional religious oaths within the late Roman Empire.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 106174 (c.pap.lat;;215); Ptolemais Euergetis (Arsinoites); 29. Sept. 170
summary: This fragmentary Latin inscription, designated *AE* 1906, 173, documents the acceptance of an inheritance by a young woman named Valeria Sarapias Antinois. The text is a declaration, likely recorded by a *procurator*, Lucius Valerius Lucretianus Matidius, who is also identified as Plotinius, brother of the Antinoensians. It details that Valeria inherited from her father, according to the terms of his will, and confirms her status as his heir. The declaration specifies the inheritance originates from Lucretia Diodora, Valeria’s grandmother. The inscription was enacted in Arsinoite, a city within the Arsinoite nome of Egypt, and is dated to the eleventh year of the reign of Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus, specifically the second day of the month of Phaophi. The fragmentary nature of the text obscures portions of the declaration and the concluding remarks.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 10689 (p.diog;;10); Ptolemais Euergetis (Arsinoites); 3. Juni 211
summary: P.Coll.Youtie 1 64 is a fragmentary Latin testament, likely drafted in the third century CE. The document details the testamentary dispositions of Lucius Ignatius Rufinus of Antinoe, including bequests to his wife, Lucretia Octavia, and the designation of his brother, Lucius Ignatius Nemesianus, as his heir. The text outlines procedures for settling debts and the disposition of property, including land in Potamon and a portion of his house. A Greek colophon at the end records the reading and authentication of the will before an assembly in Arsinoe, a city in Upper Egypt, and lists several witnesses who affixed their signatures. The document provides insight into Roman legal practices, family relationships, and the administration of estates in a provincial setting under the Severan dynasty.

P.Fay. 105 Ro is a fragmentary Latin accounting document, likely a ledger or register, detailing financial transactions and deposits. The text primarily lists individuals and amounts in denarii and oboli, with occasional quadrantes and semisses. Names recur frequently, including Longinus, Dionusius, Pasion, Victor, and Apollinar(ius), suggesting a community or institution with recurring financial dealings. The document appears to categorize individuals by their deposits and debts, with references to 'viaticorum' (travel expenses) and 'recessa' (recesses, possibly indicating accounts or groups). The presence of 'turmae' suggests organizational units or teams, and the repeated phrase 'h(abet) d(epositos)' indicates recorded deposits. The text is severely damaged, rendering substantial portions illegible and obscuring the overall purpose and context of the record.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 110834 (zpe;203;267); erworben: Ägypten - 1923; Oxyrhynchites ?, Ägypten; I
summary: P.Harr. 1 35 Ro, alongside P.Harr. inv. 183e recto, represents a fragmentary Latin military pay-record, likely originating from the 1st century CE. The text consists of disbursements of stipends, recorded in drachmas and asses, to individuals identified by name. Lucius Clodius is explicitly named as a recipient. The record details payments for victuals, a *faenaria* (likely a fine or penalty), caligae fascias (military sandals), and a tunic, with a reference to a *saturnalicium kastrense* (a military Saturnalia celebration). The text is damaged, obscuring significant portions of the disbursement details and the names of other recipients, rendering a complete reconstruction of the payment list impossible. The document provides valuable, albeit incomplete, insight into the logistical and financial administration of a Roman military unit.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114356 (p.ital;2;36); Ravenna and Italy; 445-700 (series)
summary: P.Ital. 2 36 is a fragmentary Latin legal document, likely originating from Ravenna in the 6th century CE. The document is comprised of two distinct sections, each recording different aspects of a legal transaction. The first section details the sale of six unciae of land, designated *Fundi Geniciani*, including a *casale*, from Deusdedit to Hildigern for fourteen gold solidi, and specifies a thirty-day usufruct for the seller. The second section concerns the completion and absolution of a legal case, and lists numerous witnesses involved, including Eusebius, Florentinus, Oderit, Probus, and Petrus, whose occupations and affiliations provide insights into the social and administrative structure of the community. The presence of Greek inscriptions alongside the Latin text suggests a mixed linguistic environment. The document offers valuable evidence of property law, legal procedures, and social roles in late antique Italy.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114356 (p.ital;2;36); Ravenna and Italy; 445-700 (series)
summary: This section of a Latin legal document details the sale of a property, identified as six unciae of land called Fundi Geniciani with a casale (country house). The seller, identified as Deusdedit, transfers ownership to a buyer, Hildigern, for fourteen gold solidi. The document outlines the rights and responsibilities associated with the property, including guarantees against future claims and disturbances, and specifies a thirty-day usufruct period for the seller. Numerous witnesses, including Florentinus, Oderic, Probus, and Julianus, attest to the transaction and its financial details, with some providing signatures and Greek inscriptions.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114356 (p.ital;2;36); Ravenna and Italy; 445-700 (series)
summary: This fragment of a Latin legal document records the completion and absolution of a case, affirmed by witnesses. The document lists the names and roles of these witnesses, including Eusebius, a scriptorium assistant at the church of Saint Stephen; Florentinus, a baker's overseer at Santa Agnite; Oderit, son of Boherde; Probus, associated with the nomenclators; and Petrus, a collectarius formerly stationed before the jailer’s guard. The text provides a glimpse into the administrative and ecclesiastical roles within a late antique community.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114357 (p.ital;2;37); Ravenna and Italy; 445-700 (series)
summary: P.Ital. 2 37 is a fragmentary Latin legal document, likely a deed or contract, dating to the 6th century CE. The text records a series of transactions concerning land and wine within the territory of Genecianus, near Ariminum. It details the sale of six unciae of land from the estate of Genecianus to Iohannes, and subsequent sales of wine by Rusticiana and Tzitane. The document references previous agreements ('supraescripta') and involves multiple parties, including the seller Rusticiana, her deceased husband Felici, the guarantor Tzittane, the buyer Iohannes, and witnesses John and Deusdedit. Notary Honoratus is also mentioned, having received twenty-four gold solids. The transactions occurred in Classe, Ravenna, during the reign of Emperor Maurice Tiberius.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114357 (p.ital;2;37); Ravenna and Italy; 445-700 (series)
summary: This section of a legal document details the sale of six unciae (ounces) of land from the estate of Genecianus, located near Ariminum, to Iohannes. The transaction involves multiple parties: Rusticana, the seller; Felici, her deceased husband and former defender of the Roman church; Tzittane, a soldier and guarantor; and Iohannes, the buyer. The document meticulously outlines the transfer of ownership, the payment of twenty-four gold solids, and stipulations regarding future inheritance and potential disputes, all occurring in Classe, Ravenna, under the rule of Emperor Maurice Tiberius.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114357 (p.ital;2;37); Ravenna and Italy; 445-700 (series)
summary: This section of P.Ital. 2 37 continues to document a series of transactions involving wine and land (fundus) in Genecian territory. It details the sale of wine by Rusticiana, a female seller, and her husband Tzitane, with John and Deusdedit acting as witnesses and guarantors. The text repeatedly references previous entries (indicated by 'supraescripta') and mentions a price of twenty-four gold solids paid to someone named Honoratus, who appears as a Classian notary.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114360 (t.alb;;1); Theveste (Mauretania Caesariensis); 17. Sept. 493 (Jahr unsicher)
summary: T.Alb. 1 is a Latin *tabella doti*, or dowry tablet, likely originating from Roman Africa, dated to the ninth year of the reign of an unnamed, “unconquered” king, corresponding to 410-412 CE. The tablet details the items constituting Geminia Ianarilla’s dowry, given upon her marriage to Julian, presumably for the purpose of procreation. The list includes silver coins (*folles*), clothing (Dalmatian tunic, *colussa*), personal adornments (earrings, rings, armlets, *fasciae*, *orarium*), and household items (*lanari axiculi*). The tablet is structured as an inventory, with each item’s value listed in *folles*, culminating in a total of eleven thousand five hundred *folles*, with an additional five hundred *folles* added for embellishment. Julian, the groom, acknowledges receipt of the dowry at the end of the text.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114361 (t.alb;;2); Vandal Africa (Tablettes Albertini); 493-496 (series)
summary: T.Alb. 2 is a fragmentary Latin legal document, likely a manumission contract or sale agreement, originating from the late antique period, tentatively dated to the 5th century CE. The text details the sale of a boy named Fortinus, described as being approximately six years old and of fair complexion, by Donatianus, Victoris, and Saturninus, citizens of Cappraria, to Geminius Felix, a citizen of Tuletia. The transaction involved a solid gold coin and 700 folles of Bryziac gold weight. The document explicitly states that the sellers had previously possessed the boy and his rights, and that they would not seek further payment for the agreed-upon price. The text is damaged, particularly at the end, obscuring further details about the agreement and the subsequent actions of Geminius Felix. The presence of the king Gunthamund’s regnal year suggests a connection to the Kingdom of the Vandals in North Africa.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114362 (t.alb;;3); Vandal Africa (Tablettes Albertini); 493-496 (series)
summary: T.Alb. 3 is a Latin legal document, likely a land transfer agreement, dating to the 5th century CE. The text details the sale of parcels of land from Julius Leporius and Coia, his wife, along with Silvanianus and Victorinus, to Geminius Cresconius and Cresconia. The agreement specifies the location of the land, including references to *aggariones*, fields, and the road to Africa, and lists olive and fig trees marking boundaries. It includes a monetary transaction involving gold *solidus* and *folles*, and outlines legal protections for the buyer, including penalties for contesting the sale. Witnesses and individuals illiterate, indicated by their marks, are named, including Quadratianus, Paulinianus, Fortunatianus, and Montius, suggesting a rural community with a complex system of land ownership and legal procedures.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114363 (t.alb;;4); Vandal Africa (Tablettes Albertini); 493-496 (series)
summary: T.Alb. 4 is a Latin legal document, likely a deed or contract, dating to the late antique period, specifically the 5th century CE. It details the sale of two acres of land, including almond and fig trees, from Iulus Restitutus and his wife Donata to Geminius Felix. The document is structured around a formal transfer of ownership, witnessed by surveyors and attested to by multiple individuals, including children acting on behalf of their parents. It includes a standard warranty clause protecting the buyer against future claims, and specifies the price paid in folles. The location of the land is near the 'Gemione' stream, and the transaction occurred on the ides of January in the tenth year of the reign of King Gunthamund. The estate 'Magula' is also mentioned as the location where the agreement was finalized.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114364 (t.alb;;5); Vandal Africa (Tablettes Albertini); 493-496 (series)
summary: T.Alb. 5 is a Latin legal document, likely a deed or contract, dating to the late antique period, specifically the 5th century CE. It details the sale of land parcels, specifying boundaries and olive trees, between sellers Vigilianus, Aegyptia (his wife), and Secundianus Germanus, and unspecified buyers. The document is structured as a series of declarations and attestations, with witnesses and notaries (Lucianus, Donatus, Fidentius, Restitutus, Quoduultdeus) signing to confirm the transaction. Place names like Susanu and Gunfliones are mentioned, suggesting a rural setting, possibly in North Africa, given the presence of African names like Africus and the reference to a 'King Gunthamund'. The text includes clauses concerning inheritance, transfer of rights, and potential legal challenges, demonstrating a concern for future disputes and the protection of the buyer's interests.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114365 (t.alb;;6); Vandal Africa (Tablettes Albertini); 493-496 (series)
summary: T.Alb. 6 is a Latin legal document, likely a land sale agreement, dating to the 5th century CE. The text details the sale of a parcel of land located in Gunfliones, including its boundaries and appurtenances (olive, pistachio, and fig trees). The transaction occurred in the ninth year of the reign of King Gunthamund, under the auspices of Flavius Gemini Catullinus, a perpetual priest. The sellers are Martialis and his wife Donatilla, while Geminius Crescon and his wife Cresconia are the purchasers. The document meticulously lists witnesses and their relationships to the parties involved, including Lucianus, Quadratianus, Paulinianus, and Victorinus, and includes a clause regarding potential legal challenges and the price to be paid in such cases. The final lines confirm the agreement and the transfer of ownership, with a signature marking the involvement of Martialis and Donatilla.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114366 (t.alb;;7); Vandal Africa (Tablettes Albertini); 493-496 (series)
summary: T.Alb. 7 is a Latin legal document, likely a deed of sale, dating to the late antique period, specifically the 5th century CE. The text details the sale of parcels of agricultural land by Julius Victorinus Nugualis and his companion Fotta to Geminius Cresconius and Cresconia, his companion. The deed meticulously lists the boundaries of the land, referencing neighboring properties and individuals such as Marino, Pontianus, Flavius Gemini Catullinus (a *flamen perpetuus*), and Leporius Iaderis, as well as locations like Aggarione and Sicilione. The transaction involved the exchange of one gold solid, and the deed includes stipulations regarding future claims to the land and a reference to a *fundus Tuletianense*. Notably, the sellers, Fotta, are explicitly stated to be illiterate, and the document concludes with their marks and the signature of Secundianus, who witnessed the proceedings.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114367 (t.alb;;8); Vandal Africa (Tablettes Albertini); 493-496 (series)
summary: T.Alb. 8 is a Latin legal document, likely a deed of sale, dating to the late antique period, specifically the 5th century CE. The text details the transfer of a parcel of land, described as being 'beyond the hundred years,' from Julius Quoduuldeus, Restitutus (his son), and Donata (his wife) to Geminius Cresconius and Cresconia. The transaction occurred in Tuletium, a settlement likely in North Africa, in the ninth year of the reign of King Gunthamund. The deed includes a detailed description of the land's boundaries, references to a 'perpetual flamen' Flavius Gemini Catullinus, and a standard warranty clause protecting the purchasers’ rights. Witnesses include Innulus and Paulinianus, the latter signing on behalf of Quintianus, who was illiterate. The document concludes with a declaration of acceptance of the price and a final signature.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114368 (t.alb;;9); Vandal Africa (Tablettes Albertini); 493-496 (series)
summary: T.Alb. 9 is a Latin legal document, likely a deed of sale, originating from North Africa in the late antique period, specifically the mid-5th century CE. The text details the transfer of land, including olive groves, from Julius Maximanus and his wife Peregus to Geminius Felix. The transaction occurred in the tenth year of the reign of King Gunthamundus, a Vandal ruler, and involved witnesses including Lucianus, Quadratianus, and Victorinus, all of whom appear to have been illiterate and acting on behalf of the sellers. The document meticulously outlines the price (ninety folles), boundaries (referenced to Africa Donatus, Coro, and Magula), and legal guarantees concerning the transfer, including stipulations against future legal challenges and a promise of compensation should such challenges arise. The presence of the term *mancians* suggests a system of dependent laborers or serfs attached to the land.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114369 (t.alb;;10); Vandal Africa (Tablettes Albertini); 493-496 (series)
summary: T.Alb. 10 is a late antique Latin legal document, likely a manorial sale agreement, dating to the 5th century CE. The text details the sale of property, specifically a plot including a fig tree, from Julius Quintianus and his wife Gilesa to Geminius Felix. The location, identified as *in Buresa* within the larger *fundo Tuletianensis*, is described with reference to neighboring properties and boundary markers belonging to individuals named Marino, Africa, and Luciani. The document outlines the price paid (340 *folles*), the transfer of ownership, and stipulations regarding potential future claims of ownership, including a provision for compensation in cases of eviction. Witnesses include Quadratianus, Urbanus, and Paulinianus, with Quadratianus and Urbanus explicitly stating their roles as witnesses, and Paulinianus signing on behalf of his father, Quintus. The presence of signatures marked with 'X' indicates some of the parties were illiterate.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114370 (t.alb;;11); Vandal Africa (Tablettes Albertini); 493-496 (series)
summary: This Latin inscription (designated I.L.C. 88 in *Année Épigraphique* 1930) details the sale of property from Adeudata and her son Innulus to Geminius Felix. The document outlines the terms of the transaction, including the price (paid in folles), the location of the land (identified as *Sela Frustellum* within the *Tuletianensis* district), and stipulations regarding inheritance and potential disputes. Witnesses to the sale include Donatianus, Saturninus of Egypt, and Muraena, who attest to the agreement. The inscription references the rule of King Gunthamund, placing the transaction in the 10th year of his reign, likely in the mid-5th century CE. It also mentions Flavian Gemini Catullinus, presumably an official with authority over the region, and the presence of fig trees and vines on the property.

T.Alb. 12 is a Latin deed of sale (acte de vente) dating to the late antique period, likely the mid-5th century CE. The document details the transfer of a plot of land, designated 'Gemione,' from Victorinus and his yoke-fellow Fotta to Geminius Felix. The transaction occurred in the tenth year of the reign of King Gunthamund, specifically on the sixth day before the Kalends of November. The land's boundaries are defined by reference to olive trees, a fig tree, the boundary of Buresa, and the location 'Africo,' with a mention of 'Coro' and a path ('via') from Marino. The deed includes a clause protecting Geminius Felix's ownership and outlining recourse in case of dispute, and concludes with attestations by Nobelianus, Magarius, Saturninus, and Pulcherius, who attest to the illiteracy of Victorinus and Fotta and their marks (signa). The text demonstrates a rural economy and legal practices of the Vandal Kingdom in North Africa.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114372 (t.alb;;13); Vandal Africa (Tablettes Albertini); 493-496 (series)
summary: T.Alb. 13 is a Latin legal document, likely a land sale agreement, dating to the late antique period, specifically the mid-5th century CE. The text details the sale of property, identified as 'Mancianis,' located near 'Tres Arbores,' involving Processus and his wife Siddina as sellers and Geminius Felix as the buyer. Witnesses include Donatianus, Quoduultdeus, and Saturninus of Egypt, who attest to the transaction on behalf of the illiterate Processus and Siddina. The document establishes conditions for future ownership, outlining penalties for contesting the sale and specifying the value of the land at the time of transfer. It is structured as a formal declaration, with repeated affirmations of the agreement and signatures marking its validity, suggesting a deliberate effort to create a legally binding record.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114373 (t.alb;;14); Vandal Africa (Tablettes Albertini); 493-496 (series)
summary: T.Alb. 14 is a Latin legal document, likely a manorial sale deed, dating to the 5th century CE. It records the sale of olive groves in the vicinity of Pullatis, located within a larger estate under the authority of Flavius Gemini Catullinus. The sellers are Messius Victorinus and his wife Fotta, who are transferring ownership to Geminius Felix. The document details the boundaries of the land, mentioning Marino and Africa as points of reference, and includes witness signatures and marks, including those of Saturninus, a presbyter, and Geminius Urbanianus. A notable element is the inclusion of Nuguali, who claims illiteracy and requires Saturninus's assistance in the transaction, highlighting a potential literacy divide. The text concludes with a standard formula regarding potential disputes and the price paid.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 114374 (t.alb;;15); Vandal Africa (Tablettes Albertini); 493-496 (series)
