summary: This fragmentary Latin inscription, designated *AE* 1896, 21, originates from Seleucia Pieria and documents a manumission agreement dated to the consular year of Quintus Servilius Pudens and A. Fufidius Pollio (101 CE). Caius Fabullius Macer, an *optio* in the Praetorian Fleet stationed at Misenum, purchased a boy named Abban (also known as Eutychen) from Quintus Julius Priscus, also a soldier in the same fleet. The text details the price (two hundred denarii and a port charge), stipulations regarding the boy’s health, and witnesses to the transaction, including Caius Julius Antiochus, a *manipularius* on the trireme *Virtute*, and several other officers. A Greek inscription at the end appears to record a debt owed by a tenant, Domitius Germanus, related to a school or *praseos* associated with Abban and Eutychen, suggesting a possible connection between the manumission and education. The inscription’s structure suggests a formal legal document, likely recorded on a stone tablet.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 118645 (p.oxy;73;4955); Oxyrhynchos; spätes I - frühes II
summary: P.Oxy. 73 4955 is a fragmentary Latin military roster, likely dating to the 1st century CE. The document lists soldiers organized into *centuriae* (centuries), with names appearing under various leaders. Individuals named include Quintus Voconius Saturninus, Marcus Antonius, Marcus Tullius, Titus Flauius, Marcus Dellius, Caius Iulius Firmus, Caius Iulius Crisp, Quintus Vettius Pude, Publius Vettius D..., Marcus Acillius, Lucius Antonius, and Titus Flauius Maior. The roster appears to be structured around these centuriae, with some entries noting specific locations or equipment, such as a *porticus* (portico), *castellum* (small fort), *fistulis* (pipes/tubes), and *alabastrona* (alabastrae/ointment jars). The final line indicates a distribution or allotment (*ededit*) by Publius Ac...[...]. The text is significantly damaged, rendering much of the organization and content obscure.

This fragmentary Latin inscription, designated *Année épigraphique* 1929, 13, constitutes a birth certificate for twins born to an unknown father in Alexandria, Egypt, during the reign of Emperor Marcus Aurelius. The document details the naming of the twins, Marcus Sempronius Sarapion and Marcus Sempronius Socration, and includes attestations signed by various individuals, including Gaius Julius Saturninus, who appears to have acted as a tutor or guardian. The inscription references Roman law—specifically, the *lex Aelia Sentia* and *lex Papia Poppaea*—which regulated the registration of names and aimed to prevent the listing of illegitimate or spurious individuals. The text is written on two tablets and records the date as the third day before the Kalends of May, in the eighth year of Marcus Aurelius’ reign, during the month of Pachon. The inscription also indicates that Sempronia Gemella, the mother, was illiterate, and that Gaius Julius Saturninus acted on her behalf.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 121942 (chla;21;717); Ravenna and Italy; 445-700 (series)
summary: P.Ital. 1 20 is a Latin document from late antiquity, dated to the 6th century CE, consisting of two distinct sections detailing a land donation. The first section outlines the transfer of a plot of land named Balonianum, along with its appurtenances, from Sisivera to the Holy Church of Ravenna, and includes clauses designed to ensure its permanence, referencing prior grants from Theudifara. The second section continues to elaborate on the land transfer, listing numerous witnesses including Iannes, Sisevera, Laurentius, and Iulius, and referencing sacraments and a holy cross, further establishing a religious context. The document’s structure is primarily legal, focusing on the conveyance of property rights and the validation of the transaction through oaths and witness testimony. The presence of both Latin and Greek names suggests a diverse community within Ravenna at the time. The text’s content highlights the ongoing importance of land ownership and ecclesiastical institutions in late antique Italy.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 121942 (chla;21;717); Ravenna and Italy; 445-700 (series)
summary: This section of the document details a land donation from a woman named Sisivera to the Holy Church of Ravenna. The donation includes a specific plot of land called Balonianum, along with all its associated properties and rights, including vineyards, pastures, and water sources. The text emphasizes the irrevocability of the donation and includes various legal clauses and oaths intended to prevent its revocation, referencing earlier grants from Theudifara and invoking divine sanction.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 121942 (chla;21;717); Ravenna and Italy; 445-700 (series)
summary: Part 2 of P.Ital. 1 20 continues to detail a complex land donation, likely related to a church or religious institution in Ravenna. The text lists numerous witnesses and officials involved in the transaction, including individuals with Greek names like Iannes and Sisevera, alongside Latin names like Laurentius and Iulius. The document emphasizes the transfer of property ('Baloniani') and its associated rights, alongside references to sacraments and a holy cross, suggesting a religious context for the donation.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 121943 (chla;29;865); Ravenna and Italy; 445-700 (series)
summary: P.Ital. 1 24 is a Latin legal document, likely a deed or charter, dating to the 6th century CE. The text details the transfer of a garden, described with specific features like pergulas, a well, and access points, via usufructuary donation. Gaudiosus is identified as the donor, transferring the property to a “most reverend defender” of the church of Ravenna, whose name is unfortunately lost to corruption. The document includes witness statements and affirmations, and references to holy Gospels, suggesting a formal, ecclesiastical context. A significant portion of the text is written in Greek, complicating interpretation and indicating possible bilingual practices. The presence of a *primicerius* of a school for foreigners suggests a diverse community in Ravenna.

CPR 5 13 comprises a collection of military service certificates (Latin: *Certificati di servizio militare*) likely issued from a fort near Psofthis (modern-day Tell el-Maskhuta) in Roman Egypt, dating to the late antique period, specifically the 5th century CE. The documents appear to be official correspondence between military officials, detailing the assignment of personnel to schools (*scholae*)—likely training units—and recording their stipends. Several letters are addressed to a *praefectus castri* (fort prefect) named Dionysius, and reference earlier prefects. The texts mention emperors Arcadius and Honorius, reflecting the dual Roman imperial system of the time, and name individuals such as Flavius Heraclianus, Flavius Pulcher, Sarapion, and Eleutherius. The certificates list various military ranks including *catafractarii*, *decuriones*, and *equites*, alongside their financial allotments, suggesting a system of military administration and record-keeping.

P.Ryl. 4 611 is a fragmentary Latin declaration, likely a legal document, originating from Arsinoe in Roman Egypt. The text records a testimony given by a soldier named Arsinoite, identified as belonging to the legion XXII. The declaration concerns a marriage ( *conubium* ) granted by the Emperor, presumably Domitian, to Arsinoite and a woman named Heraide. The document is dated twice, once to the seventh year of Domitian’s imperial rule and again to the same year with consuls Lucius Uolusio Saturninus and another unnamed consul. The fragmentary nature of the text obscures the precise reason for the testimony and the full context of the marriage, but it provides valuable insight into legal proceedings and imperial involvement in personal matters within the Roman military community in Egypt.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 131505 (chla;21;714); Ravenna and Italy; 445-700 (series)
summary: P.Ital. 1 6 is a fragmentary Latin testament, likely originating from Ravenna in the late antique period, specifically the 6th century CE. The document details the testamentary arrangements of a man named Mannan, including the designation of the Catholic Church of Ravenna as his heir. Numerous witnesses are listed, including individuals with diverse roles such as scribes (Emilianus), magistrates (Melminius Cassianus), and accountants (Quiriacus), alongside personal names like Iohannes, Riccitanc, and Theodosius. The text is punctuated by Greek insertions, suggesting a mixed linguistic environment. The document’s structure is somewhat repetitive, with multiple attestations of witnesses and reiterations of the inheritance clause, indicating a formalized legal process. The presence of imperial references to Justin, perpetual Augustus, firmly places the document within the reign of Justinian I.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 13757 (psi;9;1027); Ptolemais Euergetis (Arsinoites); 5. Dez. 151
summary: PSI 9 1027 is a fragmentary Latin legal document, specifically an attestation relating to the inheritance of Lucius Herennius Vales. The text details the testamentary arrangements made by Vales, naming his daughter, Herennia Helena, as his heir. The attestation is delivered by Marcia Athenaide, the mother of Herennia Helena, with Lucian Valerius Onno acting as her tutor and procurer. The document records the witnessing of the will's contents by those present, and its examination against the original records. It was drafted in the nome (province) of Arsinoite, likely in Egypt, during the consulship of Duos Aquilius Condianus and Quintilius Maximus, in the fifteenth year of the reign of Emperor Caesar (likely Augustus). A Greek colophon at the end confirms the testimony of Marcia Athenaide and identifies Gaius Valerius Onno as acting on Helena’s behalf, noting her illiteracy.

This fragmentary Latin text, likely originating from the second century CE, appears to be a draft of a protocol or record of a legal proceeding, interspersed with personal notes. The document concerns a dispute taking place in Caesarea, likely in the province of Palaestina, within a temple setting. A Roman veteran, Valerius Serenas, hailing from the village of Meason in the Pereas region, is the central figure, seemingly seeking recognition or inclusion within a group of individuals who have heard a declaration. The overseer Ailios Amphigethis, acting on behalf of a ‘revered one’ (whose identity is obscured), presides over the proceedings. References to a ‘tablet’ and a ‘matrix’ suggest the involvement of official records or documentation, and the text hints at a process of marking or signing, possibly related to validation or confirmation. The document's abrupt ending and corruptions make a complete reconstruction of the events impossible, but it offers a glimpse into Roman legal practices and veteran status in the Roman East.

This fragmentary Latin text, tentatively identified as a draft of a proceedings record or notes (PapCongr. XIII, Marburg 1971, p. 241-), appears to be a personal petition or account from a Roman veteran, likely dating to the 2nd century CE. The document details a debt owed to the veteran by a slave named Aurelius, who served in the Third Cyrenaica Legion (Legio III Cyrenaica), specifically in the century commanded by a centurion named Julius Valentis. The veteran requests intervention to compel Aurelius to repay a loan of three denarii, referencing previous inquiries about the debt. The text is heavily damaged, with numerous lacunae obscuring the precise context and intended recipient of the petition, but it provides a glimpse into the financial dealings and military service of individuals within the Roman army. The presence of a slave and the reference to a legionary’s century offer insight into the social and military structure of the period.

O.Did. 417 is a fragmentary Latin letter, likely originating from the 2nd century CE, based on paleographic assessment. The letter consists of three discrete messages, each addressed to or mentioning Claudius. The first section is a greeting and instruction from Demetrius to Claudius, concerning the receipt of goods (specifically, grain and bread) and a warning to avoid unspecified dangers. The second section is a greeting from Numisios, who identifies himself as Claudius’ brother and teacher, and requests information regarding the sale of a *contubernium* (likely a tent or shared lodging). The final section contains greetings to Crescens, described as a fellow-countryman, and a request to inquire about the receipt of an *esabarium* (a military load or baggage), alongside a greeting to a person named Diurrpain. The text’s condition prevents a full understanding of some phrases, notably the ending of the first section and a lacuna in the second.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 144990 (o.did;;429); Didymoi; vor (?) ca. 96
summary: O.Did. 429 is a fragmentary Latin letter, likely composed in the 1st century CE, written by Iulius Priscus to his brother Vettio. The letter begins with a conventional greeting and invocation of the gods, followed by an expression of affection and familial closeness. A list of names follows, seemingly intended as greetings to be passed on; these include Casillas, Didimion, Valerius (identified as a *curator*), Vibius Antonius, Doles, Tet[?]manus, and others whose names are lost due to lacunae. The letter concludes abruptly with a mention of Iulius and a military detachment (*praesidio*) and the single word 'Eros,' the meaning of which is unclear within the context. The text is damaged, particularly at the beginning and end, obscuring the full content and intended conclusion of the letter.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 14904 (sb;20;14726); Ptolemais Euergetis (Arsinoites); 1. Hälfte 399
summary: Stud.Pal. 14 p. 4 & pl. 11 [right] preserves a fragmentary letter, likely official in nature, written in Latin with embedded Greek phrases. The text appears to originate from the late antique period, tentatively dated to the 4th century CE, based on the paleography and language. It is addressed from three *praefecti praetorio* – Flavius Eutychianus, Flavius Vincentius, Flavius Anatolius, and Flavius Auienus – to an unnamed provincial prefect. The content concerns a dispute or denial within Arcadia, referencing demands and public officials, and alludes to past precedents. A significant portion of the letter consists of instructions given by “divine and magnificent governors” and a magistrate regarding the maintenance of order, and a warning about a danger requiring a response.

This is a *testatio*, or sworn testimony, likely intended for official record, dating to the second century CE. Marcus Lucretius Clemens, a Roman *eques* (horseman) serving in the first Thracian cohort of the Siluanus troop, swears an oath by Jupiter and the *numina* (divine spirits) of the August emperors to attest to the birth of his natural son, Serene, from Octavia Tamusta. The testimony details Serene’s birthdate as the VII Kal. Maias (May 7th) of the eleventh year of the reign of Emperor Trajan Hadrian Augustus. Lucretius Clemens states his reason for the testimony was to allow him to prove Serene’s legitimacy after his military service. The document was drafted at the winter camp of the cohort, near Apollonopolis in Magna Thebaidis (likely modern-day Thebes, Greece), and lists several witnesses, including Caius Antonius Maximus, Marcus Arrius Antonius, and Gaius Iulius Marcellus, all serving within the same military unit.

P.Wisc. 2 50 is a collection of fragmentary Latin documents from the second century CE, likely originating from Roman Egypt. The texts appear to be legal or administrative in nature, containing elements of a manumission decree, a birth testimony, and a related confession. The documents are dated to the consulship of M. Gaius Orfitus and L. Arrius Pudens in the fifth year of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus’ reign, and again to the sixth year of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and L. Aurelius Verus’ joint consulship. Aelia Sentia is a prominent figure, involved in the birth testimony, and the law of Papia Poppaea is explicitly referenced. The presence of Greek inscriptions, specifically the names “Ονιακὸς ἀρχιραβδοῦχος,” suggests interaction with a Greek-speaking community. The final fragments involve a Caius Iulius Noninus, a legionary, and mention individuals named Veim, Eutychus, and Vel(ius) Nemesius Rufus.

This document, published in *ZPE* 36 (1979), is a Latin *Schuldurkunde*, or debt acknowledgement, originating from the 1st century CE. The text details a debt of two hundred drachmas of Augustan and Ptolemaic coinage owed by Lucius Caecilius Secundus, a Roman *eques* (knight) serving in the *ala Paullini turma*, to Gaius Pompeius, a soldier in a cohort of the *auxilia*. The acknowledgement specifies the repayment terms, including interest to be paid monthly in drachmas and asses, and lists additional items pledged as collateral: a cash box, a signet ring, and a silver-backed dagger, all originating from Alexandria. The document concludes with a consular dateline indicating the eighth day before the Kalends of September, during the consulship of Gaius Sallustius Crispus and Lucius Lentulus Scipio. A Greek inscription at the end appears to record the same transaction, dated to the 13th year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar Augustus.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 16888 (p.oxy;31;2565); Alexandria; 26. Mai - 24. Juni 224
summary: P.Oxy. 31, 2565 is a fragmentary Latin document containing declarations of birth, likely issued as part of a larger register. The text is organized around individual birth announcements, each stating the names of the parents and the child, alongside the date of birth. The declarations were made during the consulship of Julianus and Crispinus, in the third year of the reign of Emperor Marcus Aurelius Severus Alexander. The document originates from Alexandria, Egypt, and bears the official endorsement of Aurelius Epagathus, the prefect of Egypt. The declarations are dated to the month of Pauni and the day before the Ides of August, during the consulship of Gratus and Seleucus. The fragmentary nature of the text obscures the full extent of the register and the precise details of several birth announcements, including the names of individuals and the exact date of birth.

PSI 13, 1308 is a fragmentary Latin list, likely a roster or register of sailors, dating to the 2nd century CE. The text is severely damaged, rendering a complete understanding of its organization impossible, but it appears to enumerate individuals by name. Several consular datelines are present, including those of Claro Iterum, Avito, Homullus, and Antoninus, suggesting the list was compiled or updated across a span of years. Names identifiable within the fragments include Apollinaris, Valerius Rufus, Iulius Maximus, Aponianus, Volusius Seneca, and Nephyas. The presence of the title *faber Augusti nostri* (craftsman of our Augustus) indicates a connection to imperial service, and the term *caligati* suggests a reference to a specific category of seafarers, possibly those wearing sandals. The document provides a glimpse into the personnel of a maritime operation during the Roman Empire, though its precise purpose remains unclear due to the fragmentary nature of the text.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 17284 (p.berl.zill;;4); Hermopolis (Hermopolites, Ägypten); ca. 350
summary: P.Berl.Zill. 4 is a fragmentary Latin legal document, likely a transcript of a judicial proceeding held before the *praeses Thebaidis* in the 4th century CE. The text details a dispute involving accusations of financial impropriety and potential obstruction of justice, centering on a man named Irpion and his relationship to Gaianos. Witnesses, including Strategius, a high-ranking official (identified as *vir perfectissimus, comes et praeses Thebaidis*), and Theodosius, an advocate, participate in the proceedings. The document concerns accusations of Irpion's actions regarding a treasury, land holdings, and debts, and includes appeals to the presiding official's virtue for a favorable outcome. The structure is primarily dialogic, presenting questions and responses between the officials and the accused, with references to legal precedents and the involvement of an *oikonomos* and an *exaktor* (overseer). The document highlights themes of property rights, legal process, and the responsibilities of public officials in Roman Thebaїs.

P.Ryl. 4 609 is a Latin official letter, likely emanating from the Thebaic Limitis region, dated to the 6th century CE. The letter is addressed from Flavius Constantinus Theophanes, *comes* and *vir illustris*, to Flavius Verte or Theodotius, described as *devotissimus*. It concerns the assignment of a young man, Heracleon, son of Constantinus from Hermopolis, to Verte/Theodotius’ vexillation, specifying his military suitability and lack of civilian status. The letter references Anastasius, a *piissimus* and *triumphator Augustus*, whose sacred command is invoked, and mentions the provision of supplies to Heracleon, alongside Sabinianus and Theodorus, described as *clarissimi consules*. The concluding remarks indicate Heracleon’s impending service aboard a ship and a confirmation of his age.

P.Ryl. 4 623 is a fragmentary Latin letter of recommendation, likely written in the late 4th century CE. The letter is addressed from Vitalis, identified as a *rationalis* (likely an administrator or accountant), to his lord, Delphinius. It concerns Theophanes, a man originating from Hermopolis in the Thebaid province, who is being presented for consideration, presumably for a position or opportunity. The letter references Vitalis’ brother, Philip, and Dyscol, whose office is mentioned in connection with a burdensome journey. The text is unfortunately damaged, particularly at the end, obscuring the precise nature of the recommendation and the reasons for Theophanes’ candidacy. The surviving portion emphasizes Delphinius’ benevolence and the importance of honoring those entrusted to Vitalis.

P.Ryl. 4 610 is a fragmentary Latin legal document, specifically an *antrag auf Gewährung der bonorum possessio*, a petition requesting the right to possess the property of a deceased individual named Aurelia. The text is written in Latin, with interspersed Greek words and phrases, indicating a mixed linguistic environment likely within Egypt. It is addressed to Marcus Aedinius Julianus, the *praefectus Aegypti* (Prefect of Egypt), and transmitted through Tiberius Horionem, acting as a *curator*. The petition is dated to the consulship of Mario Maximus II and Roscius Aelianus, corresponding to 13 days before the Kalends of May (May 13th), of an unspecified year. The document references a list of witnesses and a subscription, alongside names including Aurelius Asclus Eupator, Caius Terentius Sarapammonis, Marcus Iulius Felicus, Lucius Titus, and Iulius …clis Marcus Aurelius. The fragmentary nature of the text obscures the full argument and details of the inheritance dispute.

P.Cair. Cat. 10268 is a fragmentary Latin process protocol, likely originating from the Thebaid region of Roman Egypt and datable to the 3rd century CE. The text records a legal proceeding concerning the guardianship of a minor, the daughter of a man named Claudianus. Athenodorus, designated *uir perfectissimus* and *praeses Thebaid(os)* (governor of Thebaid), presides over the proceedings and issues rulings. The protocol details a dispute involving Timagenes and Helladius, who have initiated a legal action. A *curator* is appointed for the minor, and the text concerns the timing of the presentation of evidence and the proper conduct of the appointed judge. The document is written primarily in Latin, interspersed with Greek phrases, indicating a mixed linguistic environment.

P.Cair. Masp. 3 67320 is a late antique legal document, likely a decree or imperial rescript, written in Greek and dating to the 6th century CE. The text concerns the provision of grain and wine rations to soldiers of the unit *Antaios*, a military designation, and details the quantities owed for the second six-month period of the fifth indiction. It outlines a judicial order instructing local authorities to fulfill these obligations and warns of legal consequences for failure to comply. The document references the *theiou palatiou*, likely a palace administration, and identifies the author as Flavius Menas Iustinianos Demosthenes, *notarius praetorian* and *archon* of the Thebaid province. The text is structured as a formal communication, beginning with the identification of officials and proceeding to the specific requirements for the delivery of supplies, concluding with a mention of payment forms.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 18454 (chla;41;1194); Antaiopolites; 26. Mai - 24. Juni 524
summary: P.Cair. Masp. 3 67329 is a fragmentary Latin process-verbal, likely dating to the 6th century CE, documenting a land transfer dispute within the administrative district of Aphrodite, near Antaiopolis. The document records testimony concerning the transfer of land from the village of Thmonachthe to Aphrodite, involving several individuals and their properties, including arouras (land measurements). Witnesses, such as Antaiopol and Sionos, testify under oath, with Phoibammon acting as a public boatman and Psiamanobet as a notable figure. The text details specific allotments of land belonging to individuals like Besios Anoubion, Leontios, Victor Tabellion, and Eutropius Coriannus, and references a church named Euprosynos. The organization appears to be a series of testimonies and declarations related to the transfer, with a focus on legal and administrative procedures.

ZRG42 (1921), p. 452-468, is a fragmentary Latin document, likely a legal or mercantile record, dating to the 2nd century CE. The text consists of three discrete paragraphs, each beginning with a subscription indicating the consuls Gaius Curtius Iustus, Pouplius Iulius Nautones, and Sextus Nones of October. The first paragraph details a message to be delivered to Titus Memmius Montanus regarding the sending of five denarii. The second paragraph references the sale of a girl named Marmarica, with mention of Sescentius Vigenti Cyncye Pretioum Poellae Marmarica vetranes, and notes the transaction occurred at the camp of the fleet. Finally, Domitius Theophilus confirms his presence at the sale of Marmarica, acting as a witness for Aischines, son of Aischinos, Flavian of Miletus. The document’s brevity and fragmented nature suggest it is a portion of a larger collection of records.

SB 3 7181 a is a fragmentary collection of receipts, likely pertaining to the provisioning of Roman military forces. The text is written in Greek, with interspersed Latin phrases, and dates to the third century CE. It details disbursements of bread and wine, specifying quantities and associated costs. The first receipt, addressed to an unnamed recipient, records the delivery of 2841 loaves of bread and 300 additional loaves, with a price of one obol per loaf. A subsequent section, written in Latin, documents the receipt of 640 castrense rations of wine by Titus Flavius Euthenarch, commander of a cohort, at Oxyrhynchus, again with a specified price per sextarius. The document names Timos, a surveyor, Valerius Valentinus, a prefect of Egypt, and Titus Flavius Valerianus, strategos of Oxyrhynchus, as key individuals involved in the transactions. The consular dates indicate the year of Antoninus III and Comaszone II.

P.Cair. Masp. 1 67030 is a fragmentary Latin letter, likely an official dispatch, dating to the 6th century CE. The text concerns the collection and transport of grain as part of a tithe or tax obligation. It is addressed to individuals from the village of Aphrodite tou Antaiopoliton, instructing them to deliver a specified quantity of grain to Alexandria. The letter emphasizes the urgency of the task, referencing a previous assessment and warning of consequences for any negligence. Numerical data detailing grain quantities in *artabae* and *kagkeloi* are appended, suggesting a detailed accounting system was in place. The letter’s author, whose name is lost, clearly held authority within the provincial administration of Thebaid.

P.Cair. Masp. 1 67031 is a late antique (6th century CE) Latin administrative decree, likely issued in or near Thebes, Egypt. The document concerns the regulation of *sportulones*, individuals who appear to be making offerings or requests related to religious or state matters. It details a procedure for handling payments and potential disputes arising from these requests, referencing both written and unwritten regulations. The decree names Flavius Iohannes Theodorus, Menas, Nar[se]s, Chnoub[a]mm[o]ōn, Horion, and Hphaistos, who are identified as officials of Thebaean origin, and references the rulers Flavius Justinus and Aelia Sophia. The text concludes with a date: 13 Kalendas Decembris (December 13th), and mentions Antinoopolis, suggesting a connection to that region. The decree's focus on financial obligations and dispute resolution highlights the intersection of religious practice, state administration, and local customs in late Roman Egypt.

P.Ryl. 2 79 is a fragmentary Latin military list, likely originating from Roman Egypt, dated paleographically to the 2nd century CE. The text consists of a series of names, presumably soldiers or members of military units, arranged in columns, with each column headed by the names of two consuls. The consuls listed are Commodus and Pompeianus, Stloga and Severus, Rufinus and Quadratus, Sereno and Maximo, and Gallicanus and Titianus, providing a chronological sequence for the list’s composition. The presence of the name 'Domitius' and references to 'Liburnia' and 'Asiaticó' suggest connections to specific military units or regions within the Roman Empire. The text is unfortunately damaged, obscuring many names and details, but its structure reveals a systematic organization intended to record military personnel alongside the consular dates of their service.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 201528 (jra.suppl;28;132_8); Carthago (Africa Proconsularis); 373 (Jahr unsicher)
summary: This fragmentary Latin inscription, likely from the late antique period (4th century CE), appears to be a register or catalogue of individuals, each identified by a designation “centenarius” (hundred) and associated with a weight given in Roman pounds (librae). The inscription lists names such as Obbalus, Metrianus, Lampadius, Marinus, Tutus, Livianus, and Ignuus, alongside numerical values representing weights, some expressed in hundreds and others in thousands of pounds. The fragmentary nature of the text makes a complete reconstruction of the list impossible; numerous names and weight values are lost due to damage. The presence of the abbreviation 'p(ondo)' consistently preceding the weight values confirms that these are measurements. The inscription’s purpose remains unclear, but the systematic listing suggests a possible connection to taxation, military service, or some other form of communal obligation.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 201529 (jra.suppl;28;134_10); Carthago (Africa Proconsularis); 373 (Jahr unsicher)
summary: This fragmentary Latin inscription, likely dating to the 4th century CE and discovered in Keiner, appears to record weights and quantities, possibly related to a fiscal or administrative inventory. The text is structured around repeated phrases indicating 'centenarius' (hundred) and 'summa' (total), followed by numerical values expressed in pounds (librae). The inscription details quantities of ashes (as(copae)) originating from Byzace, transported to a storehouse (conditorium) in Zeugita, and packaged in twin amphorae. The presence of numerical values suggests a system of measurement and accounting, potentially linked to taxation or resource management. The inscription’s corruption obscures the full extent of the inventory, but the repeated units of hundreds and pounds indicate a large-scale operation. The mention of Byzace and Zeugita provides geographical context for the inscription’s origin.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 201935 (jra.suppl;28;141_22); Carthago (Africa Proconsularis); 6. Juni 373 (Jahr unsicher)
summary: This fragmentary Latin inscription, likely from the late antique period (4th century CE), appears to record a series of transactions involving cloth (*as(copae)*) originating from Byzace (modern-day İzmit, Turkey). The text details quantities of cloth measured in *centenaria* (hundredweights), pounds (*librae*), and references specific dates: the *III Kal(endas) Iun(ias)* (March 1st) and the *VIII Idus Iun(ias)* (June 8th). Numerical data is prominent, with repeated counts and weights, suggesting a commercial or accounting context. The inscription mentions *Iu…as(copae)*, likely a recipient or associated with the cloth trade, and references a total sum (*summa*) calculated in pounds. Significant portions of the inscription are damaged, obscuring names, quantities, and potentially the overall purpose of the record, leaving the precise nature of the transactions unclear.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 203169 (jra.suppl;28;139_18); Carthago (Africa Proconsularis); 6. Mai 373 (Jahr unsicher)
summary: This inscription, published in *Année épigraphique* 1912, 70, appears to be a fragmentary inventory or accounting record from the late Roman Empire, likely dating to the 4th century CE. The text details quantities of goods, specifically *centenaria* (hundredweights) and pounds, alongside references to various containers: *ascopae* (measures) and *amphorae*. The record lists quantities associated with individuals named Victor, Felix, Inventus, and references locations including Byzaca, Zeugitan, and Tebelbucitan. It also mentions Roman oil, a 'Roman canon' of measures, and quantities of goods originating from and destined for Byzaca and a *conditorium* (storehouse) at Zeugitan. The inscription’s organization is primarily numerical, presenting a series of weights and measures, with some personal and locational identifiers interspersed.

P.Oxy. 4 720 is a fragmentary Latin legal document, likely a petition or request, dating to the third century CE. It appears to be a formal application for the appointment of a guardian, Aurelius Plutammon, for an individual named Aurelia Ammonario. The text references the *Lex Iulia Titia* and a *senatus consultum*, suggesting the request is being made under specific legal provisions concerning guardianship. The document is addressed to Gaius Valerius Firmo, the *praefectus Aegypti* (Prefect of Egypt), indicating the request is being made to an official authority. A portion of the text is written in Greek, including a statement that Aurelia Ammonario has 'delivered' someone (likely Plutammon) and that Plutammon approves of the request. The document is dated to the consulship of Philippus Augustus and Philippus Caesar, providing a precise chronological marker.

P.Oxy. 4 735 is a fragmentary Latin military account dating to the 3rd century CE. The document appears to be a disbursement record, listing quantities of wheat (fifty *artabae*) allocated for a specific period, the month of Thoth in the 14th year of the reigns of the Augusti. Several individuals are named, including Marrius Conus, Valerius Isidori, and Oiktor Kōmarinou Kaisarōn, who is identified as an *oikonomos* (steward). Military personnel are also listed, including centurions Belei, Beleus, Zabdius, and their colleague Claudius Sabinus Ierraeus, alongside other soldiers like Macchana Gaddes and Avidus Themes. The text is severely damaged, obscuring much of the content, but it provides a glimpse into the logistical administration of a Roman military unit, likely stationed in Egypt, and the names of individuals involved in its operation.

P.Fouad 1 45 is a Latin loan agreement, likely originating from a military context in Roman Egypt. The document records a debt of fifty denarii owed by Antonius Heronianus, a cavalryman of the veteran Gallic *ala*, to Accius Anthistianus, also a cavalryman of the same unit. The text is structured as a confession of debt, outlining the amount owed, the repayment schedule (tied to a future salary), and the inclusion of lawful interest. It specifies the recipient of the repayment, extending to a procurator or heir, and guarantees the transaction’s validity without dispute or delay. The agreement concludes with a witness statement and a Greek colophon, indicating a bilingual (Latin/Greek) document likely intended for a mixed Roman-Egyptian audience. The date is indicated by the consular names Brutus Praesente and Iunius Rufinus, placing it in the Roman year 161 CE.

P.Mich. 3 162 is a fragmentary Latin military list, likely originating from Roman Egypt in the 2nd century CE. The document appears to record personnel assigned to military units, identified by their names and, in some instances, their tribal or ethnic affiliations (e.g., *Coptites*, *Anti(noites)*). The list is organized chronologically by the consuls of Rome, providing a sequence of years within which these personnel were serving. Names recur throughout the list, suggesting a roster of individuals serving across multiple years or units. Individuals named include Julius Ammonianus, Cassius, Aurelius Victor, and Pompeius Sarapionis. A final, detached fragment in Greek records a debt owed from Apollonarios, brother of someone unnamed.

P.Mich. 3 165 is a fragmentary Latin legal document, specifically a petition requesting the appointment of a guardian. The text is written on ostraca, likely fragments of pottery, and is dated to the year 3 of the reign of Emperor Maximinus Augustus (235-238 CE) based on the imperial dating formula. The petitioner, Aurelia Diodora, appeals to Mevius Honoratianus, the *praefectus* of Egypt, requesting that Aurelius Theon be appointed her guardian, citing the *lex Iulia*, the *lex Titia*, and a *senatus consultum* as legal justification. A Greek colophon at the end of the text indicates that the petition was written on Diodora’s behalf by Asclepius, son of Isidoros, as she is illiterate. The document provides valuable insight into legal procedures and social structures in Roman Egypt, demonstrating the use of legal frameworks and the reliance on appointed guardians.

This fragmentary Latin inscription, designated *Année épigraphique* 1931.88, represents a birth certificate or register entry from Alexandria, Egypt, dated to the reign of Marcus Aurelius (161-180 CE). The text details the registration of a child, Lucius Sempronius Saturninus, born to Saturnina, and references a public record maintained in the *Atrium Magnum* of Alexandria. The inscription is structured around official titles and dates, including consular names (Titus Statilius Maximo, Lucius Lollianus Avitus, Lucius Valerius Proculus) and imperial years, and mentions the prefect of Egypt, Lucius Valerius Proculus. A portion of the text is written in Greek, indicating the bilingual nature of Alexandria at the time. The document’s purpose was to record births for official purposes, likely related to civic status and taxation, and it was maintained as part of a register of professions.

P.Mich. 10 592 is a fragmentary Latin military list, likely originating from a Roman military camp or administrative center in Egypt. The text appears to enumerate individuals, possibly officers or soldiers, associated with the imperial household (*dominis nostris*). It is organized as a series of names, some accompanied by titles such as *tribunus* (tribune) and *centurio* (centurion), and linked to the imperial administration under the Tetrarchy. The list explicitly references the emperors Diocletian Augustus (6VII, 6VIII[I]), Maximian Augustus (V, VII, VIII), and Maximian Caesar II, alongside consuls Valerius Potammon, Valerius Hierax, Valerius Heracleides, Valerius Arion, Valerius Plusianus, Valerius Psentaes, Valerius Plancius, and others. The document’s dating is consistent with the late antique period, specifically the 4th century CE, based on the imperial titulature and the presence of consuls.

P.Oslo 3 122 is a fragmentary Latin military document, likely a list of soldiers attached to various *turmae* (troops) within a larger Roman military unit. The text is organized by troop affiliation, with each entry typically including a soldier’s name and, crucially, the name of the consul under whose auspices the soldier served. Several consuls are named, including Nicolaus Julianus II, Valerius Comazonte, Titus Modestus, Flaminius Agricola, Gratus, and Titus Divus Alexander. The document also records promotions (*promotus*) and mentions the involvement of a tribune in the nomination process. Recurring names include Aurelius Cronio, Aurelius Hermaiscus, Aurelius Horigenes, Aurelius Ammonianus, and Iulius Sarapion, suggesting a core of veteran soldiers or individuals of particular significance. The presence of *sesquilicarii* (soldiers of a specific rank) is noted, but the number is illegible. The fragmentary nature of the text makes a complete reconstruction of the list impossible.

P.Oxy. 12, 1511 is a fragmentary register, likely a ledger or accounting document, recording correspondence received by *tabularii*, officials responsible for managing written records. The surviving portions list senders and recipients of letters, identifying them by their military titles and units. Named individuals include a *praefectus cohortis* of the Apamea cohort, a *praefectus legionis* of Legio II Traiana Fortis, a *tabularius* named Ianius Proximus, and a *praefectus alae* named Ecrynus. The register appears to be organized by the order in which letters were received, with some entries incomplete due to damage. The document provides insight into the administrative structure of the Roman military in the 3rd century CE and the role of scribal officials.

P.Lips. 1 35 is a late antique legal petition, likely originating from Thebais, Egypt, and dating to the 4th century CE. The text details a dispute concerning a levy of gold solidi collected from the local population, intended for the recruitment of soldiers. It involves Flavius Isidoros, an official of Thebais, and references individuals like Zenagenes, Makarios, Philapollon, and a leader named Pergamos. The petition appears to be addressed to, or at least intended for the consideration of, Roman authorities, specifically mentioning emperors Flavius Valens and Gratian, and refers to imperial decrees. The document is structured as a formal plea, outlining the collection process, accusations of misappropriation, and appeals for justice, concluding with a declaration of loyalty and a request for clarification regarding the disposition of remaining funds. The presence of Thebais and references to Roman imperial figures situate the text within the context of Roman administration and military recruitment in Egypt.

ZRG32 (1911), p. 378-379, is a fragmentary legal document from Roman Egypt, likely dating to the 3rd century CE. The text appears to be a petition or copy of a legal decree concerning inheritance, specifically addressing the division of property after the death of Aurelia Hammonilla Heraclea, a citizen of Oxyrhynchus. The document involves several individuals: Aurelius Appius Sabinus, the prefect of Egypt; Marcus Aurelius Chaeremon (who also appears as Didymus); Zoiló, a priest of Antinoös; and an unnamed minor. The text references a formal edict concerning legitimate heirs and includes a Greek colophon with calendrical information (18 Kal. Oct., Aemilianus II and Aquilinus as consuls, year 7, Thoth 18) and a legal interpretation by a Roman legal expert. The document’s fragmented nature obscures the precise legal proceedings, but it clearly deals with inheritance disputes and the administration of estates in Roman Egypt.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 23403zzz (sb;22;15625); Alexandria; vor 25. Juni 221
summary: P.Bub. 1 4 is a fragmentary Latin letter, likely imperial correspondence, originating from the third century CE. The text is severely damaged, rendering a complete understanding impossible; extant portions suggest a directive or exhortation addressed to an addressee not identified in the surviving lines. The letter references marriage alliances between members of the imperial household and individuals of higher social standing, and explicitly mentions the desire to demonstrate virtuous conduct (

Stud.Pal. 20 285 is a Latin receipt, likely from a military context, dated to the 4th century CE. The document details the distribution of wine and meat to soldiers of the *legio Macedonica*, under the supervision of Gaius, a tribune responsible for daily rations (*annona*). The receipt specifies quantities: 835 units of both wine and meat, dispensed between the 15th and 14th days before the Kalends of April (March 15th and 13th). Two dinners are also recorded as part of the distribution. Following a damaged section, the text references Honorius Perpetuus Augustus and Eutychianus, alongside Sergius, an accountant, and mentions the indiction cycle (XII). A fragment of Greek text appears interspersed within the Latin.

Stud.Pal. 14 p. 3 is a Latin private letter, datable to the 1st century CE based on its language and style. The letter is addressed from Diaconus to Macedon, and concerns accusations leveled against Macedon before Iucundus and Didon, purportedly at the instigation of a freedman of Domitius. The letter writer urges Macedon to appease these individuals and mentions Nireo, a fellow freedman, who has written damaging accusations. The letter concludes with greetings from Diaconus’s companions and a request for reciprocal greetings, followed by a date expressed in both Latin and Greek (Ἐπεὶφ; κζ), indicating the 14th day before August. The letter provides a glimpse into personal relationships and legal disputes within a Roman social context, highlighting the role of freedmen and the importance of maintaining social standing.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 24002 (o.claud;2;304); Mons Claudianus; ca. 150
summary: O.Claud. 2 304 is a fragmentary Latin inscription on a truncated amphora, likely dating to the 2nd century CE. The text appears to be a *tabula servitii*, or service roster, listing individuals in a structured sequence, possibly related to military or administrative duties. Names recur throughout the inscription, suggesting a cyclical or repeating pattern of assignments. Individuals named include Julius Serapio, Ptolemaeus, Anubis, Aelius Silvanus, and various other personal names, alongside possible references to locations or festivals, though these are often obscured by damage. The repeated phrases and formulaic structure indicate a standardized format for recording service details, common in Roman administrative contexts. The fragmentary nature of the text makes definitive interpretation challenging, but it offers a glimpse into the organization of personnel within a Roman institution.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 244055 (p.ital;2;43); Ravenna and Italy; 445-700 (series)
summary: P.Ital. 2 43 is a Latin legal document, likely a charter or deed, originating from Ravenna in the late antique period, tentatively dated to the 6th century CE. The text details the transfer or confirmation of land rights, specifically a portion of a fund (fundus) located in Ravenna and Raugnes, amidst a pre-existing legal dispute (damnata litis). It involves several individuals: Marcator, Waduulf (designated 'devoted man'), Riccifrida (his wife, described as 'honourable woman'), Bassus, Hilarus, Ghiveric, Ardica, Andreas, Leo (a boatman), and the late Alexander and Titianus. The document is structured around declarations of recognition by the involved parties, marked by their signatures or symbols, and includes stipulations regarding payment and labor. The presence of witnesses and their acknowledgement of the agreement, along with the mention of a consulship, suggests a formal legal process.

PSI 13 1307 Ro represents a fragmentary collection of *Acta Diurna* – daily records – likely originating from the 1st century CE. The text appears to document military routines and personnel within a Roman legion, specifically referencing centurions and soldiers. Names mentioned include Lepid[ianus], Minicius Iustus, Varius, Bassus, Neri Antistius, Seruilius Turranius, Firmi Lucretius, and Domitius. The content details activities such as drills (*spectatum*), vigils (*vigilias deduxit*), and assignments related to the legion’s standards (*aquila et signa*) and supplies (*pondera macelli*). References to Neapolis (Naples) suggest a connection to provisioning or supply lines. The text is severely damaged, rendering much of its organization and context obscure, but the surviving fragments offer a glimpse into the daily administration of a Roman military unit.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 25160 (c.epist.lat;;81); Panopolis oder Oxyrhynchos; 2. Hälfte I - 1. Hälfte II
summary: CLA 2 228 is a fragmentary official letter of introduction, composed in Latin during the 1st century CE. The letter’s content centers on the recommendation of a slave named Hermerotus to an unnamed recipient. The sender, Celer, describes Hermerotus as a domestic slave and a man dear to him, requesting that the recipient treat him with favor. The letter’s opening and closing are damaged, obscuring the precise nature of the request and the sender’s concluding remarks. The letter concludes with a dedication to Tiberius Claudius Hermerotus, the procurator of Augustus, and notes that it was issued in Panopolis to Celer, an architect. The document provides insight into the social and administrative practices of the Roman Empire, particularly concerning the movement of individuals and the reliance on letters of introduction for securing patronage.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 26179 (chla;42;1210); Myos Hormos; I - Anfang II
summary: P. Quseir 18 is a fragmentary Latin name list, likely originating from Egypt and datable to the 1st century CE. The text appears to be a series of personal names, possibly drawn from a military or administrative register, though the precise context is lost. Names include Roman cognomina like 'Antoninus,' 'Severus,' and 'Tiberius,' alongside others of uncertain origin, suggesting a diverse population. The list is severely damaged, rendering many names incomplete and obscuring any potential organizational structure. Mentions of 'Serenus curator' and 'Leucius Limenis' offer tantalizing glimpses into the roles of individuals within the document's original context, but their significance remains unclear due to the fragmentary nature of the text. The presence of Greek names like 'Heraclianus' indicates a Hellenistic influence within the Roman sphere.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 27080 (c.epist.lat;;141); Alexandria; frühes II
summary: P.Mich. 8 467 is a private letter written in Latin, likely dating to the 2nd century CE. The letter is from Claudius Terentianus to Claudius Tiberianus, whom he addresses as *dominus et pater carissimus* (lord and most beloved father), suggesting a patron-client relationship. The text details a request for military equipment—a sword, lance, shield, and other items—to be sent via Valerius, and mentions a previous shipment of goods including olive oil amphorae. Terentianus also expresses frustration regarding a denial of a request, references a negative interaction with a man named Marcellus, and includes greetings from family members and associates, including Aphrodisiam and Isitychen. The letter provides glimpses into military life, trade routes (Alexandria, Kalabel, Delta), and personal relationships within the Roman world.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 27081 (c.epist.lat;;142); Alexandria; frühes II
summary: P.Mich. 8 468 is a private letter written in Latin by Claudius Terentianus to his father and patron, Claudius Tiberianus, likely in the early 2nd century CE. The letter details Terentianus's possessions, which he received from his father, and requests further supplies, including caligae and a mallet. It also mentions individuals Terentianus wishes Tiberianus to greet, including military personnel like Arrius and Saturninus, as well as civilian figures like Terentius, the governor, and Sempronia Italicus. The letter reveals a hierarchical relationship between the two men, with Terentianus dependent on Tiberianus for material support and information, and provides a glimpse into the logistics of military life and the importance of patronage in Roman society. The concluding lines indicate a familial connection, with Terentianus sending greetings from his mother, brothers, and others at home.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 27082 (c.epist.lat;;144); Alexandria (?); frühes II
summary: P.Mich. 8 469 is a private letter written in Latin by Claudius Terentianus to his father, Claudius Tiberianus. The letter, composed in the second century CE, concerns a request for the purchase of a German slave woman, previously freed by an unnamed individual. Terentianus’s mother also expresses a desire for certain household goods, specifically beds, which Terentianus had previously acquired. The letter includes a brief discussion of other items, including *situlae* and a *furca*, and a reluctance to request them. The tone is informal and familial, with a concluding blessing invoking divine favor and a farewell to loved ones. The recipient, Claudius Tiberianus, is identified as a *speculator*, a term denoting a surveyor or overseer, likely in a military or administrative context.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 27083 (c.epist.lat;;145); Alexandria (?); frühes II
summary: P.Mich. 8 470 is a fragmentary Latin letter, likely composed in the second century CE, addressed from Terentianus to Tiberianus. The text is severely damaged, rendering a complete reconstruction of the content impossible; however, discernible fragments suggest a personal and somewhat agitated tone. References to a 'balteum militare' (military belt), 'Heraclides', and a discussion of a debt involving sixty-five denarii point towards a dispute concerning property or a transaction. The letter mentions a 'byssinus' garment and a maternal lineage originating elsewhere, indicating a discussion of family or inheritance. The writer expresses concern for Tiberianus's well-being and requests reassurance regarding a previous 'missio' (mission) and the security of funds, specifically one hundred denarii, with thirty-five remaining. The letter’s fragmented nature obscures the precise nature of the conflict, but it clearly involves financial matters and personal relationships.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 27084 (c.epist.lat;;146); unbekannt; frühes II
summary: P.Mich. 8 471 is a private letter written in Latin, likely composed in the early second century CE. The letter is addressed from Claudio Terentianus to Claudio Tiberianus, and details a series of financial and familial difficulties. The author recounts a father, Ptolemy, who prioritizes his own business and neglects his family, specifically failing to provide financial support. The letter mentions a pregnancy, childbirth, a dispute, and a planned journey to Alexandria, where the author intends to travel with his mother and belongings. Ptolemy’s departure for Alexandria with recruits is also described, alongside the involvement of a third party, Saturninus, who is asked to intervene in a dispute. The letter conveys a sense of dependency, frustration, and economic hardship.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 27085 (c.epist.lat;;147); Alexandria; frühes II
summary: P.Mich. 8 472 is a private letter written in Latin, datable to the second century CE. The letter is addressed from Claudius Tiberianus to Longinus Priscus, whom Tiberianus refers to as *dominus* and *rex*, suggesting a hierarchical relationship. The content concerns Tiberianus’s travel plans and a missed opportunity to depart from Alexandria, and includes instructions for a messenger, Sempronius Clemens, who is responsible for delivering a ship and letters. Tiberianus requests Longinus to inform him of his location so that Tiberianus can arrange for a ship to find him, and mentions sending signed documents. The letter concludes with greetings to several individuals, including Aristus and Qarium, and a closing from Tiberianus’s son, Claudius. The letter’s fragmentary nature obscures some details, particularly regarding the reasons for the delay and the nature of the documents sent.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 27148 (chla;4;249); Philadelphia (Arsinoites); 2. Hälfte II
summary: This is a fragmentary marriage contract (dosymbiosis) composed in Latin, likely dating to the second century CE. The document records the marriage of Zenarion, daughter of Caius Antistius Nomissianus, to Marcus Petronius Seruilius. It details the dowry provided by the father, including land (one acre, two and a half iugera), household goods, livestock (sheep), and personal items like tunics, pallia, and a slave named Heraida. The contract specifies a location, likely the paternal estate near Philadelphia, and lists witnesses who sealed the agreement, including Marcus A…golenos, Marcus Valerius Montanus, Titus Flavius Julianus, Lucius Valerius Loicritanas, and Popplius M…thinus. The text is significantly damaged, particularly in the sections describing the dowry's precise contents and the concluding clauses, rendering some interpretations uncertain.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 27228 (p.athen;;50r); Philoteris? (Arsinoites); II - III
summary: P.Athen. 50 Ro is a fragmentary papyrus document, likely originating from Egypt, written in Latin and dating to the 2nd century CE. The surviving portions suggest it is a report (ὑπηρεσιακὴ ἀναφορὰ), potentially concerning agricultural revenues (βιβλίον γεωργικῶν εἰσοδημάτων). The text is severely damaged, rendering a complete reconstruction impossible; however, it appears to detail a dispute or assessment related to land and resources. Mentions of a *strategus* (military governor) and a woman named Hippodromia suggest involvement of official and personal elements. The document's fragmented nature makes it difficult to ascertain the precise context or scope of the agricultural assessment, but it provides a glimpse into the administrative practices and social relationships of the Roman period in Egypt.

This fragmentary document, published in *JJP* 6 (1952) as no. 4a, appears to be a mixed-language (Latin and Greek) receipt or record concerning the delivery of grain. The Latin portion requests Silvanus, a dispenser ( *dispensator*) for the Caesar, to acknowledge the delivery of grain owed for two months, July and August, during the consulship of Gratus and Seleucus. The Greek portion, written in a cursive hand, contains greetings from Isidoros Serapion, described as a Roman *hippeus* (horseman), to Silvanus, referred to as an overseer (*oikonomos*) of Caesar. The text further mentions a measurement of grain, a *praetor’s* portion, and references Taureion Melanos, who appears to have written on behalf of someone else. The document’s mixed language and reference to a *hippeus* suggest a context within the Roman military or administration in a region with a significant Greek-speaking population, likely in the 3rd century CE.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 27901 (p.coles;;19); unbekannt; 2. Hälfte I (?)
summary: P.Ryl. 2 223 is a fragmentary Latin inventory, likely a shipping manifest or similar document relating to the transport of goods by water. The text details the movement of various materials – pitch, oil, wax, resin, and iron lamellae – in amphorae, small chests (liburnae), and containers (istegi). Weights are consistently recorded, suggesting a concern for accurate accounting. The document is organized chronologically, beginning and ending with references to the *idus Maias* (the 13th and 14th days before the Kalends of May), and lists deliveries to individuals named Lucius and Timetus, as well as a destination identified as the *praetorium*. The presence of iron lamellae suggests the transport of armor or related military equipment, and the repeated use of weights indicates a commercial or administrative context within Roman Egypt.

P.Ryl. 2 273a is a fragmentary Latin pay record, likely originating from Roman Egypt and datable to the 2nd century CE. The document details disbursements of *denarii* to auxiliary soldiers, recording amounts received and dates of payment. Individual names appear, including 'Marinus Crisp-' and 'Maeg-' (both likely soldiers), alongside the mention of 'rat-' (possibly a military rank or official). Payments are noted as being made on the Kalends of January ( *Kalendis Ianua[ri]*) and other unspecified dates. The text is organized as a list of payments, with the amounts often partially preserved, and is unfortunately heavily damaged, obscuring much of the content. The surviving fragments provide a glimpse into the financial administration of Roman military personnel in a provincial context.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 28696 (p.hamb;1;72); unbekannt; II - III
summary: P.Hamb. 1 72 is a fragmentary Latin formulary, likely intended for use in the drafting of manumission testaments. The text provides standardized clauses concerning the inheritance of children born to a testator’s wife after his death, stipulating a larger share for the surviving child if one dies. It references the *lex Fufia Caninia*, a law concerning inheritance, and includes provisions addressing the potential conflict between manumission and the status of fugitive slaves. The formulary also contains clauses intended to ensure the validity of prior acts of donation or prohibition regarding slaves and free women, and a declaration of the testator’s honesty. The document’s structure is formulaic, presenting pre-written phrases and clauses to be incorporated into a complete testament. The text is damaged, particularly at the beginning and end, obscuring some of its original scope.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 35065 (analpap;25;32); Oxyrhynchos (Oxyrhynchites, Ägypten); 1. Hälfte V
summary: PSI 13 1309 Ro is a fragmentary Latin text, likely dating to the late antique period (5th century CE), documenting a legal proceeding before a *praeses* (presiding official) in Arcadia. The text consists primarily of direct speech, revealing a dispute involving multiple individuals: Rufinus, a *protector* and seemingly the presiding official; Anicius, whose actions are under scrutiny; Zenon, Apronianus, Aristides, and Eustathianus, a sophist. The arguments revolve around accusations of torture and the presentation of evidence, with references to legal procedures and the role of orators. The *praeses* attempts to maintain order and guide the proceedings, while the participants accuse each other of withholding information and manipulating the legal process. The text’s abrupt endings and corruptions make a complete reconstruction of the case impossible, but it offers a glimpse into the complexities of legal argumentation and the social dynamics of late Roman Arcadia.

P.Lond. 5 1792 is a private letter written in Latin, likely originating from Egypt and datable to the 4th century CE. The letter is addressed from Eulogius, who identifies himself as an *epitropos* (overseer or guardian), to his brother Mercus. The content revolves around a dispute concerning a young woman, likely a slave or servant, who was given to Eulogius and for whom he now seeks payment. Eulogius requests Mercus’s intervention to ensure the payment is made promptly and without impediment, invoking divine assistance and appealing to Mercus’s sanctity. The letter demonstrates a concern for legal and financial matters within a domestic context, and provides insight into the social and economic relationships of the period, including the practice of transferring individuals and the expectation of compensation. The text is fragmentary, with significant portions missing, particularly at the beginning and end, obscuring the full context of the exchange.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 35623 (c.epist.lat;;243); Oxyrhynchos; spätes IV - frühes V
summary: P. Oxy. 18 2193 is a fragmentary Latin letter, written in a mixed Graeco-Latin style, likely originating from Egypt in the 4th century CE. The letter begins with a brief theological reflection on mortality and divinity, addressed to a recipient named Pascentius. The main body of the letter concerns a woman’s request for assistance, conveyed through written correspondence, alleging injustice suffered by herself and her son. She seeks a ‘rightful explanation’ ( *diciolgia* ) and requests that someone act piously on her behalf. The letter concludes with a brief instruction to return something to Pascentius, described as a ‘slave of God’ (*servo dei*). The text is damaged, particularly at the end, obscuring the full context of the request and the nature of the item to be returned.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 35624 (c.epist.lat;;244); Oxyrhynchos; spätes IV - frühes V
summary: P. Oxy. 18 2194 is a fragmentary Latin letter, likely composed in the late antique period, specifically the 4th century CE, based on paleographic assessment. The surviving portions of the letter contain a mixture of prose and Greek phrases, suggesting a context where Greek was still in common use alongside Latin. The letter's content is highly fragmented, but appears to discuss divine favor, possibly related to a religious or communal undertaking, and mentions financial obligations or 'repayments' owed, potentially to a deity or a leader. References to 'emperors' and 'senators' suggest a connection to the Roman elite, while the inclusion of a 'veteran' named Paulus indicates a military or service-related context. The letter is addressed to a recipient named Pascentius, and concludes with a pious invocation, 'in God’s time.'

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 35728 (sb;1;5357); Arsinoites; V - VI
summary: SB 1 5357 is a fragmentary Latin text, likely a transcript of a legal proceeding from the late antique period, tentatively dated to the 5th century CE. The document details a dispute concerning inheritance and accusations of ingratitude, involving Roman law and customs. It appears to concern the transfer of property and the obligations of familial relationships, with references to a 'familiar brother' and a father defending his son. The text is structured as a series of statements and arguments, interspersed with Greek phrases, suggesting a multilingual legal environment. Key figures mentioned include Flavius Paulus, Leontius, Marinous, Petronius, Hsouchius, Iulianus (an advocate), and Romanus, the accused. The place name 'Transtigritan' is also present, indicating a geographical element to the dispute.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 35870 (p.rain.cent;;166); Ravenna; VI - VII
summary: P.Marini 124 is a Latin sales document, likely a deed or contract, originating from Ravenna and dated to the 6th century CE. The text details the sale of one ounce of land on the *fundus Paonine* (estate of Paonine) and repeatedly references preceding stipulations (*supra scriptis*). The sellers are not named directly but are associated with a man named Pitione, who provided assent regarding a “yoke” (presumably a debt or obligation) of Petronia. Witnesses include Solomon, Gaudiosus (an archpriest), Mauro, and Petronia herself, all described as *viri/feminae honesti* (respectable people). The price of the land is stated as six gold solidi, which were reportedly paid and delivered. The document's repetitive structure and formulaic language are characteristic of late antique legal documents.

Ch.L.A. 13 563 is a Latin text likely representing a land exchange agreement or charter, originating from the late 10th or early 11th century. The document details the transfer of land parcels between Landeb[erctho], abbot, and Magnoald, abbot of the monastery of Tucioneuall[e], and Hramnino, a hereditary successor of Landeb[erctho]. Specific locations mentioned include Pinsiacinse, Francorecurte, and Roccon(e)curte, suggesting a localized settlement within a larger region. The text outlines the terms of the exchange, including stipulations for future transfers and penalties for violation, and is signed by numerous witnesses, including priests, deacons, and a lictor, indicating a formal and legally binding transaction. The charter’s structure follows a typical formula for land conveyances, emphasizing communal agreement and divine sanction.

Ch.L.A. 13 564 is a Latin legal document, likely a charter or deed, concerning the foundation and endowment of a monastery dedicated to the Virgin Mary and Christ. The text is divided into two distinct sections: the first details the transfer of land and property, including vineyards and fields at Mummola, Brocaria, and Pladano, to the monastery, with Charichard acting as a temporary custodian. The second section outlines legal consequences for violations of unspecified stipulations, including excommunication and financial penalties, and records deliberations regarding an inheritance potentially involving the monastery. The document concludes with a substantial list of signatures, including Chrothilde, Bishop Aggilpertus, Ermenrigo, and Abbot Chrodecarius, suggesting a significant local involvement. The composition of the document appears to have taken place in Morlacas during the reign of King Chlothachariae, and it addresses themes of ecclesiastical law, inheritance, and spiritual redemption.

This section of the text details the foundation of a monastery dedicated to the Virgin Mary and Christ, initiated by an unnamed benefactor. The benefactor outlines the transfer of land and property, including vineyards and fields, to the monastery, intending it as a means of spiritual redemption and a legacy for future generations. The text includes legal stipulations regarding the monastery's independence and restrictions on the alienation of its assets, with Charichard designated as a temporary custodian.

This section of a legal document outlines consequences for an individual who violates unspecified stipulations, including excommunication and financial penalties. It details a deliberation concerning an inheritance, potentially involving a monastery, and emphasizes its permanence. The document concludes with a lengthy list of signatures, including prominent figures such as Chrothilde, Aggilpertus (a bishop), Ermenrigo, and Chrodecarius (an abbot), alongside numerous other individuals identified by their names and occasionally their roles (e.g., 'requested,' 'a sinner'). The text was likely composed in Morlacas, a public place, during the reign of King Chlothachariae.

Ch.L.A. 13 569 is a Latin document comprising two distinct sections. The first portion presents a testamentary donation, detailing bequests of property and rights to various basilicas and associated lands situated in *pagi* including Sociaco, Porcariorum, Binando, Ghinnachario, Uuarnaco, Fauariolas, Castanito, Lecterico, and Uuadreloci. This section also includes provisions for manumission and curses against those who would tamper with the will, referencing Judas Scarioth. The second section consists of an oath or declaration, likely of ecclesiastical legal significance, compelling priests and bishops to uphold the sanctity of designated sacred locations and forbidding interference with the declaration's proceedings. The document is dated and signed at Artegia, within the district of Velcassino, and bears the attestations of Aldus and Olenus.

This section of the Latin text is a testamentary donation, outlining the distribution of property and rights to various sacred basilicas and associated lands. The testator, whose name is not given, details bequests to specific villas and districts including Sociaco, Porcariorum, Binando, Ghinnachario, Uuarnaco, Fauariolas, Castanito, Lecterico, and Uuadreloci, all located in different *pagi* (districts) within the broader region. The text also includes clauses regarding the manumission of slaves and curses against anyone who attempts to alter the will, invoking divine retribution and referencing biblical figures like Judas Scarioth.

This text is a Latin oath or declaration, likely part of a legal or ecclesiastical document. It compels priests and bishops to maintain the sanctity of specific sacred locations, and forbids anyone from interfering with the will or deliberations of those making the declaration. The document is dated and signed at Artegia, in the district of Velcassino, and includes multiple attestations of its authenticity, with the signatures of 'Aldus' and 'Olenus'.

Ch.L.A. 13 571 is a Latin legal document, likely a charter or deed, composed of two distinct sections. The first section details a series of land donations from an unnamed donor to various ecclesiastical institutions and individuals, listing properties including Ingolinocurti, Fraxineto, and Oxma, alongside the presiding abbots and priests. A personal note within this section is addressed to the donor’s wife, Ercamberta, concerning her inheritance and continued support of these religious bodies. The second section focuses on the governance of the Church of Paris, outlining penalties, including excommunication, for those who would challenge its stipulations. This portion was ratified at Camillaco and dated to the seventeenth year of King Theoderic’s reign, and concludes with signatures from individuals such as Acerelio, Boson, and Uuademiris. The document’s themes revolve around land tenure, ecclesiastical authority, and legal validation.

This section of the text details a series of donations of land and property to various churches, monasteries, and individuals. The donor, whose name is not given, grants estates named Ingolinocurti, Fraxineto, Oxma, Nouiolio, Uuabuniacas, Gomariouilla, and many others, specifying the abbots or priests presiding over each location. The text also includes a personal note from the donor addressed to his wife, Ercamberta, outlining her future inheritance of certain properties and expressing a desire for their continued support of the religious institutions.

This section of a legal document concerns the recording of the church of Paris and stipulations regarding its governance. It outlines penalties for those who would attempt to alter or contradict the agreement, including excommunication and financial penalties. The document was ratified at Camillaco and dated to the seventeenth year of King Theoderic’s reign, and concludes with a list of signatures, including several prominent individuals such as Acerelio, Boson, and Uuademiris.

Ch.L.A. 14 580 is a Latin charter or privilege concerning the foundation and operation of a monastery dedicated to Saint Mary and other saints, situated near the river Legeris. The document details the monastery’s governance, specifying an abbot and a spiritual father, and establishes protections against interference from secular and ecclesiastical authorities, notably the bishop of Carnotensis (Chartres). The charter’s issuance involved the consent of Deodatus, a former bishop, and references the deacon Chrotcharius, likely a key figure in the monastery’s establishment. Following the initial stipulations, the text presents a list of ratifying individuals, each preceding their name with the phrase *etsi peccator*, indicating humility. This ratification occurred in Captona during the second year of the reign of King Childeric, on the sixth day of March, and includes several bishops, clerics, and an abbot.

This Latin text is a charter or privilege granted to a newly established monastery dedicated to Saint Mary and other saints, located near the river Legeris. It details the terms of the monastery's operation, including its governance by an abbot and a spiritual father, and outlines protections from interference by secular authorities and clergy, including the bishop of Carnotensis (modern Chartres). The charter was issued with the consent of Deodatus, a former bishop, and references the venerable deacon Chrotcharius, who appears to have been instrumental in the monastery's founding.

This section of the document lists numerous individuals who purportedly ratified or subscribed to a privilege. Each name is preceded by the phrase 'etsi peccator' ('as if a sinner'), suggesting a self-deprecating acknowledgement of their own failings. The document specifies that the ratification occurred in Captona during the second year of the reign of Childeric, on the sixth day of March. The individuals include bishops, servants of Jesus Christ, and an abbot, all seemingly participating in a formal act of confirmation.

Ch.L.A. 14 582 is a Latin charter, likely originating from the late Merovingian period (7th century), detailing a land exchange between Adalric and Uualdromar, abbot. The document outlines the transfer of land near Mairilaco, situated within the district of Penesciacinsi, and specifies the boundaries adjacent to Bertin and Ansbert. It establishes conditions for the exchange, granting full ownership and rights to the recipients, and includes a curse against those who would violate the agreement. Witnesses include Baldoaldus, Ursinus, Chramlenus, Arisulfus, and Sicharius, a lictor, indicating a formal legal process. The charter is dated to the third year of the reign of Childibert, a Merovingian king, and concludes with the signatures of several individuals, some expressing unworthiness.

Ch.L.A. 14 592 is a Latin testament, apparently incomplete, detailing the testamentary dispositions of an unnamed testator. The document is structured in two distinct parts, each focused on bequests and stipulations. Part 1 lists numerous bequests of land, livestock, slaves, and valuables to individuals and institutions, with specific references to locations on Mount Maurilion, Mount Metobaure, Tauriniaco, and Mount Uultoricino, and mentions individuals named Deoruald and Deorouald. Part 2 continues the testamentary stipulations, primarily concerning the manumission of slaves and outlining their subsequent obligations, and names witnesses including Mummolus, Erminethruda, and Scupilio. The text also references basilicas in Paris and the church of Vicus Bonisiacensis, as well as basilicas dedicated to Saint Martin of Ciperente and the Lord Sinfuriani, and locations including the mountains Maurelion and Blixata.

This section of the testament details numerous bequests of land, livestock, slaves, and valuables to various individuals and institutions. The testator, whose name is not given, distributes vineyards, sheep, cattle, silver and gold objects, and slaves, specifying cultivators and locations on Mount Maurilion, Mount Metobaure, Tauriniaco, and Mount Uultoricino. Several bequests are made in the names of Deoruald (likely a son or relative) and Deorouald (likely the same person), and the document also outlines provisions for the maintenance of several basilicas in Paris and the church of Vicus Bonisiacensis.

This section of the text continues the testamentary stipulations of an unnamed testator, detailing the manumission of numerous individuals and their property. The beneficiaries include servants, freedmen, and others, with specific instructions regarding their obligations, such as providing timber or lamps for religious institutions. The document also mentions several locations, including the mountains Maurelion and Blixata, and basilicas dedicated to Saint Martin of Ciperente and the Lord Sinfuriani, alongside names like Mummolus, Erminethruda, and Scupilio who serve as witnesses.
