This Latin text, designated Ch.L.A. 17 654, is a royal charter issued by Childeberthus, king of the Franks, likely dating to the early 7th century. It details the grant of the forest of Corniol[etus], situated on the Sequana river near Paris, to the monastery of Saint Mary, Saint Peter and Paul, and presided over by the abbess Leudesinda at Argentoialo. The charter outlines the forest’s history as a royal fiscal domain and emphasizes the king’s intention to protect its integrity and prevent any diminishment or slander against Leudesinda or the monastery. It establishes a perpetual arrangement, ensuring the monastery’s continued use and benefit from the forest, and is sealed with royal subscriptions and the endorsement of Wulfolaecus, likely a royal official. The document’s formal language and detailed stipulations are characteristic of Merovingian-era land grants.

Ch.L.A. 18 659 is a fragmented Latin text comprising ten distinct sections, likely originating from a monastic or ecclesiastical context in a Roman or Romanized settlement. The document primarily functions as a series of agricultural accounting records, detailing the distribution and assessment of grain—wheat (*triticum*), rye (*secale*), barley (*hordeum*), and oats (*auena*)—alongside occasional timber allotments. Numerous individuals are named throughout, including Aigomarus, Berthericus, Leofred, and Genmarus, alongside references to settlements such as Exsolicia, Colonia Antoniaco, and Patriciaco. The text appears to document a complex system of land tenure, tribute obligations, and grain distribution, with occasional notes indicating refusals or returns of goods. Recurring themes include agricultural yields, taxation or tithes, and the management of resources within a rural economy, with a final summary calculation from Caniaco appearing in Part 9. Due to its fragmentary nature, a complete understanding of the occasion or purpose remains elusive.

This fragmented text appears to be a list of donations or allotments of grain and timber, likely associated with a monastic or ecclesiastical context. The names of numerous individuals are recorded, each followed by quantities of wheat, rye, oats, and barley, alongside timber donations. The text mentions several *coloniae* (colonies or settlements), including Exsolicia, Calo[…], and Siluiaco, suggesting a regional distribution of these goods. The repeated use of abbreviations and the fragmentary nature of the text make a complete understanding of the occasion or purpose difficult.

This section of the text appears to be a fragmented agricultural census or accounting, listing quantities of grain (wheat, rye, barley, oats, and spelt) attributed to various individuals and communities. The amounts are given in *modii*, with occasional notes of

This section appears to be a fragmented accounting or roster, likely related to land holdings or tribute obligations. It lists quantities of grain (wheat, rye, barley, and oats) assigned to various individuals and communities, including names like Aigomarus, Hadoald, Berthericus, Milareto, and numerous others. The text also mentions several locations, including Colonia (appearing repeatedly), Iogundiaco, and Milciacus, and references a feast or occasion marked by the abbreviation 'spt v.'

This section (Ch.L.A. 18, 659, Part 4, sections 31-42) appears to be a fragmentary inventory or accounting document, likely related to land or agricultural produce. It lists quantities of grain—wheat (*triticum*), rye (*secale*), barley (*hordeum*), and oats (*auena*)—distributed or assigned to various individuals, alongside their names and, occasionally, the *coloniae* (colonies or settlements) they are associated with. Numerous personal names are present, including Leu[g]iselus, Abroardus, Maurinus, Rigomarus, and many others, suggesting a local context within a Roman or Romanized settlement.

This section of the text details distributions of grain—wheat, rye, barley, and oats—by various individuals to a location identified as *Colonica Monte* and *Colonica Braciadello*. The distributions are recorded in a list-like format, with each person’s name followed by the quantity of each grain they provided. Several individuals, including Ur[...], Dalhomirus, Leudosindus, and numerous others with Germanic-sounding names, are listed. The text also includes occasional notes indicating refusal of distribution or a return of wood, suggesting a complex system of obligations and contributions.

Part 6 of Ch.L.A. 18 659 presents a detailed accounting of grain distribution from a villa, likely Patriciaco, listing numerous individuals and the quantities of wheat, rye, barley, oats, and spelt they received. The text appears to be a record of agricultural yields and allotments, with names like Genmarus, Aigobertus, and Colonica recurring, suggesting they are landowners or officials. The final section details totals for each grain type, culminating in a sum of 100 and five measures, and then trails off into fragmentary names and quantities.

Part 7, sections 57-64 of Ch.L.A. 18 659 presents a list of individuals and the quantities of grain (wheat, rye, barley, and oats) they contributed, likely as part of a tithe or other form of assessment. The names include Gunsoaldus, Leboald, Bertemarus, Deoroaldus, Audosind, Fredoramn, and many others, with each entry specifying amounts of grain. The text appears to be an inventory or accounting document, possibly related to landholding or taxation within a specific locality, though the precise location is not stated.

This section appears to be a fragmented inventory or accounting document, likely related to land tenure or taxation. It lists quantities of grain – wheat, barley, and rye – assigned to various individuals, alongside occasional references to oats. The names listed include Gisellus, Asindus, Urso, Burgolenus, Maurontus, and numerous others ending in '-bercthus,' suggesting a localized community or familial network. The text also contains phrases indicating the return of timber, possibly related to forestry management or construction.

Part 9 of Ch.L.A. 18 659 presents a detailed accounting of grain distributions, likely as part of a larger estate inventory or tax record. Numerous individuals are listed, each receiving varying amounts of wheat, barley, rye, and oats, often measured in fractions of a *modius*. The text also includes a summary calculation at the end, totaling the quantities of wheat, rye, barley, and oats distributed, alongside a brief note from Caniaco. The names listed suggest a rural, Gallo-Roman context.

This fragmentary text appears to be a register or accounting document, likely related to agricultural yields or distribution. It lists quantities of grain—wheat (triticum), barley (hordeum), rye (secale), and oats (auena)—measured in *modii*, alongside the names of numerous individuals: Laudolfus, Rigobodis, Arnoaldus, Alsendus, Bertoramnus, and many others. The repeated names suggest a system of taxation, tithes, or perhaps allotments of grain to specific people. The text is heavily damaged, with many names and quantities illegible, making a complete reconstruction impossible.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 382974 (chla;20;709); Ravenna and Italy; 445-700 (series)
summary: P.Ital. 1 3 is a fragmentary Latin inventory or accounting document, likely originating from a rural estate in late antiquity (6th century CE). The text details quantities of livestock (sheep, geese, hens, chicks), eggs, honey, lard, and milk, alongside monetary values expressed in solidi, tremisses, and scales. The document appears to list holdings across multiple locations, identified as 'xen(iis)' (enclosures or storehouses) and colonies, including Saltus Erudianus, Noviciana, Simpliciaca, Candidiana, Valeriaca, and Severiaca. Named individuals include Maximus (overseer), John, Vigil, Bassus, Valerius, Quintulus, Sabinionem, Leonem, Achillem, Victurinum, Severum, and the presbyters Victor and Proiectus. The presence of weekly work obligations and references to 'territorio Patavino' (territory of Patavium) suggest an organized agricultural system with associated labor and taxation.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 382975 (chla;20;710); Ravenna and Italy; 445-700 (series)
summary: P.Ital. 1 9 is a fragmentary Latin legal document, likely a will or a related testamentary instrument, dating to the 6th century CE. The text details the disposition of property and obligations related to individuals and holdings. It concerns the transfer of land (fundi), specifying amounts of solidi (Roman bronze coins) paid for each property and listing locations such as Agelli and Apranus. The document also outlines stipulations regarding the treatment of slaves' ashes and mentions obligations to Firmina, the author's mother, and concerns the distribution of private property or pensions. Key individuals named include Flavius Iohannis, a man of high standing, Laurentia (a woman's name, likely a wife), Adaucte (a daughter’s name), Bilesarium, and Sifilone (likely Bilesarium’s wife). The text is organized around a series of conditional clauses and obligations, suggesting a complex legal arrangement.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 382976 (chla;20;711); Ravenna and Italy; 445-700 (series)
summary: P.Ital. 1 2 is a fragmentary Latin document, likely a register or account roll, dating to the 6th century CE. The text details financial transactions related to a patrimony, likely associated with the church of Ravenna, involving payments of solidi (gold coins) for various purposes, including masses, tithes, and grants. It lists individuals involved in these transactions, including Titianus, Iohannes (a canon), Cumquod[e]us, Adon, Eventius, Honorius, and Agnello, an archiepiscop. The document references the archiepiscop of Ravenna, and mentions the transfer of land previously belonging to Arian churches. The text concludes with expressions of gratitude to Christian and peaceful lords and references imperial authority, suggesting a connection to the Byzantine administration.

Ch.L.A. 22 722 is a Latin charter, likely pertaining to a land donation. The document records the act of a donor, identified as Albanus, an 'agellanarius,' and details the transfer of property, specifically two 'fundi' belonging to Sclariano and Domicilio. Witnesses to the transaction include Theophanius, Vitalis, Secundus Tiberiacus, Iohannites, and Petrus, each identified by their roles and affiliations, such as 'miles numeri invicti' (soldier of an invincible cohort) and 'tribunus numeri Iuniorum' (tribune of a junior cohort). The charter’s scribe, a member of the Ravenna city administration, confirms the details and lists Apollinaris as a witness. The text is fragmented, with several lacunae obscuring portions of the witness list and the concluding remarks.

Ch.L.A. 29 877 appears to be a fragmentary land transfer document or agreement, likely originating from Ravenna (Ravennatis). The text details the conveyance of two measures of land, along with associated rights concerning entrances, exits, courtyards, wells, and a designated foot-rule measurement. Several individuals are named as witnesses and participants in the transaction, including Petrus, Acastus, George, Urso, Apollenaris, Iubentinus, Constantinus, and Anastasius, with various military designations (miles, domesticus) and roles (sartor, adiutore). The presence of references to 'bandi' (bands) and 'draconariorum numeri invic[ti]' (units of dragoners) suggests a military or organized communal context. The document concludes with a formal declaration and the signatures of witnesses, indicating a legally binding agreement.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 383110 (chla;29;880); Ravenna and Italy; 445-700 (series)
summary: P.Ital. 1 13 is a Latin legal document, likely a donation charter, composed in the late antique period, specifically the 6th century CE. The text details the transfer of property, including land and associated rights, from an unnamed donor to recipients designated as lords and procurators. It specifies quantities of silver and solidi, references territories of Urbinati and Lucense, and outlines stipulations regarding tenants, boundaries, and mancipia. The charter invokes divine sanction and imperial authority, mentioning Emperor Justinian and referencing a prior mandate from the donor's father, Aderit. Witnesses, including Severus of Forum, Laurentius, Arborius, Bassus, and Amantius, attest to the transaction, and the document concludes with the scribe, Severus, affirming its completeness.

P.Mich. 7 450 is a fragmentary Latin text, likely a section of *acta diurna*, official daily announcements common in the Roman world, dating to the 3rd century CE. The surviving portions detail military deployments, personnel assignments, and administrative actions within a Roman military presence. Names prominent in the text include Sarapion, Ammonianus (appearing multiple times as a centurion), Didumachi, Diosdorus, Severianus, and Iulius Alexandrus. Geographic references are scant, but suggest activity in or near Alexandria, with mentions of Therape, and the presence of units like the *Ala Gallica*. The text appears to list personnel, their assignments to various posts (custodiarum bal, dromadarius, signa), and dates, including references to *idus Augustas*, suggesting a structured, calendrical organization. The fragmentary nature of the text makes a complete reconstruction of the events described impossible.

PSI XI 1183 is a fragmentary Roman census declaration dating to the years 47/8 CE. The document records declarations of citizenship granted by Emperor Tiberius Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus and Emperor Tiberius Plautius Silvanus Aelianus. It details property holdings and shares within Oxyrhynchus, a city in the Egyptian nome of Oxyrhynchus, and lists individuals declaring themselves and their sons as citizens. The declarations involve several named individuals, including Hapio, Serapion, Didymus, Apollonius, Hatrio, Ischyra, Theonis, Hamyn, Seleucus, and Pol Nigma. The text is organized around individual declarations, with each entry specifying the property, the shared ownership, and the proportion assigned to each party. Significant portions of the text are damaged, obscuring details of the declarations and the names of some individuals.

C.Pap.Lat. 324, commonly known as the Feriale Duranum, is a Latin calendar from the 3rd century CE detailing observances of the imperial cult alongside traditional Roman religious festivals. The text is organized chronologically, outlining rituals scheduled throughout the year, including animal sacrifices (bulls, cows, oxen) dedicated to deities such as Jupiter, Juno, Minerva, Mars, and Salus, alongside dedications to the *Genius* of emperors. Honored emperors specifically mentioned include Marcus Aurelius, Severus Alexander, Trajan, Antoninus Pius, and Severus. The calendar documents occasions such as imperial birthdays, military victories (particularly relating to the Parthian campaign), and festivals like the Rosalia and Neptunalia. A fragmentary section details the birth anniversaries of Divine Faustina and Divine Augustus, alongside a damaged reference to a 'supplication' in January, though significant lacunae impede a complete understanding of this portion.

This section of the Feriale Duranum details a series of imperial cult observances scheduled throughout the year, primarily focused on honoring emperors such as Marcus Aurelius Severus Alexander, Trajan, Antoninus Pius, and Severus. The rituals involve animal sacrifices (bulls, cows, and oxen) dedicated to various deities including Jupiter, Juno, Minerva, Mars, and Salus, alongside dedications to the *Genius* of the emperors. Specific occasions include birthdays of emperors and their family members, military victories (particularly the Parthian campaign), and festivals like the Rosalia and Neptunalia, demonstrating the intertwined nature of imperial and divine worship in the 3rd century.

This fragment of the Feriale Duranum lists two imperial cult observances. The first concerns the birth anniversaries of the Divine Faustina and Divine Augustus, celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of October and the day of the birth of the Divine Augustus respectively. The second observance, heavily damaged, references the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January and mentions a 'supplication' within the context of the ninth day of the Kalends, likely of the same month. The text is fragmentary and difficult to interpret due to significant lacunae and corruption.

P. Dura 55 A-B constitutes a file of letters, likely official correspondence, written in Latin during the 3rd century CE. The fragmentary nature of the texts makes reconstruction difficult, but the content appears to concern military administration and discipline within a Roman cohort. Several letters are addressed to an unnamed recipient, and reference is made to Valerius Comazontis, who acts as an authority issuing instructions. The letters mention the 20th Palmyrene cohort, and allude to troop movements towards Syria, and a dispute or incident involving soldiers, potentially related to desertion or unauthorized departure. A section is written in Greek, discussing the obedience of soldiers and their actions, and includes references to 'our company' and a town populated by soldiers. The document provides a glimpse into the challenges of maintaining order and control within Roman military units during a period of potential unrest.

C.Pap.Lat. 330 is a fragmentary Latin document consisting of letters originating from a provincial headquarters, likely in the Roman East. The letters detail the assignment of horses to cavalrymen within the 20th Palmyrene cohort, accompanied by financial records indicating the value placed on each animal. The correspondence is addressed to and from various military officials, including Marius Maximus Valens, a legate, and Ulpian Valentino, a tribune, and references Emperor Antoninus Augustus and Caesar Geta. The document is organized as a series of discrete assignments, each recording the horse’s characteristics, its assigned recipient, and the associated payment. Dates are provided using Roman calendar conventions, with locations including Hieropolis and Antioch, suggesting a wide geographical scope for the administrative operations described.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44781 (rom.mil.rec;1;114); Dura - Europos; ca. 241
summary: C.Pap.Lat. 329 is a fragmentary Latin letter, likely an official dispatch originating from Syria in the third century CE. The surviving portion of the text is addressed to Attius Rufinus, who holds the title of *legatus Augusti pro praetore*, indicating a high-ranking imperial official. The letter references the sixth year of the reign of Emperor Gordian III and mentions Claudius Pompeianus, who served as consul. It also names Aurelius, the *praepositus cohortis* (prefect of a cohort), and identifies a unit as *cohors XX Palmyrenorum* (20th Palmyrene cohort), suggesting a military context. The text is unfortunately damaged, obscuring the precise content of the message and the recipient's role in the communication, but it provides valuable insight into the administrative and military landscape of Roman Syria during Gordian III’s reign.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44786 (chla;6;316); Dura - Europos; ca. 216

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44788 (zpe;207;210); Dura - Europos (Syrien); ca. 216 - 220
summary: P.Dura 62 is a fragmentary Latin legal document, likely a petition or record of a judicial proceeding, dating to the 3rd century CE. The text is severely damaged, rendering a complete reconstruction impossible; extant portions suggest a discussion of property or debt. Mentions of *Germanus*, *Marinus*, *Cassianus*, *Aurelius Mocimus*, and *Aurelius* (likely a person's name) appear, indicating involvement of these individuals in the matter. The presence of the name *Gordianus* and *Aurelius* suggests a connection to prominent Roman families. The document’s structure is unclear due to the fragmentation, but it seems to contain statements or testimonies relating to a legal dispute.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44791 (rom.mil.rec;1;88); Dura - Europos; vor 1. Juli 211
summary: C.Pap.Lat. 332 comprises a fragmentary collection of letters, likely personal correspondence, written in Latin during the 3rd century CE. The surviving portions suggest a network of individuals involved in commercial or legal dealings, evidenced by references to the sale of a person and the involvement of a *procurator*. The letters are addressed to 'Agathion' and 'Saturninus', and mention 'Seleucus', 'Iulius Pomp[onius]', 'Gentian', 'Bassus', 'Themar[s]', '[Zebi]da', 'Hiereum Abe[d ...]', 'Appada[na ...]' and a 'dominus' (master). The dating formula indicates the letters were composed during the consulship of Gentian and Bassus, likely in the mid-2nd century CE, though the papyrus itself dates to the 3rd. The fragmented nature of the text makes a complete reconstruction of the correspondence impossible, but it provides glimpses into the social and economic life of the time.

C.Pap.Lat. 337 comprises a series of letters addressed to a man named Iustillus, identified as a *tribunus cohortis* (tribune of a cohort). The letters are penned by Aurelius Rufinus, a *praepositus praeturae* (official in charge of the praetura) and *procurator* (financial administrator) for the Augusti (emperors). The correspondence concerns requests for the provision of grain from estates to auxiliary cavalry and mule-drivers serving in a vexillation of the Appadanens cohort, and also involves a request directed to a *librarius* (librarian) named Sozontem of the Legio XVI Flavia Firmana Antoniniana to satisfy a Haniae. The letters are dated by the consulship of Gratus and Seleucus, placing them in the early third century CE. Antonius Seleucus, a *uir clarissimus consularis* (most illustrious consular), is also mentioned, seemingly as the originator of a previous communication that Rufinus is responding to. The fragmentary nature of the text obscures the full context of these exchanges, but the content reveals aspects of military administration, provisioning, and imperial bureaucracy.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44795a (rom.mil.rec;1;89_1); Dura - Europos; Juli 216
summary: P. Dura 66 A is a fragmentary Latin letter, likely official in nature, written in the third century CE. The text is severely damaged, rendering a complete understanding of its content difficult. It appears to concern the dispatch of soldiers, specifically a cohort (XX Palmyrenorum Antoniniana) engaged in military activity, possibly a skirmish, within a wooded area. The letter is addressed to recipients styled as 'dominis' (lords), and mentions Aurelius Mucianus, a *stator* (a military official, possibly a standard-bearer), and Postumius Aurelianus, a tribune of the cohort. The letter was sent by an unnamed author, and references the consulship of Sabinus II and Anullinus. The letter concludes with a wish for the recipients' continued well-being and prosperity.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44795bb (rom.mil.rec;1;89_28); Dura - Europos; vor 23. Aug. - 8. Sept. 216
summary: P. Dura 66A is a fragmentary Latin inscription, likely a public notice or official record, originating from Dura-Europos and datable to the 3rd century CE. The surviving text mentions the seventh day before the Kalends of September, suggesting a date related to a festival or official business. It also names the consuls Sabinus II and Anullinus, providing a chronological marker for the inscription’s creation. Further lines reference Postumius Aurelianus, identified as a tribune of a cohort, but the remainder of his designation is lost due to damage. The mention of Palmyra suggests a connection to the region, although the precise nature of this connection is unclear from the fragment. The inscription’s purpose remains obscure due to its fragmentary state, but it offers valuable insights into the administration and calendar of Dura-Europos during the Roman period.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44795d (rom.mil.rec;1;89_4); Dura - Europos; vor 8. - 15. Juli 216
summary: P. Dura 66A is a fragmentary Latin document, likely an official register or roster, originating from Dura-Europos and dated to the 3rd century CE. The surviving text appears to list soldiers, numbering twenty-eight, belonging to the 20th cohort of Palmyrenes. The document is addressed to the *dominus cohortis*, and was produced under the authority of Aurelius Theodorus, a procurator of the Augusti. Numerous personal names, including Barsemia, Ulpius Silvanus, Zebidas, and Aurelius Alexander, are present, suggesting a military or administrative context within the Roman presence in Palmyra. The register was transmitted by messengers, and the date of composition is indicated as the *Ides* of July in the consulship of Sabinus and Annulinus. Significant portions of the text are lost, rendering a complete understanding of its purpose and organization impossible.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44795g (rom.mil.rec;1;89_7); Dura - Europos; vor 16. - 23. Juli 216
summary: P. Dura 66A is a fragmentary Latin letter, likely written in the third century CE. The surviving portions suggest a personal correspondence, addressed to an individual named Aurelius. The letter’s opening contains greetings and mentions Postumius Aurelianus and Aelius, alongside a 'genius,' a term often associated with a person’s protective spirit or divine ancestor. A reference to 'Lupo' and a cohort (cohors) of Palmyrenae, specifically the XX Palmyrenorum, indicates a military connection, potentially involving soldiers from Palmyra. The letter also names 'Tines' and 'Sorianus,' suggesting a network of individuals involved in the communication. The text is unfortunately damaged, obscuring much of the content and the precise nature of the message being conveyed, but it provides a glimpse into the social and military landscape of the Roman Empire during the 3rd century.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44795j (rom.mil.rec;1;89_10); Dura - Europos; vor 16. - 23. Juli 216
summary: P. Dura 66A is a fragmentary Latin inscription, likely a military dispatch or official communication, dating to the 3rd century CE. The text is severely damaged, rendering a complete interpretation impossible. Surviving portions suggest a communication originating 'from...abep...' and addressed 'to Antonio' within a military context, potentially referencing a legion and a cohort. The mention of 'hibernia' (Hibernia, i.e., Ireland) indicates a connection to Roman activity in that province. A centurion, Postumius Aurelianus, is named, identified as a *tribunus cohortis* (tribune of a cohort), suggesting a position of command. The inscription’s purpose appears to be administrative or logistical, detailing movement or status updates within a Roman military unit operating in Hibernia.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44795n (rom.mil.rec;1;89_14); Dura - Europos; vor 23. Juli - 1. Aug. 216 (Monat und Tag unsicher)
summary: P.Dura 66A is a fragmentary Latin inscription from Dura-Europos, dating to the 3rd century CE. The text appears to be a legal or administrative document, likely related to military affairs given the mention of *cohors XX Palmyrenorum* (20th Palmyrene cohort). A *procurator Augusti* (procuretor of the Augustan emperor) is also named, suggesting official business. The inscription is severely damaged, rendering much of the content illegible; discernible fragments mention a *barchalba*, a term of uncertain meaning, and a person named Aurelius. The text’s arrangement is linear, with significant gaps and lacunae obscuring its original structure and purpose. The presence of Palmyrene soldiers and an Augustan procurator indicates interaction between Roman administration and local military units in Dura-Europos.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44795y (rom.mil.rec;1;89_25); Dura - Europos; vor 22. Aug. 216
summary: P. Dura 66A is a fragmentary Latin inscription, likely a military notice or dispatch, originating from Dura-Europos and dated to the third century CE. The text is severely damaged, rendering a complete interpretation impossible; however, it appears to record a military action led by a tribune of the twentieth *miliaria cohors*. The mention of Palmyrene individuals suggests a connection to the Roman presence in Syria. The inscription is dated to the consular year of Sabinus and Anullin(us), placing it within a specific, albeit narrow, timeframe. A Postumius Aurelianus is also named, identified as a tribune, and the text references an Aurelius, whose name is incomplete. The inscription’s fragmented nature hinders a full understanding of the event it describes, but it provides valuable insight into the administrative and military context of Roman Dura-Europos.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44796 (rom.mil.rec;1;92); Dura - Europos; 13. März 222 - Dez. 225
summary: C.Pap.Lat. 338 is a fragmentary copy of a letter, likely official in nature, originating from the Roman province of Osrhoene in the 3rd century CE. The document primarily consists of lists of names, organized by centuries (centuriae) and turmae (troops or companies), suggesting a military context. These lists appear to be associated with a forthcoming military expedition, with references to assignments, musterings, and troop numbers. Individuals named include Roman citizens and local dignitaries, such as Iulius Romanus, Aurelius Magnus, and Abgarus Themasa, alongside less familiar names like Zebida, Iarhaei, and Vabalathi, indicating a mixed Roman and local population. The text’s condition is severely compromised, rendering many sections illegible and obscuring the full scope of the letter’s original purpose.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44797 (rom.mil.rec;1;94); Dura - Europos; ca. 232 - 238
summary: P. Dura 68 comprises fragmentary letters written in Latin during the 3rd century CE. The surviving portions are severely damaged, rendering a coherent narrative reconstruction impossible. The texts appear to consist of isolated phrases and names, suggesting correspondence of a personal or administrative nature, though the precise context remains obscure. Individuals mentioned include Vibianus, Paulus, and Aurelius Gaianus; place names, if identifiable, are lost to fragmentation. The presence of the term 'turma' (cohort/detachment) hints at a military or administrative association. The mention of 'Gaulian' suggests a connection to Gaul, though the precise location within Gaul is unknown. The text offers a tantalizing, albeit frustratingly incomplete, glimpse into the communication practices of the Roman period.

P.Dura 69 is a fragmentary Latin document from Dura-Europos, likely dating to the 3rd century CE. The surviving portions consist of lists of soldiers’ names, interspersed with what appear to be fragments of personal letters. The lists are organized by groupings of names, separated by consular datings. The document mentions the consuls Aufidius Marcellus II, and Albino and Maximus, and includes names of individuals, including Zebidas Iarh, Lo, Salme, and Themarsas. The presence of names like Demetrius and Maal suggests a diverse military population, potentially including individuals of non-Roman origin. The fragmentary nature of the text makes a complete reconstruction of its purpose and context impossible, but it offers a glimpse into the administration and personal correspondence within a Roman military unit at Dura-Europos.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44804 (chla;7;330); Dura - Europos; ca. 210 - 220
summary: P.Dura 75 comprises fragmentary letters written in Latin during the 3rd century CE. Recurring phrases suggest a formulaic opening, including expressions of well-wishing (“felicissimum…bene ualere”), and a request to send something (“mittas”). The surviving portions consist of three discrete lines, suggesting a larger, now lost, correspondence. source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44811 (chla;7;335); Dura - Europos; ca. 235 - 245
summary: P.Dura 80 comprises a small collection of fragmentary Latin letters originating from Dura-Europos, likely dating to the 3rd century CE. The surviving portions consist of isolated phrases and words, making reconstruction of complete letters impossible. Mentions of a *tribunus* (tribune) and *cohors* (cohort) suggest a military context, possibly relating to the Roman garrison stationed at Dura-Europos. The presence of the name

C.Pap.Lat. 326 is a fragmentary morning report, likely originating from a Roman military installation in the East, dated six days before the Kalends of April (March 28th) of the 3rd century CE. The document details the composition of a legionary contingent, listing troop numbers, unit types (duplicarii, sesquiplicarii, dromadarii, equites), and cohort designations, specifically mentioning Palmyrenes, Severians, and Alexandrians. Named individuals include the tribune Julius Rufianus, and various centurions and other officers like Timinius Paulinus and Aurelius Silvanus, alongside soldiers like Nigrinus and Iarhaboles Odeati. The report also references logistical concerns, including grain procurement and the prosecution of hoarders, and mentions deployments and returns of soldiers, alongside a brief mention of a holy sign of Mercury. The text is heavily damaged, rendering portions unintelligible, but reveals a glimpse into the administrative and military routines of a Roman legion.

C.Pap.Lat. 339 is a fragmentary morning report, likely originating from a Roman military installation in the Eastern Roman Empire. The text appears to list personnel and units, specifically mentioning the *centuriae* of Pudentis and Ptolemy, and the 20th cohort of Palmyrene soldiers assigned to the Severian Alexandrian detachment. It also references consuls Maximus and Paternus, whose names appear in two separate datelines, the first dated to *pridie Nonas Septembres* and the second incomplete. The document details orders for the units to proceed to camp and mentions Demetrius, designated as *magister campi* (camp master). Further fragmentary sections include names like Bellaeus, Malchus, Zebida, Gora, and Abidn, alongside references to cavalry (*equites*) and a standard of Jupiter (*signum Iovis*), suggesting a detailed accounting of military assets and deployments.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44816 (p.dura;;85); Dura - Europos; ca. 230
summary: P. Dura 85 is a fragmentary Latin document, likely originating from Dura-Europos and dating to the 3rd century CE. The surviving text appears to be a morning report, or a similar type of administrative record, judging from the presence of military titles. Mentions include a *tribunus* (military tribune) and *tribubres* (plural, likely referring to subordinate military personnel). The text is severely damaged, rendering a full reconstruction of its content impossible; discernible fragments suggest references to a “salu…” (possibly a greeting or salutation) and “exem…” (potentially an exemption or discharge). The document’s organization is lost due to the fragmentation, but it seems to list personnel or activities. The presence of military terminology indicates a connection to the Roman military presence in Dura-Europos.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44818 (p.dura;;87); Dura - Europos; ca. 230
summary: P.Dura 87 is a fragmentary Latin text, likely a military report, originating from Dura-Europos and datable to the 3rd century CE. The surviving portions suggest a roster or accounting of personnel, specifically mentioning *equites* (cavalrymen) and *turmae* (cavalry units). Names are present, including the imperial cognomen *Antoninus*, which likely refers to Marcus Aurelius Antoninus (r. 161-180 CE) or a successor, and a personal name, “Cari.” The text appears to list numbers of individuals, with references to “lx” (sixty) and “cc” (two hundred), and a corrupted reference to a centur(y). The fragmentary nature of the document makes a complete reconstruction of its purpose and scope impossible; it is unclear whether it represents a daily, weekly, or other periodic report. The presence of military terminology and imperial association firmly places it within the Roman military context of Dura-Europos.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44820 (p.dura;;89); Dura - Europos; 26. - 29. Mai 239
summary: C.Pap.Lat. 331 is a fragmentary morning report, likely issued from a Roman military camp in the third century CE. The text details troop deployments, personnel assignments, and readiness for duty, specifically within the 20th Palmytrene cohort of the Gordianae unit. Named individuals include Aurelius Germanus, the appointed leader, Ulpius Marianus (signifer), Aurelius Priscus (bucinator), and Avitus (centurion). The report lists various roles such as tessararius, signifer, deciman, and duplicarii, alongside numerical strength of units and equipment. References to Jupiter Dolichenus and the Kalends of June suggest a blend of military administration and religious observance, and the document provides valuable insight into the organization and daily life of a Roman legionary cohort.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44822 (p.dura;;91); Dura - Europos; ca. 225 - 235
summary: P. Dura 91 is a fragmentary Latin tabulation, likely a morning report or similar accounting document from the 3rd century CE. The surviving portions detail military personnel, specifically listing absent soldiers (dcclxv, or 675) and camel drivers (dromadarii, xxvii, or 27). The text appears to be organized as a roster, with names partially recoverable: 'Salmes Them[...]', 'Iulius Mari[...]'. The presence of the month 'Iunius' (ccxxvi, representing the 226th day of the year, or June) suggests the report was compiled during that month. The fragment is unfortunately damaged, rendering portions of the text illegible and obscuring the full scope of the information it originally contained. The document provides a glimpse into the logistical and administrative practices of a Roman military unit.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44827 (p.dura;;95); Dura - Europos; Okt. 250 - Juli 251
summary: P. Dura 95 is a fragmentary Latin military report, likely originating from Dura-Europos, dating to the late 3rd century CE. The text details troop deployments, personnel assignments, and numerical counts of soldiers, organized around specific dates and consuls. It references several individuals, including military officials like a *praesidus* and centurions Marinus and Aurelius Malchus, and consuls Sabinus, Dionysius, Decius, Gratus, Pontianus, and Aquilinus. The document appears to record changes in military personnel and their movements, alongside references to decrees concerning stipends and rations. Notably, the text includes references to Germanic and Achean centuries, suggesting a diverse military composition, and mentions a military procurator, indicating administrative oversight. The repeated mention of *Dominus noster Decius Augustus* suggests the reign of Emperor Decius.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44828 (p.dura;;96); Dura - Europos; ca. 245 - 255
summary: P. Dura 96 is a fragmentary Latin document, likely originating from Dura-Europos and datable to the late 3rd century CE. The text appears to be a military roster or list of personnel, specifically detailing individuals holding various ranks within a Roman unit. Visible abbreviations indicate the positions of *signifer* (standard bearer), *vexillarius*, and *mensor* (measurer), suggesting a focus on logistical or ceremonial roles. The presence of numerals, notably 'xii' (twelve), implies a structured organization, possibly denoting the number of individuals holding a specific rank or assigned to a particular cohort. Names are present, including Iulius and Heliodorus, but are largely obscured by damage; the name Iarabolēs is also partially recoverable. The document’s fragmentary nature prevents a complete reconstruction of its purpose or the unit to which these individuals belonged.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44829 (p.dura;;97); Dura - Europos; nach 31. Aug. 251
summary: C.Pap.Lat. 325 is a fragmentary Latin inventory, likely from a military or administrative context, dating to the late 3rd century CE. The document meticulously lists horses and their owners, alongside associated financial transactions (denarii payments). Each entry includes details such as the horse’s age (often ‘quadrimus,’ meaning four years old), markings (notably on the thighs and arms), and the individuals responsible for proving their ownership. Recurring figures include the procurator Pomponius Letianus, the leader Licinnius Pacatianus, and the prefects, whose presence is noted alongside dates. The document is organized chronologically by consular years and calendar dates, providing a snapshot of horse ownership and administration within a specific Roman community.

C.Pap.Lat. 333 is a fragmentary roster, likely a military or administrative list, dating to the 3rd century CE. The text consists of numerous personal names, many of which appear to be of Eastern origin, alongside references to Roman consuls and centuria. The roster seems to be organized by groupings of individuals, with some entries explicitly noting their position within a centuria. Recurring names like Aurelius, Malchus, and Themarsa suggest a mixed Roman and Eastern population, possibly within the Roman East. The frequent mentions of consuls indicate an attempt to date or contextualize the individuals listed, though the repeated and sometimes overlapping consulships create chronological ambiguity. The presence of names like Abgarus and Seleucus points to connections with regions like Syria and Mesopotamia.

C.Pap.Lat. 335 is a fragmentary Latin roster, likely documenting military or administrative personnel across the late 2nd and 3rd centuries CE. The document is organized into sections, each presenting lists of individuals identified by their names and occasionally their titles or military ranks such as *signifer*, *vexillarius*, and *explorator*. Consular years are frequently included, providing a chronological framework that spans the reigns of Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius, Commodus, and Severus III. Recurring names include Aurelius (in various forms), Becchufrain, and Appadan(a), suggesting individuals of authority or association with specific units. References to locations like Parthia and Appadana, alongside names with Eastern etymologies, indicate a context of frontier administration and a diverse military contingent, while mentions of feasts and legal proceedings further illuminate the document's administrative and social context. Significant damage obscures many names and locations, hindering a complete reconstruction of the roster’s contents.

This section of C.Pap.Lat. 335 presents a roster of individuals, seemingly military personnel, organized into centuries and ranked by status. The text lists names, often preceded by the prefix 'Aurelius,' alongside consular dates spanning the late 2nd and 3rd centuries CE, including names like Mucianus, Fabianus, Tertullo, and Severo. The roster appears to document transfers or assignments, with some individuals noted as *translatus* (transferred) and references to *ad dominum nostrum* (to our lord), suggesting a possible connection to imperial service or military administration. The repeated names of Becchuf(rayn) and Appadan(a) Aurelius suggest they held positions of authority or were associated with specific units.

This fragmented roster (Latin: *tabula stipendiaria*) lists individuals, seemingly military personnel, identified by their Latin names and often followed by parenthetical designations like 'consul' or 'explorator'. The names are heavily damaged, but recurring individuals include Aurelius (in various forms) and the place name Appadana, suggesting a connection to a region east of Roman control. The text also mentions feasts (Neon), Roman officials (consuls), and deities (Sacrahim, Dom(inum) n(ostrum)), indicating a context of Roman administration and religious observance in a frontier setting.

Part 3 of C.Pap.Lat. 335 continues a roster, listing individuals with their names and titles alongside the names of Roman consuls under whose administration they served. The individuals appear to be officials or soldiers, identified by their *cognomina* and occasionally by their military rank (*signifer*, *vexillarius*, *explorator*). The roster spans several decades, with consuls from the reigns of Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius, Commodus, and Severus III appearing repeatedly. The text is heavily damaged, rendering many names and titles illegible, and the geographical locations of *castella* are also obscured.

Part 4 of C.Pap.Lat. 335 presents a roster of individuals, likely military personnel or officials, associated with various locations and titles within the Roman Empire, possibly in a context of frontier administration. The names are predominantly Latinized versions of local names, suggesting a diverse population. The text includes references to consuls, emperors (Antoninus Augustus), and military ranks (duplicarius, vexillarius, decurio), alongside mentions of feasts and legal proceedings (prosecution of hordiators). The repeated name 'Becchufrain' and locations like Parthia and Appadana suggest a connection to the eastern frontier.

Part 5 of C.Pap.Lat. 335 continues the roster, listing individuals with their *cognomina* and occasionally their roles (vexillarius, explorator, duplicarius). The text appears to document personnel associated with military or administrative units, with frequent references to consuls and offices held. Proper names are predominantly Latin, but include elements suggestive of Eastern origins, and the document seems to span several years, indicated by the succession of consuls named. The text is heavily damaged, rendering many lines illegible.

Part 6 of C.Pap.Lat. 335 consists of fragmented rosters, likely military or administrative personnel lists, spanning several decades of the 3rd century CE. The lists contain numerous personal names, many of which appear to be of Eastern origin, suggesting a diverse military contingent. Consular years are frequently cited, providing a rough chronological framework for the entries, and include names like Severus III, Anullinus, and Dextrus. The repeated name “Becchufrain” suggests a title or designation rather than a personal name.

P. Dura 101 is a fragmentary Latin roster, likely documenting personnel associated with the Roman military presence at Dura-Europos during the 3rd century CE. The document comprises four distinct sections, each presenting a list of individuals identified by personal names, titles, and potentially military rank. Recurring names include Abgarus, Seleus, Ulpius, Aurelius, and Iulius, alongside Roman cognomina such as Antiochus and Heliodorus. Chronological markers are provided by repeated references to Roman consuls, including Severo, Cilone, Antonino, and Victorino, alongside mentions of feasts dedicated to d(ivus) Antoninus. Geographic references include Appadana, Castello Arabum, and Magdalena, suggesting administrative or military districts within the region. The text’s organization appears to be primarily by individual name, with some sections suggesting groupings by unit or role, and the phrase 'ad mamm' indicating periodic updates.

P. Dura 101, Part 1, sections 1-18, appears to be a roster or register of individuals, likely military personnel or officials, associated with various names and titles. The text lists names like Abgarus, Seleus, Aelius Heliodorus, and Aurelius Antiochus, alongside repeated references to offices like 'signifer' and 'officio'. Consuls are frequently mentioned, including Severo, Cilone, and others, providing chronological markers within the document. The repeated name 'Appad(ana)' and the presence of terms like 'Becchuf(rayn)' suggest a specific regional or ethnic context.

This fragmented roster (Part 2, sections 19-32) appears to be a list of individuals, likely military personnel or officials, associated with the Roman presence in Dura-Europos. The names are predominantly Latin, but include numerous Eastern personal names, suggesting a mixed population. The text repeatedly mentions consuls of various years (divo Severo iii, Geta Seniore ii, Antonino iii, Faustino, Dextro ii, Annullo ii, Victorino, Pompeiiano, Apro et Maximo, Sabino ii, Grato), and references locations such as Appadana, Castello Arabum, and Magdalena, indicating administrative or military districts. The repeated use of the term 'singularis' suggests a categorization or rank within the listed individuals.

Part 3 of P.Dura 101 presents a roster of individuals, likely military personnel, associated with various names and titles. The text is heavily damaged, obscuring many names and titles, but it repeatedly mentions individuals named Ulpius, Aurelius, and Iulius, alongside eastern names like Zenobius, Malchus, and Appadana. The roster includes references to Roman officials (consuls, praetors) and military ranks (centurions, explorators), alongside mentions of feasts (divo Antonino) and locations (Magdala), suggesting a military or administrative context in the Roman East.

Part 4 of P. Dura 101 presents a roster, likely of military personnel or officials, associated with the Roman garrison at Dura-Europos. The text lists numerous individuals, many with names of clear Eastern origin, alongside Roman names like Ulpius and Aelius, suggesting a mixed military population. The roster is organized seemingly by units or roles, with frequent references to consulships (both Roman and potentially local) and military ranks such as vexillarius, signifer, and decurion. The repeated mention of 'ad mamm' (to the month of) suggests the roster may have been updated periodically.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44834 (p.dura;;102); Dura - Europos; ca. 222 - 228
summary: P. Dura 102 is a fragmentary roster, likely a military or administrative list, organized by centuries. The text primarily contains the names of individuals, consistently prefixed with “Aurelius,” suggesting a predominantly Roman or Roman-influenced population within the Dura-Europos region. Alongside these names, the document includes references to individuals named Seleucus, Salmanes, and others of potentially non-Roman origin, indicating a diverse community. The list is punctuated by references to Roman consuls, including Laetus, Sabinus, and Faustinus, providing chronological markers for the document’s composition, likely within the 3rd century CE. The presence of terms like “dromon” (likely referring to a ship or transport) and “Appadana” (a Persian term) suggests involvement in trade or military activities. The text is heavily damaged, rendering many entries illegible and obscuring the full scope of the roster.

P. Dura 103 is a fragmentary Latin list, likely originating from Roman Dura-Europos in the early third century CE. The text appears to enumerate cavalrymen, judging from the military nomenclature present. Names are listed sequentially, but significant portions of the text are lost, rendering the precise arrangement and any potential organizational structure (e.g., by unit, rank, or geographical origin) unclear. The names themselves suggest a diverse group, including individuals with Latin (Aurelius, Ulpius, Iulius) and potentially Aramaic or other Near Eastern personal names (Nisamsus, Zabdibo[li], Maccaeus, Iadei, Barnaei, Apoll[ona], Maccaei, Vab[alathi]). The presence of these varied names reflects the cosmopolitan nature of Dura-Europos' military population.

P. Dura 104 is a fragmentary Latin list of names, likely dating to the third century CE based on paleographic and linguistic assessment. The text is severely damaged, rendering a complete reconstruction impossible; the surviving portions consist of isolated names and potentially titles or honorifics. Several names appear multiple times, suggesting a possible repetition of categories or a listing of individuals associated with a specific group or event. Individuals identifiable include Germ[anus], Abdeus, Fusc[o], Malchus, and Rabbelus. The presence of the consular titles 'Crispino co(n)s(ul)' and 'ii co(n)s(ul)' indicates a connection to Roman political life, though the precise context remains obscure due to the fragmentary nature of the document. The text offers a glimpse into the personal nomenclature of the Dura-Europus region during the Roman Empire.

P. Dura 105 is a fragmentary Latin roster, likely originating from Dura-Europos and datable to the late 3rd century CE. The document lists individuals, seemingly organized by some form of military or administrative unit, with designations like *singularis* and *duplicarius*. Numerous personal names are present, predominantly those of individuals named Aurelius, suggesting a significant presence of this *nomen* within the group. The roster also includes consular dating, referencing several years with consuls such as Sabinus, Lucius Iulianus Fuscus, and Albinus, providing a potential chronological anchor. References to *d(omino)* Alexandro, appearing multiple times as consul, suggest a recurring figure of importance. The text is severely damaged, rendering much of the organization and context unclear, but it provides a glimpse into the personnel structure of a late Roman community.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44838 (p.dura;;106); Dura - Europos; 5. Sept. 233 - 241
summary: P. Dura 106 is a fragmentary Latin guard roster, likely originating from Dura-Europos and datable to the 3rd century CE. The document lists personnel assigned to various gates (portae) of a Roman military installation, specifically mentioning the Porta Praetoria, an aquaria, and ballistae. Names appear to be organized by gate assignment, with each line containing a sequence of names, often preceded by fragmentary centuria designations. Individuals named include Aurelius (appearing repeatedly), Alexander, Heliodorus, Bargas, Claudius, and Julius, alongside less common names like Zebida, Malchus, and Germani. The roster provides a glimpse into the military administration and personnel structure of a Roman garrison in a frontier setting, demonstrating a mix of Latin and potentially other names, suggesting a diverse military population.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44839 (p.dura;;107); Dura - Europos; 22. - 24. Mai 240 (Jahr unsicher)
summary: P. Dura 107 is a fragmentary Latin guard roster from Dura-Europos, likely dating to the 3rd century CE. The document lists personnel assigned to various centuriae and turmae, identifying them by their personal names, all of which are preceded by the cognomen 'Aurel(ius)' or 'Flauius'. The roster includes names like Iarhaeus, Nismosa, Siluanus, and Antiochus, suggesting a diverse military contingent. Recurring place names, such as porta praetoria and porta aquaria, indicate the roster's connection to specific locations within the city's fortifications. The text is heavily damaged, rendering many entries illegible, but the surviving portions provide valuable insight into the administrative organization and personnel of a Roman military unit stationed at Dura-Europos.

P. Dura 110 is a fragmentary Latin document from Dura-Europos, likely dating to the 3rd century CE. It constitutes a guard roster, listing soldiers organized into *centuriae* (centuries). The roster names individuals, including Marinus Apollus, Iarhaboles, Sfetules, Malchi, and Aurelius, alongside the centurions Bargillus and Bargarelus. References to *porta aquaria* (aquatic gate) and *porta praetoriana* (pretorian gate) suggest a military installation with specific access points. The presence of names like Germani Aurelius and Aurelius Abedmalch indicates a diverse military population, potentially including individuals of Germanic or other non-Roman origin. The text is severely damaged, obscuring much of the organization and full list of personnel.

P. Dura 113 is a fragmentary Latin inscription, likely a military register or roster, originating from Dura-Europos and datable to the 3rd century CE. The text appears to list individuals, possibly soldiers, organized into centuriae. Names visible include Bassus, Chabseus, Malch[...], Zabdibol, and Demetrius, suggesting a mixed population, perhaps including individuals with names of non-Roman origin. The presence of the name Flavius Demetrius indicates a Roman citizen or someone integrated into Roman society. The inscription is severely damaged, rendering much of the content illegible, but the recurring mention of centuriae suggests a military context, possibly a unit within the Roman army stationed at Dura-Europos. The fragmentary nature of the text prevents a more precise determination of its purpose or scope.

C.Pap.Lat. 334 is a fragmentary Latin document from the 3rd century CE, likely a military register or roster. The text is organized primarily by *turmae* (units, possibly equivalent to centuries or companies) and then by *centuriae* (centuries) within those units. It lists individual names, seemingly soldiers or members of a military cohort, alongside some titles like *dupl(icarius)* (double-soldier). Recurring names include Aurelius, Themarsa, Mocimus, and Malchi, suggesting familial or tribal connections within the unit. The document also records dates, specifically mentioning the consulship of Lupo and Maximo, which allows for a tentative chronological placement. Significant portions of the text are lost or too damaged for reconstruction, hindering a complete understanding of the register’s purpose and scope.

P.Dura 117 is a fragmentary Latin text from Dura-Europos, likely dating to the third century CE. It presents itself as a list of personal names, organized into groupings designated by the numeral 'dcc' (seventy) and 'pdcc' (one hundred and seventy). The names appear to be arranged by centuries, although the precise chronological framework is obscured by lacunae. Individuals mentioned include the Roman Emperors Maximinus Augustus and Africanus, serving as consuls at the time of the document’s creation. Recurring personal names such as Iarhaeus, Zebida, Aurelius (in various forms), and Malchus suggest a community with diverse origins, possibly including elements from Syria and Mesopotamia. The text offers a glimpse into the personal nomenclature and social structure of a Roman frontier settlement.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44852 (p.dura;;120); Dura - Europos; Okt. - Dez. 222
summary: P. Dura 120 is a fragmentary Latin document from the third century CE, likely originating from Dura-Europos. The text appears to be a list of names, organized by centuries (centuriae), and further subdivided by dates expressed as day and month. Each entry includes a name and a consular dating formula, indicating the consuls of the year. The document references the consuls Antoninus Laetus, Aurelius Antoninus, Aurelius Silvanus, Extricatus, and Alexander Augustus, suggesting a connection to the Roman administration of the region. The presence of dedications 'to our Lord' (d(omino) n(ostro)) before the name Alexander Augustus suggests a possible imperial cult association. The fragmentary nature of the text makes a complete reconstruction of the list impossible, but it provides valuable insight into Roman administrative practices and nomenclature in the region.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44853 (p.dura;;121); Dura - Europos; nach 28. Juni 239 (Jahr unsicher)
summary: P. Dura 121 is a fragmentary Latin record, likely originating from Dura-Europos, documenting the transfer of military personnel. The text consists of repeated entries, each recording a number of individuals 'reported' (relatus) based on correspondence from Attus Rufinus, a *vir clarissimus consular* serving under the authority of Gordian, who held the consulship. The entries are dated by consular names, specifically Heliodorus Fuscus (in his second consulship) and Aurelius Macrinus (in his seventh), suggesting a timeframe within the early third century CE. The record appears to list units, with references to a 'century' and mentions of 'Germani' and 'Iulius,' potentially indicating troop designations or tribal affiliations. Significant portions of the text are lost, obscuring the precise nature of the transfers and the full extent of the personnel involved. The document provides a glimpse into the administrative processes of the Roman military presence in Dura-Europos.

P. Dura 122 is a fragmentary Latin military roster, likely originating from Dura-Europos, dating to the 3rd century CE. The text lists soldiers organized by centuries (centuriae), and each entry is associated with the same consular year, indicated by the phrase 'eodem consule.' The names recorded are largely of Roman soldiers, but include individuals with non-Roman ethnic names, suggesting a diverse military contingent. Several names appear multiple times, potentially indicating repeated service or errors in transcription. The fragmentary nature of the document makes a complete reconstruction of the roster impossible, and several names are only partially preserved. Consuls named in the text include Aurelius Bernicianus and an unidentified consul associated with the Mocimi and Achei centuries. The document provides valuable insight into the composition and organization of Roman military units in the eastern frontier.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 44862 (p.dura;;128); Dura - Europos; ca. 245 (?)
summary: C.Pap.Lat. 336 is a fragmentary collection of official records, likely from a public journal or archive, dating to the 3rd century CE. The surviving portions consist of discrete entries, seemingly organized chronologically but with significant gaps. The text is primarily in Latin, interspersed with Greek phrases and words, suggesting a bilingual administrative context. Recurring individuals mentioned include Pacatianus, identified as a man of merit, and Castor, who appears to be an official issuing decrees or pronouncements. The fragments contain references to decrees, copies of documents (ἀντίγραφον), and administrative actions, including the dispatch of an individual to an unspecified location. The content also alludes to a 'dimiourgos' (a craftsman or official) and a peculiar reference to a 'goose' (χην), the significance of which is unclear given the fragmentary nature of the text.

C.Pap.Lat. 342 is a fragmentary Latin letter, datable to the third century CE based on paleography and script conventions. The surviving portions indicate a correspondence involving horses, likely relating to their management or sale, given the opening phrase 'epistulae equorum'. The letter’s sender is identified as Zabnibolus of Maccaeus, while the addressees appear to be Aurelius Claudius and Aurelius Archelaus. The text is severely damaged, obscuring the precise content of the message and the nature of the relationship between the individuals involved. The presence of personal names suggests a private, rather than official, context. The fragment offers a glimpse into the administrative and economic activities surrounding equestrian ownership in Roman society.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 45366 (c.epist.lat;;175); unbekannt; II - III
summary: Ch.L.A. 10 434 is a fragmentary Latin letter, likely dating to the 2nd century CE based on the paleography and language. The opening identifies the recipient as Iulius Agrippinus, a soldier in the Legio II Traiana. The letter’s content is severely damaged, but discernible phrases suggest a request or appeal concerning a matter of duty ('munus') and a possible captivity ('in captivitate'). The writer expresses a desire to learn something about the recipient ('ut possim te cognoscere') and mentions an adversary, implying a conflict or dispute. The letter’s abruptness and lacunae make a full reconstruction of its argument impossible, but it appears to be a personal communication of some urgency.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 62953 (chla;5;304); Tebtynis (Arsinoites); II - III
summary: P.Tebt. 2 686 is a fragmentary papyrus containing a combination of accounting records and exercises in cursive writing, likely produced in the second century CE. The document details expenditures and quantities of various materials, including timber, reeds, oil, lead, cloth, and pitch, measured in talents, drachmae, and minae. Alongside these accounts are lists of personnel involved in various tasks, such as lead-layers, painters, and workers, along with associated costs. The text also includes a brief, damaged passage that appears to be a personal note, mentioning a Feneto and alluding to a debt or obligation related to gifts and time. The mixed nature of the document—combining administrative records with calligraphic practice—suggests it may have been a training exercise for scribes or an informal record kept by an official.

P.Aberd. 133 is a fragmentary Latin accounting document, likely originating from a Roman military auxiliary unit in the 2nd century CE. The text comprises two distinct sections, both detailing payments and disbursements related to military equipment (specifically *lorica*, or body armor) and provisions (*viatico*). Accounts are organized primarily by individual recipient or payer, recording sums in denarii, oboli, semisses, and quadrantes. Individuals mentioned include military personnel such as Maximus Nicanianus and Luccius Agillius, and officials Orfito, Maximo, Pollio II, and Quintillus. Imperial connections are indicated by references to Lucius Commodus and Quintillus, and the geographical location of Babylon is noted in the second section alongside the individual Tinhius Val[...]. The document provides a glimpse into the financial administration and logistical support of a Roman military unit.

This text is a fragmentary accounting document, likely from a military auxiliary unit. It details payments and disbursements related to equipment (lorica) and provisions (viatico), listing individuals involved and amounts in denarii, oboli, semisses, and occasionally a quadrant. The accounts are organized by individual, and mention several officials, including consuls Orfito and Maximo, Pollio II, and Quintillus, as well as military personnel like Maximus Nicanianus and Luccius Agillius. The document also references imperial officials Lucius Commodus and Quintillus.

This section of P.Aberd. 133 details the accounting of a military unit's equipment and finances, specifically concerning lorica (body armor) and associated payments. It appears to be a record of disbursements and receipts, listing individuals and amounts owed or held in deposit, often in denarii, oboli, and quadrantes. The text mentions the consuls Lucius Commodus and Pertinax, and references a location identified as Babylone (Babylon), and a person named Tinhius Val[...].

This fragmentary Latin text, designated BGU 7 1689, appears to be a segment of a ceremonial or triumphal inscription, likely related to a fast or religious observance, given the presence of military organization and consular titles. The surviving lines list individuals—soldiers, consuls, and representatives of various nations and provinces—arranged under the authority of consuls. Named individuals include Catilius Severus (in his second consulship), Annius Verus (also in his second consulship), and references to locations such as Syria, Capitol, Egypt, Africa, and Noricum. The text details the number of units or individuals associated with each location, with numerical values (ii, iv, v, vi) indicating quantities. The presence of the term 'giribit' is unclear, as its meaning within this context is unknown. The inscription's purpose and the full scope of the event it commemorates remain obscure due to the fragmentary nature of the surviving text.

source: papyri.info DDbDP TM 64894 (chrest.mitt;;380); unbekannt; IV - VI
summary: P.Amh. 2 27 is a fragmentary Latin legal text, likely originating from a collection of imperial rescripts or legal opinions, datable to the late antique period, specifically the 5th century CE. The fragment appears to concern judicial procedure, specifically addressing issues of witness testimony and the permissible length of legal proceedings. It references a *rescriptum* (imperial decree) concerning enactments, and mentions the consul of the day, whose name is unfortunately truncated as 'top...h[ ...]'. Individuals named include Aurelius Severus, and the text alludes to a provincial governor (*rector prouinciae*). The fragment discusses the potential harm caused by false testimony (*narratio falsi*) and the limitations placed on prolonging litigation, even for those who abandon a case. The concluding portion is highly corrupt, mentioning 'extraordinary judgments' and a partially legible term 'po...n...inonil...'.

P.Cair. Masp. 2 67131 Vo is a fragmentary legal document, likely a written confirmation or record of a transaction related to property and debt. The text appears to be a declaration made by an individual, possibly a magistrate or official, concerning a debt owed to them by Isidoros. It involves a transfer of property, specifically a house, and a payment of fifteen thirds of gold solidi towards a city exchange. The document includes a request for Theodosius, a messenger, to verify the details and confirm Isidoros’s acquisition of certain items. A ‘defensor’ is present, indicating a legal context, and the text concludes with instructions for the recording of the declaration by Psiō, a numerary of a canonical chest, and its availability for public viewing. The presence of references to a ‘military order’ and a ‘canonical chest’ suggests a connection to official or ecclesiastical institutions.

BGU 2 611 is a Latin oration, likely delivered in the Roman Senate during the reign of Claudius (41-54 CE), concerning judicial reform. The speech addresses concerns about the conduct of accusers and judges, proposing measures to curb frivolous lawsuits and ensure fairer proceedings. The speaker, whose name is not given, criticizes the practice of defendants being brought before courts by vengeful accusers and laments the lack of due process. He suggests limiting the power of accusers, imposing deadlines on judges, and establishing clearer guidelines for judicial conduct, referencing the *Lex Laetoria* and proposing a system of accountability. The text is fragmentary, particularly towards the end, but reveals a significant concern with the abuse of legal processes and a desire to restore integrity to the Roman judicial system.

BGU 7 1690 is a Latin birth announcement (genessancia) from Roman Egypt, dating to January of 125 CE. The text records the birth of a daughter, Loginia, to Epimachus Longinus, a soldier (miles) in the second cohort of Theban auxiliary troops serving under centurion Octavian Alexander. The announcement explicitly mentions the presence of Arsute, daughter of Lucius, as a guest in Epimachus’s household, and explains the insertion of this notice as a consequence of a military division (districtio) that occurred at Philadelphia during the winter. The document is notable for its inclusion of Greek phrasing at the end, likely reflecting the multilingual environment of Roman Egypt. The consuls Sergius Octavius Laenate and Pontius Marcus Antonius Rufinus, and the reign of Emperor Trajan Hadrian are specified, providing a precise chronological marker. The text’s fragmented condition obscures portions of the phrasing, particularly in the concluding remarks.

BGU 7 1691 is a fragmentary Latin birth announcement, likely originating from Alexandria, Egypt. The text details births registered on a public tablet, specifically referencing the *tabula albi professionum* – a register of professions used for recording births. The announcement is dated twice, first to the consulship of Aulus Cornelius Palmus Frontonianus and Publius Calvisius Tullus in the twelfth year of the imperial reign of Nerva Trajan Augustus, Germanicus Dacicus, and again to the consulship of Appius Annius Gallus and Marcus Atilius Bradua in the same twelfth year of Trajan’s reign. Individuals named include Lucius Sentius Saturninus and his son, Charita, and Marcus Sentius, son of Lucius, alongside Pollia Marcus Aquila. The text appears to be a formal record, intended for public display in the *Atrium magnum* of Alexandria, and mentions a Prefect of Egypt, likely Servius Sulpicius Similis.

BGU 7 1692 is a fragmentary Latin birth announcement, likely a public record from Roman Egypt. The text details the registration of a child, Marcus Valerius Turbo, born to Marcus Valerius Maximum and Antonia Casullute. It references multiple years and consular pairings, specifically mentioning Lucilius Lollianus Avitus and Titus Statilius Maximus, and later Lucius Valerius Proculus, prefect of Egypt. The document explicitly states it was copied from a public tablet of professions displayed in the Great Atrium of Alexandria, indicating a formalized system for recording births. The text is interrupted and corrupt, particularly regarding the page divisions and some names, making a complete reconstruction impossible. The presence of both the Egyptian month Phaophi and the Roman month September suggests a bilingual calendar system in use.

BGU 7 1693 is a fragmentary Latin birth announcement, likely originating from Alexandria in Roman Egypt. The text details the registration of newborn children, recorded on a public tablet displayed in the Great Atrium. It provides a date, identifying the consuls Lucius Lollianus Avitus and Titus Statilius Maximus, and the eighth year of the reign of Emperor Marcus Aurelius (Caesar Titus Aelius Hadrianus Antoninus Augustus Pius). The prefect of Egypt, Lucius Valerius Proculus, is also named. The inscription’s purpose was to formally announce and record these births, presumably for civic or administrative purposes. Significant portions of the text are lost, particularly concerning the causes or reasons for acceptance of the children’s professions, rendering the full context unclear.

BGU 7 1694 is a fragmentary Latin birth announcement, likely originating from Alexandria, Egypt. The text records births registered according to official procedures, and is presented as a transcript from a public register ('tabula professionum') displayed in the Atrium Magnum. The announcement is dated twice, first to the consular year of Marcus Pontius Laelianus and Aulus Iunius Pastores, and then to the following year under Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Verus. The register was overseen by Marcus Annius Suriacus, the Prefect of Egypt. The surviving fragment details the birth of Marcus Lucretius Numisianus, son of Publius Cornelius Bassus and Julia Cuaiane, and notes a payment of 400 sestertii made by Marcus Lucretius Octavianus. The text’s organization appears to be chronological, listing births sequentially on a register page.

BGU 7 1695 is a Latin funerary testament, likely inscribed on a tomb stele, originating from Alexandria, Egypt, and dated to the 2nd century CE. The text details the deceased, Flotten, a soldier in the Alexandrian fleet, and outlines his wishes for burial and the disposal of assets. He requests to be buried and his body consumed, bequeathing 200 denarii from a source identified as *dolus* (deceit/fraud). The testament is dated to the 21st year of the reign of Emperor Hadrian, specifically the 10th day of the month of Phaophi, with consuls Barbaro and Regulus. Several witnesses are named, including Safinnius Herminus, a soldier in the Alexandrian fleet, and a series of individuals identified by their Greek names and professions as householders, suggesting a local community of mixed language and cultural backgrounds.

BGU 7 1696 is a fragmentary Latin testament, likely dating to the 2nd century CE. The document concerns the disposition of property, specifically a *vicus* (farm or village) located at Philadelphia. The testator, whose name is lost in the surviving fragments, names Gemellus as a key figure, likely a slave or freedman involved in the estate's management. The beneficiaries include Chrestias, who receives a portion of the property, and the heirs are to be surveyed according to some unspecified process. The text also mentions Caius Numissius, whose role is unclear but who appears in connection with a potential condemnation or legal action related to the inheritance. The document's structure is disrupted by lacunae, making a complete understanding of the testamentary arrangements impossible, but it provides a glimpse into Roman property law and the complexities of manumission and inheritance.

Ch.L.A. 1 7 a-b is a fragmentary pay record (stipendium) from the Roman army, likely dating to the 1st century CE. The document details payments to individual legionaries, listing amounts in drachmas and obols, and itemizing expenditures for food (faenaria, victum), military equipment (caligae fascias), clothing (vestimentis), and other expenses. Several individuals are named: the consuls Lucio Asinio and Quintus Iulius Proculus, Damasco, Rennius Innocens, and Gaius Valerius Germanus Tyro. The record appears to track payments across three years, with recurring entries for standard allotments and deductions. The text is damaged, with numerous lacunae obscuring portions of the names and amounts, making a complete reconstruction impossible.

Ch.L.A. 1 7 a-b is a fragmentary Latin record detailing detached military service, specifically relating to grain supply duties, spanning from February 80 to September 87 CE. The text lists individuals, their assigned tasks (primarily *frumentum* – grain supply), and the years of service under the reigns of both Titus and Domitian. Entries are organized *viritim*, meaning by individual soldier, and include dates of departure and return, often specified by Roman calendar dates (e.g., *xii Kalendas*). Notable individuals mentioned include Marcus Papirius Rufus, Titus Suetus Clemens (a camp prefect), Titus Flavius Satur, Titus Flavius Vale[rius], and Titus Flavius Celer. The record references locations like Neapolis and Mercury (likely a place name, not the Roman god), and mentions roles such as centurion and freedman. The fragmentary nature of the text obscures some details, leaving gaps in names and dates.

Ch.L.A. 1 7 a-b represents a fragmentary monthly summary, likely a report from the Legio III Cyrenaica, dating to the 1st century CE. The text appears to detail the status of a century within the legion, listing numerical data concerning personnel and their assignments. Several names are present, including Porcius, Carrarius, Plotinus, Julius Severus, Flavus, Domitius, and Celsus, suggesting a record of individuals fulfilling specific roles within the unit. The document mentions various roles such as *armorum custos* (armourer), *conductor*, *secutor*, *custos domi* (house custodian), *librarii* (scribes), and *cieapi* (camp followers or servants), providing insight into the logistical and administrative structure of a Roman legionary century. The presence of references to “supranumerarii” (above the number) and a “goat” (curitius capra) introduces elements of uncertainty and potential administrative anomalies within the record. The text is severely damaged, rendering a complete reconstruction of its contents impossible.

Ch.L.A. 1 7 a-b is a fragmentary duty roster, likely associated with the Legio III Cyrenaica, dating to the 1st century CE. The text details shifts and assignments across multiple days, beginning with the Kalends of Domitius and extending to the Nones of Domitius. It appears to list individuals and their roles within various units, often referencing bathhouses (
